According to Alaska Dispatch News, Sitka, Alaska–based artist Cynthia Gibson made a dress out of 20,000 salmon bones — and the result is something pretty fantastic.Gibson's fishy fashion creation has been four years in the making. She put the final touches on the look in December, just ahead of Sitka's Wearable Arts Fashion Show in February, where she showed off her work on the runway. The goal was to illustrate how art and fashion interact, and we think she performed... swimmingly.Salmon is a revered species in Gibson's community of Sitka. She told Alaska Dispatch News, "I always wondered why no one was doing much with salmon vertebrae because they're everywhere and they're easy to bead. They already have a hole in the center of them from the spinal cord."The result is a knee-length dress crafted to look like a "giant salmon vertebrae," created entirely from fishbones, save for the seams. Even the high neck collar is an ode to high fashion. It's only gaining real viral traction now, with interest from museums and art organizations like The Salmon Project coming in waves.Gibson's labor definitely didn't come without its challenges. According to Hello Giggles, she had to smooth over each individual vertebrae to ensure it wouldn't latch onto material. She let maggots and other sea creatures to clean the delicate bones of any residue. Threading each individual bone was no easy feat either, but what's most impressive are the Gatsby-inspired sleeves.Talk about attention to detail!More in unconventional dresses:Zac Posen Explains the Anatomy of a Dress:Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItEight Top Dermatologists Reveal Their Skin Care RoutinesLegendary Makeup Artist Bobbi Brown Is Now Giving Makeup Lessons on MasterClassMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. McCartney is a fan of the artist—they starred together in one of Sundance's Iconoclast episodes in 2008.Known for his enigmatic use of text in his paintings, Ruscha superimposed phrases like "NO LEATHERS FEATURES OR FUR," "VEG OUT," and "MEAT FREE" over images of model Amber Valletta. The words and the choice of model (Valletta is an advocate of ethical fashion) are a show of commitment to McCartney's stance on cruelty-free fashion.In honor of the campaign, which will appear in the September magazine issues, let's take a look back at our five favorite fashion collaborations to date.Comme des Garçons and Cindy ShermanIn 1994, American photographer Cindy Sherman collaborated with Japanese label Comme des Garçons on its ad campaign. Sherman, who is known to dress up as exaggerated female and male archetypes in her photos, personified different characters and disjointed mannequins while wearing CDG's latest collection. Sherman has worked with other companies since then, among them Chanel, Marc Jacobs, and Balenciaga.Louis Vuitton and Yayoi KusamaBack in 2006, while filming Loïc Prigent's documentary Marc Jacobs & Louis Vuitton, Jacobs went to Tokyo to meet the mythical Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama. He called the day "charming and special." Six years later, they released a capsule collection featuring bags, shoes, coats, and dresses covered in the artist's trademark polka dots. Following the launch, Kusama designed custom installations for Louis Vuitton's New York flagship store, which coincided with her retrospective at the Whitney Museum of American Art.Raf Simons and Sterling RubyThe Belgian fashion designer and the American artist have had a long-term partnership since they met in 2005. Simons used the artist's prints in countless collections for his eponymous line, including the pair's collaborative fall 2014 collection. But perhaps one of the best moments the two have had is when Simons made his Dior couture debut in 2012. The show featured dresses printed with paintings by the artist.Louis Vuitton and Daniel BurenAfter working with Kusama, Marc Jacobs enlisted French artist Daniel Buren to work on his spring 2013 collection for Louis Vuitton. Jacobs reportedly gave Buren full creative freedom to design an installation for the runway show. The result? Four long escalators covered in Buren's iconic yellow stripes, which models rode down two by two before walking the runway. The checkered clothes were also inspired by Buren's work. After the show, Jacobs commissioned him to design the window displays at the Louis Vuitton flagship store in New York.Alexander McQueen and Damien HirstIn honor of the tenth anniversary of Alexander McQueen's iconic skull scarf, McQueen and British artist Damien Hirst teamed up on creating 30 limited-edition scarf designs. Adapted from Hirst's "Entomology" series, which includes bugs, butterflies, and spiders in kaleidoscopic patterns, the artist's prints were reworked to form the classic skull pattern. The two are known for their use of skulls—McQueen for his scarves and Hirst for his famed diamond-encrusted skull piece, For the Love of God (2007).Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. This is because popping on a pair of glasses  can change up your look as quickly and easily as swiping on a bold lipstick or some eye-catching liner. Whether you wear glasses every day, reach for them only on occasion, or just throw a pair on sometimes for a little extra fun, the frames you choose can ultimately dictate the way the world sees you — and more importantly, how you see yourself. (Get it? Eh?) Factors like frame shape, color, and style all come into play and can alter your aesthetic, so when picking a pair, it's helpful to be aware of your face shape and to have some idea of what you're going for to make the shopping process more seamless. You know what also helps? A little inspiration, that's what. That's why we went ahead and tapped five of our staffers with different face shapes to showcase which styles suit each best. Without further ado, allow them to help you find your favorite frames yet.Makeup: Stephanie Peterson. Hair: Ashley Rubell."A square face is all about the angular features, like your prominent jawline and a wider forehead," says New York City–based stylist Ross McCallum, who adds that in order to add dimension and contrast to these features, it's best to choose frames that soften your angles. For this, he recommends frames that are more curved and/or circular as well as thinner, such as this pair by Zenni Optical."These were by far my favorite pair," says writer, model, trans advocate, and editorial assistant Devin-Norelle. Ze adds, "I really liked them because they accentuate the shape of my eyes — and I don't normally wear glasses, but I think I'll wear these pretty often."Starting at $30 (Shop Now)Another top pick of McCallum's for those with square faces is a classic cat-eye style, as they have the desired curved effect that complements the angles of the face. New York City–based stylist and creative director Rachael Wang concurs, explaining that the strong geometry of a square face is flattered by the thick framing on the upper half that's common in cat-eye styles, like these from Warby Parker.Starting at $145 (Shop Now)Another top pick of McCallum's for those with square faces is a classic cat-eye style, as they have the desired curved effect that complements the angles of the face. New York City–based stylist and creative director Rachael Wang concurs, explaining that the strong geometry of a square face is flattered by the thick framing on the upper half that's common in cat-eye styles, like these from Warby Parker."I love how these clear frames opened my face up," says Choi. "I've worn glasses for years because of my terrible vision, so it's refreshing to have frames that make a subtle statement without sacrificing my eyesight."Starting at $145 (Shop Now)Another glasses style that flatters a round face is a retro cat-eye frame with thicker rims. "The youthful softness of round faces is complemented by strong geometric and angular frames," says Wang. "Glasses with lenses that are wider compared to taller can also help for height so they don't sit on your cheeks," adds McCallum, who says one of his top picks would be a fun cat-eye style, like these from Zenni Optical."I always wear a cat eye with my makeup, so I thought that a similar shape in my glasses could be overkill. However, I was pleasantly surprised at how they seemed to complement the overall look," muses Choi.Starting at $13 (Shop Now)"People out there with heart-shaped faces are revered for their high cheekbones and sharply tapered jawline," says McCallum, who also notes that they tend to have a longer chin and wider forehead. "Look for frames that are a bit wider than your forehead, as they usually suit you better," he says, adding that his top choices would be styles that sweep up the face, such as cat-eye frames or these rectangular frames by Warby Parker. Wang agrees, adding that folks with heart-shaped faces should aim for bottom-heavy frames to balance a narrow chin."I loved discovering what glasses actually worked for my face shape rather than just picking out the trendy frames," says Allure associate social media manager Madisen Theobald. "This tortoiseshell pair is a great option if you are bored with the more traditional silver/black frames."Starting at $145 (Shop Now)As McCallum mentioned, another frame shape that flatters heart faces is cat-eye glasses, as they "sweep up the face." These frames by Warby Parker are a perfect example. They do a solid job of highlighting prominent cheekbones while balancing out the rest of the face at the same time."I loved the cat-eye style of these because they lifted my face and accentuated my eyes," says Theobald.Starting at $145 (Shop Now)You could say that those with oval faces are pretty lucky, as both Wang and McCallum explain that almost any frame will work for you since oval faces are nearly perfectly proportional. "Round or aviator-style frames complement oval faces as they’re slightly wider than the broadest part of your face and bring all your features to the forefront," says McCallum. That said, Wang says you can also play with bold textures or playful shapes, too, because you can get away with it."I’ve always wanted glasses even though I don’t need them — yes, I’m a fraud. I have 20/20 vision, but there’s nothing chicer than a good pair of glasses that frame your face, and I love how the gold [from these Eye Buy Direct frames] radiates against my skin tone," says Lara Adekola, an associate social media manager for Allure.Starting at $32 (Shop Now)These funky green frames from Zenni Optical are playful and accentuate both the brows and the eyes, as they allow them to come forward slightly in a super flattering way. They're also a medium-size style, which McCallum recommends because oversize or too-small frames can throw off the face's proportions."This colored pair were fun because they're so different from anything I'd normally pick out for myself, but I loved how they made my eyes look bigger," says Adekola.Starting at $26 (Shop Now)If you're not one to play by the rules or you're not 100 percent sure you fall into any of the aforementioned face-shape categories, McCallum says you can't go wrong with a pair like these, as he explains a light tortoiseshell color, like this shade of frames from Eye Buy Direct, goes with most skin tones and hair colors without clashing. What's more, he says, their slightly curved style will flatter most face shapes, including round and square."Typically, I stray away from tortoiseshell glasses because I thought they coordinated too well with my hair," says Allure's digital beauty reporter, Devon Abelman. "However, these ones convinced me otherwise because they have more golden tones to them."Starting at $32 (Shop Now)Similar to the tortoiseshell pair, these light-colored frames by Zenni Optical will flatter nearly any and every skin tone and hair color. What's more, if your face is somewhat oval, like Dev's, you can get away with the oversize style without it detracting from any of your features. No matter what your face shape, though, it's important to remember to just have fun with it and choose a pair that makes you feel like your best self."My retro aesthetic is fully realized with these glasses; plus, the clear finish lets me get as bold as I want with my makeup without the two aspects of my look competing for attention," says Abelman.Starting at $28 (Shop Now)More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. I asked guests how many pairs of the iconic shoes they have in their closets—and which pair is their favorite.Camila Alves: "I don't know—you've got me on that one. It was unusual to have that many shoes at that time. Obviously, I'm a shoe maniac, but it's really about Manolo. I love him as a person, and I am a monogamous Manolo client, beginning in 1985. I wore them to my wedding in 1986. Right now, I'm thinking about the next pair. They're arriving tomorrow—Kelly-green boots."Julie Macklowe:"I always say, a woman shouldn't disclose her age or her shoe count. I wore my favorite pair today. They're croc Manolos. But I can tell you about my first Manolos, which were the most fun. They were pumps. And then, when I became president of my company, I bought the super-duper high-heeled version. And I still keep the two pairs next to one another in my closet. The tall ones are five inches, but Manolos are made for walking. Did people respond differently when I wore the tall ones? Of course, they did. It was like, The Boss is here!"Sharon Bush: "Maybe ten pairs. I have this snakeskin kitten heel in five different colors. They last forever. The tall ones are my next purchase, but I twisted my ankle, so I'm a little afraid of them."Hilaria Baldwin: "How many? That's a secret. And you know what, I don't even know. For me, it's all about the comfort of Manolos. A shoe can be very beautiful, but if they're uncomfortable, then you're not going to have a good time."Simon Doonan: "I have very small feet, so there has been many a time that I've popped on a Manolo. They are incredibly comfortable. I think you can't go wrong with anything that's black patent leather. Online shopping is already an exercise in risk, but for plus-size shoppers, there's also the added need for a good imagination. Clothes are typically photographed on sample size models, who have measurements far from folks who make up the majority of the population. For the rest of us, it means mentally Photoshopping a dress that's depicted on a model onto our own bodies. Thankfully, retailer PrettyLittleThings is calling an end to the madness. The fast fashion site has started modeling its clothes on both straight size and plus size models. That's right: The same dress, on two different body types.Fans first noticed PLT's new initiative with the launch of Hailey Baldwin's holiday collaboration. Instead of only showcasing the clothes on Baldwin's supermodel frame, PLT also shot every item in the collection with a plus-size model. For some items, both models even appear side by side.For others, there are additional slides for the plus-size model. But the effect is the same: Plus-size shoppers will be able to see how a garment looks on a body more similar to their own.Fans on social media thanked PLT and called on other brands to follow their example. One fan tweeted, "i absolutely LOVE how @OfficialPLT hailey holiday campaign has plus sizes for all the outfits hailey wore." Others are celebrating the brand's inclusion of more models of color.This is certainly an exciting and noteworthy step made by PLT, but as anyone who has tried to shop for plus-size clothes online will know, there's still work to be done. As one fan put it on Twitter, "Why should this be an amazing thing and not the norm? When Robbie made an appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live! earlier this month, she wore a black printed pajama set with red piping by Thakoon paired with the covetable metallic Gucci crossover sandals in gold, proving that the look is all about the balance between casual and formal. While the clothes may suggest that she just rolled out of a (very chic) bed, the heels add some polish.RELATED: [#article: /articles/577ff05e8adb777d7e930f83]||||||Moretz and Saldana took a slightly different approach by pairing classic pajama tops with dark-wash jeans and ankle-strap heels. Wearing the matching top and bottom is a fun way to get in on the coordinating-pieces trend, and it takes away the problem of trying to find the right bottom to pair with the pajama top. The advantages of pairing the top with jeans? The combination can be unexpectedly dressy.The shirts are easy to style and comfortable. And while they may seem better suited to the cooler months, wearing a pajama top—which has more structure than, say, a T-shirt—in the summer can make you feel more dressed up.It’s day-to-night dressing at its best. Now they sell men's magazines, inspire diligence in dieters, and (evidently) enhance the performance of beach-volleyball players. So in honor of National Bikini Day on July 5 (yes, like National Lipstick Day and National Rubber Eraser Day, it is a thing), we add up the tiny numbers of the bikini's racy history.1943: Year in which wartime rationing led the U.S. government to order a 10 percent reduction in the fabric used in women's swimwear, resulting in a bare midriff and the removal of skirt panels.3: Number of years later that French engineer Louis Réard invented the official bikini, naming it after Bikini Atoll in the Pacific, where atomic bombs were tested that year.30: Square inches of fabric he used.13: Square inches of fabric used to make a thong bikini bottom today.50,000: Number of fan letters received by French nude dancer Micheline Bernardini (shown below), after she became the first woman to be photographed in a bikini (professional models refused to wear the new design because they deemed it too shocking). As a result of the shoot, Bernardini moved to America to work as an actress.10: The most common size for a woman wearing a two-piece swimsuit.80: Percentage of women who try on swimwear and leave the store empty-handed.$2,625: Starting cost of a Bikini Boot Camp six-night-stay at the Amansala Resort in Tulum, Mexico, including daily body-sculpting sessions.1948: Year in which bikinis were banned from the Miss America pageant because officials thought they detracted from the competition's purpose—awarding scholarships.1997: Year in which bikinis were allowed back in the pageant.1960: Year in which the song "Itsy Bitsy Teenie Weenie Yellow Polkadot Bikini" was released.1965: Year Annette Funicello filmed How to Stuff a Wild Bikini (because she was pregnant, she was shot mostly from the waist up).1962: Year Ursula Andress wore a belted white bikini in the James Bond Film Dr. No.$60,000: Amount Andress's famous white bikini sold for at an auction in 2001.2002: Year in which Halle Berry wore a similar suit in Die Another Day.2: Number of weeks it took for Bloomingdale's in Manhattan to sell out of string bikinis in 1974.60.4: Percentage of all Sports Illustrated swimsuit issue covers that have featured a model wearing a bikini.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”$30 million: Cost of the 150-carat diamond bikini worn by Molly Sims in the 2006 Sports Illustrated swimsuit issue.1983: Year Carrie Fisher wore a gold bikini as Princess Leia in Return of the Jedi.$309,206,384: Total box office earnings of the film, making it the highest-grossing of the three original films in the Star Wars trilogy.1996: Year Jennifer Aniston, as Rachel on Friends, wore a similar gold bikini to fulfill Ross's fantasy.1993: Year in which the bikini became the required beach-volleyball uniform for women in the Olympics. According to international ruling, the side of the bikini bottoms had to have a maximum width of 2.5 inches.__19:__Years later that the International Volleyball Federation dropped the mandatory bikini requirements, allowing players to wear shorts and sleeved tops out of respect for the cultural beliefs of some participating countries.75: Percentage of women who would rather have a root canal than wear a thong bikini in public.2015: Year Women's Health editor in chief (and former Allure beauty director), Amy Keller Laird, banned the term "bikini body" from the magazine.*Additional reporting by Sophia Panych. *Watch Kayla Itsines teach us three workout moves you can do at the office:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The collaboration is part of a long-term initiative on behalf of the makeup brand to bring fashion labels to a wider, more global audience, according to the Business of Fashion."M.A.C. is intrinsically tied to fashion through its many initiatives and partnerships with the industry globally," says Karen Buglisi Weiler, the global brand president of the cosmetics company. "M.A.C. has a significant global footprint which will help designers break into new territories outside of the United States."The private, appointment-only event will have a strict rule of no social media, and all images associated with the collection will be embargoed until the clothes hit stores. Moda Operandi cofounder Lauren Santo Domingo will host an intimate party at her Paris home after the presentation. For members of the American fashion set who plan to stay in the States for the Independence Day weekend, the brand will host private appointments back in New York City with the same set of rules later in the season.The fashion week calendar as we know it is changing, and Proenza Schouler's decision to show its resort collection in Paris is just another shake-up to add to the mix. Major industry heavyweights Tom Ford, Vetements, Burberry, and Public School have all recently abandoned the traditional fashion calendar by either showing in different cities or announcing that they will offer direct-to-consumer fashion. Public School announced that it would present two collections a year—one in June and another in December—while Tom Ford pushed back its fall 2016 show to September this year to align with the retail calendar.For the past 14 years, Proenza Schouler, the label designed by Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, has been showing at New York fashion week. The label has become known for the "It" bag status of its PS1 bag and an aesthetic that focuses on clean lines, heavy construction, and lots of handcrafted details.M.A.C. and Proenza Schouler have been working together for 16 seasons at New York fashion week. The cosmetics brand will be backstage working on makeup for more than half of the haute couture shows—so it's a partnership that comes naturally.We reached out to Proenza Schouler for a statement and will update this post as we hear more.Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItEight Top Dermatologists Reveal Their Skin Care RoutinesLegendary Makeup Artist Bobbi Brown Is Now Giving Makeup Lessons on MasterClassMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The label, which launched in 2009, will not show at Paris fashion week next month, as Vaccarello will debut in his new role with YSL during that time.“This adventure has been amazing but I now feel the need to fully focus on this new project,” the designer said in a statement.In April, Vaccarello was appointed creative director at Saint Laurent, succeeding Hedi Slimane. Vaccarello had previously served as a guest designer for Versus Versace since 2013 and was named as the brand’s creative director in January 2015. Before that, he worked under Karl Lagerfeld at Fendi, specializing in fur designs.RELATED: Tommy Hilfiger Shows Have a Flair for DramaThis past June, Vaccarello released his first campaign for Saint Laurent, with ads that lacked clothing but included black-and-white portraits shot by fashion photographer Collier Schorr. At Vaccarello’s own label, the designer was well-known for his power dresses, body-con silhouettes, and asymmetrical hemlines.Let’s take a look back at some of the designer’s best red carpet hits.Designer Anthony Vaccarello and model Anja Rubik at the 2013 Met Gala.Anja Rubik at the 2013 Met GalaThe Polish model wore a red leather mini dress with popped collars and a chainmail panel from Vaccarello’s fall 2013 collection at the Met Gala in 2013. The look perfectly encompassed Vaccarello’s feminine-meets-rock-and-roll aesthetic.Jennifer Lopez at the 2013 Grammy Awards.Jennifer Lopez at the 2013 Grammy AwardsThe singer-actress has worn Anthony Vaccarello’s pieces on multiple occasions and our favorite look is the one-sleeved, floor-length gown with a thigh-high slit at the 2013 Grammys. Which is why we are living for Reformation’s NYE capsule collection designed with the consummate cool girls of Haim.The '70s-inspired collaboration between Reformation and sisters Este, Danielle, and Alana Haim, who dominate festival circuit—and festival style around the globe—while rocking out with besties like Taylor Swift—is as killer as you might expect. “Our closets are filled with [Reformation’s] pieces. When they approached us about doing a collaboration for New Year’s Eve, it was literally a dream come true,” the Haim sisters tell Allure.The result is an effortlessly glamorous dream come true for us, too. Picture plunging necklines, Rita Hayworth-worthy silks, lots of un-intimidating sparkles, and rich velvet silhouettes that will hold up way past midnight. “We were channeling full-on '70s vibes when creating the collection and looking to #RefBabes Cher, Bianca Jagger, and Diana Ross for inspiration,” say the Haim sisters. “There’s no better way to ring in 2017 than with a little 1970.”More '70s trends we love:Given the peak level of laid-back glamour, all the pieces in the cool-girl collab are made to outlast the champagne—after the ball drops, you’ll be left with pieces to dress down for your 2017 style resolutions, just like Reformation’s CEO and founder Yael Aflalo. “My favorite piece is probably the black patent jacket. I wear it with denim, but it's good with a silk slip dress for NYE,” Aflalo tells Allure.For Haim, Reformation’s commitment to sustainability and making eco-fashion more mainstream was just as important as nailing the band’s style for the collection. “We have so much respect for how Reformation destigmatizes eco-fashion and affects positive change on the fashion industry and environment,” the sisters say. “Their clothes are stunning, but also happen to be sustainable, and we are so proud to be supporting this incredible mission.”The best part? Each piece looks comfy as hell. “I think more girls are moving away from typical New Year's stuff, like sequins, and more into sexy dresses that are also really comfortable,” says Aflalo. “The new collection has plenty of fancy silks and stretchy metallic knits so you can look good and feel good all night.” Important no matter where you’re waiting for the ball to drop.How to get a festive New Year’s Eve makeup look:Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItEight Top Dermatologists Reveal Their Skin Care RoutinesLegendary Makeup Artist Bobbi Brown Is Now Giving Makeup Lessons on MasterClassMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Pronounced “Kate,” the line’s moniker alludes to the Greek word meaning "long, flowing hair,” and its offerings (dreamed up by creative director Catherine Holstein) meld subtle 1970s influences with modern silhouettes and lines. Since the Line’s Los Angeles location has become an Instagram-able hot spot for California stunners, we imagine Khaite will soon be a mainstay in the wardrobes of some of our favorite coastal cool girls.Likewise, a host of under-the-radar, California-centric collections are helping to define the aesthetics of trendsetters all over the world, allowing the insouciant, sun-drenched, vintage feel often associated with the state to permeate modern clothing culture.Here, four up-and-coming West Coast brands favored by “It” girls.FREDA SALVADORThe girls at Freda Salvador, based in Sausalito, California, create understated yet awesome shoes designed to effortlessly complement contemporary ensembles. “We deconstruct classic styles and give them a modern feel,” says Megan Papay, who cofounded Freda in 2011 with her like-minded friend Cristina Palomo-Nelson. “We feel that makes our shoes understandable but also unique and exciting.” Gigi Hadid and Kristen Stewart have both slipped into the line’s unique oxfords, while Taylor Swift was recently spotted in the Glide mule while vacationing in Europe.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”RE/DONEThose unwilling to scour their local thrift store in search of the perfect pair of Levi’s 501s will find instant old-school gratification with Re/Done. The Los Angeles luxury label—founded by Sean Barron and Jamie Mazur—reconstructs vintage Levi’s to pitch-perfect effect, offering the beloved styles as well as unique cuts inspired by influencers. (The Leandra, a high-rise cropped flare, was designed in collaboration with Leandra Medine of Man Repeller). Recently, Re/Done added T-shirts to its e-commerce selection, crafting ’50s-inspired tees in conjunction with Hanes. “We’ve started a movement that embraces individuality, sustainability, and American heritage,” says Barron of the venture. The reworked offerings have found fans in basically everyone: Selena Gomez, Cara Delevingne, Kylie Jenner, Bella Hadid, Beyoncé, and others.NEWBARKWith each slip-on shoe handmade in Los Angeles, it’s safe to say Newbark is quintessentially Californian. “Newbark is our way of life, our story: the California effortless life with a rock-and-roll-chic aesthetic,” says Maryam Malakpour, who created the brand in 2009 alongside sister and fellow stylist Marjan. The loafers, boots, and sandals that comprise the collection meld luxury with comfort and a classic feel, resulting in shoes that will stand the test of time in more ways than one. The Row’s Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen have been spotted in Newark’s contemporary-cool loafers, as have models Rosie Huntington-Whiteley and Constance Jablonski.AMO DENIMA desire for the perfect pair of jeans—cozy and formfitting, with vintage notes and present-day appeal—led to the creation of Amo. The line was launched in 2014 by Kelly Urban and Misty Zollars, both Los Angeles natives, when fruitless searches for the ideal denim left them dreaming up designs of their own. “We set out to create a vintage-inspired denim collection with a modern, comfortable fit,” says Urban. “Los Angeles is known as one of the very best places in the world to manufacture denim—we wouldn’t make our jeans anywhere else.” The well-tailored, feminine cuts are favored by Kendall Jenner, Olivia Wilde, and Heidi Klum.Conde Nast Traveler: A Day in Los Angeles:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Louis Vuitton and Supreme have made their collaboration official. This morning, the French luxury house unveiled its much anticipated collection with the skatewear brand at its men’s fall 2017 runway show in Paris. The collection features denim, sneakers, gloves, scarves, and a wide range of bags, including a backpack, messenger bag, and fanny pack in the brand's signature materials like red and black Epi leather fabrics. It has even produced a red-and-white skateboard that comes with a matching trunk and tool kit. “We thought it was quite nice to do it properly,” creative director Kim Jones told WWD, in reference to the cease-and-desist letter the French brand sent to Supreme back in 2000 when the streetwear brand repurposed LV's monogram print on its skateboards.This collab has been circulating the Internet for weeks, ever since a mysterious photo of a Louis Vuitton sweater with a Supreme logo surfaced online. Last June, Supreme's founder James Jebbia was spotted at the Louis Vuitton's spring 2017 menswear show, which also fueled rumors of a collaboration. Jones is also a well known streetwear fan, who has worked with cult-favorite labels, including Nike and Hiroshi Fujiwara of Japanese streetwear label Fragment Design, in the past.The new line will go on sale at select Louis Vuitton stores on July 17, and potentially, at a few pop-up locations. Until then, check out some of the sneak peek preview of the collection.A Supreme x Louis Vuitton backpack on the runwayDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Originally posted on January 4, 2017:Those of us who were teens in the early 2000s might remember Louis Vuitton's entrance into the streetwear scene. The luxury brand became the darling of everyone and everything related to the streetwear craze, thanks to its then-creative director Marc Jacobs. Celebs and fashion fans alike went gaga over artist and designer Stephen Sprouse's graffiti bag collection for the label in 2001, while musicians like Pharrell Williams and Kanye West were commissioned to design capsule collections of their own in 2008 and 2009, respectively.Now, the French brand is rumored to be in cahoots with none other than Supreme, the skater apparel brand that reigns supreme (pun intended) over streetwear fans everywhere. We have reached out to Louis Vuitton to confirm and will update this post accordingly.While the dream collaboration is just a rumor for now, all signs point to "in stores soon." A photo of a possible piece from the supposed collection was posted by Supreme fan account @MrBld this week. The pic shows a cozy white sweater with a Supreme emblem and Louis Vuitton's classic logo woven all over the knit. The photo's caption reads, "sweater got spotted by a model at a LV casting show." The post also mentioned that there is a bag in the works by Louis Vuitton's menswear director Kim Jones.After the leak, Jones posted (then deleted) an image of a Supreme sticker on top of the LV monogram, according to Racked. But it wasn't deleted fast enough to stop the Supreme reddit sub-forum from obsessing over it, of course.More on Louis Vuitton:The fanfare over the possible collab might not be all about the sweater. According to Complex, Louis Vuitton sued Supreme way back in 2000 after the streetwear label used the French label's monogram print on a skateboard deck. A sweater bearing the names of both brands, then, would indicate a reunion of sorts—one fans would be happy to support.Celebs who love Louis Vuitton:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Specifically, using the late Alexander McQueen as an example. Back in 1992, McQueen claimed to have used his own hair in his graduate project, “Jack the Ripper Stalks His Victims.” And as a designer who loved to push boundaries and provoke intense reactions with his work, it’s fitting that McQueen is one source of inspiration behind Gorjanc’s own school project.For her exhibition “Pure Human,” Gorjanc wanted to investigate a process called de-extinction, in which anyone can extract genetic information from a source and use it to biologically program an already-existing skin graft (which could later be theoretically used to produce luxury goods, like a designer jacket or bag). Gorjanc says that material usually comes from a preserved hair, skin, or bone, which makes McQueen’s “Ripper” project a perfect outlet for exploration.Although Gorjanc wasn’t able to use McQueen’s actual genetic material for this project (she says she contacted some owners of McQueen’s collections to get information on whether the hair was really his but never finalized an agreement about acquiring the hair), that wasn’t the point of her work. Instead, she applied for a patent that was “theoretically based on [having] Alexander McQueen’s genetic information as a source of a procedure,” she says. Meaning that if she did have it, the process that would be used to make laboratory-grown leather from human tissue would be plausible. And thus, her project shines a light on her real concern: how easy it is to exploit biological information .A sample bag made out of pig leather that mimics the surface of McQueen's skinDavid Whelan, a cofounder and former chief strategy officer of the New York Genome Center, says growing McQueen’s genetic information into skin, tanning it, and turning it into leather jackets and bags could be akin to a found-object art piece. “What if we created a piece of art with a private letter from McQueen that we found in the trash? Or his cell-phone bill? While there could be a bit of invasion of privacy here, it’s not exploitive,” he says.Though there has been much confusion in the press as to whether Gorjanc actually has McQueen’s hair (which, again, she does not), she says she purposefully chose to include his name in her project and her request for a patent.Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItEight Top Dermatologists Reveal Their Skin Care RoutinesLegendary Makeup Artist Bobbi Brown Is Now Giving Makeup Lessons on MasterClass“Because of the lack of legislation surrounding the protection of genetic materials, I wanted to showcase how someone can gain hold of biological material from sources you would usually think [are] extremely protected,” she says. “McQueen’s genetic information was interesting from the perspective that he is dead, has an enormous brand empire that is protected with numerous copyrights, and still has relatives that have inherited his possessions. Despite all that, though, his genetic information is still not well protected.”In other words, even though McQueen’s name is basically as big as it gets, Gorjanc—someone who has zero connection to the designer's family or his brand—could still potentially get a piece of his genetic information and use it to make these luxury materials.It’s kind of mind-blowing, and that’s exactly Gorjanc’s point. This is not the first time that genetic information has been used to create artistic projects, either. In 2012, artist Heather Dewey-Hagborg debuted “Stranger Visions,” which featured portrait sculptures made from analyses of genetic material from items like cigarette butts collected in public places.“A person loses the ownership of his biological materials as soon as they leave his body,” says Gorjanc. “Which essentially means that if you get a haircut at the hairdresser’s, you don’t own the hair that’s cut off.”As for Gorjanc’s “Pure Human” project, she’s currently waiting on patent approval for both the bioengineered genetic material and the process to make it. She doesn’t have any plans to turn it into a commercial project.And while the thought of someone grabbing your genetic information and using it to create whatever the F they want—and getting away with it—is slightly alarming, that doesn’t mean it’s an entirely bad idea. The technology that would be required to pull something like this off on a mass-production scale isn’t available yet, but Whelan says that once it is, it’s something that could be useful in developing more-sustainable lab-grown leather. Translation: We wouldn’t have to slaughter animals for their hides.“Start-ups are using synthetic biology, the spiritual successor of genetic engineering, to fabricate leather that is biologically identical to leather from an animal but doesn’t have any animals involved,” says Whelan. And it wouldn’t feel, well, weird. “Let’s not think about Leatherface from Texas Chainsaw Massacre just because we hear the word ‘skin.’ We really are talking about leather that will look and feel like leather.”This project could be a breakthrough that leads to more people wearing sustainable fashion pieces—and a prompt to start investigating the protection of people’s genetic material, and whether the laws concerning genetic material should change with these advancements in biotechnology.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The dress, from the house's spring 1998 haute couture collection, had people talking online. (A sampling of headlines: "Kim Kardashian Wore the Sexiest/Craziest Dress Ever and Was THIS Close to Having a Nip Slip," "Kim Kardashian Wore Her Most Revealing Dress Yet and Twitter Is Shook," "Kim Kardashian Debuts Her Most Shocking Dress Yet (and Avoids a Wardrobe Malfunction).") And within hours it had been knocked off.By Monday, shoppers could go on Fashion Nova's website and purchase the "Winning Beauty Cut Out Gown," a black maxi featuring cutouts and slits similar to those on Kardashian West's Mugler dress. Its product description doesn't reference her or her look, but it still sold out. (There's an option to join a waiting list.)Fashion Nova, often referred to as a retailer for the Instagram age, releases merchandise at an incredibly fast pace and promotes it on influencers ranging from Cardi B to Kylie Jenner and Kourtney Kardashian. Over the years it's been accused of ripping off designers on multiple occasions, some instances more brazen than others: Never forget how it re-created Jenner's twenty-first-birthday outfits and put them up for purchase on its site within hours of her party.The timing of Fashion Nova's latest Kardashian-inspired release — which theoretically involved designing a dress, making a sample, and photographing a model wearing it before putting it on its e-commerce — raised some eyebrows. Shortly after the dress appeared online, the fashion watchdog Instagram account Diet Prada shared its own theory as to how FashionNova was able to turn it around so quickly: Could it have gotten a tip from Kardashian West herself?Diet Prada based its speculation on an Instagram Story from a reported Fashion Nova e-commerce model, Yodit Yemane, in which she shares images of the "Winning Beauty Cut Out Gown" on February 14, days before Kardashian West would wear the vintage Mugler dress. So Diet Prada asked its 1.1 million Instagram followers: "Did Fashion Nova whip up the dress overnight in their Los Angeles atelier after seeing Kim in it or is she peddling her vintage finds to mass retailers ahead of debuting them for a calculated, timely release?" (Diet Prada wasn't available to comment for this story.)Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Kardashian West herself responded to that question on Tuesday. In a series of tweets, the reality star and businesswoman addressed allegations that she cooperated with Fashion Nova to replicate her looks, saying that she's "not leaking my looks to anyone"—and that it's "devastating" to see the designer pieces she wears knocked off at any retailer."Only two days ago, I was privileged enough to wear a one-of-a-kind vintage Mugler dress, and in less than 24 hours it was knocked off and thrown up on a site," she said. "This is a way to get people to sign up for their mailing list and make people believe there is some kind of relationship between me and this fashion site. There is not."Kardashian West contextualized her remarks in past accusations against Fashion Nova of copying Yeezy, her husband Kanye West's label: "I’ve watched these companies profit off my husband’s work for years, and now that it’s also affecting designers who have been so generous to give me access to their beautiful works, I can no longer sit silent."She ended the thread by explaining how she'll often plan outfits months in advance — and setting designers up to be copied would only undermine them. "I’m not leaking my looks to anyone, and I don’t support what these companies are doing," she wrote.When asked to comment, a representative for Fashion Nova told Glamour that the brand has not been in contact with Kardashian West, nor did it intentionally copy her dress."We respect the fashion community and work with a variety of vendors, designers, influencers, and celebrities to keep our style offering fresh and relevant," a representative for Fashion Nova said. "Kim Kardashian West is one of the top fashion icons in the world that our customers draw inspiration from. However, we have not worked with Kim Kardashian West directly on any of her projects but have been driven by her influential style."This is the first time Kardashian West has publicly addressed fast-fashion sites' copying her and her family's outfits. Although she herself has been accused of ripping off the work of other designers: In 2017 her children's clothing label, Kids Supply, was called out for its similarities to Vetements outfits worn by her daughter North West.More Kardashian smackdowns:Now, a Rihanna-inspired makeup challenge:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Chiuri replaced Simons, who left the position in October 2015 after three years at the helm.“The arrival of Raf Simons as chief creative officer signifies a momentous new chapter for Calvin Klein,” said Steve Shiffman, CEO of Calvin Klein. “Not since Mr. Klein himself was at the company has it been led by one creative visionary, and I am confident that this decision will drive the Calvin Klein brand and have a significant impact on its future. Raf’s exceptional contributions have shaped and modernized fashion as we see it today and, under his direction, Calvin Klein will further solidify its position as a leading global lifestyle brand.”Calvin Klein has also announced the appointment of Pieter Mulier as creative director. Mulier has long been known as Simons’s “right-hand man” and his studio director at Dior. He was the breakout star of Dior and I, Frédéric Tcheng’s 2014 documentary on Simons’s process leading up to his debut couture collection at the French house, much like Grace Coddington in R. J. Cutler’s 2009 film, The September Issue.Raf Simons and Pieter Mulier (left) at Dior fall 2015 show.Simons will lead the creative direction of the company's labels, including Calvin Klein Collection, Calvin Klein Jeans, and ck Calvin Klein. The designer will also be responsible for the company’s imagery for other divisions, including underwear, fragrance campaigns, and home goods. Simons began his career in furniture design. He has also teamed up with Danish company Kvadrat to release a new range of upholstery textiles in 2014.The new appointment presents an opportunity for Simons to apply his vision and reshape the iconic brand in all aspects—from the clothes to its celebrity campaigns. It was speculated in reports that Simons resigned from Dior last fall because of the lack of creative control and the time to experiment—the designer’s vision didn’t extend to areas such as the store designs and the celebrity campaigns.Simons trained as an industrial designer before launching his menswear brand in 1995. He joined Dior in 2012 after John Galliano’s dismissal in 2011. Prior to that, the designer spent six years as creative director of Jil Sander, his first foray into womenswear.Simons’s first collection for Calvin Klein will debut for the fall 2017 season at New York's fashion week.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Luckily, we’ve seen a recent trend in chic, affordable nuptial duds that has us falling in love all over again.Love is definitely in the air over at Joie, the feminine with an edge brand known for its silky fabrics and straight-from-a-fashion-blogger styling playbook. Today, the brand is launching its first bridal collection, and the affordable results deliver the expected dose of dreaminess with an edge.Save these ideas for later—and follow Allure on Pinterest!“The muse is definitely our customer,” Rachel Wilder-Hill, VP of design, tells Allure. “Our woman tends to have a sense of effortlessness, and that should be reflected in her dress—having something that is of course elegant and beautiful, but carries a sense of ease in the styling.”The Ishild from the Joie bridal collectionThe springy four-piece collection clocks in at under $1,000 and features romantic, ethereal silhouettes in fluttery silks and lace. There’s the Elmira, a delicately embroidered tiered gown; the Gertie, a woodsy, off-the-shoulder number; the Gerda, a cotton voile concoction begging for a flower crown; and the Ishild, a romantic take on a slip dress. All four of the looks are sweet enough to stand on their own but simple enough to support some serious customization. “It really depends on the setting, but I think the personalization really lies with accessories,” says Wilder-Hill. “Don’t be afraid to wear a bold shoe, antique jewelry, or a vintage fur or silk wrap—these details are what will set your bridal look apart.”With all the cash you’ll save on the dress, just think of the room you’ll have to splurge on wear-it-again accessories. Her latest show is no exception.In addition to a bevy of edgy blue ball gowns and workwear-inspired jumpsuits, the designer brought back a major '60s trend that looks totally fresh: the beret. Rather than the prim and proper classic French felt versions of yesterday, Chiuri's black leather chapeau looked back on the beret's revolutionary roots—the style originally began as a military uniform and evolved into the artsy signature of counterculture beatniks in the '60s.Dior’s latest interpretation shares similar rebel ties. Paired with a wide range of blue looks (the color of strength and power that’s come to be a signature of the empowered woman in pop culture), the new beret adds the edge of an arched “you really want to try me?” eyebrow to each look—even the most airy, romantic date-night look. In other words, it’s the perfect accessory to pair with a “We Should All Be Feminists” tee from Chiuri’s debut collection for the storied French house.Rihanna wearing the beret at the Dior show at Paris fashion week.To pull off the rebel-ready trend, go for the same mix of edgy and feminine seen on the runway. "The beret feels very revolutionary and provocative, so I wanted to keep the hair very soft and floaty and very easy,” Guido, Dior’s backstage hairstylist, tells Allure. “You have this balance of tough and pretty in one look."Who knew the '60s would be the inspiration for one of the freshest takes on empowering trends for 2017?If you love the color blue and Dior, check out these stories:Check out the four true-blue denim trends we love:Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The model chooses to wear her dark, curly shag naturally, and it's a beautiful statement that stands out from the typical sleek style popular in the industry. Her brow-skimming bangs are also seriously covetable. Arganaraz's natural curly do was enhanced with a little help from a friend in Argentina, according to Vogue. As if Fashion Nova hadn't already cleared out your wallet in the pursuit of dressing like the rapper, prepare to just throw your money at the fashion brand now.In an interview with Business of Fashion, Fashion Nova CEO Richard Saghian revealed that the brand is gearing up to expand well beyond its current offerings. "We are transforming FashionNova.com into a one-stop shop lifestyle destination," Saghian said, noting that part of the plan includes a launch of a makeup line called Nova Beauty.While Fashion Nova currently has a few basic beauty offerings on its site — NYX lip glosses, various fake eyelashes, and blinged-out makeup brushes from Bebella Cosmetics, to name a few — this would mark the first time that it would be developing products of its own. Eventually, says Saghian, the brand wants to expand its beauty offerings to rival those of Sephora and Ulta.Fashion Nova isn't the first fast fashion brand to make its foray into the beauty world. Topshop, Boohoo, and PrettyLittleThing have all introduced their own beauty offerings recently, giving Internet fans a dose of drugstore-priced beauty from somewhere other than an actual drugstore.Sadly, the Nova Beauty rollout won't happen until later this year or early next, so it will be some time before we'll be able to paint our lips and eyelids with any Fashion Nova originals. In the meantime, though, you will be able to get your hands on some of the pieces that Cardi B collaborated on with the brand, which should be enough of a dose of Fashion Nova to hold you over until 2019.More fast beauty:Cardi B's makeup artist Erika La'Pearl breaks down her best beauty looks:Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. We asked Lori Goldstein, a fashion stylist, editor, and designer of Logo, to give us some tips on wearing sparkle in the daylight. "Anything that sparkles invokes a sense of joy, and wearing something shiny, especially during the day, always makes me feel more confident," she says. Here are Goldstein's four daytime sparkle mantras.Look for starter sparkle. "Venture into this trend with a shirt, skirt, or jacket that's partially shiny. I have an army jacket with sequined sleeves that's perfect. For day, I wouldn't do more than two, maybe two and a half, sparkly items—a skirt with a sequined panel and a sparkly necklace, but not much more than that."Keep it grounded. "Glitter and sequins are inherently girlie, so I like to pair them with something masculine. A sparkly T-shirt looks amazing with a heavy tweed jacket or trousers. I also love a brocade jacket with gold threading paired with a crisp white shirt."Stay in one color family. "For day, stick to a monochromatic look—navy pants with a navy sequined top. It's work-appropriate but with a kick."Think small. "Big sequins demand a lot of attention. After a particularly contentious string of headlines in 2016, the fashion world has gotten particularly politically charged, with designers voicing their opinions and upping the political ante with their brand campaigns. Case in point: Kenzo’s superchic, supercharged, statement-making short film.The French label—known for bringing the funk to its clothes, its runways, and its campaigns thanks to a California-cool reboot by Opening Ceremony geniuses Carol Lim and Humberto Leon—is keeping tempo with a film-slash-ad campaign dubbed “Club Ark Eternal.” Like most of the brand’s ventures over the past year, the campaign is dance-inspired (Spike Jonze directed the superplayful film for Kenzo’s debut perfume this summer) and funky as hell. Rather than plaster the campaign with familiar faces and social media megamodels, Kenzo cast a diverse lineup of dancers and choreographers to show off its resort  and men's spring/summer 2017 collections.The ensuing seven minutes, directed by Partel Olivia, are a multisensory feast of movement, color, and soul-tangling beats. In a series of gritty, artistic underground vignettes cut with pensive nature scenes, all set to a sick soundtrack, the multicultural and supremely talented cast offer up the world's coolest look at a luxury label. "Club Ark Eternal" embodies that got-to-have-it cool factor Kenzo is known for.The short movie also has a subversive and timely-as-hell message. According to the brand’s statement accompanying the video on YouTube, the film and the 2017 collections are about paying homage to global club culture “as a powerful source of alternative energies against racism, sexual oppression and class violence.”  The link between Kenzo’s distinctive and individualistic aesthetic and club culture’s rich history of progressive communities and “crucibles of self-invention” is unmistakable, proving Kenzo has its finger just as squarely on the pulse of the current political climate as it does on razor-sharp trends. And her latest outfit of choice proves she’s both practical and minimally chic when it comes to fashion.The star was recently spotted on the streets of Toronto, where she is currently filming her legal drama, Suits. To combat the arctic chill that has descended across the city, the actress has developed a foolproof winter ensemble that consists of a classic puffer, knit beanie, oversize sunglasses, and a pair of foolproof duck boots. Made famous by L.L. Bean (a.k.a. the purveyor of winter survival gear), the classic, preppy footwear is a favorite of East Coast dwellers traversing through the snow-filled streets every year. Though L.L. Bean is one of the original producers of the style, the duck boot has been reinterpreted by various brands like Sorel and even Yeezy. Incredibly durable and waterproof, when it comes to winter snowstorms, puddles, or just freezing temps, a pair of duck boots will keep you warm and dry. Guaranteed.More winter style inspirations:Even better, Markle’s shoes cost under $120. They’re made by Canadian heritage brand Kamik, and feature all the classic elements of a duck boot with the addition of tweed panels and bright yellow laces. You can still get your hands on the boots, which also comes in two other color options (black and taupe). They’re an affordable (and chic) option to ward off your sartorial winter weather woes.The actress, like Harry's sister-in-law, Kate Middleton, certainly knows how to mix and match high and low fashion. This also means, should she become a princess (one day, we hope), you can expect her accessible fashion picks to sell out quickly. Like the Duchess of Cambridge, we wouldn’t be surprised if she has a penchant for Zara, too. But despite being a groundbreaker, she apparently can't wear whatever she wants to wear. Over the weekend, Meghan Markle joined many of her new in-laws at Trooping the Colour, Queen Elizabeth II's official birthday celebration, and has since been brutally dragged on the Internet by people claiming that her outfit was "inappropriate."To attend the outdoor event, Meghan opted for a pale pink, off-the-shoulder Carolina Herrera dress with a matching wide-brimmed fascinator. She rode to Buckingham Palace in an open-top carriage with Prince Harry, who wore his full military uniform; once at the palace, they joined Prince William, Kate Middleton, and their kids, as well as many other members of the extended royal family, to watch as the Royal Air Force flew overhead. Though Meghan's outfit looked very classy — not to mention season- and weather-appropriate — Cosmopolitan notes that many people still came for the Duchess of Sussex online, attacking her decision to (gasp!) show her shoulders, and comparing her to new sister-in-law Kate.For the record, The Sun reports that "fashion tradition usually dictates that Royal women do not wear off-shoulder or other more revealing styles." That said, this outdated rule has been broken several times before by Kate herself: The Duchess of Cambridge wore a bright red Alexander McQueen off-the-shoulder dress for an outdoor event in Berlin last summer, a white Barbara Casasola shoulder-baring gown to an event in London the summer before that, and yet another gorgeous Alexander McQueen off-shoulder gown to the 2017 BAFTA Awards.Furthermore, Prince Harry's mother, Princess Diana, was also a big fan of off-the-shoulder dresses back in the '80s and '90s — proving that this is one "rule" that has been broken for decades now, and that the Markle-haters need to do better research before they start comparing her to other royals who have worn even more "scandalous" outfits. Aside from that, Shayne Oliver, the designer behind the brand, values performance art as a part of fashion shows. A traditional show without any aspect of unconventional beauty or runway antics would be unusual for the brand.Oliver started his label when he was a teenager in 2006 with a collection of tees printed with the word “Hood.” The logo remains a major part of the brand and has transformed to “HBA,” which is featured on pants and sweatshirts every season. In 2014, the designer was a finalist for the LVHM Prize for his boundary-pushing fashion.In honor of the label’s upcoming show at New York Fashion Week this Sunday, let’s take a look back at some of the brand’s most outrageous moments.A model walks the runway at the Hood By Air fall 2013 fashion show.A Star Is BornDespite the fact that Hood By Air has been around for more than a decade, it seems like the industry took notice after one collection: fall 2013. Shayne Oliver decorated models in light-up mouthpieces and white-out eye contacts, dressing them in baggy shorts, tees, padded parkas, and sweatshirts with his now signature logo: “HBA.” The mix of daring facial accoutrements paired with luxury streetwear pieces defined the brand and earned a write-up in the New York Times and Complex, which named the designer as one of the 25 Greatest Black Fashion Designers.Models voguing on the runway at Hood By Air fall 2014 fashion show.Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItEight Top Dermatologists Reveal Their Skin Care RoutinesLegendary Makeup Artist Bobbi Brown Is Now Giving Makeup Lessons on MasterClassBringing Voguing to a New LightFor Hood By Air’s fall 2014 show, models sported multi-colored extensions and streetwear-inspired jeans. For the finale, shirtless models appeared on the dark runway, frantically voguing. Voguing was born out of the culture of ‘80s ballroom dancing in Harlem. It’s a highly stylized form of dancing, with fast movements and dramatic poses. Hood By Air brought a very particular kind of street culture into a traditional runway space, and it was shocking to many. It also exposed voguing to new generations who had never heard of it before.Boychild walks the runway at the Hood By Air spring 2015 fashion show.Redefining Walking Down the RunwayFor his spring 2015 collection, the designer sent down models wearing denim, white shirts, basketball shorts, and large plexiglass collars down the runway. If the accessories weren’t eye-catching enough, the show also featured a model who slowly moved down the catwalk with the help of crutches and an appearance by performance artist and Oliver’s muse, Boychild, who paraded through the venue with a Great Dane.A model walks the runway at Hood By Air fall 2016 show.The Provocative PerformanceHood By Air sent male models down the runway in plastic-y red and black fabrics, knee-high heeled boots, and white turtlenecks printed with the word “bitch” for its fall 2016 collection. Midway through the show, a model by the name of Hirakish twirled, posed, and seductively grabbed another male model by the neck. He perfectly epitomized the gender-bending playful spirit of Hood By Air.Rihanna performs onstage during the 2016 MTV Video Music Awards.Rihanna’s Pink EnsembleLast month, Rihanna performed at the 2016 VMAs wearing a pastel pink Hood By Air logo ensemble, which consisted of a T-shirt, corset contraption, and thigh-exposing chaps. Of course, her back-up dancers matched her and wore cotton candy pink hoodies, lace-up boots, and beanies. The singer has never strayed away from dramatic, rule-breaking fashion, and Hood By Air delivers on both accounts.Watch a Young, Pre-Hood By Air Shayne Oliver Vogue for Rashaad Newsome:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Last September, the duo organized a politically-charged fashion show starring a group of empowering actresses and activists, including Whoopi Goldberg, Rowan Blanchard, Aubrey Plaza, and Rashida Jones, who each presented a serious (yet comical) thought on the issues facing the United States amid a tumultuous election. The public uproar over the crises that have shaken the nation has escalated since then, leading the brand to take a firm stance again—this time, in collaboration with New York City Ballet.Instead of a traditional runway show during New York fashion week (which officially starts on February 9), Opening Ceremony collaborated on a protest-inspired ballet in celebration of immigrants and the American melting pot at the David H. Koch Theater last Saturday. Dubbed The Times Are Racing, the piece was choreographed by NYC Ballet's resident choreographer, Justin Peck, and starred 20 members of the company who were outfitted by Leon. Accompanied by a selection of exhilarating tunes from Baltimore-based composer Dan Deacon’s 2012 album, America, the ballet made its official debut earlier in the week, but no doubt, seemed all the more poignant on a night full of political unrest.Trading tutus and pointe shoes for streetwear and sneakers, the dancers wore vibrant tees and tank tops with '80s-style slogans like “Defy,” “Protest,” “Unite,” and "Fight," (the pieces make up Opening Ceremony’s new "Action" capsule, available now). The rest of the costumes—brightly hued trench coats, cutoff shorts, and a denim overall—were adapted from the brand's spring 2017 collection, which drew inspiration from photos of Ellis Island, the portal which welcomed over 12 million immigrants to the U.S. in the 19th century. The newly-launched collection decidedly felt relevant given the global backlash against President Trump's executive order, which temporarily suspends immigration from seven predominantly Muslim countries. The refugee ban instigated a new wave of protests at airports around the nation, drawing parallels to Opening Ceremony's own demonstration that same evening.The coincidental timing of the event was not lost on Leon and Lim, who were both born in Los Angeles to immigrant parents. Indeed, the duo seems to attract the most evocative dates when it comes to scheduling: Their fall 2016 show took place on the 15th anniversary of the September 11 terror attacks, while this collection debuted exactly one week after the inauguration.New York City Ballet dancers perform The Times Are Racing.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”This isn't the first time the brand has collaborated with Peck. Two years ago in September, the creative team has caught the eyes of the fashion set when it sent down seven NYC Ballet dancers on the runway for the spring 2016 show. The "models" took a series of falls—meticulously choreographed by Peck—inciting a collective gasp (and rolling camera flash) from the crowd. The next month, Leon debuted a set of unitard costumes for Peck's new ballet New Blood.“Justin has become a friend now, and we met the day after the election, and we were pretty bummed,” Leon told the Hollywood Reporter. "What’s great about this piece is that it debuted four days after the inauguration, while all this stuff was happening; but 20 or 30 years from now, this ballet will still be performed, and these clothes will be part of it. That definitely means something.”The spring 2017 collection is available now for pre-order at openingceremony.com.More on the world of ballet:Ballerina Lauren Lovette shares her foot-care routine:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Following last week's reverse suspender situation, we bring you — wait for it — rompers for men.No, really. The RompHim, a Kickstarter launched by Evanston, Illinois-based Aced Design, is determined to give the men of the world their own version of the shortened, summer-inspired jumpsuits typically worn by women. And if the promo video is any indication, the RompHim looks like the kind of one-and-done piece frat boys will love."Is it a romper designed for men? Sure. But it's also pretty darn comfortable, and it may just be the start of a fashion revolution," the RompHim claims on its Kickstarter page.The romper design, which comes in pastel, printed, and even polka-dot options, features a front shirt pocket, an adjustable waist, and — get this — a fly zipper. (Why don't previously-existing rompers come with this option?!)Know someone who'd love to romp (sorry, couldn't resist) around in one of these numbers in the coming summer months? Well, lucky for them (and maybe you?), the RompHim will be available beginning May 15. All you have to do is pledge $90 now (the original retail price is $119 per onesie), and your jumpsuit will be shipped around July. Oh, and if you're interested in a RompHim for Independence day, the guys behind the design say they are "committed to getting the 4th of July RompHims to backers in time for the holiday." After the astounding success of her collections of pleated skirts and jersey dresses, just five years later she started her own couture house in Biarritz, France. Her revolutionary approach to fashion—putting women first and often using herself as a model—is reflected in almost everything we wear today. Whether it’s a piece of costume jewelry or a pajama top paired with jeans, you can bet there’s a way to connect it back to the French designer.Chanel also left her mark on the industry with an unforgettable line of fragrances that would set the standard at future fashion houses. Chanel No. 5, created in 1921 by the designer and perfumer Ernest Beaux, was revolutionary for its composition, name, and presentation.Let’s take a look back at the biggest moments in Chanel's fashion career.Coco Chanel wearing a pocketed jersey jacket and white blouseThe Introduction of JerseyChanel opened a boutique in Deauville, France, in 1913. The shop offered her first collection of sportswear, which included jersey garments. It was the first time the fabric had been used in a mainstream womenswear collection, as it had previously been reserved for undergarments only. Today, jersey is a wardrobe essential in T-shirts and dresses and on the runways of luxury brands from Acne Studios to Dior. Fashion’s favorite rule breaker Vetements recently presented jersey T-shirts as a part of its couture debut.Coco Chanel with Duke Laurino of Rome on beach at the LidoDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Inventing the Garçon StyleToday, women’s wardrobes consistently take inspiration from menswear, and Chanel practically invented that look. Regarding her love for masculine style, she once said, “I liberated the body, I discarded the waist, I created a new shape.” She created elongated evening fashion that was easy to wear and consisted of shirtwaists made from cotton knits—a refreshing take on womenswear that challenged the politics of looking feminine (as championed by Christian Dior’s “New Look”). The borrowed-from-the-boys approach can be seen in labels such as DKNY, Calvin Klein, and Alexander Wang.Coco Chanel in 1944A LBD Is ForeverThe little black dress is largely considered a wardrobe staple and a never-fail piece in every woman’s closet. Chanel created the style in 1926. American Vogue called the piece “the Chanel ‘Ford’ dress, the frock that all the world will wear.” It was revolutionary because of the simplicity of the garment, as well as because of the color. Before the 1920s, black was typically reserved for mourning. The designer’s admiration for the color came from years spent as an orphan in a convent in Aubazine during her childhood.Coco Chanel at her atelier, circa 1960Workwear for WomenChanel began designing workwear-worthy pieces for women as early as the 1930s. The designer introduced her classic tweed suits in 1954, and in 1957, she released her signature flattering two-tone slingback pumps, which featured a black toe cap and nude exterior and elongated the leg. Proenza Schouler’s fall 2016 boots take inspiration from the toe cap, and tons of fast-fashion chains released their own versions of the shoe this year.Actress Mia Farrow carrying a Chanel bagThe Iconic BagIn 1955, Chanel released its 2.55 bag (the name is derived from its creation month and year, February 1955). The bag’s simple yet luxurious quilted leather accented by a long gold chain allowed women to keep their hands free. The design inspired fashion houses such as Christian Dior, Hermès, and Chloé to create their own “It” bags. The 2.55’s value remains at an all-time high: The year it was released, it cost a mere $220; today, the similar Classic Flap costs $5,500.Coco's Chanel and Karl's Chanel: The Evolution of a Fashion House:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Faced with an uncertain income and the prospect of finding a new—and, by necessity, more economical—living situation via Craigslist, I decided instead to leave New York.And why not? Never before had I been so free from professional and personal commitments, and the opportunity might not come around again. So I sold most of the furniture to my (still friendly) ex, consigned and donated about 70 percent of my clothes, and bought a one-way ticket to Paris. I’ve been living out of a suitcase (and one very handsome-looking carry-on bag) ever since.This year has taught me a great deal: to live with almost constant uncertainty, to be smarter about money, to be more proactive about seeking new experiences, and how to avoid penalty fares for missed flights (be polite, and cry). It’s also changed my relationship to clothes.Call me superficial, but the idea of packing nine months’ worth of clothes, toiletries, and electronics into a suitcase and a weekender bag— nine months that would take me through multiple seasons and climates; fashion weeks in New York, London, and Paris; beach holidays in Ibiza and Sicily; a half-marathon in Vancouver and muddy hikes in southwest England—was a little daunting to someone who spends as much time thinking about clothes as I do. I didn’t want to drag around a lot of stuff, but I did want to feel equipped for any situation I might encounter.More shopping advices:What I discovered is that you really can pack just about everything you need in a suitcase, if you’re smart about it. And while I did enjoy having lots of styling tools at my disposal in New York—I can’t resist a sleeveless coat, however dubiously practical—having a streamlined wardrobe of basics made getting dressed easy in a way that I’d long craved. And I generally felt more confident in what I was wearing, too, because I was rarely trying to pull off something new.Here’s what else I learned about dressing with a limited wardrobe—principles I’ll use not just on future trips, but when I finally settle down and have a closet at my disposal again.RELATED: The Fashion Staples You need to Survive Living Out of a Suitcase1. Everything you own should go together. This seems obvious, but when packing for a trip, it can be really tempting to pack a series of outfits: blouses, skirts, and shoes that work perfectly together, and maybe with one or two other things. Don’t. Every piece of clothing should be an interchangeable unit that can be worn with everything else.2. Pick a simple silhouette, and stick to it. In my early and mid-twenties, I was fanatical about experimenting with new cuts and proportions. (If a J.Crew model could look that fantastic in cropped brocade pants, I ought to be able to give it a pass! Sadly, not so.) The only thing I’ve ever looked consistently good in are A-line skirts and dresses. Sure, that can be a little bit boring at times, but when you stick to the same shapes—for me, that’s midi skirts that sit an inch or two below my natural waist, crew-neck sweaters and blouses cropped at the hip, and single-breasted coats that end at the knee—it means you’ll never have to fuss in front of the mirror.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Having a streamlined wardrobe of basics made getting dressed easy in a way that I’d long craved.3. Develop color discipline. Ensuring that all of your clothes go together isn’t just a matter of proportion—color is critical, too. Study your wardrobe and see what colors are already working together. If you tend to favor graphic brights like red and yellow, but find that your brown cords never seem to go with anything, toss ‘em—and avoid brown in the future. Limiting yourself mostly to neutrals makes it easy.4. Don’t be afraid to wear the same things again and again. It’s easier, and makes your “look” more identifiable.5. Learn to layer. In the past, I wore T-shirts only in the summer, trading them out for light and medium-weight sweaters in the fall and heavy knits in the winter. Since I no longer have room for several sweater weights, I’ve embraced layering: a white tee makes for a great base under a lightweight bomber, sleeveless puffer vest, and trench on crisp fall days.6. Buy multiples of key pieces. This rule may seem counterintuitive when you’re tight on space. But when you’re doing laundry on a 90-degree day, you’ll be really happy you packed more than one tee.7. Opt for season-neutral fabrics whenever possible. You might love a double-faced wool dress, but you’ll get a lot more use out of one in a technical fabric that’s light enough for summer and can be easily layered over tights and long underwear in the winter. I like viscose and neoprene.8. Keep dry clean-only to a minimum. It’s a hassle, and it’s expensive. Enough said.9. You only need four pairs of shoes. Shoes can easily monopolize a suitcase, and I regret how many I packed. In the end, all I needed was a single pair of white sneakers, loafers, black kitten heels, and running shoes. (Sandals would have been nice for the beach holidays, too, but I could make do in sneakers.)10. Leave room for new purchases. While I tried to pack for everything I could think of, there were certainly things I forgot, or thought I could do without. Plus, you’ll never know what you’ll discover—I was very happy I’d left some room in my carry-on for a pristine vintage Pierre Cardin trench I found at a secondhand shop in Paris.Now learn how to pack like a supermodel:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast.
