Before that, he was artistic director of Emilio Pucci and had served in that role since 2008. In 2015, some called the move to Cavalli a homecoming of sorts. Dundas previously worked with founder Roberto Cavalli and his wife, Eva, as head designer from 2002 to 2005. Roberto Cavalli’s “design team will carry on and the appointment of a new creative director will be made in due course,” according to Gian Giacomo Ferraris, the company's CEO.One thing’s for certain: Celebs love wearing Roberto Cavalli on the red carpet. It’s an iconic brand for a reason: Its naturally glam, rock-and-roll aesthetic easily lends itself to the flashiest events. Let’s take a look back at some of our favorite Cavalli moments in recent history.Bella Hadid at the Cannes Film Festival, 2016On the Cannes Film Festival red carpet, the model wore a nude floor-length gown from Roberto Cavalli by Peter Dundas. The lacy details combined with the crisscrossing straps in the front showed off the designer’s penchant for glamorous pieces with a '70s bohemian twist.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Ciara at the CFDA Awards, 2016Ciara looked pretty in pink in this ruffled, off-the-shoulder dress at this year's CFDA Awards. The dress—from the brand's spring 2016 collection—complemented the singer's dewy skin and soft pink cheeks.Peter Dundas on designing Ciara's wedding dress:Kendall Jenner at the Cannes Film Festival, 2016The model stunned the crowd with a show-stopping sheer gown that hugged every inch of her lithe frame. The glam, gothic dress—with embroidered scrolls that morph into snakes—perfectly suited Jenner's fearless sense of personal style.Naomi Campbell at the Met Gala, 2016A long-time muse of the brand, the model radiated elegance in this floor-length gown. The sleek silhouette and the intricate beading complemented the futuristic theme of the fashion exhibition.Kim Kardashian West at the Met Gala, 2015In true Kardashian form, the reality star opted for a daring gown that would become the talk of the night. Dundas showed off his skills and flair for details with the careful positioning of crystals on the sheer fabric. As the runway looks rack up, some surprising trends are emerging that we can’t seem to get enough of—one of which danced onto our radars at the start of the first day.The unofficial NYFW opening/fundraiser for Hillary Clinton (co-hosted by Anna Wintour, which is about as official as unofficial can get), was packed with big name designers. But what really caught our attention in the sea of fashionable political power players was the models—or should we say non-models. The “Made for History” collection was modeled by basketball players, musicians, and principal dancers from the New York City Ballet (NYCB), who in particular called to mind a long history of dual inspiration between two aesthetic art forms.RELATED: Marc Jacobs, DVF and More Take Part In Hillary Clinton’s Fashion ShowLucky for the inner ballerina in all of us, that was just the start of the trend for the spring collections. More NYCB muses were back at Cartier’s afterparty as models and entertainment; while Mikhailovsky Theatre's Julian MacKay performed at the Ryan Roche presentation. Ballerinas also stole the stage, er, runway, at the Sachin & Babi show, which was designed with dancers in mind from its very conception.New York City Ballet dancers perform at the Cartier afterparty."We started the season looking at images of ballet dancers in motion and were fascinated by the composition of grace and strength and how they complement each other,” Sachin and Babi Ahluwalia, the designers behind the namesake eveningwear brand, told Allure. “As a married couple who design together we see the same interplay between the two of us—there is always a push and pull.”The idea of the performance art world influencing the wearable art world is not a novel one. There’s a reason the ballerina is a perennial archetype of style—both aesthetic arts revolve around the body as a means of expression. “The fashion industry has really related to the grace and beauty of ballet, but also how powerful and confident it is,” Sara Mearns, principal dancer with the NYCB, told Allure. This week’s iteration of the pas de deux between the two disciplines reinforces that common thread.RELATED: A New Pas de Deux: Puma Partners With New York City BalletDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”With the idea of cocreation and inspiration between the two art forms in mind, dancers from Ballet Beautiful, who received special consulting from Mearns, modeled the entire Sachin & Babi spring 2017 collection this week. “We asked ballerinas to model the collection because we design looks with motion in mind,” the designers said. “We wanted to show how these evening wear pieces are still easy to move in and the ballerina was the perfect vessel.”A Ballet Beautiful dancer at Sachin + Babi spring 2017 presentation.You don’t have to be a dancer (or have the body of a ballerina for that matter) to wear the ballet-inspired looks this season. The trend is surprisingly wearable. To score the off-duty dancer look, “simplicity is key,” according to Mearns. “You can always tell when someone is trying to hide their body when they are wearing way too much,” she said.And more than the clothes, achieving true ballerina-inspired style is about the carriage. If there’s one thing that kept the dancers’ style en pointe this week, it was that seemingly effortless air of graceful posture. Of course, for us mere mortals, a little effort is needed to achieve the elegance. “Imagine there is space between each backbone and walk with confidence,” said Mearns. Excuse us while we take her advice and dust off our childhood prima ballerina dreams before the curtain falls on NYFW.Go Inside the Miami City Ballet Costume Shop:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Instead, thin women were shown modeling all of the clothing items that were available in 1X and 2X sizes — and we mean all. Tops, bottoms, dresses, and the sale pages were all devoid of any plus-size models, with the largest size modeled being a medium (which is definitely not plus-size). We noted here at Allure how this was problematic for numerous reasons, most prominently because it reinforced unrealistic and unfair beauty standards. Not to mention, it falsely represented what the plus-size outfits look like.Athleta has issued a statement on the matter that doubles as a promise to be more aware of its practices in the future. "This is a place where we can do better. The positive portrayal of women in the media is very important to us," the company's statement said, according to  Hello Giggles. "We celebrate women of all body shapes, sizes, ethnicities, and ages across our stores, website, campaigns, and social media channels. The Power of She campaign is what we really stand for. It’s really important for us to acknowledge the strength, health, and beauty all women have. This is something we’ve been looking at and working fervently to solve.”As mentioned in the statement, Athleta has a prominent body-positive campaign called The Power of She, which celebrates women and girls around the world who make a positive social impact in various ways. Here's hoping this was just an unfortunate, honest error on Athleta's part and not indicative of a bigger trend to come.Related:Watch:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. Not only has she made us go gaga over her eponymous brand and its throng of relaxed yet structured dresses and outerwear, the former Spice Girl surprised us all with the announcement of her upcoming line with Target (set to launch in April); she's even designed a T-shirt with her adorable five-year-old daughter, Harper.But perhaps what we love most about Beckham is her undeniably chic sense of style. The style icon usually sticks to a uniform that consists of baggy trousers, cool kicks, and a chunky knit—a classic combo we'll undoubtedly see at her upcoming show on Sunday, February 12, at New York fashion week. To put a girly spin on her boyish ensembles, the designer has lately been opting for a wardrobe full of pretty pastel colors over fashion’s favorite neutrals like navy and black. Just this week, she was spotted wearing an tangerine-hued dress with a pair of bright turquoise shoes from her pre-fall 2017 collection. The outfit reminded us of the equally vibrant ensemble she wore while en route to Paris a few weeks ago—though this around, she opted for a pair of orange pants and an oversized powder blue shirt.While the color combo usually has us conjuring up images of the Knicks in our heads, Beckham's latest style choices have proven that the complementary shades can elegantly amp up any look without heading to the Tony the Tiger territory. In addition to blue and orange, the designer's been introducing other groups of bright palettes to her look recently. Combined with everything from deep berry sweaters paired with gray trousers to a scarlet red dress worn over a blue button-down, the style star has truly mastered the art of wearing color with aplomb—a pretty surprising feat coming from the woman who made the little Gucci dress a thing.One thing to keep in mind if you want to mimic Victoria Beckham's style? She typically wears a pair of dark, oversized sunglasses with almost every outfit. This not only adds a bit of mystery to her look, but also helps ground all the colors of the ensemble. Though according to the designer, the dark shades hold a more practical purpose: "I may make it look easy, but the reason I wear sunglasses all the time is, because let me tell you, I'm up every night with the children!" she said at a recent talk at Saks Fifth Avenue.The designer also opts for pretty minimal makeup looks, as well, which makes it a whole lot easier to play with every color of the rainbow when it comes to your wardrobe. Trust us, it’s harder choosing the right red lipstick when you’re wearing orange and blue. At London fashion week, Christopher Kane presented his spring 2017 collection full of slinky dresses, T-shirts with colored grommets and religious iconography, and knitted tops with floral appliqués. But one bedazzled accessory stood out among these beauties and became the star of Instagram: the Crocs shoes.RELATED: The Shoes at Marc Jacobs Will Help You Soar to New Heights (Literally)Crocs on the runway at Christopher Kane's spring 2017 show.The runway collaboration between Kane and the footwear brand included the classic sandals embossed with an array of crystals and stones in shades of navy blue, brown, and gray. Most people associate these rubbery shoes with nurses, cooks, gardeners, and the occasional style-challenged neighbor. They’ve undoubtedly been the butt of many style jokes, and the hatred for these comfy sandals rivals that of another fashion faux pas: Uggs, which London-based label Preen by Thornton Bregazzi also coincidentally collaborated with for its spring 2017 collection.RELATED: 9 Eye-Catching Shoes From NYFWPreen sent models down the catwalk wearing black and white flatforms and sandals adorned with bows and styled with lace tights and socks. True to the Ugg brand, they looked surprisingly comfortable.Ugg flatforms on the Preen by Thornton Bregazzi runway.And while you may not be ready to jump on the bandwagon of the seemingly ugly footwear trend just yet, it doesn’t come as too much of a surprise that Uggs and Crocs have popped up on the runway this season. The Birkenstock and Teva sandals enjoyed their 15 minutes of fashion fame in past seasons, with labels, including Marni, Prada, and Céline, creating their own renditions. Now it’s time for the Crocs and Uggs to shine—and we’re ready.If you want to try the trend before the designer versions are released next year, you’re in luck. The classic Crocs retail for just $35, while most pairs of Ugg sandals or boots will only cost you between about $100 to $200. Typically, the content of the site or app is used to make inferences about your interests, which inform future selection of advertising and/or content.Select All3 PurposesConsent PurposesLocation Based AdsConsent AllowedLegitimate Interest PurposesPersonalizeFeaturesLocation Based AdsClear FlitersFor Syro, fashion is about way more than selling shoes — it's an opportunity to carve out an empowering, celebratory space for people of all identities. Writer Evan Ross Katz spoke with the queer, POC-owned brand's founders to learn more.In fashion, questions surrounding gender swirl around the industry: Who gets to wear which clothing items? Do we still need siphoned-off menswear and womenswear runway shows? What really comprises a gender-neutral garment or fashion line? Amid those conversations, Syro emerged. Founded just three short years ago, the shoe brand's goals are not to break the rules so much as to create a new paradigm for an oft-underserved consumer demographic in the market: men and gender-nonconforming people who want to wear high heels.When you head to the "About" section of the brand’s website, its self-description is equal parts concise and intentional. “Syro is a queer POC business based in New York City,” it reads.“It’s simply the truth,” co-founder Henry Bae tells me. “And I think we want that really to be known because we had a fear early on that gender-nonconforming style would be eaten up by a larger mainstream in upcoming years. And we wanted to protect what was genuine about our identity and our femininity — our identity as minorities, really.”This purposefulness, and the ease with which they articulate it, is central here. For instance, the brand does not call itself “gender-neutral” (as is the preferred term for many companies these days), but “gender-nonconforming“ instead, which is to strip the gendered modifier of its power over the clothing itself. Sure, anyone of any gender can technically wear anything — same goes for makeup, skin care, and nearly any subsection of beauty and fashion — but it is one thing for a brand to say its products are for all customers and an entirely different thing to create it with emphases on size inclusivity and gender-inclusive marketing right from the start.Bae, who is 28 and identifies as a gender-nonconforming queer/gay man, and co-founder Shaobo Han, who is 28 and also identifies as gender-nonconforming and queer, first met in New York City in 2012 via Facebook. “Henry knew me as this loud, Asian city kid in NYC, while I revered his writing on his now-hidden blog,” Han recalls.Syro co-founders Henry Bae (L) and Shaobo HanBae chimes in, “It wasn't until I met Shaobo that I had a friend who reflected such polarizing parts of my identity — being feminine, gender-nonconforming, and yellow-American — back at me. It was a thrilling and liberating chemistry from the very beginning.”Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept Bangs“I've always needed high heels to fit my look, but could only fit into the absolute largest women's shoes I could find. Even then, they would be narrow and it would hurt.”The idea for the brand came out of necessity for Bae, who first formed the idea for Syro before bringing Han on board. “I've always needed high heels to fit my look, but I could only fit into the absolute largest women's shoes I could find,“ Bae remembers. “Even then, they would be narrow as eff and it would hurt, but I still did it.”One day, it dawned on Bae, who had been working in the shoe industry for years as a buyer, seller, and marketer, that he could create this himself — though not on his own. That’s when Han, who had been working in graphic design, came into the business. The brand officially launched in 2016.“At the time, I was going through a lot of gender-related problems that I was facing, and doing Syro with Henry truly informed my own personal gender journey,” Han tells me. “It has really shaped who I am now and my own sense of self.”They also saw it as an opportunity to cater to an underserved and even unacknowledged demographic of consumer. “Society doesn't want to acknowledge, let alone cater to, femme-presenting gender-nonconforming folx,” Han says. “It's so important for Syro not only to sell heels, but also to carve out space where femme folx can celebrate and empower each other — where we can focus our attention on creating joy, and reclaiming the moments of triumph in our narratives.“So, who is the average Syro customer? “Anyone who wears a U.S. men’s size 8 to 14 shoe,” according to Bae, who adds that the brand is particularly excellent for those in search of “something to give them a more cunty experience on the street.”Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsThe founders agree that the biggest hurdle in the brands early days was the lack of assurance around an audience for larger-sized high-heeled shoes. While they did not necessarily create Syro’s shoes for the stage (”Syro is shoes for the street,” Bae proudly declares), one of their biggest clients to date is none other than the mother of mainstream drag, RuPaul. “Shaobo and I screamed when we had sold a pair to her highness, RuPaul,” Bae recalls. The feeling of seeing a pair of Bruce Red Syro heels on RuPaul’s Drag Race was extremely validating, says Bae.The founder admit that, at times, balancing friendship and business can be tricky. “It’s like we had a baby, so suddenly, we are more than just friends,” Han tells me. “And sometimes we have different styles of parenting, of what we think is best for the baby.” It’s a story not unfamiliar to anyone who has experienced the pangs of working alongside somebody you're close to, particularly when attempting to bring new ideas into an industry.Alongside the rise of the brand has been a slowly percolating trend toward greater gender-deviant expression on red carpets, runways, and society writ large from men and male-presenting public figures. This cannot be credited wholly to brands like Syro, Paloma Spain, Eckhaus Latta, and Telfar, but that there are now non-custom options for folks of varying gender expressions is crucial. And one needs only to glance through the brand's extensive lookbook to get a feel for its powerful messaging, including gorgeous shots like the ones throughout this story, which were taken by photographer Hao Nguyen and feature models Cory Walkers and Serena Tea.Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsOf course, there is the issue of safety — a pervasive and anxiety-inducing concern for transgender and gender-nonconforming people. “I [had] a friend who got punched in the ear on the train for just dressing like a [complete] Bratz doll, so this place is still not as safe as you would expect from a neighborhood you call gentrified,” Bae shares. “But it's one of the safest places in the world where you can get a get away with being yourself...and, as this business does well, I guess I can't help but hope for more and hope for better for all of us.”“Society doesn't want to acknowledge, let alone cater to, femme-presenting gender-nonconforming folx.“On paper, Syro is a footwear brand. However, in talking to both of its founders, the most prominent theme is the idea of what its footwear represents: a deliberate ethos to offer people — particularly those untethered to the constructs of the gender binary — the tools and validation to fully express themselves. Many companies do not care for their customers after their credit card transactions are accepted, but to Bae and Han, it is important to push compassion far beyond that.Syro wants to support folks who experience violence and harassment for merely expressing their authentic selves — or even batted eyelashes and raised eyebrows — by letting them know that they are not alone, and that they are part of a larger community who not only hold space for them but is willing to fight for them, too.To pick up shoes from Syro for yourself (or for a loved one who deserves an extra-special gift), head to Shopsyro.com, or follow the brand's Instagram page to stay up-to-date on what they're rolling out next.Read more stories about gender and inclusivity in beauty:Now see what this genderqueer person love most about how they look:Follow Allure on Instagram and Twitter, or subscribe to our newsletter for daily beauty stories delivered right to your inbox.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Armed with about 100 pound trunks of clothes, I need to be able to move freely and get through security with ease. Even if you aren’t dealing with trunks, dressing yourself for comfort and efficiency seem to prove difficult when traveling on a long flight. You’re either going to be too cold, too hot, or too tired to even be bothered with it all. Alas, here’s a formula on how you can achieve the ultimate comfort in coach. With these tips in mind, you won’t even mind spending $7 on that can of Pringles.Since airplane temperature is so erratic, it is important to dress in easily removable layers. We love this soft and chic cashmere cardigan from Equipment. Equipment cashmere sweater, $318 (equipmentfr.com).A great T-shirt is the cure to all comfort issues. Acne makes the perfect breathable, thick cotton tee that is almost wrinkleproof. The fabric is thick enough to last you many months before it wears out and will hold its perfect boxy shape for many vacations to come. Acne Studios cotton T-shirt, $170 (acnestudios.com).There's nothing worse than getting up after a long flight and seeing your legs drenched in sweat. Over the years I have come to the conclusion that jeans are the best solution to your comfort problems. A nice, worn-in denim, like this Simon Miller pair, is perfect for sitting on a cramped chair for hours because it doesn’t get baggy. Plus, the thick denim prevents the fabric from clinging to your skin. Simon Miller jeans, $320 (simonmillerusa.com).The worst part of airport security is taking off your shoes, especially if you’re not wearing socks. I always love a slip-on shoe for the airport because it provides the comfort of a sneaker without the hassle of tying and untying. Common Projects makes the perfect slip-on shoes in sleek leather, and they also come in nude and black. Common Projects leather shoes, $305 (thecorner.com).I like carrying a backpack every day. But for non-backpackers, this is the time to utilize one. You don’t have to worry about your goods spilling out onto the X-ray conveyer belt. Plus, you’ll have two free hands for double-fisting snacks. Proenza Schouler twill-and-leather backpack, $1,495 (barneys.com).More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. (And, let's be real, we all scooped up a few new pairs in celebration.)But wearing flat sneakers 24/7 doesn't mean you're automatically destined for pain-free peds. According to Jackie Sutera, DPM, a New York City-based podiatric physician specializing in the prevention and treatment of foot pathology, foot issues aren't so much about shoe style as they are how much you're wearing your go-to pair of kicks."Everyone is born with a fat pad at the bottom of their foot think of that chubby, bottom part of a baby's foot—but, over time, the overuse of 'bad' shoes wears it down," Sutera explains. "So while heels definitely do that to you, it may be more surprising to know that flats and unsupportive sneakers will cause that fat pad to wear down just as quickly."This means that while Beckham—along with most of the athleisure-loving female population—may have made the switch to Stan Smiths, simply ditching heels isn't enough to save feet from painful things like inflammation, tendonitis, and pinched nerves. And living solely in your favorite flats can do just as much damage.The cure? Make sure to mix up your footwear, says Sutera."Sneakers are comfortable and now fashionably complete a look, so I'm not saying you have to sacrifice your style," Sutera explains. "But don't wear them on the walk to the subway, and then all day at work, and then all night to go out—and the same goes with flats and heels."She suggests alternating your trend-driven kicks with super-supportive options—they do exist!—or buying a supportive insert that can seamlessly slip into any shoe, like Vionic orthotics.If it means we get to hold on to our go-to Adidas low-tops, that's a pretty small price to pay. Instead of professional models, the ads feature a diverse group of 16 "influencers" (including students, artists, musicians, and writers) of different genders, sizes, and ethnicities. It is, undoubtedly, the brand's most progressive campaign yet.More on diversity in fashion:According to a joint press release, the goal of the campaign is to spread social awareness: Each model involved was chosen because of his and her commitment to "challenging the status quo" through activism. As part of the project, each influencer designed a Hanes T-shirt featuring personal slogans and empowering messages. They will also star in their own short social videos and curate blog posts, showing off their custom made tees and discussing their work.The project is notable for several reasons. For one, "The Class of 2017" features plus-size model Barbie Ferreira and transgender model Hari Nef, marking a decidedly progressive shift in the brand's identity. Second, it focuses on social issues rather than fashion: In fact, the associated collection's only offerings are Hanes T-shirts and a range of Champion sweats. While the influencers individually offered personal slogans dear to them, the overall statement is pretty loud and clear: Be true to yourself and love one another—an uplifting message we can all get behind.Last year decidedly marked a shift in fashion's focus on diversity. Retailers like Aerie and Free People invited real women to model in their campaigns, while J.Crew and Christian Siriano enlisted women of diverse shapes and sizes to showcase their collections at New York Fashion Week. Here are the direct-to-consumer collections to watch out for this season.Instant fashion is the new mentality of many designer brands on the runway today.Along with Tom Ford, Burberry, and Tommy Hilfiger, smaller brands are also taking on the retail model of see now, buy now. Why make shoppers wait the usual lead time of four to six months for seasonally appropriate fashion that’s been unveiled and promoted on social media months earlier?Let’s take a look at some of the direct-to-consumer collections available to shop straight from the runway this season.1) Rebecca Minkoff: Last season, Rebecca Minkoff presented immediately shoppable looks from her collection at NYFW and saw a 200 percent increase in sales, according to Business of Fashion. For the designer’s upcoming show on Saturday, she’ll take a similar approach. Minkoff will stage a runway show outside her New York City boutique for buyers, influencers, editors, and select consumers. Most of the products will be available immediately after the show in the store, where the designer will host a meet-and-greet.2) Baja East: Buzzy brand Baja East will release a see now, buy now capsule collection immediately after its NYFW show on Friday. The label is collaborating with Minions for its spring 2017 show. Merchandise from the runway will be available at the afterparty and on baja-east.com.RELATED: Topshop’s Spring Collection Will Be Up for Grabs After the Show3) Topshop: British retailer Topshop is also getting in on the shopping action. Following Topshop Unique’s spring 2017 fashion show at London fashion week later this month, over half of the runway items will be for sale in stores and online the same day, September 18. The rest of the collection will become available on November 11.4) Club Monaco: On Friday, Club Monaco will present its first on-schedule presentation at NYFW. The brand will show its men’s and women’s collections together. Items will also be available to purchase immediately in select stores and online.Tom Ford5) Tom Ford, Burberry, and Tommy Hilfiger: These three major brands are the leaders of the direct-to-consumer movement. Tom Ford took a season off earlier this year to reset and prepare for his fall 2016 collection, which showed at the Four Seasons restaurant space on Wednesday. You’ll be able to find the new collection online and in stores immediately after the show. Mytheresa.com has also added a “show and shop” feature that will allow shoppers to pick and choose pieces from these designer collections straight from the runway.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”RELATED: Tommy Hilfiger Shows Have a Flair for DramaMisha Nonoo6) Misha Nonoo: Misha Nonoo released her first see now, buy now collection this week via Snapchat. The designer has been known to present her collections through social media in the past. The new collection is available exclusively on the designer’s own website, mishanonoo.com.7) Thakoon: The designer recently rebranded with a completely new business model. The changes come after the Hong Kong–based investment firm Bright Fame Fashion acquired a majority stake in Thakoon’s 11-year-old company late last year. Going forward, all of Thakoon’s collections will be available for purchase in his new SoHo store and at his own website exclusively, with new merchandise dropping approximately every two weeks.8) Banana Republic: Banana Republic has partnered with Olivia Palermo who will act as the brand’s first ever women’s global style ambassador. To celebrate the occasion, more than a dozen pieces from the brand’s spring 2017 presentation will be available for immediate purchase on bananarepublic.com and in the label’s Flatiron location in New York after the presentation on Saturday.Ralph Lauren9) Ralph Lauren: The brand announced that its new collection would be available in stores and online seconds after it's presented on the runway this Wednesday at NYFW. The fringed jackets, plaid shirts, and leather coats will likely be in high demand—and fit into your fall wardrobe perfectly.Urban Zen10) Urban Zen: According to Donna Karan, she's been preaching the see now, buy now idea for ten years. Now comes the designer's first collection via her philanthropic line, Urban Zen, which utilizes the retail model. Right as I walked in, I saw it in the corner of my eye: a blush crushed-velvet mini slip dress that looked like one of Courtney Love’s castoffs from her Hole days. That’s it. We have traveled back to the '90s.In fashion, it’s common for what’s old to be new again. Just think of last year’s '70s resurgence with short, Ossie Clark-esque dresses parading down Hedi Slimane’s Saint Laurent runways and Nicolas Ghesquière’s French bourgeois style at Louis Vuitton. For fall 2016, we saw a veritable '90s invasion, from oversized streetwear hoodies at Vetements to tubular wire chokers at Loewe.RELATED: Velvet for Summer? Why Celebs Are Making the Case for the Season's Hottest FabricNow, I hadn’t worn that exact slip dress from Zara when I was a 'tween in 1996 for an obvious reason—it was far too sexy for a 13-year-old— but I did wear a crushed-velvet, short-sleeved, mock turtleneck in sweet baby blue to death (What can I say? I was obsessed with Gwyneth Paltrow’s velvet Gucci suit by Tom Ford). Fast forward to 20 years later. How was I supposed to wear the clothes I wore as a child again?Gwyneth Paltrow at the 1996 MTV Video Music Awards.Those obsessed with the style today don’t necessarily see the trend as a throwback. After all, “It” girls like Gigi and Kendall, who were recently seen rocking overalls and frayed jeans, were wearing diapers in the late ‘90s. Tome co-designer Ryan Lobo, who cites Michelle Pfeiffer’s Catwoman in 1992’s Batman Returns as one of the inspirations behind his fall collection, agrees. “[The trend] is something we can't help but cringe at sometimes because it's very much a part of our youth in a very literal way,” he says. “But all of these ‘It’ girls, like Kendall and Bella, who are sporting the look right now, they were babies when the trend was around the first time—if they were even born.”RELATED: The Ultimate Fall Fashion Shopping GuideThat’s not to say other women haven’t successfully worn the trends of yore before. Charlotte Rampling still manages to wear mod, '60s-style ankle boots with aplomb today, while Catherine Deneuve’s printed wrap dresses and trench coats look like she literally pulled them from her '70s closet.So for those of us who are literally #TBT-ing it, styling becomes paramount, whether you are wearing slip dresses, Tommy Hilfiger overalls (which, of course, recently relaunched at Urban Outfitters), or even choker necklaces. “A head-to-toe look is strong and difficult, unless you've got a body like Gigi and feel comfortable fitting into a crop-top corset and high-waisted Shannon-Doherty-in-Beverly Hills, 90210 pair of Levi's,” says Lobo.Bella HadidNew York-based designer Tanya Taylor feels similarly. “Empire Records was my idea of the '90s—those short, fluffy sweaters and mini kilts—but now the style is more about moderation,” says Taylor, who, like me, was a tween in the ‘90s. “It is a balance between the elements of an outfit that feel nostalgic versus the ones that feel really modern.”Taylor says take baby steps when it comes to adopting this movement this time around. Pick out one '90s-inspired element and style your outfit around it so that you don’t head toward the shudder-worthy costume territory. For example, if wearing a Spice Girls-esque, chunky platform, Taylor suggests pairing it with a modern silhouette like a voluminous poplin shirtdress. Same goes for a choker: Complement that with a simple pair of sneakers.Which brings me back to the crushed-velvet slip dress from Zara. Perhaps I could get away with it, just not paired with a slouchy Kurt Cobain-inspired cardigan and a tattoo necklace. Moderation, as they say, is everything.Lily Aldridge Talks Beauty and Wellness:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. It’s practical.” And we left it at that.Cut to present day, and there’s 15-year-old Kaia Gerber—Cindy Crawford’s daughter, aspiring model, style influencer, “It” girl—tying her white Converse Chuck Taylor high-tops the very same way. Um is my boyfriend the ultimate trend-setter? It looks to be that way.But there are a couple of differences between these two shoelace-tying looks, like the fact that Gerber tied hers with sneakers versus boots, and how she put them on display (my boyfriend always had his tucked away from sight beneath the cuffs of his pants—also side note: If he ever wore tiny denim shorts, I might have to reconsider some things). As a result, the mere presence of those two darling little bows gives a swift kick of sweetness to Gerber’s street-chic, downtown-cool edge. And combined with frayed cut-offs (to show off her enviably long legs, of course), a ‘90s flame-printed hoodie, her fur pom-adorned cross-body, and retro frames, it’s model off-duty perfection at its finest.And frankly, who wouldn’t want bows bedecked on everything and with every look? It’s already a spring fashion trend and an emerging fall hair one. Maybe that was the whole idea behind Gerber’s look. Or perhaps her shoelaces were just too damn long.Love Kaia Gerber's style? Among the former First Lady’s many accomplishments (reporter, polyglot, book editor), her role as a globe-trotting trendsetter is impossible to ignore—particularly while shielding our gazes from the summer sun with a pair of oversize shades.The iconic Onassis first started building her reputation as a jet-setting style savant with a trip to the Kennedy compound in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, in 1953, where the then lighter-haired style icon took to the waters with JFK for an afternoon of sailing wearing a sleeveless button-up blouse featuring oversize pockets, demonstrating her soon-to-be signature brand of timeless taste.Later visits to Greece featured darkened, saucer-like sunglasses, while jaunts to Capri called for a coif covered by one of her trademark head scarves. Ensembles ranged from chic and demure—calf-grazing pea coats paired with kitten heels and ladylike hats—to casual, with tees and blouses effortlessly complementing tapered slacks and sandals. But wherever the location, it was Onassis's grace, composure, and confidence that carried off each outfit.Here, six of Jackie Kennedy Onassis's best moments in travel style.1. In 1953, the then Jacqueline Bouvier and John F. Kennedy went sailing and sunning in Hyannis Port—activities that called for a cute and causal uniform of high-waisted Bermuda shorts and a sleeveless blouse.2. A seaside snap was elevated by the First Lady’s 1960s-era coif, peach pout, moss-colored scarf, and textured cream coat.3.  A trip to Ireland—with two children in tow, natch—requires a chic, buttoned white coat; demure white gloves; and  simple black flats.4. A flared wool coat, boxy bag, and signature oversize sunnies transform a simple arrival at the airport into an iconic moment in style.5. For a 1968 trip to Paris, Onassis opted for a brushed-out bouffant, geometric shades, and a black turtleneck that peeked coyly from beneath a classic camel coat.6. She's one of the new faces for Calvin Klein's fall 2016 campaign.The ads, which the brand teased on Snapchat last night, debuted today and feature a major cast, including Kate Moss, Frank Ocean, Zoe Kravitz, Margot Robbie, Bella Hadid, Henry Rollins, and more. They're a continuation of the "I _______ in #mycalvins" concept we saw last season. Seriously, we're obsessed with the diversity and hope to see more like this in the future. "Across generations and genres, these incomparable individuals are changing culture. Making history on the stage, screen, runway and field," the campaign touts."Through our fall 2016 global campaign, we push the boundaries of traditional advertising with our content and our cast," proclaimed a company statement.The campaign images show Coddington in two black looks designed by Francisco Costa, Calvin Klein Collection's former creative director, who announced his departure earlier this year.Calvin Klein isn't the first brand to cast models who are older than 20. In fact, older models and faces have been dubbed the new "It" girls, thanks to pairings such as Céline and Joan Didion, Saint Lauren and Joni Mitchell, L'Oréal and Helen Mirren, Marc Jacobs and Jessica Lange, Catherine Deneuve and Louis Vuitton, and Dolce & Gabbana's spring 2015 ad, which featured a trio of elderly women. And of course, there's Iris Apfel, who not only has her own line but was cast in an Alexis Bittar campaign. We can probably thank Advanced Style for this moment in fashion.But beyond the incredibly fun casting is the digital explosion that's gone along with it. The multimedia extravaganza is full of interviews, videos, and "stories," with releases happening on Periscope and Snapchat. There's also a 24-hour video takeover of the Calvin Klein site in the U.S. happening today. The company has always been digitally savvy, but they're going to a whole new level."We are inviting the consumer into our world to experience personal storytelling that no other brand can offer them," the statement said. "Our approach is digital-first, video-led and socially powered, providing our audience with an authentic and intimate experience that they can consume and share."Check out the videos for yourself, including some behind-the-scenes vids. There might be a solution in the form of a fresh new relaunch from Adidas. With the help of a supermodel named Kate Moss (you might've heard of her?), the brand is relaunching its classic Gazelle, and if everything falls into place, it has major potential to give the white-and-green classic a run for its money.Moss was photographed wearing a pair of Gazelles In 1993, and the image has become an iconic reference for the brand. To celebrate this new generation of the style, the company teamed up with artist Doug Abraham to "hack" the photograph for the campaign. Like the revamped image of Moss (below), there won't be any drastic changes to the design—only small tweaks—keeping that nostalgic factor we love."With the relaunch of Gazelle, we looked to the original cultural references that defined the authenticity of the style," said Nic Galway, VP of global design at Adidas Originals, in a statement. "Kate Moss has always had a connection to the Adidas Originals brand, and her affection for Gazelle during the '90s is a testament to the ways the silhouette has been adopted into style and pop culture."Speaking of style and pop culture, the renaissance of Stan Smiths was arguably prompted by their frequent appearances on the trend-dictating feet of Céline's Phoebe Philo. But the craze reached nearly every nook and cranny of the world, even outside the high-fashion set, thanks in large part to Instagram. The fact that Adidas paired up with Abraham, who's known for his social-media presence (@bessnyc4), shows that the company values and understands the power of new media.If the Gazelle is the next Stan Smith, it'll definitely mean a lot for the brand, but more importantly, our feet will rejoice. The shoes take a cue from festival-inspired rock and roll style: A pair of open-toed sandals just doesn’t cut it on a muddy field or at a live concert in the desert—and Kate Moss, the queen of rock and roll model-off-duty style, has been rocking the look for years now.Bella HadidThe trend is easy to pull off. Plus, it adds a tough edge to an outfit that otherwise might feel pretty basic. Take a look at Bella Hadid, who recently opted for a long-sleeved minidress paired with platform ankle boots and socks.If that isn’t enough to make you consider tossing your strappy sandals out the hot, humid window, Kendall Jenner also sported the look with black leather shorts, a black crop top, and a fringed jacket, while Rita Ora donned a pair of platform ankle boots with a pair of shorts and an oversize shirt.Kendall JennerWant to take the trend a step further? Try pairing a knee-high boot with your favorite summer sundresses and denim shorts. LVMH, the luxury conglomerate behind everything from Louis Vuitton to Sephora, has confirmed that it has teamed up with Rihanna to launch Fenty Maison.Business of Fashion reports that the new fashion line isn't just an in-the-works project — it's a fully realized ready-to-wear collection that will be ready to show in just a couple of weeks. A presentation of the looks — which will reportedly include clothing, shoes, eyewear, and jewelry — is scheduled for a Paris debut on May 22. So for all those fans complaining about a lack of new music, it wasn't just Fenty Beauty taking up Rihanna's time; she's been quietly working on an entire fashion collection.“Designing a line like this with LVMH is an incredibly special moment for us. [LVMH chairman and chief executive Bernard] Arnault has given me a unique opportunity to develop a fashion house in the luxury sector, with no artistic limits," Rihanna said in a statement. "I couldn’t imagine a better partner both creatively and business-wise, and I’m ready for the world to see what we have built together."This isn't the first time Rihanna has dabbled in apparel. In addition to Savage x Fenty lingerie, the multitalented mogul has teamed up with Puma in the past to collaborate on sneakers and other sporty clothing. And while Fenty Maison obviously not the first fashion brand under the LVMH umbrella (which covers Dior, Fendi, Marc Jacobs, and many more), it is the first one it has launched from scratch since 1987, Business of Fashion reports, and according to Essence, Rihanna will be the first black woman in the company's history to head up one of its fashion brands.Clearly, everything Rihanna touches turns to gold, so it's understandable that LVMH would want to partner with such a superstar for a new high-end fashion line. From New York City to Denver, Los Angeles to Dallas to D.C., museums are presenting shows that explore media beyond painting and sculpture. Fashion, photography, porcelain, and a work titled Vase With Hair are all fair game for the fall.“The end of summer is always a good opportunity to retreat indoors after focusing so much on outdoor activities during the summer,” says Florence Müller, the Avenir Foundation curator of textile art and fashion at the Denver Art Museum. “After enjoying so much recreation and leisure, it is a good moment to reengage the mind, coinciding with the start of the fall academic calendar.”Shannon Stratton, the William and Mildred Lasdon chief curator at New York City’s Museum of Arts and Design, echoes that thought. “September is such an exciting time of the year in the visual arts as it’s the annual launch of a museum or gallery’s new program,” she says. “It's time to get people back into culture as they return from holidays and reenter the city for the fall and winter ahead.”Ditch the beach for one of these museum shows and gain new perspectives that’ll stay with you longer than that sand at the bottom of your purse.Bruce Hulse and Talisa Soto, Bellport, New York 1982"Bruce Weber: Far From Home" at the Dallas Contemporary (September to December)Must be tough to be Bruce Weber, traveling around the world and photographing the most beautiful people on the planet. Since the early '80s, when he began rising to international prominence, Weber’s name has become synonymous with a certain sense of luxury, sophistication, and sensuality. Think: campaigns for Helmut Lang, Bottega Veneta, Calvin Klein, and Pirelli. That’s just scratching the surface, not even beginning to delve into his editorial work.Glibness aside, the guy has proven himself through an astounding number of projects: directing seven short and feature length films, publishing 39 books, acting as a director for a creative agency, shooting images for the world’s most elite publications and companies, etc. In "Far From Home," the Dallas Contemporary presents more than 250 of Weber’s photographs, the majority of which have never been exhibited. Travel-related short film works will also be on view. As executive director Peter Doroshenko says, Weber “helped establish our current visual vocabulary.” Ogle Weber’s depictions of fabulous personalities, clothing, and locations while learning more about his masterful technique along the way.Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsChris Antemann in collaboration with Meissen®, Little Maid, 2014"Chris Antemann: Forbidden Fruit" at the Museum of Arts and Design (September 22 to February 5)Does the word “porcelain” remind you of dusty objects in your grandmother’s cabinet? Time to rethink that association. The upcoming Chris Antemann show of porcelain works at the Museum of Arts and Design is more “sexy” than “granny.” Stratton describes the work as “unapologetically suggestive, combining seductive contemporary characters in the form of a traditional porcelain figurine like you might expect to find in someone’s china cabinet.”If you can’t see the show in New York City, the traveling exhibition will provide other viewing opportunities. In March, it will open at the Crocker Art Museum in Sacramento and will run through July 23.Gaetano Pesce, Vase With Hair, 2015"Gaetano Pesce: Molds (Gelati Misti)" at MOCA LA (September 3 to November 27)Be forewarned: Gaetano Pesce’s objects might inspire some serious design envy. From Vase With Hair, which kind of looks like a really hip sea creature, to other vases that recall a tree and dripping paint, Pesce’s works blur the line between craft and fine art, utility and beauty. You’ll never want to put your flowers in some boring clear glass again. The exhibition will also include a selection of chairs, lamps, and two-dimensional cast-resin reliefs that the designer calls “industrial skins.” His work evokes nature and the body, the appealing and the grotesque.Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsItalian-born Pesce has worked in architecture, urban planning, and design for over four decades. If you’re into the MOCA show, check out his work in over 30 permanent collections around the world, including MoMA in both New York City and San Francisco, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, and the Pompidou Center in Paris.Barbara Kruger, Untitled (Your Gaze Hits the Side of My Face), 1981"In the Tower: Barbara Kruger" at the National Gallery of Art (September 30 to January 22)A former graphic designer and magazine art editor, artist Barbara Kruger has created striking images that look, at first glimpse, like advertisements. Kruger’s signature style has made her one of today’s most recognizable contemporary artists. Her images include red bands with white wording in Futura Bold typeface that stretch across black-and-white pixilated images. You’ll know them when you see them.Fifteen works will be on view at the National Gallery in Washington, D.C. With messages such as “Know nothing / Believe anything / Forget everything,” “You thrive on mistaken identity,” and “Your creation is divine / Our reproduction is human,” the exhibition will leave you with some messages to reconsider, particularly regarding what it means to be a woman and a consumer of popular culture today.Comme des Garçons, Bump Dress"Shock Wave: Japanese Fashion Design, 1980s–90s" at the Denver Art Museum (September 11 to May 28)Can’t make it to fashion week, but craving some sartorial inspiration? The Denver Art Museum’s exhibition "Shock Wave: Japanese Fashion Design, 1980s—90s" might begin to quell the FOMO. The exhibition will feature 70 looks by designers including Issey Miyake, Kenzo Takada, Kansai Yamamoto, Yohji Yamamoto, Comme des Garçons, and Junya Watanabe.Two of curator Müller’s favorite pieces from the show include an Issey Miyake jumpsuit that “looks like an art piece, with a kind of paint-dripping pattern, like a Pollock painting” and a Comme des Garçons "bump dress" that “distorts the body in a monstrous way.”"Shock Wave" is one of many fashion exhibitions now finding a home in an art museum. Müller explains the trend: “Through these last 25 years, fashion has become one of the spotlights in our world.… Museums offer a more serious platform to consider fashion as an art historical subject and simultaneously the best expression of the ‘air du temps’ or the evolution of our society through fashion.” It’s also relatable—not all museumgoers may own artwork, but they’ve all (hopefully) worn clothes at some point in their lives.A Film From the Night and Day Books of Bruce Weber’s Adventures in Hollywood:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The musician garnered a lot of attention leading up to the show, which originally conflicted with Marchesa’s time slot at 5 p.m. After a little beef with the Council of Fashion Designers of America, West decided to reschedule his show two hours earlier at 3 p.m at Pier 59 Studios, a NYFW-favorite venue.While most fashion insiders have come to expect West's runway shows to pretty much be an anything-can-happen kind of event, this season proved them wrong.Vanessa Friedman of The New York Times summarized it best:Attendees entered the show to a near pitch black room, which of course, made it difficult to find their seats or see who was actually at the show. Turned out guests in the front row included buzzy-designer and West's right-hand man, Virgil Abloh, Hailey Baldwin, La La Anthony, ASAP Ferg, and of course, Kim Kardashian West.The show started 25 minutes late, which is actually considered early in the fashion world (it's also a big improvement from Yeezy Season 4, where guests suffered in the heat for two hours at Franklin D. Roosevelt Four Freedoms Park). It began with a voice-over followed by images of the models projected on a big black screen at the center of the runway.The most notable additions to the Yeezy line were the denim pieces, like high-waisted jeans and shearling-lined jackets (a.k.a. everything we've been seeing on the runways). The Snapchat-famous Calabasas track pants also made their runway debut in red and orange colorway. For sneakerheads, the show introduced a new pair of kicks, dubbed the "Yeezy runner," which came in black and burgundy.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Perhaps the most significant moment of the show was when Halima Aden, the Somalian-American model who has recently been signed by IMG models, made her highly-anticipated fashion week debut. While she was shrouded in a massive fur coat, her foray into fashion was certainly momentous.Halima Aden made her runway debut at the Yeezy Season 5 show.After being projected on the screens, the models then strutted down the catwalk IRL. The show then ended rather abruptly. Unlike most designers, West didn't come out to take a bow after the finale. Instead, attendees sat awkwardly for a few minutes until his wife got up and headed backstage.The fans' biggest complaint was that the show was not being live streamed as it had previously. In fact, there were signs barring media, although many attendees captured a great deal of the show.After so much controversy leading up to the show, it was surprising to see West's latest Yeezy installment to be, well, normal. Will there be another show next year? Who knows. But Meryl Streep stole the hearts of many fashion fans with her patriotic American flag shirtdress.One might assume the red-white-and-blue number was tailor-made for the occasion, but this look made its first appearance on Streep seven years ago. The Oscar winner wore the chiffon dress by French designer Catherine Malandrino to promote her film Doubt in Paris. The Malandrino dress has also made many other red-carpet appearances in the past. Halle Berry sported a sleeveless version during her press tour for Swordfish in 2001, and Katy Perry wore the dress on the Fourth of July in 2013 (which she celebrated with her then boyfriend John Mayer).Streep wore the dress in 2009 to promote her film Doubt."When I saw Meryl in my dress, I was speechless," Malandrino told Allure. "Her talk was clear, her gesture powerful. I had chills all along my body and was moved to see my dress associated to that historical moment. This dress is my American dream."According to a press representative for the Catherine Malandrino brand, Streep got the dress through a publicist. Since then, the actress has kept it in her closet, until yesterday, when she appeared at the convention to make her rousing speech about Clinton’s “grit and grace.”“We were ecstatic to see Meryl wearing the flag dress at the DNC,” says Mo Hedaya, the marketing director at Bluestar Alliance, which acquired the French label in 2013.  “It was definitely the ultimate arena for this piece, and who better [to wear it] than such an iconic and acclaimed actress.”Catherine Malandrino fall 2001 collectionThe dress, Malandrino’s breakthrough design, made its debut at New York fashion week as part of the designer’s flag-motif fall 2011 collection, which also included a patriotic skirt that Madonna wore during a concert tour. Once reserved for the Fourth of July weekend, stars-and-stripes garb became a symbol of remembrance after the September 11 attacks. Kelly Ripa wore a dress from Malandrino's collection for the September 18, 2001, episode of Live With Regis and Kelly, her first show after the attacks.RELATED: [#article: /articles/5790d7b8e1c20f8b68d407bf]||||||The designer relaunched the pattern in 2008 to commemorate President Obama's election and her tenth anniversary. "It has been my lucky dress. Relaunching it proved to me that the dress has a long life and it will be iconic in my history,” she told the Cut in 2009. The dress was also featured on the cover of her eponymous book.Unfortunately, the dress is currently sold out. Clothing sizes aren't exactly standardized, and many brands participate in vanity sizing — or the practice of putting smaller numbers on bigger sizes to make folks feel "better" about the clothes they're able to fit into, and thus, more likely to make a purchase. However, it seems ASOS just decided to employ the opposite tactic, as they recently put an item of clothing up on their website and listed the "large"-sized offering as a U.K. size 10, which is the equivalent to a U.S. size 6.The garment in question is a pair of high-waisted shorts by the brand Pull&Bear with a ruffled hem and a floral pattern. After noticing the strange (and limited) sizing range, Twitter user @GrrlGhost posted a screenshot of the sizing drop-down, followed by a tweet that reads, "Screaming into the void rn." Many of the people who have responded to her tweet seem to agree that the sizing is indeed worth a scream into the void.ASOS has since responded and apologized on Twitter, saying there was a "glitch" that affected the sizing of all of their Pull&Bear offerings. The shorts are now available in a wider range of sizes, but the largest size available is still only a U.K. size 12 (equivalent to a U.S. size 8). Given that the average woman in the U.S. is a size 16-18, only offering to sell an item of clothing to those who can fit a size 8 and below (and calling a size 8 a large) sends a pretty unhealthy message to women about body standards.It also sends a message about who should be wearing what kind of clothing. People are often body-shamed for their clothing choices under the assumption that only folks with certain body types should wear certain garments — in fact, everyone from Lady Gaga to this beauty queen to this Congresswoman has felt the pressure to conform to cultural beauty standards. However, everyone (regardless of size) should feel free to wear whatever makes them feel comfortable and fabulous — and with hot weather coming up, who couldn't use a cute pair of shorts?More on body image:Rapper and Singer Lizzo Talks Bodysuits and Body Image:Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Luckily, our favorite designers feel the same way. For those of us with a serious case of nostalgia, Lucky Brand is bringing us a capsule collection that delivers big on old-school vibes.RELATED: The Backpack Is Back: Back-to-School Options For AdultsThe fashion retailer is teaming up with Los Angeles-based artist Ornamental Conifer—known for his punk-y yet brightly colored artworks featuring idioms and eye-catching typography—for a capsule collection of graphic tees, vintage bandanas and one-of-a-kind hand-painted denim and leather jackets.“I want the collection to emphasize that we, as humans, are all unique,” Conifer told Allure.  “I understand that sounds very corny, but I feel very strongly that we, as a society, have yet to really comprehend the impact that the digital age we live in has had on us as people....Each jacket I made is completely unique, there is no chance that you will meet someone else wearing the same piece as you.”Lucky Brand and Ornamental Conifer denim jacketRELATED: How To Get Runway Inspired Back-to-School LooksThe customized denim trend has been picking up steam this season. For such a style staple, the denim jacket has been reinvented more times than we can count. This latest take on the wardrobe essential is adding an extra dash of cheekiness to your fall closet. Part wearable art, part killer fall outerwear, the Ornamental Conifer denim and leather jackets feature hand-painted punny yet thought-provoking verbal messages—adding some edge to the pretty standard jeans company.“For us, collaborating with someone as authentic and creative as Conifer came very naturally because we’ve always embraced individuality....His aesthetic is so original and brought such a fun and optimistic touch to iconic Lucky Brand pieces,” Kin Ying Lee, Lucky Brand’s chief creative officer, said in a statement.The entire capsule collection will launch online and in select Lucky Brand stores on October 14. The vintage bandanas and graphic tees will both sell for $50 and under, but the jackets will cost you. For one of the 59 unique denim and leather jackets, you’ll have to shell out at least $750. Despite the price tag, there is a major case to be made for investing in one-of-a-kind closet items—with an Ornamental Conifer original, you’re literally getting a piece of wearable art. Giorgio Armani's international makeup artist, Linda Cantello, based the entire look around one of the house's iconic black-and-white advertising images from the '90s."Reworking the strong Armani Beauty Code of the early '90s, we emphasized the top lashes for a simple, graphic eye," Cantello told Allure. "It's really a diva-like attitude to celebrate Armani. It's very much the DNA of the brand and the only focus is on the eyelashes."To get the vintage-inspired look, Cantello's team applied false lashes, curling them with a spoon to get an extreme, cat eye-like shape. She then applied Armani Beauty's Eyes to Kill Classic Mascara and Armani Beauty Smooth Silk Eye Pencil (#4, Black) to get a more intense gaze."Armani really wanted to have a very long, straight eyelash that doesn't go up and doesn't go down," explained Johan Lundin, international marketing director for Giorgio Armani. "This morning, we straightened them using a spoon and blow-dryer and a little bit of brow gel for some hold."Considering the show itself was all about a glamorous '90s look, the fashion also mirrored  the drama of the beauty look: Models walked down the runway and stopped to spin in slow motion to show off the intricate beadwork, luxurious fabrics, and stunning, sparkling gowns that paid tribute to the codes of the house of Armani.Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsThe hair also had a '90s, vintage sensibility. Aldo Coppola's team created slicked-back, sculptural works of art on the backs of models' heads. The end result looked like a more sophisticated version of pin curls in progress.Finally, for a more antiquated take on base makeup, Cantello used foundation shades two shades lighter than the natural skin tone on models' faces and necks. She also applied the brand's Crema Nera Supreme Reviving Cream Light Texture as a base, along with Armani Prima Day-Long Skin Perfector Trouble Zones all over the forehead and on the T-zone to mattify the skin.She topped the faces off with the Best of Beauty-winning Power Fabric Foundation and used Neo Nude A-Contour in shade #20 (Light) under the cheekbones to lihtly sculpt the face. Taking even more influence from the era, her team used Armani's Lip Maestro Freeze in shade #204, "Nuda" for a soft, pale lip.Nineties beauty is back, baby. Say hello to CIE Denim's upside-down shorts, which literally invert the fitted waistband and raw hem of a pair of vintage jorts to give you a whole new perspective on your old jean shorts.According to CIE Denim, a New York City-based vintage shop, each pair of the upside-down shorts is handmade and one of a kind. The shorts are a high-waisted cut with a hidden zipper and tab closure around the raw hemline up top and the original waistband, belt loops, and pockets down below. The shorts retail for $385 (custom vintage denim doesn't come cheap) and, unfortunately, are only available in sizes 23 through 29.The inverted shorts come in two slightly different washes and styles, named the Nancy and the El, a reference to the two main female characters of Netflix's Stranger Things. CIE Denim took the reference to the Upside Down even further with its "Will," "Mike," and "Lucas" pants, which are similarly inverted full-length jeans, all in relaxed fits and various distressed washes, and each of which retails for $500. (Though CIE Denim posted about "Dustin" upside-down denim on Instagram in February, that pair no longer appears on the website, having presumably sold out or gone too deep into the Upside Down.)Who What Wear was first to report on the mind-bending jean shorts, after they appeared on the Instagram feed of Alyssa Coscarelli, a fashion editor. Dior is expected to announce the move after its couture show in early July.If confirmed, Chiuri will be the first female creative director in the company's 70-year history, following the likes of John Galliano, Yves Saint Laurent, and most recently, Raf Simons, who announced his departure last October.Chiuri is the one half of Valentino's design duo. Valentino Garavani handpicked Chiuri and her design partner, Pierpaolo Piccioli, to be the the Italian brand's joint creative directors in 2007. During their tenure, the brand has become known for romantic, fairy-tale-esque designs. Earlier this year, Valentino topped $1 billion in annual sales, according to WWD.While Dior has yet to issue statements to confirm the appointment, a rep for Valentino said, "We have no comment at this time as nothing has been confirmed."The next couture season, scheduled for the week of July 4, will mark Chiuri's final Valentino show with Piccioli. Typically, the content of the site or app is used to make inferences about your interests, which inform future selection of advertising and/or content.Select All3 PurposesConsent PurposesLocation Based AdsConsent AllowedLegitimate Interest PurposesPersonalizeFeaturesLocation Based AdsClear FlitersStock up on the ethical clothing brand's famous basics and classic silhouettes at hugely discounted prices.Twice a year like clockwork, one brand goes above and beyond to remind us why it's still head and shoulders above the rest. I'm referring, of course, to Everlane's Choose What You Pay event, which still feels too good to be true no matter how many times it comes around.Here's how it works: The promotion allows customers to select from one of three prices for any given item, no strings attached, and it's been applied to literally hundreds of products from shoes, to dresses, to outerwear, to intimates and beyond. Now, you're probably already running and not walking to Everlane.com to peruse the offerings, but in case you need a bit more explanation to wrap your brain around this improbable gift, the retailer has you covered, with a mega-dose of the radical transparency that informs its day-to-day operations.Everlane has built its brand on chic, ethically-made pieces offered without the traditional retail markup, so you wouldn't think its prices had anywhere to go but up. But when the brand overproduces a certain item, it double down on its policies to clear out the overstock, transferring that benefit to the customers by slashing the costs even further. Ultimately, the lowest of the three possible prices reflects only Everlane's basic costs to produce the item, with absolutely no overhead whatsoever. If you're feeling in the mood to pay it forward, the midrange price and the higher price go toward the costs of office costs and future product development, but there's no obligation to shell out more than you want to.Mmmhmm, now you're picking up the pace and trotting over to see for yourself, and not a moment too soon because items are going fast. As of this writing, there are 405 pieces available with the Choose What You Pay pricing — which is inflated slightly because multiple colors of the same item are counted separately — enough to account for your head-to-toe fashion needs. Regular old models wearing regular old collections down regular old runways? Not in the age of social media. This season—along with the seemingly endless wish list of items we already want in our wardrobes—NYFW is also sending some important messages down the runway.In the midst of a particularly tumultuous election season, Opening Ceremony’s Carol Lim and Humberto Leon, who are both children of immigrants, took advantage of their platform to make the clothes about a bigger cause, allowing the standard runway fare to feature women talking about serious issues like immigration, police brutality, economic inequality, and gender discrimination.RELATED: Marc Jacobs, DVF and More Take Part in Hillary Clinton’s Fashion Show“Since our very first show, Opening Ceremony has participated in Fashion Week as a platform to express ideas,” the designers said in the show’s program. “This year, no ideas are as critical as the one’s our country will consider on Election Day.”RELATED: These Women Posed Nude to Send a Message to the Republican National ConventionThe “Pageant of the People,” hosted by Portlandia’s funny-as-hell duo Carrie Brownstein and Fred Armisen, featured a diverse and impressive catwalk cast with famous and empowering women, including Natasha Lyonne, Rowan Blanchard, Rashida Jones, and even Whoopi Goldberg. Fittingly hosted on the fifteenth anniversary of the September 11 attacks, the runway-show-slash-pageant-slash-town-hall-debate got right down to business, asking each of the 11 special guests a specific question regarding today’s societal issues.When asked how she juggles family and career, comedian Ali Wong questioned why men never get asked the same question. “[Men] just ignore the child and that’s perfectly socially acceptable,” said Wong. “But dads get so much praise for doing so much little. My husband occasionally changes the diapers, and people, they can’t believe it. They go, ‘Oh, my God, I can’t believe your husband changes diapers, what a doting father.” Girl Meets World star Rowan Blanchard gave her thoughts on feminism, a topic she has been a strong advocate of on social media. “Feminism could be more inclusive if we choose to listen to people instead of talking over people,” said the 14-year-old.Each participant was then asked why Americans should vote this November. The crowd erupted in applause when Whoopi Goldberg answered, “You should vote because if you don’t, you can’t bitch.”RELATED: 3 Times Beauty Pageants Actually Did Something RightThis is certainly not the first time fashion and politics have joined forces. In its purest form, fashion is political: “When we get dressed, we make decisions about which aspects of ourselves to present to the world,” the Opening Ceremony program read. Designers have been magnifying that connective thread for as long as we can remember, but what’s particularly notable about Opening Ceremony’s presentation is that it gave this connection a voice. Gymnastics leotards.When the competition begins, there’s no doubt that we’ll see gymnasts decked out in crystals. In fact, Team USA’s leotards will be emblazoned with more than 5,000 Swarovski crystals, according to The New York Times.It makes perfect sense. Women’s gymnastics is one of the most viewed Olympic sports. It’s highly publicized, and female gymnasts aren’t allowed to wear any jewelry except for small stud earrings. The shiny, sparkly leotards demand attention.Before competition, Olympians receive a package of eight leotards to compete in and 12 to practice in. The custom-fit leotards studded in high-quality crystals would cost an average of $1,200 on the open market.RELATED: The Style Olympics: What the Athletes Will Wear in RioIn 2008, Nastia Liukin won the gold medal in the individual all-around competition at the Beijing Olympics while wearing a pink leotard studded with 184 crystals. “It’s our ball gown. It’s our moment to go out there on the biggest stage we’ll ever be on, so it’s really important not just to feel confident but to look confident,” Liukin told Allure.Liukin, who’s designed her own line of leotards for GK Elite, said that before the competition, she and her teammates put on a fashion show and used the hotel hallway as a catwalk to pick out their uniforms.In honor of tomorrow’s opening ceremony in Rio, let’s take a look back at some of the most iconic leotards of all time.RELATED: Olympian-Inspired Fashion for Champion ShoppersNadia Comaneci at the 1980 OlympicsNadia Comaneci, 1980In 1980, Romanian gymnast Nadia Comaneci took home the gold medal while wearing a simple white leotard with the Romanian-flag tricolor stripes down the side. She also worn a gold chain necklace, a signal that she was aiming for first place.Mary Lou Retton at the 1984 Olympics.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Mary Lou Retton, 1984Mary Lou Retton won the all-around gold medal at the 1984 Olympics (plus four more medals) while wearing a white leotard decorated with the American flag. The uniform became so iconic that in 2012, Jordyn Weiber and Aly Raisman wore leotards resembling Retton’s (with more sparkles, of course).Shannon Miller at the 1996 Olympics.Shannon Miller, 1996At the 1996 Olympics in Atlanta, Shannon Miller performed a routine on the balance beam while wearing a simple white leotard with a big blue star on it. Miller won 16 World Championships and Olympic medals between 1991 and 1996 and ranks as the most decorated gymnast in U.S. history.Gabby Douglas at the 2012 Olympics.Gabby Douglas, 2012At the 2012 Olympics in London, Gabby Douglas won her all-around gold medal while wearing a metallic-pink leotard decked out in 1,188 decorative crystals. The shiny fabric, which the majority of Olympic gymnasts wear today, is called Mystique. It’s a spandex base covered with foil, which results in a glossier finish.Simone Biles at the 2016 Olympic trials.Simone Biles, 2016Anticipation is building for this year’s Olympic performance. Simone Biles, heralded as a gymnast to watch, will be wearing some fantastic uniforms. Biles wore a bright red leotard embellished with, you guessed it, crystals during the Olympic trials in San Jose, California.—With additional reporting by Macaela MackenzieThe Athleticism of Simone Biles:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. But Kendall Jenner and Gigi Hadid are sure as hell making me feel like one.The stylish model BFFs have been spied around town flashing peeks of their hipbones in high-cut bodysuits, which they pair with hip-skimming bottoms. The "peekaboo pelvis," if you will. It is a trend that Who What Wear calls "polarizing." But I'm calling it "my old swag." The whole high-cut one piece with low-slung bottoms thing was totally my jam back in 2006 when I arrived on campus for my freshman year of college.I remember the mid and late aughts as the years when everyone was wearing American Apparel. Their straightforward basics were a little pricey for me (at the time I wasn't trying to spend more than $8 dollars on a t-shirt. Don't judge me, I was on a microwave mac and cheese budget), but I was willing to shell out extra dollars I'd had stashed away from my summer job on some of their sexier fare. I loved their Gold lamé leggings (I bought a pair and served Karen O realness as I stomped up and down my grassy rural Ohio campus,) their plunging halter bodysuit, their micro mini skater dresses. But my favorite piece from the now-fading brand was their thong leotard, which had (of course) a low neckline and a high cut.Myself in 2006, preemptively and unintentionally on-trend with Kendall Jenner and Gigi Hadid. Photo: courtesy Jihan ForbesI owned three different versions of the piece — one in black, another in white, and a pale yellow one. I am not ashamed to say I still have them in my possession, somewhere tucked away in a bin in my closet.Obviously, I know Kendall and Gigi care as much about my sartorial proclivities in 2006 as Maxine Waters cares about Bill O'Reilly's opinions on her hair, but I couldn't help but feel a little bit of vindication seeing them rocking the combo I used to love when I thought 25-year-olds were old.Sure, these girls are working international models and household names. OK, so they can count Olivier Rousteing amongst their fans. Yeah, I can't open a fashion magazine without seeing multiple images of them. I'll let them have that (all of that). But did they ride into off-campus frat housing sporting the peekaboo pelvis on the shoulders of their slender 6'3" homie? I don't think so! Such everyday iconic moments are reserved for the non-rich and famous. Sorry, gals.Of course, I know I wasn't the first to rock this style, nor will I be the last. And Kendall and Gigi didn't "steal" the look from me. But at the very least, KenGi's contemporary love of high-cut bodysuits and jeans just affirms that while there are some outfits I regret from 2006, at least I know that there is one combo I favored that wasn't totally heinous. Hey, the aughts were rough fashion-wise for almost everyone... with the exception of maybe Gwen Stefani, so it's nice to see a win from that era.Anyone else rocked high-cut bodysuits and jeans back in the day?
