Following in the footsteps of fast-fashion brands like H&M, the retailer just launched a new sustainability initiative and ethical clothing line. Dubbed Zara’s #JoinLife initiative, the new collection, which is designed for “a woman who looks into a more sustainable future,” is made with materials aimed at reducing environmental impact, like organic cotton or recycled wool.RELATED: 10 Eco-Friendly Fashion Brands to Reduce Your Buyer’s RemorseThe collection is next-level chic. The androgynous pieces inspired by earthy, mineral tones are right on trend for fall. Think: the kind of high-wasted pleated trousers you’d expect from a killer '90s power suit, a bevy of bell-sleeved dresses and architectural tops, and a handful of oversize trenches.Zara’s sustainability efforts go beyond the clothes—the retailer is applying the sustainable mind-set to everything from the products to the packaging. As part of the overall brand overhaul, Zara is committing to using boxes from 100 percent recycled cardboard. The “boxes with a past” initiative means that boxes are packed and reused in stores up to five times before the cardboard is recycled and made into fresh boxes. According to the retailer’s website, 56 percent of all online orders are currently delivered in these recycled boxes. Zara also teamed up with a list of cool designers, photographers, and all-around creative individuals—such as interior designer Ciszak Dalmas and photographer Pierre-Ange Carlotti—to turn the recycled boxes into ultrachic DIY projects complete with make-it-yourself tutorials on its website.Finally (and seriously finally), the brand is starting to do something about all the clothes we’re tossing out every time we go for a new fast-fashion wardrobe update. Like H&M, Zara now has a recycling program that will make getting your old clothes into the right hands supereasy. The retailer currently has drop-off points in stores across Europe and will be doing the same for U.S. stores in 2017. In Spain, Zara will even pick up clothes right from your home. All the clothes you ditch when you pick up some new seasonal must-haves will be donated to either the Red Cross, Oxfam, or Cáritas in Spain, who will sort and reuse them in the most sustainable fashion.RELATED: Your First Look at H&M’s Natural and Organic Beauty LineThe #JoinLife initiative is arguably a little ironic—the fast-fashion industry has taken a lot of heat for its largely negative environmental issue. According to an investigation by MSNBC earlier this year, most items are worn only seven times before we ditch them for a closet upgrade, which means the clothing industry is churning out 150 billion new items a year. All that fast-fashion-fueled production means a need for supercheap labor and an increase in the world’s sweatshops, not to mention a massive carbon footprint left by the collective production facilities.So are initiatives like Zara’s #JoinLife or H&M’s Conscious just greenwashing? Maybe. But for retailers that currently make around $20 billion in sales every year, even the smallest green step matters.Allure fashion director Rachael Wang shares her style tips:Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. In fact, the first New York Fashion Week plus-size showing actually happened in September 2013 when designer Eden Miller of Cabiria sent her line down the runway as part of The Fashion Institute's showcase. Back then, it was still called Mercedes Benz Fashion Week, but now it's called NYFW: The Shows under IMG. While it's true that Torrid is the first brand to show under the new name of NYFW, they're not the first plus-size label to ever show, and this distinction is important — Cabiria paved the way, and their hard work should be acknowledged.If you're not familiar with Torrid, they're a brand that creates super cute clothing for sizes 10 to 30. Given the fact that shopping while plus-size can be pretty difficult, Torrid makes it easy with their affordable and stylish options. Now, they're changing the industry in a different way with some major news — they've just shared the exciting news that they're becoming the first plus-size brand to show at New York Fashion Week, and we couldn't be more excited to see what their runway show will look like.Come September 2017 they'll be presenting their Spring/Summer 2018 collections with the best of them at NYFW. The collections will feature 40 looks, which, according to a press release obtained by the LA Times, include key trends for the Spring/Summer 2018 seasons, like "edgy rock ‘n’ roll, romantic boho, hand embroidery and painted elements." Given that they're a plus-size brand, they'll be using all plus-size models, and Torrid has been conducting a model search to find 10 lucky models who will go to New York Fashion Week and represent Torrid. The search started in May with online submissions and has continued through the summer with live casting in Seattle, Houston, Atlanta, and Ontario, Canada — it officially ends on August 13. The 10 finalists will be flown to New York for fashion week, and one of them will be selected and given the title of "Face of Torrid 2018" along with a wardrobe and modeling contract. Judges for the contest are designer Ashley Nell Tipton, supermodel Candice Huffine, and celebrity model Priscilla Ono.The inclusion of a fully plus-size brand with all plus-size models at NYFW is a huge step in the right direction for inclusion and representation, as Bustle writes the Spring/Summer 2017 shows included less than one percent plus-size models. This show could nearly triple that percentage, if they bring in one model per look. Regardless of statistics, it's wonderful that the brand is getting such huge recognition for their work. Their clothes are fantastic, and it'll be a wonderful show.More on fashion:Rapper and Singer Lizzo Talks Bodysuits and Body Image:Follow Rosemary on Instagram and Twitter.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. W. Anderson’s spring 2017 show may be tomorrow afternoon, but the brand has already solidified its presence at fashion month with its infinitely relevant accessory: the J. W. Anderson Pierce bag. The inevitably eternally chic shoulder bag, which made its debut last year for the designer's prefall 2016 collection, boasts clean lines and an elegant trapezoidal silhouette. It features a flap struck through by the everyday-goth appeal of a septum ring, hence the name. It’s basically the personification of the new-era "It" girl: a modern classic with on-trend details and a heavy dose of irreverence. (Speaking of, here's how you should carry fall's new "It" bags.)The J. W. Anderson Pierce Bag has been spotted on the arms of influencers like Susie Lau of Style Bubble, Pernille Teisbaek, Irene Kim. “I love it because it's deceptively small," Lau says of the bag. "The multiple pouches means you can actually fit a lot of stuff in it, and I think it takes a ladylike shape and subverts it with the giant ring hardware on the front.“ Lau says she currently has her eye on the colorful patent design from the men's spring 2017 show. (Who says men can't rock a purse?)The Pierce bag at J. W. Anderson's spring 2017 menswear show.Sarah Blair, senior vice president at Barneys New York, cites the Pierce’s combination of minimalism and attitude as factors that make the piece stand out effortlessly among the seemingly endless over-the-shoulder offerings. We expect to see even more of the supremely Instagrammable accessory as London fashion week—and the quietly rebellious street style synonymous with the city—continues. With facial piercings becoming as ubiquitous as a timeless topknot, the transmutation from beauty to fashion is inevitable—after all, the punk-driven charm of metallic adornments are far more accessible minus the needle and the pain.The Perfect Mini Bag:Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Now, the multitalented star is back with a clothing collection under the same label. But don't think it's just like any other celebrity fashion line. Daya by Zendaya is seriously for everyone. Though it's technically sized for women, most items are unisex. Plus, the entire collection retails for less than $160 and comes in sizes 0-22. How many celebrity lines can say all of that?I caught up with Zendaya at the New York City pop-up launch of the collection, where she was showing off her exciting new baby, while wearing a casual-cool outfit from the line. In addition to New York, she'll be making appearances at pop-ups in Chicago and Los Angeles this weekend. If you can't make it to one of those cities to shop the line, it's all available online today.What's Inside a Celebrity Makeup Artist's Kit:Why was inclusivity so important to you? That was something that was a no-brainer, a deal-breaker, something that had to happen for me. I can’t just talk the talk. I can’t just say all this stuff about inclusivity and loving people and you know, breaking barriers, and then actually not do it when it comes down to my own stuff. That’s fake. I wanted people to have quality pieces that were realistic [when it comes to price]. If you’re a college student, you're not going to be able to buy a $500 jacket. It doesn’t make sense.Sizing was a huge thing. I want my mom to be able to wear my clothes. I want my older sister to be able to wear my clothes. There are too many shapes and sizes in my family to say, oh, you can’t wear that, though. That’s not even something that would cross my mind to do. I want everyone to feel included—like this is for them. I made sure in my e-commerce photos that there were thick girls in there. It should feel normal.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Also, with the gender-neutral pieces, it’s about people being able to wear what they want and do whatever they want. There are things that are technically made for women, but that doesn’t mean a woman has to wear it. It’s about wearing things that make you feel good.Were you inspired by any designers? I’m inspired more by people. Law [Roach, her longtime stylist] and I are always looking at people because that’s who this is for. This isn’t for me. I’m not designing clothes so I can go wear them. It’s for them; it’s what they ask for. I just went to Capri with Dolce & Gabbana, and what Domenico [Dolce] told me, which is what I’ve been preaching, is: It’s for the people. What you do is for the people. It’s not about you. That’s the driving force.You have shoes and clothes. How else do you see your brand expanding? When I think of a brand I would like to have in the future, I think of Oprah because she’s able to do everything. And she's able to keep it so positive. What Oprah says is trusted. If she says it's the best latte, it’s the best latte. It’s a trusted brand. There’s also a level of empowerment and goodness. Everyone feels like they’re related to Oprah.Why launch a collection only online and not in a department store? Most people order stuff online. My mom orders stuff online. It’s the new wave. And I just feel like it's easier. But now, seeing this, I feel like I need a store. The pop-up looks so dope.You wear a lot of loose clothing. Are those the pieces that make you feel most confident? I don’t really know what makes me feel most confident. I’ve gotten to a point where I feel good in anything. I would show up today in pajamas and I wouldn’t give a dang at all.  In most of my videos on my app, I’m not wearing makeup because I don’t need to do that. But there are times when I want to beat my face down and be all glamorous and that’s also exciting.What are some of your favorite items in the line? There's a velvet jumpsuit that I love. It’s so comfortable it’s like wearing a onesie that you can go to dinner in and look presentable and still be comfortable. [I love that there are] different layers of who I am in the clothes. You’ve got the glam, you’ve got the toned-down, you’ve got the rough, you’ve got the tough—it’s everything.Could a beauty line be next? Obviously I’m with CoverGirl, which is a great partnership. But hopefully one day I can do my own line.Switching gears a bit, is there a particular issue in this upcoming election that you’re passionate about? If there’s a time to vote, it’s now. We’re in a very pivotal time in our history. This is going to be your country for a long time and who do you want representing you? Be educated and try to inform other people. We’re dealing with a lot of issues right now. Big issues. We’re dealing with a specific, giant issue. But I think [we'll] be good as long as people go out there and vote.RELATED:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. Typically, the content of the site or app is used to make inferences about your interests, which inform future selection of advertising and/or content.Select All3 PurposesConsent PurposesLocation Based AdsConsent AllowedLegitimate Interest PurposesPersonalizeFeaturesLocation Based AdsClear FlitersWhat do you do when an entire season's worth of runway trends don't exactly speak to you?I have a problem with white jeans. Not for what they are—which is bleached cotton cut into a pair of tubes and sewn together—but for what they represent. Because white jeans tend to be unforgiving. It takes a woman with healthy self-esteem to pull them off. Historically speaking, I have not been a woman with healthy self-esteem. Therefore, I have not been a woman who wears white jeans. And until recently, I felt a pang of spite every time I passed a woman who wore white jeans and looked great in them. The aversion is like a self-inflicted allergy: irritating, unpredictable in its emergence, and entirely my own fault.It may also be universal. Every woman I know has a similar irrational intolerance for a particular item of clothing. Rompers, for example. Or kitten heels. Or sleeveless turtlenecks. Or peplums. Or empire waists. Or combat boots. Or whatever. It's the item that you tried on once as a teenager, and it looked so miserable that it still makes your skin crawl to think of it. The item that, when you see another woman looking great in it, injects you with petty, unfeminist feelings. None of this is reasonable, but neither is fashion. Which brings me to the runways this season.Prada fall 2016The runways were—what's the best way to say this? It's as though all the designers held a secret conference where they came up with a master list of the most difficult-to-wear items and then populated their fall runways exclusively with those items. There were oversize, rough-edged trench coats belted perilously high on the waist and tweedy menswear-inspired trousers that would seem to require at least 40 inches of leg to pull off (or on, as it were). There were fuzzy midcalf skirts. There was double-breasted everything. Miuccia Prada, who is the undisputed queen of challenging fashion, outdid herself with argyle tights and drop-shoulder jackets bearing fur sleeves, just in case any of us want our legs and arms to look four times as big as they are. Sheer madness, all of it.It's as though all the designers came up with a master list of the most difficult-to-wear items.And yet if we know anything about designers, it's that their madness always has a method. While grappling with the fall forecast and its high-concept gear, I found myself turning to the French-born notion of jolie laide. That phrase—which Google helpfully translates as “pretty ugly”—refers to the unconventional glory of the not quite perfect. It's used to describe people, typically women, who sport an idiosyncratic, non-textbook beauty. The gorgeous lady with a gap tooth or a crooked nose or a slight asymmetry in her eyes (or all of the above)? She might qualify as jolie laide. Anjelica Huston is a commonly cited example. Jolie laide is the opposite of Barbie dolls and Kate Upton and Joan Smalls; it's Charlotte Gainsbourg and Daphne Groeneveld and Lady Gaga. Beauty icons are not jolie laide, but style icons often are. And in clothing terms, jolie laide might be exactly what has marched off the runway and into our lives for the brisker seasons ahead.Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsAnjelica HustonSound intimidating? I thought so, too, until I realized that a bit of jolie laide fashion might be a relief after all the flesh-baring pageantry of summer. Gone are the sandals and off-the-shoulder sundresses of June. Gone are the crop tops and featherweight slip dresses of July. Come fall, nobody is mistaking your outerwear for underwear, unless you habitually fall asleep in a floor-length mustard velvet turtleneck dress. Best of all, you won't hear the phrase “body-con” for at least six months, guaranteed. See? You're breathing more deeply already.4 denim styles that go beyond the basic blues:Balenciaga fall 2016Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsPlus, the new fall clothes raise imaginative possibilities that crop tops can't touch. Can you see yourself draped in a tent-loose, pin-striped pantsuit? Or buttoned into a brocade tuxedo jacket with overstated shoulder pads and a matching necktie? Probably not, and that's the fun of it. Experimenting with new identities is one of the great privileges of getting dressed every day. Each time you open your closet, you're given a chance to shock your coworkers to pieces, startle your family to bits, and make your boyfriend or girlfriend question your sanity. Surely it's worth exercising that right every once in a while, if only to see the looks on their faces. Fortune favors the bold, as they say.Proenza Schouler fall 2016This doesn't mean you have to exchange your perennial fall staples (trench coat, cashmere V-neck in a tasteful neutral) for a rack of runway costumes. Baby steps in a quirky direction can be just as satisfying as giant leaps. If you're not ready to sport a statement pantsuit, you can try houndstooth trousers. If thigh-length leather jackets are a step too far, stick with a bomber. If full fur sleeves make you nervous (about your silhouette, about PETA, or about attracting stray wildlife), a coat with a faux-fur collar will accomplish the job. The only taboo is playing it safe. And once you discover the pleasures of being unpredictable, you might just find yourself strapping into that pantsuit after all.A fashion alchemy was occurring before my eyes: I'd worn an outfit so wrong that it started looking right.In my case, it was the white jeans that got me. After decades of avoidance, I woke up in a perverse mood one morning last year, opened my laptop, and, from bed, ordered a pair of Levi's 501s in a snowy selvedge. It seemed like the mature thing to do. If I could force myself to wear a pair of white jeans for even one day, I figured, it might have the effect of a vaccine, curing me of my spiteful thoughts and hypersensitivity for good. When the pants arrived, I let them sit in their plastic wrapping for a full weekend. On Monday, I forced myself to wear them to work. At 9:15 a.m., I got a compliment. By noon, I was passing reflective surfaces on purpose in order to clock myself in the pants. I didn't recognize the woman in the mirror, but I was starting to respect her style. In fact, a fashion alchemy was occurring before my eyes: I'd worn an outfit so wrong that it started looking right. By lunchtime, I'd ordered a second pair.Now I wear them all the time. My favorite outfit—regardless of the season—consists of white jeans, white brogues, and a white silk shirt. I think it makes me look like a big, sexy glass of milk. If there's a lesson here, it's that our sartorial antipathies might be worth exploring for precisely the reasons they make us squirrelly and anxious. And the timing couldn't be better: This season offers more opportunities than ever to face your fashion allergies head-on. Or feet first. Or, you know, however you get dressed in the morning.RELATEDMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. Robbie is consistently well dressed on and off the red carpet, so in honor of her much awaited The Legend of Tarzan release, we rounded up our top five favorite looks from the actress.At the 88th annual Academy Awards in 2016, she coordinated with Oscar itself with a slinky gold Tom Ford gown. This time, however, she accessorized her décolletage with a vintage Van Cleef & Arpels tassel necklace.At Givenchy's spring 2016 show in New York, she reminded us just how great it looks to wear white after Labor Day. Fashion rules are archaic, to be honest.Another cool fashion moment went down at the recent Los Angeles premiere of The Legend of Tarzan, when she showed up in a cheongsam-inspired Gucci dress from the fall 2016 runway. Between the embroidery and the fur-trimmed sleeves there's a lot going on, so kudos to the actress for her simple and chic styling.In 2014, when The Wolf of Wall Street gave her a boost to the Hollywood A-list, she showed up to the Oscars with dark hair (for her role in Z for Zachariah) in a Saint Laurent gown. There's a sense of old-Hollywood beauty about the look, with the bow in the back and retro curls, but the dark lip gave her an edge.Robbie is one of the newer players on the best-dressed lists, but we think she'll be around for a while. But there’s one part I dread every year: dressing up. I don’t mean in elf costumes or ugly sweaters. I mean dressing up for cocktail parties, sit-down dinners, and family gatherings (if I show up in jeans, my mother will not-so-subtly ask: “When are you getting ready?”). The thing is, putting on “fancy” clothes is not fun. I find that most sophisticated looks are uncomfortable, time consuming, and usually constructed from sheer fabrics that leave me shivering and miserable. That’s no way to party! It’s not like I lounge in sweats all day, though. My daily uniform consists of cropped or slim jeans, a crisp button-down, and some sort of flats, like oxfords or pointy ballerinas. It’s fine for 9 to 5, but pretty basic after sundown.Luckily, the fashion community is on my side. With sporty-cool riffs on formalwear from brands like Gucci and Off-White, now seems like the ideal time to up my game and invest in some pieces that are both sleek and easy-going. Could this be the year I find the dressy version of myself, buried under my parka? I decided to consult a few experts to coach me to holiday glory.“Most people equate dressing up with discomfort, and it becomes an emotional thing,” says Claire Distenfeld, the perennial chic founder of Fivestory boutique in New York City. “But you need to erase that thinking because you can look elevated and comfortable.” She might be onto something. As a kid, I hated dressing up—those tights and scratchy dresses were awful! Perhaps I have negative associations I just need to get over."Most people equate dressing up with discomfort, and it becomes an emotional thing. But you need to erase that thinking because you can look elevated and comfortable."Distenfeld advises me to think about the go-to pieces I already love, then find their dressier next-of-kin. Since I’m all about jeans with a subtle stretch, she suggests that I try a relaxed-fit suit. “When I worked in the art world, I wore suits all the time,” Distenfeld points out, adding that those from Alexander Wang fit well and look great in grey and navy tones (not black; “a black suit means you didn’t try,” she warns). Allure fashion director Rachael Wang also favors menswear-inspired suits for their posh yet practical attitude. “They’re neat and tidy, and I get them tailored so the hem hits right at the ankle,” she says. “They can be worn with flats, heels, or even sneakers with a tee, a crisp shirt, a silky blouse—or just a lacy bra” (the latter might be a stretch for me, but #goals!). Another option: the tracksuit-meets-tuxedo pants from Valentino and DKNY—pair the suit with a white T-shirt and pumps for a cocktail-ready ensemble.More holiday style inspirations:Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsBut back to my jeans—do I need to give them up entirely? “It depends on the context,” says Los Angeles-based fashion designer Rosetta Getty (i.e. not at my mother’s Christmas party or any champagne affair). Getty prefers wearing a pair of cropped skinny denim with a low heel for a polished touch. In more casual-festive situations, Distenfeld likes pairing jeans with an interesting top. “Blouses are really huge right now, and going forward this is what I’m buying more of,” she says. “Anything in silk will elevate an outfit to be a little more fancy, and I love a bold color, like mustard or orange.” Wang is all about “Victorian high-neck blouses” at the moment, which I can appreciate not only for their feminine charm, but the fact that they don’t reveal too much skin on negative-zero days. Or to go all-out, Wang suggests I “step it up with some gold or sparkly ankle boots,” like those from Brother Vellies or Anine Bing.Now for those ultra-dressing occasions: Rather than grit my teeth and force myself to wear a barely-there silky frock, Distenfeld says I consider long-sleeve knit dresses that cling to the body but don’t fall into the alarming (for me, anyways) “body-con” category. This dark emerald one from Lemaire checks all the boxes. And since I obviously have childhood issues with tights, Distenfeld says I should pull on tall suede boots to stay cozy. “I have a pair from Stuart Weitzman that hit mid-thigh that I wear with skirts and dresses. On cold days, it’s like having on pants.”A look from Rosetta Getty resort 2017 collectionOr I could really wear pants, says Getty. “I like pairing a caftan or dress with trousers as an alternative to a traditional cocktail dress.” Her recent resort collection featured a hammered satin caftan dress paired with straight flare pants in stretch cady. Another statement-making idea: add oversized earrings—it requires almost no effort, but brings a lot of glamour to any outfit. Distenfeld recommends the Rebecca de Ravenel “Bonbon” earrings, which have developed a cult-following and often sell out. “They are by far the easiest way to elevate a look in a milli-second. And they have a little shimmer to them, just like fairy dust.”No matter the outfit, though, dressing up should be fun. “You want to develop a formula for dressing up that makes you feel like the best version of yourself,” says Getty. “I keep a tight-edit of go-to pieces, so I always have an idea of what will work. Being prepared in that way makes it a lot easier to pull together a look.” And if what you reach for is dressy in your eyes but defies a few dress codes? “It’s good to be unconventional if you’re remaining true to your personal style,” says Getty. (Hear that, mom? I still love you, of course).Best holiday looks from the past 100 years:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. In a long Facebook post written on Thursday afternoon, Høyer alleges that she was fired from the French fashion house's recent Cruise show in Kyoto for being "too big" — and she's a size 2.As the model says in her post, she was initially flown to Paris to try on the outfits and audition for the show, and she was allegedly confirmed to model the Cruise collection before she even left the fitting. "I was excited to go to Japan and happy to know that even though I wasn’t in my skinniest ‘show-shape’ Louis Vuitton would still have me in their show," she wrote. The day after she arrived in Kyoto, she had an additional fitting. "That day I ate a very small breakfast and had just water and tea before the fitting, because that’s how we do it … I tried my dress and the coat which I was confirmed fitted in Paris. I changed shoes and trousers a couple of times. Afterwards I tried on a puffy dress with a semi bare back and then I was done."However, problems soon arose. "Later that night my French agent called me and told me that [the show's casting agent] had said that there had been some problems during the fitting," Høyer wrote. "According to her, I had 'a very bloated stomach,' 'bloated face,' and urged me to starve myself with this statement: 'Ulrikke needs to drink only water for the next 24 hours.' I was shocked when I heard it." The following morning, Høyer even said that the casting agent checked to see what she was eating for breakfast, something she didn't do with the other models: "She said good morning to me and the other girls and then looked at me, then down on my nonexistent plate and up at me again. She was checking if I had been eating food."Sadly, later that day, Høyer said she found out that she was dropped from the show and would be sent home. Louis Vuitton had allegedly contacted her primary agent in Denmark, outlining that the decision was made because her "belly," "face," and "back" areas were problematic and bloated.Høyer wrote that wanted to share her story not because she's seeking revenge over being cut from the show, but rather due to the cruel treatment she experienced. "Such lack of respect and decency have let me to decide that I will never work under such conditions again," she said. "I cannot accept the ‘normality’ in the behavior of people like this. They find pleasure in power over young girls and will go to the extreme to force an eating disorder on you ... these sizes of the show pieces are made for women to have eating disorders. Go watch the show and see for yourself, even the smallest tightest pants are loose on the models they book."We've reached out to Louis Vuitton for comment and will update when we hear back.More on body image:This Woman Used to Shave Her Entire Body — Here’s Why She Finally Stopped:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. This year alone has seen increased representation of Muslims at New York fashion week, Nike’s pro hijab announcement, and the introduction of Halima Aden – and it’s still only March. What used to be a one-off occurrence has become almost commonplace with Muslim designers, entrepreneurs, and influencers making worldwide headlines every month. Megastars of the Halima-variety aside, Muslim women are leaving their mark on the industry every day in various capacities, at all levels, and not solely in modest or Muslim-focused markets. From holding it down in executive positions at established brands to forging their own paths as intrepid entrepreneurs, these women exhibit unique perspectives, diverse backgrounds, and of course, fierce style. In the spirit of empowering one another, we asked dynamic Muslim women working in beauty and fashion to reveal the inspirational women they call style icons.“Princess Deena Aljuhani Abdulaziz, Saudi royal and the first editor-in-chief of Vogue Arabia. You can tell that high-fashion is like second nature to her. She always looks glamorous, elegant, and dynamic. Also, Emmanuelle Alt, editor-in-chief of Vogue Paris. Her style is leather, lots of black, and oh-I-just-threw-this-on Parisian edge – very much goals.”— Anum Tariq, fashion illustrator“I've been following U.K. influencer Dina Tokio for years and love how she uses bold colors and patterns. Sometimes it's just easier to reach for a black hijab, but she makes me want to pair things in my own wardrobe more boldly. I also love how blogger Brittany Xavier can make something traditional like flowered embroidery look really contemporary by using a bold lipstick or a high, clean ponytail. Of course, my favorite style icon is my mom. I love going home and stealing some of her old ‘80s blazers and blouses that are still in great shape. I hope my kids feel that way about my wardrobe one day!”— Arshiya Kherani, founder & CEO of Sukoon Active, a modest activewear company“I love Aaliyah’s style from the ‘90s. I love how she was very feminine and had the best makeup, but was kind of tomboyish at the same time. It’s so me. I’m always in something oversized but I’ll be pretty glammed up [in the face].”— Farah Dhukai, beauty vlogger“Women in the Qajar era (a 19th century dynasty of Iran known for their distinctive style) knew their patterns!”— Hoda Katebi, activist fashion blogger, author & photographer of Tehran Streetstyle“I love Olivia Palermo's style. It's super wearable and classic yet eclectic. I love adding a little twist to timeless pieces. I also love the ‘40s throwback vibe of Victoria Beckham. The wide-leg trousers and longer length skirts and dresses are so glamorous and feminine.”— Melanie Elturk, CEO of Haute Hijab“Alicia Silverstone in Clueless and Kareena Kapoor in the Bollywood film, Kabhi Khushi Kabhi Gham. When it comes to runway-worthy shoes for a fraction of the price, the retailer's Who What Wear collection offers some of the most perfect velvet booties we’ve ever laid eyes on. Target's designer collaborations are also pretty unparalleled when it comes to price point and style. Take, for example, the upcoming Victoria Beckham line that’s set to be released early this year.On January 31, the retailer is launching a line of affordable jewelry that just happens to be the sartorial solution you need if you’re missing some sparkle from your wardrobe. Designed in collaboration with BaubleBar, the new line, dubbed SUGARFIX, will be exclusively available at Target with new releases dropping every month, similar to the Who What Wear collections. Although BaubleBar’s collections are already superaffordable, SUGARFIX's price point will be even more wallet-friendly—the average BaubleBar piece retails for $50, SUGARFIX pieces average around $14.99.The collection includes statement pieces, such as oversized, dangly earrings and sparkly chokers, as well as more subtle styles similar to some of BaubleBar’s best sellers. This isn’t the first time BaubleBar and Target have teamed up either—the two retailers collaborated in late 2015 on an exclusive collection of tech accessories.The best part, however, is the amount of options SUGARFIX will offer. The line is expected to release 50-150 brand new pieces each month, so you can really have options to add some glitz to your #OOTD. With more statement-making earrings on the runway than ever before (Delpozo, J.W. Anderson, Topshop Unique are just a few of the labels that sent out over the top earrings), this is likely one of the chicest and cheapest ways to get in on the trend.Sugarfix choker necklace and bracelets, available at target.comSugarfix beaded necklaces and earrings, available at target.comSugarfix necklaces and earrings, available at target.comMore of our favorite collaborations:Learn how to make your own charm bracelet:Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. But before you consider a total closet overhaul, keep in mind that with some strategic styling, your favorite summer whites (and even those off-the-shoulder numbers you’ve collected) can be repurposed for cooler months. We asked fashion insiders to share their expert tips on how to seamlessly transition our wardrobe from summer to fall—and the fresh pieces they can’t wait to buy.1. Elevate summer colors with monochrome dressing.While your warm-weather uniform may have involved LWDs jazzed up with brightly colored sandals and accessories, you should opt for a neutral palette for fall. Los Angeles–based stylist Anita Patrickson relies on monochrome combinations to elevate pale shades that are typically reserved for the hot season. “White or cream wide-leg trousers are always so chic,” she says. “You can pair them with a tank and flats in the summer, and later with a white cashmere sweater and white coat for an elegant, wintery-white look.” Bonus: A head-to-toe one-note ensemble lengthens the silhouette.RELATED: The Ultimate Fall Fashion Shopping Guide2. Layer up for maximum wear.When a crisp chill enters the air, layering adds warmth and a sophisticated element to skin-baring pieces. Give those slip dresses, cold-shoulder tops, and jumpsuits some extra mileage by layering them over tees, thin turtlenecks, and button-downs. “You can play with colors and patterns to keep it fresh and make it feel like a new outfit every time,” says Hannah Dilworth, the owner of the Brooklyn-based boutique Concrete + Water. The same goes for shoes: Keep those mules, slides, and platforms in rotation long past Labor Day with tights or ankle or knee socks.3. Mix in structured menswear-inspired details.Sharpen the casual, softer silhouettes of summer with tailored pieces. Tabula Rasa designer Emily Diamandis incorporates structured garments to update her warm-weather staples. “I have a stack of lightweight gauzy knits that I transition for fall by pairing them with Altuzarra pencil skirts, which make for a less summery, sharper look,” she says. “I also button up light shirts—that I have worn open over tanks all summer—to the collar and tuck them into my favorite vintage Levi’s high-waisted jeans.”Similarly, Laura Vinroot Poole, the founder of Capitol boutique in Charlotte, North Carolina, steals styling inspiration from her husband. “I love the idea of dressing like a boy—it’s smart and chic and tightens me up after a summer of chilled-out caftans and easy-breezy dresses,” she says. “Saint Laurent’s Le Smoking jacket over the shoulders on top of virtually anything sharpens everything to look just right.”Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsRELATED: Why the Kimono Is the Perfect Summer-to-Fall Transitional Piece4. Invest in outerwear, boots, and luxe textures.If you’re feeling overwhelmed even after brushing up on the season’s top trends, focus on practical wardrobe workhorses that are always worth the investment. “I like to start with my coats and shoes, and then work around those key pieces,” says Diamandis. “I have had a classic Burberry trench for years, and it always feels relevant. It's the perfect final layer when the temperature is variable. I also live in ankle boots; they are perennially in fashion and a worthy investment.” As temperatures increasingly dip, these are the styles you’re bound to wear on a daily basis.Along with surprisingly summer-friendly velvet, plush fabrics like corduroy, shearling, and lace add a chic update to any outfit. “I'm really into the baroque and medieval vibes we've been seeing,” says Patrickson. “I’m in the market for a velvet suit. I love suits for their versatility. You can wear it together for a sexy cocktail look, or pull it apart and use as a blazer or pants.” Keep it from veering into holiday territory by pairing with neutral colors and minimalist jewelry. Corduroy can similarly be set free from its nostalgia-ridden roots when worn in modern silhouettes. “Now it's shown in updated styles like wide-leg trousers and culottes and workwear-inspired outerwear,” says Dilworth. “YMC did an incredible corduroy jacket I can't wait to wear this season.”5. Think outside the (storage) box.Once you’ve sorted the wardrobe mainstays from the season-specific pieces you’ll be putting away, get creative with storage opportunities. Homepolish interior designer Megan Hopp uses items that cleverly double as decor, like an elegant vintage suitcase that’s secretly stuffed with sundresses in the winter. “I keep sandals in a supply closet next to backup lightbulbs, and winter scarves in a drawer with surplus stationery,” she says. “As long as your closets and drawers have a system, there are no rules as to what they need to look like. The best organization is tailor-made—not from a playbook.”Allure Fashion Director Rachael Wang Shares Her Style Tips:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. The company has released a new style of jeans called the Wedgie Fit that claims to lift and shape your butt.According to the Levi's website, the new jeans "hug your waist and hips, showcasing your best assets." In other words, they give you a good wedgie. Three weeks ago, Kylie Jenner posted a picture of herself on Instagram wearing the unfortunately named jeans:In an interview with Mashable, Jonathan Cheung, the senior vice president of Levi's Global Design, said the jeans were modeled after the way the company saw women wearing vintage Levi's. "Just as the 501 CT was inspired by girls wearing the 501 a little bit slouchy, the Wedgie is inspired by girls [who] were downsizing a vintage 505 and wearing it very close and almost vacuum-packed to the rear ends," he said. You may be thinking, big butt be damned, who the hell would ever want to wear jeans that gives them a wedgie all day? The brand told Mashable that the Wedgie jeans were created with stretchable fabric so that the wedgie it creates is tolerable. We're glad they thought that one through.If you're interested in trying the style, you can buy them now for $158 a pair. The 26-year-old can pull off just about anything when it comes to red-carpet fashion, from ladylike gowns to edgy dress-over-pants ensembles. On the promotional tour for her highly anticipated film Beauty and the Beast, the actress has been demonstrating her love for fashion—more specifically, eco-conscious duds—with a new Instagram account, aptly called The Press Tour.Created in partnership with the star's stylist, Rebecca Corbin-Murray, the account—which currently boasts 284,000 followers—chronicles Watson's looks as she attends promotional events and parties around the world. Each posts give a behind-the-scenes look into how the eco-conscious outfits were put together, along with a note of validity from Eco-Age, a brand agency that helps designers achieve growth through sustainability. Though there are only a handful of posts so far, Watson's press-junket wardrobe includes stellar outfits by Oscar de la Renta, Stella McCartney, and Louis Vuitton.The latter, headed by creative director Nicolas Ghesquière, created a custom look for the star: a cobalt-blue number reminiscent of Belle's countryside getup. According to Watson's Instagram post, the asymmetrical dress was created with fabrics made from recycled plastic bottles. "These are sourced, mechanically processed and spun into yarns in Italy, with a fully traceable supply chain," the actress writes in the caption. "This saves energy and reduces CO2 emissions compared to creating brand new polyester fibre. The arm band was created in a carbon-neutral mill." The gathered, tea-length skirt evokes the charm of the mid-eighteenth-century pinafore the actress wears in the film, while the leather ankle boots subtly suggests a modern take on men's footwear from the same era.The actress has long been an advocate for sustainable fashion. In 2015, she joined the Green Carpet Challenge, an organization that champions ethical efforts of fashion designers, by taking the initiative to wear brands that were “considering local craft and production, artisan skills, the environment, sustainability, and the longevity of fashion.” Last year at the Met Gala, the actress made headlines when she wore a Calvin Klein outfit made out of recycled plastic bottles.Considering the fact that we have three more weeks to go until the film's release, the actress has plenty of time to showcase her eco-conscious sartorial choices. His first collection for the brand will be for fall 2017.Simons has a history of taking brands and raising their cool factor. Take, for example, the way he transformed Dior when he was appointed in 2012. The designer left Dior in October of last year and had expressed his disdain for the lightning-fast pace of the fashion industry.RELATED: [#article: /articles/57a0be0aa52e53a71e7b51d8]||||||Prior to that, Simons designed furniture as well as menswear for his namesake line since 1995. From 2005 to 2012, Simons also served as the creative director of Jil Sander.In anticipation of the new Calvin Klein collections, let's take a look at Simons’s greatest runway hits.Raf Simons spring 2005When Simons established his eponymous brand in the ‘90s, he continually took inspiration from the youth culture and the underground music scene. Simons turned these obsessive codes into covetable menswear pieces with hints of punk culture and indie slogans. The brand took a bit of a different direction for the spring 2005 collection: Simons refocused on his tailoring skills and delivered a collection full of clean- cut suits transformed by unexpected baggy trousers and sleeveless jackets.Jil Sander spring 2011 fashion showJil Sander spring 2011Simons debuted his first womenswear collection as creative director of Jil Sander in 2005. However, Simons was one of the earliest proponents of putting women in menswear in the early ‘90s at his own label. Season after season, he kept the minimalist menswear-inspired codes he lived by at his own label. But for his Jil Sander spring 2011 collection, he feminized it with voluminous dresses, bright colors, and sleek tailoring. The collection was a part of Simon’s experimental couture phase at Jil Sander, which consisted of three collections called the “Couture Trilogy.”Dior fall 2012 haute couture fashion showGabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsChristian Dior haute couture fall 2012Simons made his highly publicized debut at Dior for the fall 2012 haute couture collection, defining a new era for the brand. Simons took Dior’s signature pieces and reinvented them, such as the classic Bar Jacket turned into a modern tuxedo, and the billowing skirts embellished with floral details. Silk dresses were covered in prints by artist Sterling Ruby, who collaborated with Simons on his namesake collections in the past.Dior 2016 resort collection showChristian Dior resort 2016Staged at Pierre Cardin’s terracotta-colored Le Palais Bulles, located between Cannes and Monaco, Simons presented his 2016 cruise collection for Dior. The designer went back to Dior’s roots, presenting silhouettes nipped at the waist. Floral prints were everywhere, and Simons infused his own hint of irony and style by sending formal black pantsuits down the runway paired with flip-flops.Raf Simons spring 2017 showRaf Simons spring 2017Simons’s namesake collection for spring 2017 was not only one of his best—it may just be a hint of what’s to come at Calvin Klein. An exhibition staged in tandem with the show at Pitti Uomo in Florence showcased some of his archival menswear looks on female mannequins, proving that he still loves a menswear-inspired women’s silhouette. Simons worked with the Robert Mapplethorpe Foundation to print the photographer's beautifully harrowing images of flowers and portraits on T-shirts, knitwear, button-down shirts, and apron-like cloths.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. To signal the major change at hand, Ralph Lauren moved his show date and venue from Thursday morning in a downtown event space to Wednesday night on Madison Avenue next to his Upper East Side boutique. A glass case was built around the perimeter of the store, where guests including Jessica Alba, Julianne Moore, and Rosie Huntington-Whiteley sat in the front row.RELATED: "See Now, Buy Now" Collections You Can Shop TodayTo celebrate the new business model, the designer enlisted “It” girls Kendall Jenner, Bella Hadid, and Imaan Hammam to present his new clothes—together, they boast about 72 million Instagram followers. But true to the brand’s timeless appeal, the show also featured runway icons from the pre–social media generation: Carolyn Murphy, Liya Kebede, Liisa Winkler, Sasha Pivovarova, and Stella Tennant (a.k.a. the OG supermodels). The presence of these runway veterans showed the real women, the consumers of the brand, a relatable yet aspirational image. Plus, the five women showed that in the age of instant gratification and the season of instant shopping, good talent, and certainly good fashion, are ageless.Liya Kebede walks the runway at the Ralph Lauren fall 2016 show.The same could be said about the new collection, as well. The clothes remain true to the brand’s sophisticated-Americana aesthetic but include elements of the Wild West in pieces such as fringe suede jackets, cowboy hats, and slinky metallic dresses. And though the designer previously presented his fall 2016 collection back in February, this runway show was dubbed the September Collection and is an extension of last season’s English-countryside-inspired designs.Following Tommy Hilfiger, Burberry, Tom Ford, and even Topshop, Ralph Lauren’s decision to show an immediately shoppable runway show is a powerful statement about the changes that may soon become the new normal in the fashion industry. The Democratic presidential nominee and self-acclaimed pantsuits aficionado—she’s made several jokes about her beloved style staple—hasn't shown much interest in fashion, but she certainly knows how clothes can be used to her political advantage.Case in point: the birth of National Pantsuit Day. On Election Day, November 8, Clinton supporters will not only vote for the candidate, they’ll also sport their own version of Clinton’s blazer-trouser attire.To organize the effort, they’ve created a private Facebook group that has gathered more than 1.3 million members in three weeks. The invitation-only page features words of support for the Democratic nominee and uplifting stories for its members who’ve been significantly stressed by the election, according to The Wall Street Journal."After the third presidential debate, I was thinking about how beautifully and stoically Hillary embodies women's fight for equality, and how the pantsuit is a kind of emblem of that struggle itself," Libby Chamberlain, the creator of the Facebook group, tells Allure. "It's a symbol that might be lost on younger women, and so I wanted to do something to re-appropriate that symbol and everything that it means to me as a feminist and Clinton supporter."Due to the overwhelming response, Chamberlain says she hasn't found the time to browse the aisles for her pantsuit. Instead, she ordered three outfits online, two from Macy’s and one from Amazon, and plans to wear white—the unofficial color of Clinton supporters—on Election Day.Hillary Clinton's iconic beauty moments:On the opposite side, Donald Trump backers are seeking to show their support for the Republican candidate by encouraging each other to wear red—the color closely associated with the party.This is not the first time Clinton’s signature two-piece has garnered the public’s attention. Last month, more than 200 dancers clad in pantsuits staged a flash-mob dance party in Manhattan’s Union Square Park. Dubbed “#PantsuitPower,” the pop-up performance featured principals from the Martha Graham Dance Company, members of Broadway’s Fiddler on the Roof, break-dancers, and ballerinas dancing to Justin Timberlake’s Can’t Stop the Feeling. The video has more than 1.1 million views on Vimeo so far.From left: Tibi, Ralph Lauren, Tory Burch, GucciFor those in need of a pantsuit, consider some of the options from the fall 2016 runways. Office-appropriate pairings ran the gamut, from relaxed, fluid shapes at the Row and Tibi, to slimmer, sleek versions at Gucci and Tory Burch. Ralph Lauren, who’s dressed Clinton for her most recent televised appearances, sent down an array of suits in wool and even suede for both of his fall 2016 collections. And just in time for the final presidential debate last month, Reebok released sketches of athleisure-inspired versions of the two-piece—complete with a cross-strap sports bra.If you're not convinced the style is for you, consider the suit as a wardrobe investment. You can maximize your outfit by separating the pieces—try a pair of skinny jeans with the blazer or rock a crop top with the trousers like Gigi Hadid. For a more casual look, forgo the pumps and put on your favorite pair of sneakers instead. Comfortable workwear? Your best bet at finding pieces from the current season before the aforementioned launches would have been department-store websites, such as Saks Fifth Avenue and Neiman Marcus (the company that owns MyTheresa.com), but the selection there focuses on bags and shoes rather than runway pieces.According to WWD, runway styles attracted Net-a-Porter to the idea of selling the Prada collection. "The [fall 2016] show ticked every box across every different category," Sarah Rutson, the vice president of global buying, told WWD. "It had that pioneering spirit, but it's also going to sell."Net-a-Porter has partnered with multiple fashion brands that have long eschewed e-commerce in the past. Last year, the company secured an online exclusive with Chanel's capsule jewelry collection, dubbed Coco Chanel—the first time the French brand has sold anything other than beauty products online.Prada's fall collection features lush fabrics, tailored jackets with dropped shoulders, fur-trimmed coats, argyle tights, and kitschy waist corsets. Accessory-wise, the Italian label presented eccentric sailor hats, belts, and necklaces with small booklets attached on them. Now, she's taking her empowering message beyond her home state and into the world of fashion.The Somali-American has signed with modeling agency IMG Models—home of Gigi and Bella Hadid, Gisele Bündchen, and Hari Nef—and today, she'll make her New York fashion week debut at the highly-anticipated Yeezy Season 5 runway show, according to the Business of Fashion. That's not all: It turns out Carine Roitfeld, editor-in-chief of CR Fashion Book, is also a fan. Aden will be featured in an high-fashion editorial in the magazine's tenth issue, set to release in March.The fashion industry has often been criticized for its lack of diversity. But over a couple of seasons, we've been seeing some excellent improvements from brands and designers who are pushing for more inclusivity on the runway and in editorials. Just this week, Tome’s Ryan Lobo and Ramon Martin sent models of all ages and sizes down the runway to presents their fall 2017 collection, while Brandon Maxwell made a strong stance for inclusivity with a diverse range of cast. Often hailed as the champion of diversity, Christian Sirano presented his most empowering show yet, which featured almost half non-white models, as well as ten plus-sized models.IMG's signing of Aden not only affirms the fashion industry's commitment to diversity, but also represents a small victory for the Muslim community. When Aden competed in the Miss USA competition not only did she make her inspiring message clear by wearing the religious garbs, she also made history by being the first woman to ever do so in a major beauty pageant.Aden, who moved to the States at age 7 when her family relocated from a refugee camp in Kenya, said modeling was not in her mind, but regardless, she "wanted to spread a positive message about beauty and diversity, and to show other young Muslim women that there is room for them."We can't wait to see where Aden's promising modeling career will take her.More on fashion's industry commitment to diversity:Now, watch how one plus-sized model learned to love her body:Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Somehow over the course of the brand’s 160-year history, it’s maintained its heritage and classic design aesthetic while simultaneously managing not only to stay relevant, but actually be considered an industry leader in innovation and digital savviness.Though the British brand has an artistic—and always surprising—take on their classic, functional aesthetic roots, no one item has remained so representative of the brand than the trench. It's icon-meets-innovation.Like most classic staples, the Burberry trench was created with function in mind, which, if left in the wrong hands, can be a one-way ticket to dowdy. Instead, the brand has managed to build an entire ecosystem around the classic coat, including bespoke design options, fresh new takes on the trench (we’re fawning over the python prints for fall), and a crowdsourcing project called “The Art of the Trench.”RELATED: Burberry Reveals Details About Its First See Now, Buy Now CollectionKarlie Kloss wearing a Burberry trench coat.In 2016, designers have to appeal to a whole new set of consumers—namely legions of social media fans and street style bloggers. And “The Art of the Trench” project, which launched with The Sartorialist’s Scott Schuman in 2009, does that flawlessly, showing off the iconic look IRL through street style photos just begging to be pinned or shared with hoards of hungry followers. You might think staring at images of trench coats would get dull after the first dozen or so pics, but as a true digital democracy—the project is curated by the hundreds of thousands of Burberry wearers who frequent the site—each look is totally novel. It’s a living wall of outfit #goals capable of making the likes of even Kate Middleton and Kate Moss equally excited.RELATED: Gucci Just Won Social MediaIf you had to pin the success of the dynamically chic trench—and really the entire brand revolution that’s backing it—on just one person, it could easily be Christopher Bailey. The head-designer-turned-chief-creative-officer-turned-CEO-turned-president (he recently stepped down from his CEO duties after a two-year tenure) has been helping to shape the company’s strategy from sketch to stitch to social media since he took the helm of the design team in 2001. Under Bailey’s influence, the brand, which was originally the go-to gabardine outfitter for explorers, aviators, and military men, became the outfitter for the modern day versions of all three: Less aviator, more jetsetter; less explorer, more vintage thrift whisperer; less military personnel, more street style conqueror.Today, it’s easy to take for granted that the fashion world and the digital world haven’t always been so well-paired. Burberry was on the front end of the digital revolution, bringing digital experiences into their stores, their advertising, and straight to their consumers’ social media feeds—a trend they’ll be keeping up with as they debut their see now, buy now collection at London fashion week. The brand’s evolution from royally sanctioned outdoorsy outfitter to the digitally savvy paradigm it is today has set the standard for the rest of the industry—and for that, we can thank one classic cornerstone coat.Christopher Bailey on see now, buy now runway strategy:Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The moment transcended what she was wearing, although Clinton’s sharp white suit also garnered plenty of support and compliments.Clinton was known as the anti-fashion queen of pantsuits in her 30-plus years in politics, but she gradually started using her wardrobe—and the fashion industry—as important branding tools to communicate her key messages. Earlier this year, the self-proclaimed “pantsuit aficionado” was featured in the March 2016 issue of Vogue (with portraits by Mario Testino). Anna Wintour has been hosting fund-raisers for the candidate, even donning a Hillary Clinton T-shirt at Marc Jacobs's fall 2016 show. Indeed, it’s been reported that the editor has been advising Clinton on her wardrobe choices for this year’s campaign trail, according to The Business of Fashion. Clinton has also hired Kristina Schake, Michelle Obama’s former aide, to help shape her style.In honor of last night, let’s take a look back at some of Clinton’s most significant outfits.The White Suit, 2016Clinton chose a crisp white suit (update: The suit was designed by Ralph Lauren, a representative from the brand confirmed with Allure) rather than one of the colorful ones she'd worn along the campaign trail. The look was flattering and did not distract from her powerful speech. Also worth noting: Whether it was intentional or not, white was one of the official colors (along with purple and gold) of the women's suffrage movement. Fictional character Olivia Pope from the political drama Scandal wore a similar white suit in season four.The Tweed Suit, 2012At the Women in the World summit in 2012, Clinton wore a turquoise-and-black bouclé jacket with black pants. It wasn’t the only time she wore a Chanel-esque jacket that year. Clinton is also a fan of the French brand’s white J12 diamond watch.The Black Pantsuit, 2008Clinton wore a simple black pantsuit with a subtle silver necklace when President Obama nominated her for Secretary of State in 2008. Again, no distraction from a major, career-defining moment.The Blue Pantsuit, 2001Clinton celebrated her victory of becoming a member of the U.S. Senate in a blue pantsuit, proving that her personal style and fondness for pantsuits had been a long time in the making. When she was elected, she was the first American first lady to ever win a public-office seat.The Pink Skirt Suit, 1995As first lady, Hillary Clinton frequently experimented with her look. Case in point: a pink skirt suit with matching gold details and red sunglasses. In addition to that, everything will be live-streamed using 360-degree virtual reality technology, there will be wearables on the runway, and a meet-and-greet will be hosted immediately after the show at the Rebecca Minkoff flagship so that consumers can get the runway look right then and there. The brand is also partnering with Maybelline New York to debut two new makeup products on the runway, which will be available for sale following the show.We caught up with the designer to talk beauty routines, technology, and her favorite piece from her new collection.Why is the see now, buy now retail model so important to your brand right now?We saw the success of our show in February. We did comparisons and our sales were up more than 200 percent. Our consumer wants to see something and buy it right away and not have to wait six months. So, we’re giving her what she wants when she wants it. I think that’s the driving force, to give our girl what she wants.RELATED: See Now, Buy Now Collections You Can Shop TodayTechnology has long been an integral part of your brand—from virtual-reality live streams to wearables. Why are you so interested in it?Even though we are inviting consumers to be at our show, not everyone can make it or come to it. This is just another way to get closer to our consumer and really make sure that if you can’t go, you still feel like you got to experience it as live as you can, without being there yourself.We also have some new wearables that will be in the show. It looks like a piece of jewelry—we’re designing it to be beautiful. We’re also using an app called Zeekit, which, if you take a picture of yourself and upload it, it will actually show you what the clothing going down the runway will look like on you.What’s the inspiration behind the show?This idea of a 'gypset' lifestyle that a modern millennial woman lives—traveling to a lot of places and picking up the best of the best of the things you find along the way. It’s just the things you want to have in your wardrobe come fall that have a touch of where you’ve been and where you’ve experienced global cultures. "Coming from St. Petersburg, I learned early on how to layer—silk undershirt, blouse, sweater, coat, scarf," she says. "You want to look like you could be in Doctor Zhivago, but not too fancy." Here are five of her best tips for looking cute but also not freezing your ass off.Work from a black base. "I often start my outfit with black pants or stockings and add layers of color to enliven it. Camel and red coats or details go particularly well with black. They prevent the look from being too heavy."Mix it up."Winter is great for mixing textures; there are so many to choose from. I love the look of a faux-fur bomber jacket with a wool kilt, for example. I try to keep textures in the same color family—forest green, deep teal, and navy."Keep your coat open. "If I'm wearing an overcoat, I tend not to close it, unless it's freezing. It adds another layer of style when people can see the belt or the sweater under the coat."Stay down. "I usually wear flat, durable boots—anything with treads or thick soles, which are practical and balance the bulk of a coat. If I do wear heels, I make sure they're chunky—they feel substantial in bad weather."Prepare for glare. "Unless it's snowing, I wear giant sunglasses to protect my eyes. Add that laissez-faire yet put-together approach to style with the comfort of activewear, and you’ve got A.P.C.O.V., the latest collaborative collection by French fashion label A.P.C. and Outdoor Voices, a New York-based athletic brand.The collection, available in stores and online starting this week, includes a sensible yet stylish range of women’s basics, from casual warm-up leggings and a slim bodysuit to baseball caps and a grab-and-go tote bag. Prices range from $60 to $290, with pieces just as fit for the gym as they are for Sunday brunch. And don’t worry gentlemen, there are men’s options for you, too.RELATED: Meet Nike’s Unexpected Film Star: An 86-Year-Old NunWhen you think of activewear, the first words that generally come to mind are probably “sports bra” or “track pants.” The collection includes those everyday workout staples, but pieces can easily be worn with equestrian-style knee-high boots or ladylike ballerina slippers for your next workout at the barre. In fact, the bodysuit was specifically designed with classically trained ballerinas of the ‘80s in mind. “Traditionally, we would style everything with tennis shoes and accessories that help you jump right into an activity,” Tyler Haney, the 27-year-old founder of Outdoor Voices, tells Allure. “But A.P.C. brought to the table this idea of being able to style your workout clothes with everyday pieces. We can see the customer wearing A.P.C.O.V. under an A.P.C. trench coat. And when she gets to the studio, she takes off the coat, and there you have it, your clothes to work out in.”Though the A.P.C. and Outdoor Voices collaboration was in the works since early last year, the two cult-favorite brands officially came together last October when Jean Touitou, the founder of A.P.C., announced its investment in Outdoor Voices, which has raised an impressive $22.5 million in funding thus far. While the partnership between the outspoken yet elusive 64-year-old designer and the young entrepreneur from Boulder, Colorado may seem like an unlikely match, Haney says she naturally bonded with Touitou over their obsession with fabric materials. “We both look at the materials first and then design,” she adds. “We focused on simple but still perfect fitting silhouettes that almost become beautiful to wear everyday–that’s my mentality for Outdoor Voices. And that’s the mentality Jean had with A.P.C. when he started it almost 30 years ago—making clothes that people would want to wear everyday.”That design approach is displayed in the campaign ad, as well. Instead of featuring sweat-drenched professional athletes with super-human endurance, the duo enlisted Sasha Hutchings and Ephraim Sykes, a real-life couple and Hamilton cast members who choreographed and performed the pas de deux presented in the video ad. Haney says the premise was inspired by what the dance partners do on their days off with friends and other cast members—head upstate to have dance parties free from the structure of rehearsal and performance on stage.“Rather than positioning ourselves around competition or physical performance like running, we are all about making activities fun and redefining what recreation means to today’s consumers,” she says. “Movement, for us, is more about being outside and participating.” Pretty activewear that we don’t need to sweat in? But (rejoice!) this one has nothing to do with ignoring the bread basket at dinner. The "carb" in question here is carbon—specifically, your carbon footprint.For Earth Day (today, if you somehow hadn't heard) the sustainability-focused fashion label Reformation has introduced a new initiative to raise awareness about how your clothing can contribute to your carbon footprint. Every item the label sells will have a "RefScale," a chart of eco stats that'll inform consumers exactly how much water and carbon dioxide it took to produce the garment, compared with the industry standard.To get things off the ground, they're debuting their Low-Carb collection (modeled by ultimate RefBabe and all-around cool girl, Atlanta de Cadenet Taylor). The collection will be their most eco-friendly one to date, created using the least amount of CO2 ever in the brand's history.Because Reformation's flowy summer dresses are a far cry from the sad, shapeless sacks you might normally associate with eco-friendly fashion, it's no surprise that celebrities like Taylor Swift, Alexa Chung, and Karlie Kloss (who also happens to be a financial backer of the company) are fans. The “It” bag has been dead for a few seasons now, and fashion is always in the search for the next big thing, whether it’s inventing an unconventional way to carry a bag or personalizing the luxe sacks with fun accessories. After all, fur puffs, key chains, leather stickers, and patches and pins have been adorning the bags of the fashion set this year.Most of these new bags are about to hit the market soon, and we have no doubt that street-style stars and celebs will be rocking them at fashion week next month. But after a decade of deliberately hiding socks from plain sight with ankle styles or no-show footies, they have returned to the public spotlight. And we have The Row's Ashley Olsen to thank for that. Because we all know that if one or both of the Olsen twins have endorsed something, that something is bound to be a trend (they single-handedly—double-handedly?—launched the normcore movement several years back, after all).Spotted on the streets of New York City, the eldest Olsen sister was snapped in an enveloping olive green robe coat to which she styled with two bags (a classic Olsen move), a pair of clean white sneakers, and what looks to be shin-high pink socks that she bunched around her ankles. It’s not the most groundbreaking look, but the way it’s so casually presented makes it so nonchalantly cool (and dorky even), so effortless, so Olsen-like in every way.But of course, the fashion set has toyed with socks for awhile now. First, there was the controversial sock-and-sandal pairing that was presented on the runways (see: Burberry spring 2010 and Hermès fall 2014), and then it was eventually embraced by today’s most influential street style stars, who were partial to glittery versions with their platform sandals or fishnet socks with their strappy mules. Also, the rise in both logo-mania and streetwear has made socks irresistible to some, namely Gucci’s web stripe tube socks and the Vetements x Reebok sock collaboration.A guest wearing a pair of Vetements x Reebok socks.If you love Ashley Olsen's style, check out these celebs:How to be stylish in sneakers, according to Veronika Heilbrunner:Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Even the most casual Kendall Jenner observer knows that this woman is no huge fan of the bra. Sure, she wears one — sometimes outside of her clothes — but she often takes the opportunity to skip it and, nope, it makes no difference to her what she's got on when she does. Kendall has proudly #FreedTheNipple while wearing everything from a baggy tee to a totally sheer shirt (and one very memorable crocheted jumpsuit).In fact, Kendall has basically made freeing the nipple her signature lewk: So much so that even when she decides to cover up, she sometimes chooses to wear her trusty Never Fully Dressed T-shirt featuring — what else? — a simple line drawing of boobs. See what she did here?.Kendall's braless looks might send the world into a frenzy, but to the supermodel herself, it's NBD. As she wrote on her blog in 2016: "I really don't see what the big deal is with going braless! I think it's cool and I really just don't care! It's sexy, it's comfortable and I'm cool with my breasts. That's it!" Say it, Kendall!Ahead, 11 times Kendall Jenner freed the nipple — and if you're feeling inspired, here's how to get the braless look, no matter what your size.On July 31, Jenner went braless in a sheer floral top, denim cut-offs, heeled sandals, and her trusty Louis Vuitton fanny pack to do some shopping at the Adidas store in New York City.The day before that, Jenner rocked another #FreeTheNipple look when she wore a sheer red blouse with vintage Levi's and pointy white boots in New York City.On July 26, Jenner chilled in Tribeca in her signature look: vintage denim, Louis Vuitton monogrammed accessory, sexy heels, and a T-shirt sans bra.In June, Jenner wore one of her most arresting looks yet: a white eyelet dress by Opening Ceremony, which she paired with a sheer white camisole for a statement that's somehow both sexy and demure.For our money, Kendall's most iconic #FreeTheNipple moment was the time she went braless while wearing a nude crocheted jumpsuit and tan Yeezy lace-up boots at LAX airport, inspiring literally everyone to up their airport style game forever.For a night out with Cara Delevingne, Kendall didn't technically free the nipple — but her cheeky tee by Never Fully Dressed did.In March, Jenner hit the town in Paris wearing a stunning cherry-red dress by Balmain with straight-off-the runway thigh-high python boots. Slaying.In January, Kendall gave us this amazing outfit featuring lace-up, high-waisted pants and a totally sheer shirt with glittery, star-shaped nipple pasties. This is everything.For her twenty-first birthday, Kendall wore a teeny silver chain-mail dress, custom-made by LaBourjoisie, and inspired by none other than Paris Hilton.In June 2016, Kendall looked relaxed and cool in a fresh white tee, white sneaks, and high-waisted pants topped by a dramatic duster.And, just to prove Kendall's been doing this look for a long time, here's her runway debut at Marc Jacobs back in February 2014, where she went without a bra — and eyebrows — in one of her edgiest looks ever.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. A few of his all time-favorite trips? Mongolia, Easter Island, the Galapagos Islands, and Rajasthan. He's traveled to Japan over 70 times in the past ten years.The designer also happens to be a self-proclaimed sneaker buff, so it makes sense that he's partnered up with NikeLab on a forthcoming collaboration. "I have about 500 or 600 pairs of sneakers in my archives, probably," he said in a release. "I've got them in my house in London and just lots and lots of cupboards in Paris. I've got lots of Jordans and tons of pairs of Huaraches. When they first came out, I bought them in bulk because I loved them so much."Available online and in stores on July 23, the NikeLab x Kim Jones: Packable Sport Style collection was designed with the global colors of Rio in mind. Offered in both men and women's silhouettes, the collection also take inspiration from Jones's jet-set lifestyle, and all the clothes are easily, what else? Packable. For example, one of the jackets in the collection is designed so that it can easily be rolled into a pouch."The Windrunner is [made from] just one piece of fabric, so looking at how that would be cut and how that would be graded were the most challenging details," he said. There will also be one footwear option in the collection, available only in select NikeLab stores.In the past, Jones has infused his love of travel into his menswear collections. For his spring 2017 collection for Louis Vuitton, the designer took inspiration from a trinity of locations: Africa, London, and Paris. The result? Contrasting aesthetics and materials such as exotic skins, punk-y silhouettes, and beige palettes."I always look at culture (more than fashion) as a reference—and travel, which is the key thing," said Jones. "I love going to South Africa. I really enjoy the energy down there—also in Tokyo, New York, and Los Angeles. But I like to look in different places, too. Effortlessly chic and laid-back cool, it was a look that marked the beginning of normcore athleisure and an era of Stan Smith domination.In the seven years since, sneakers have come and gone, with bold ones touted to be the "Next Stan Smith," but never really coming close. Who could compete with the ubiquitous minimalist white sneaker distinguished by its perforated stripes, green heel tab, and the outlined portrait of tennis star Smith on the tongue?But now it looks like the Next Stan Smith sneaker is, well, a Stan Smith sneaker. Unveiled a few days ago, the Stan Smith Boost Primeknit is a breathable, summery version of the classic. It boasts all the same beloved identifiers, including the colored heel tab and the Stan Smith portrait, but the leather upper has been replaced by a knit construction using Adidas’s Primeknit technology, which delivers “lightweight comfort that wraps seamlessly around your foot, while fewer materials produce less waste.”Another difference: The new Stan Smith integrates the brand’s revolutionary Boost cushioning system (you know, the same one found in Yeezy Boosts), which uses individual absorbent capsules for the sole, as opposed to traditional foam-based materials, to increase durability and a high-energy return.So the question you probably want answered: Is the new Stan Smith better? From a fabrication, technological POV, it’s a winner on all fronts—but we still love our classics.The Stan Smith Boost Primeknit isn’t available yet stateside, but they’re up for grabs at overkillshop.com for $160 in both green and navy colorways.More shoes we love:How to be stylish in sneakers, according to Veronika Heilbrunner:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast.
