It’s how to find the calm in the chaos of fashion.”In 2015, Karan announced she’d be stepping down as chief designer of Donna Karan International, a company she founded in 1984, remaining only as an adviser. Dao-Yi Chow and Maxwell Osborne, founders of New York-based brand Public School, succeeded Karan as creative directors of DKNY last year. “I loved it,” Karan told us of Chow and Osbourne’s spring 2017 collection for the brand, which showed Monday at NYFW. “It kept to the energy of New York, and I’d wear it!”RELATED: Donna Karan and DKNY's Best Fashion MomentsWhile the fashion world mourned the loss of one of the most groundbreaking American designers of our time, it seems that Karan is making a comeback by doing fashion week her own way.At Karan’s Urban Zen presentation, which was held at the brand's West Village boutique, models wore tufted silk coats, long shearling vests, heavy leggings, moto jackets, reversible kimonos, and artisanal knits—all perfectly fit for a cozy fall wardrobe. Live music played in the background while a falconer, who was part of the presentation, greeted guests while holding the real-life bird. “Now Ralph [Lauren] is only showing in season,” Karan said of the American designer’s recent decision to show a direct-to-consumer collection this week. “It makes sense. [The consumers] don’t want you to show the spring collections now, they want you to show fall collections now. Let’s get the customer excited again.”RELATED: "See Now, Buy Now" Collections You Can Shop TodayEditors, buyers, and guests had the option to purchase the clothing worn by the models immediately after the presentation at the boutique and online, which follows the “see now, buy now” retail model that countless brands have started to adopt in recent seasons: Tom Ford, Burberry, Rebecca Minkoff, Tommy Hilfiger, and more included.A look from Urban Zen presentation.Karan founded Urban Zen as a nonprofit organization to fund culture preservation. The Haiti Artisan Project, which she created to raise jobs and spread awareness for the cause, inspired the fall collection.Still, Karan insists that she takes a similar approach to designing pieces for Urban Zen as she would for her namesake line or DKNY. After all, this is the designer who brought us the Seven Easy Pieces. “I think the beauty of it is that the jersey is timeless, it’s seasonless,” she says of her new collection. “It evolves to how you want to wear it. But Bella Hadid may have just introduced a brand new way to pull it off. Yesterday, the model sported a thick black choker that read her name, “Bella,” in oversize white gothic font. She paired the choker with black skinny jeans, a lingerie-inspired bodysuit, and a duster coat. The neck piece takes the ubiquitous choker trend—stemmed from fashion's current obsession with the '90s—and gives it a new twist.Kendall Jenner tries nine things she's never done before:Bella Hadid wearing her Abel necklace.The look is reminiscent of nameplate necklaces that, admittedly, have been making a bit of a comeback, as well. Earlier this year, Gigi Hadid proved she and her boyfriend, Zayn Malik, are #relationshipgoals when she rocked a Zayn necklace by jewelry designer Lola James. And rather than swapping broken heart pieces, the model and her BFF Kendall Jenner tapped the jeweler to create personalized friendship necklaces featuring a combined version of their names: KenGi Little sister Bella followed suit with a tiny, delicate Abel necklace—in honor of her boyfriend, The Weeknd. Like everything in their wardrobes, the trend decidedly harkens back to the late '90s and early 2000s—the supermodel trio's favorite fashion decades.To show off her personalized choker last night, the younger Hadid pulled her hair up into a simple topknot and added a bit of glitz with a pair of silver hoop earrings. In terms of makeup, however, things have been kept rather simple, the beauty focus shifting mainly to the hair. I'm not complaining; I think it's wildly exciting that we're finally willing to get more experimental when it comes to our hair (shout out to Schiaparelli, Chanel, Armani Privé, Christian Dior, etc.), but despite the fact that the couture customer is far from relatable, the couture shows are where we beauty obsessives keep an eye out for makeup magic. With this in mind, spring 2016 has been a bit disappointing, until this morning's Maison Margiela show in Paris.Backstage at John Galliano's third collection for the house, makeup artist Pat McGrath delivered some seriously amazing makeup. Aligned with the spirit of couture, she created unique looks for each model, and to our satisfaction, many seemed to be inspired by David Bowie. We're talking graphic zigzag lines around just one eye, sequin stars sprinkled across the face, heart-shaped lipstick, and lipstick-shaped tattoos. The hair, by Eugene Souleiman, was equally as inspired, with colorful mullets and purple, mermaid-esque mini braids. Basically, it was the stuff beauty dreams are made of.Moral of the story: Thank you, Maison Margiela, for satisfying our beauty appetites today—and for paying homage to Bowie in a most beautiful way.Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept Bangs13 Cyber Week 2019 Deals That Allure Readers Are BuyingDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedPat McGrath Labs's LuxeTrance Lipstick Is $10 Right NowTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesLast fall, when Maria Grazia Chiuri sent down a T-shirt that read, “We Should All Be Feminists” on the runway for her debut spring 2017 presentation for Dior, the pro-women rallying cry rang out loud and clear. Fast forward to the fallout after the election, and the desire for such slogans—whether on T-shirts, signs or patches—has now risen to a fever pitch, with brands like Versace, Prabal Gurung, and Tome incorporating politically-charged messaging into their recent fall 2017 collections.Clothing, of course, has always served as a form of self-expression. The recent wave of activist-minded garments not only represents a symbol of solidarity against the current political administration, but also as a form of bonding among those who share the same beliefs. Whether printed on tops, tunics, or jackets, these messages stand out as a visual marker of what you believe in—and that can be a powerful catalyst for change.The pulse of the movement isn't limited to the runways—it's found on a more grassroots level, as well. That’s where DIY artists and creative polymaths have been producing some of the most culturally relevant and virally strong apparel, putting out their wares on maker platforms like Etsy as a way to take a stand against Trump’s particular brand of prejudice, false truths, and social injustice. And unlike large-scale fashion houses, which can take months to incubate collections, these independent designers can be more reactive and nimble in the moment.Katy Perry wearing the Nasty Woman T-shirt.Amanda Brinkman, the co-founder of Google Ghost, conceived her Zeitgeist-defining “Nasty Woman” T-shirt last October while watching the infamous debate in real time. “I first designed the Nasty Woman shirt moments after Trump uttered the words,” she says. “I was shocked by his audacity, but my initial reaction was that if Trump found a smart, prepared, and qualified woman so threatening that he had to call her names, then that made me a nasty woman, too.” And she didn’t waste any time spreading that message. “I was on my computer during the debate, designed the T-shirt, and put it online before the debate was even over.” Her creation went “viral overnight,” with it quickly gaining traction among A-list celebs, including Katy Perry and Kristen Bell. (“There was one point where Hilary Clinton tweeted a video of Will Ferrell wearing my shirt,” says Brinkman with glee).Others started making feminist apparel long before Trump stumbled onto the public stage. Rachel Berks, the founder of the hybrid retail store and design studio Otherwild, first put her “The Future is Female” T-shirt into circulation the summer of 2015. “I’ve been interested in reactive political slogans from the 1970s and 1980s,” she says. (In fact, the phrase first appeared on a T-shirt that was made for Labyris Books, a women’s bookstore that opened in 1972. Most recently, Prabal Gurung adopted the slogan for his fall 2017 collection tees). Berks now has an extensive collection of upstanding apparel and accessories, including “Gender is a Drag” and “How Dare You Assume I’m Straight” pieces, which she created in collaboration with Herstory, a curated Instagram project founded by Kelly Rakowski. Getting in the studio is a way of taking action. “We have a dysfunctional body politic, to stay the least,” says Berks. “I feel compelled to find ways of disseminating empowering messages, to which we can speak and dedicate ourselves in our lived practices.”Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”A woman wearing Otherwild's "The Patriarchy is a Pyramid Scheme" political T-shirt at Milan fashion week.To combat against the increasing threats of defunding community organizations, many designers of slogan apparel have been donating a portion of the proceeds to such non-profits as a form of resistance. Brinkman’s Nasty Woman T-shirts, for example, have raised more than $126,000 for Planned Parenthood so far. And giving back has been part of the DNA behind Boy Meets Girl, which designer and creative director Stacy Igel launched in 2001. “Contributing to causes that can help make a stand or help one in need gives me a sense of hope that others will follow and continue to show their support,” she says. Every month, Igel releases a limited-edition collection with 10 percent of the sales dedicated to organizations that “impact communities in need in a positive way.” Her most recent cropped sweatshirts, which read, “Women Crush Everyday,” support Planned Parenthood, while her oversized “F*ck Racism” tees give back to the ACLU.“The fashion industry is an extremely fast-paced environment where it’s a constant race to catch up,” says Igel. “Dedicating myself to other passions of mine allows me to take a step back and see the big picture. It allows me to slow down for a second to breathe and think, how can a make a difference today?” Still, that raises the question: Can wearing outspoken clothing really spark lasting change?Kristina Haugland, the Le Vine associate curator of costume and textiles at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, believes that such highly visible messages can serve as important conversation starters. “You empower and encourage others to speak up or become more active as well,” she says, adding that political slogans are nothing new. Haugland is currently spearheading an upcoming exhibition, Text in Fashion, that explores the use of words and letters on garments from the 18th century to the present day. “We have a child’s cotton dress from the 1860s, printed with Civil War union shields all over the dress, and then if you look at the French Revolution, colors were used to show your support for various factions.” In the early 20th century, wearing white, she says, became associated with the women’s suffrage movement, similar to how today’s pink hats signify standing up for women’s rights.Suffragettes on the Euston Road procession in London, 1908.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”But fashion apparel really started to get political in the 1960s and 1970s with the rise in silkscreen printing. The technique made it easier for anyone to print a custom T-shirt to help speak their mind during the Vietnam War protests, says Haugland. Today, people still want to find an outlet for their frustrations. “I’m not the only one to say the country is very polarized, and people are trying to find ways to express an opinion and make their views known,” she says. “It’s a way to add cohesion to groups and show support for people who feel the same way as you do.”Think of it as a sartorial form of banding together. Or as Brinkman puts it, “When you wear a T-shirt, like the Nasty Woman T-shirt, you’re not only making some of your beliefs known, you’re identifying with a larger group of individuals who feel the same way,” she says. “I’ve given high-fives to women in parking lots wearing the shirt: It’s a simple and positive way to note that we’re on the same team.”More on political messages in fashion:We shot this before Trump won, here's why we posted it:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The fashion fallout: Aestheticians like Joanna Vargas, the founder of Joanna Vargas Salon in New York City (and facial fairy godmother of celebs like Karlie Kloss, Naomi Watts, and Dakota Johnson), are extending skin-care wizardry all the way to the waist."Cutouts are getting more and more popular, but the body skin does get dull," Vargas explains. To make her clients' midriffs as smooth and radiant as the skin on their faces before events, Vargas exfoliates with a diamond-tipped microdermabrasion tool, then softens skin with a shredded-coconut-and-green-tea compress and a hydrating mask.Unless you're actually going to the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute Gala, though, you don't need a diamond-tipped sloughing wand—or 60 spare minutes—to shape up your midsection. In everyday life, Vargas recommends getting the job done with a coconut-oil-rich sugar scrub, which physically dislodges dead skin cells and conditions skin with omega-3 fatty acids. We moped around in thrift-shop threads and lank hair, proclaiming our love for Sylvia Plath and Rainer Werner Fassbinder—not entirely aware that neither was the ideal romantic hero. We played Joni Mitchell and cried. This wasn't depression of the DSM variety; it was an affectation. Happiness seemed facile while we wanted to be dark and deep.Well, so much for that. I've become a diligent student of joy, with my Flipboard set to articles about happiness. I can't go a week without finding a new study that reveals exactly what to do to boost your spirits: Make your bed, eat more vegetables, take a walk, write a thank you note, pet your dog, chat in an elevator. This was once called civilized behavior. Now, it's a checklist sprinkled with magic.My favorite fact from one study is that even a fake smile increases happiness—of the smiler and the smiled upon. I also like this bit of news from recent research: that Botox reduces depression because it inhibits the ability to frown. This is science I can get behind.With this wealth of evidence, it makes no sense to me that so few models smile in photographs or on runways. I'm constantly begging for smiling pictures in Allure, and I'll even settle for a slight upward curve of the lips. At a dinner with a supermodel years ago, I asked her why she looked so glum in pictures when she was so cheerful in life. She explained that after analyzing photographs of herself, she came to the conclusion that smiling makes her nose look wider and her eyes smaller. Simply that. And that made me sad.Maybe this is why many fashion shows resemble funeral marches. Or perhaps the designers, like my college roommates and me, think happiness looks superficial and commercial. Still, I fully believe that if a designer really wanted to be subversive, he'd send the models down the runway wearing big, beautiful smiles.It's worked for Kate Moss, Gisele, Cindy Crawford, and Karlie Kloss, who seem unconcerned about the face-distorting effects of a smile. Their joy is radiant and contagious, and there's nothing facile about that.How to age like a supermodel:Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”13 Cyber Week 2019 Deals That Allure Readers Are BuyingDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedPat McGrath Labs's LuxeTrance Lipstick Is $10 Right NowTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Unconventional. Bold. These are the first words that come to mind when describing international style icon Yasmin Sewell. The style.com fashion director, whose elegant and quirky ensembles have made her a street-style favorite, never fails at serving up a killer look. Sewell is a staple at fashion weeks and can be seen rocking a myriad of looks that range from boho-chic to futuristic glam, putting most onlookers to shame. What do we love most about her style? That she is never stagnant. As Sewell describes it, “Someone who has innate and timeless style, it’s who they are. Fashion is of a moment. It’s always changing and evolving, which I love.”Above everything, it’s her personal journey that makes her a true fashion inspiration. At the age of 19, Sewell moved from her home country of Australia to London, eventually opening up Yasmin Cho, a short-lived boutique that spotlighted up-and-coming designers like Rick Owens and Pierre Hardy. During her career, she served as buying director for British department store Browns in 2005, opened up her own consulting agency in 2008, and became cofounder of French label Être Cécile in 2013.More inspirational fashion and beauty stories:When she’s not curating the hottest fashion and beauty products on the market, she’s blessing us with her beauty and fashion tips. Eckhaus Latta, J.Crew, and Chromat are among the few that have eschewed a narrow standard idea of beauty in favor of personality-driven casting and unconventional models. Inspired by “friends and fans,” as well as their “confidence and personal style,” designer Rio Uribe of New York-based label Gypsy Sport has long been a champion of diversity and inclusivity—both in clothing and casting.Gypsy Sport runway shows are effortlessly filled with people of color, transgender, and who represent a diverse range of backgrounds and body types. By fusing New York-inspired streetwear with unexpected feminine flourishes and luxe materials, the unisex label has continuously challenged gender norms.In the past, with the help of Uribe’s longtime friend and casting director, Anthony Conti, Gypsy Sport shows have included a range of personalities, from rapper and reality TV star Cardi B to indie singer Maluca and Harlem-born model Slick Woods. This season, Conti has cast a number of empowering activists to showcase the brand’s new collection inspired by “outdoor living both by choice and circumstance.” Just before Gypsy Sport’s fall 2017 show at New York fashion week, we spoke to Conti about his casting process, the industry’s responsibility to diversity, and how he came across Jesi Taylor, one of the stars of Allure’s “Dispelling Beauty Myths” video series.Where and how do you find your models?I’ve always been into street casting (now social media casting), so I’m constantly making a running list of people whom I’ve found on Instagram or Facebook. The process is really just going into what I call a “black hole.” It’s just going deeper and deeper online, click on someone’s page and just get lost in Instagram, get lost in Facebook. We post on the Gypsy Sport Instagram page, saying that we are doing an open-call casting. We set up an E-mail address for them to send photos, and then we take it from there.What do you look for in a Gypsy Sport model? What do they have to represent?From the start, Gypsy Sport has always been about inclusion. We’ve always been setting up this global village, where we kind of celebrate everyone and anyone, and really try to embrace the world and all of its beauty and its people. We try to be representative without being token—we try to keep it very organic, but there’s certainly not a check-list of “OK, we have this kind of person, that kind of person.” With Gypsy Sport, we are being diverse for the sake of being diverse, which I feel like most people are doing now and are doing it because they feel the responsibility to do it. We didn’t set out saying, “Oh, we are going to become a multi-cultural brand.” It’s just innately in the brand. It’s like breathing. It’s how we function. For us, diversity was never not going to be part of the conversation. That’s how Rio sees the world. He’s always seen it in many colors. We truly see uniqueness in every type of human experiences.Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsWhat can we expect in the fall 2017 show?This season, we’re focusing on activism, and that we did because it would be irresponsible not to certainly in the climate we are currently living in. It’s our responsibility as a brand that supports inclusivity to highlight and promote people who are getting themselves out there in a way that will positively affect the community. I found Kelvin Pena of Everybody Eats on Instagram ever since his campaign went viral. He started a non-profit organization that helps feed single-parent families and after-school kids. Diandra Forrest, she’s an activist for albinism and women empowerment. We have a young girl named Kabrina Adams of Free My Boobs movement.  There’s also Khoudia Diop. She’s a brand ambassador for the Colored Girl and is an activist against bullying.And you’ve also cast Jesi Taylor from our “Dispelling Beauty Myths” video series?Yes, Jesi Taylor, whom I’ve found on the Allure beauty series. It was so freaking good. The moment I saw her and heard her story, I knew I had to reach out to her. She told me she’s running for local government office, so that’s incredible. When you first reach out to people, there’s definitely apprehension because they’re not models. There are certainly people on Instagram who are set up and ready to go and become a supermodel, but most people are still pretty timid. I spoke to Jesi last night because I wanted to make sure that I represented her properly. During the conversation, she told me she was so excited for Sunday.A model backstage at Gypsy Sport spring 2017 show.What is the process like when working with people who are not professional models?It’s really about being themselves. When I tell them to walk it’s like, ‘I want to see what you look like when you’re walking down the street, don’t give me supermodel, don’t try to do this or the other. I want to see how you look like when you’re in New York City.’ I’m not trying to get them to be something they’re not because I tell them, “We picked you to celebrate you, not you the person we want you to be.”Last year, we've seen more brands making the initiative to become more inclusive. Do you see the industry's commitment towards inclusivity being progressive—or is it just a trend?Let’s hope it’s not a trend. I see efforts being made. I think there are a ton of brands in New York City, just like Gypsy Sport that are very inclusive from inception. I think there are older brands that have quite a bit of way to go. I can only affect what I can affect. My hope is that what we do will inspire people. People are definitely taking notice, but for me, it’s unfortunate that it had to be a thought process to get to this point when it should have always been there. I mean, we live in New York City, you are a New York City brand, you are inundated with people everyday and they certainly don’t all look like you. It’s unfortunate that people have to think to get to that point, but hey, better than completely ignoring.More on fashion's push for diversity:Watch Jesi Taylor speak about her experience living with vitiligo:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Seriously. While we were busy writing the hoodie off as an innocuous sweatshirt to be reserved for post-gym brunches or shameless evenings of Netflix and chill, it was subverting its way right into the fabric of our cultural consciousness. We don’t often think of clothing as having an agenda, but the hoodie definitely does.“Most people see the hoodie as the representation of anything anti-social,” says Laura McLaws Helms, a New York–based fashion historian. “It’s this anti-establishment, anti-social thing, and probably the ultimate garment that represents those ideas.”The hoodie has what you might call a paradoxical history. When it first hit the retail scene in the ’30s, the hoodie had a pretty practical intent: keeping athletes warm, a purpose that was quickly appropriated by blue-collar laborers. But not too long after its vanilla beginnings, the hoodie started to get a rep on the streets. According to McLaws Helms, this, too, was purely practical—the hood provided the perfect shroud for ne’er-do-wells up to no good. From there it really took off. In the ‘70s, the hoodie solidified its counterculture rep, largely thanks to the army of graffiti artists sporting the style as they left their marks on major urban centers. In rapid succession came the hip-hop crowd and the skater scene of the ‘80s and ‘90s—two more countercultures borrowing the uniform of their predecessors.Sweatshirts on display in the ’50s.For a brief second, it looked like the hoodie might swing back toward its squeaky-clean roots, says McLaws Helms. “The hoodie has had this other tread that’s all about leisurewear and resort wear,” she says. “You can go through old issues of WWD and Vogue from the ’70s, and it’s all pictures of pretty blondes on the tennis court wearing hoodie sweatshirts.” It provides an interesting commonality between the country club set and some of the era’s most relevant counterculture movements.But the hoodie held down its street cred heading into the 21st century, when it was adopted by the early recluses who pioneered Silicon Valley—most notably, Facebook’s Mark Zuckerberg.How to wear a hoodie all day:Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Which brings us to the latest incarnation of the hoodie. In an almost poetically perfect throwback, the athleisure trend has taken the preppy hoodie of the ‘70s country club set and the humble uniform of the 1930s football star and married the two. But there’s also a much more ironic trend happening with the modern sweatshirt. As the street-style trend has moved away from the fringes of fashion into the mainstream, so has the most authentic piece of street-style wear. All of a sudden, labels like Supreme, Vetements, and Yeezy are slapping three- and four-figure price tags on oversize versions of the uniform of graffiti artists and tech nerds in a kind of modern-day counterculture move that might have you scratching your head.From left: Alexander Wang, Vetements, YeezyThroughout all of these different incarnations the hoodie has had throughout history, there’s been one common thread in its narrative: subversion. “The hoodie has been inserting itself into some of the biggest cultural conversations of the past century, and we’re only just now starting to pay attention. That’s part of why designers like Kanye West and Vetements are drawing on that history. They have hoodies in their collections because it has such a strong cultural background,” says McLaws Helms. “For any designer, when you take something from history, even if it’s just contemporary history, it’s always going to come with a certain amount of cultural connotation."Herein lies the hoodie’s genius. It’s managed to pass through some of the most important counterculture movements of our time, only to end up right in the focal point of high-end trend watchers. With one simple item of clothing, modern designers are referencing not only a broad-spectrum history of youth culture, but also a very relevant political conversation.Madonna wearing a hoodie on the set of Saturday Night Live in 1985.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”So what gives a simple item of clothing that kind of power? It starts with the form and then becomes about the narrative that we, as a culture, write around it—what started out as a totally functional way to keep high school athletes warm became one of the most potent symbols of subversion. The crazy thing is just how much narrative power the hoodie has managed to garner over the past century. "For such an omnipresent garment and such a common thing, it’s really unlike any other piece of clothing in terms of the amount of stories people have about it," says McLaws Helms.The hoodie now has such cultural cache that it’s become prescriptive—when you see one in the wild, you start filling in the narrative about it’s wearer. Take for example the Black Lives Matter movement, which sprang from the murder of Trayvon Martin and the huge amount of time the court spent discussing the role his hoodie might have played in his death. The hoodie rose to such importance in that case, that many attributed Martin’s death to his clothing choice that day.If history is any indication, the hoodie is here to stay—but it won’t be staying quietly.RELATEDMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. This deal will provide rehearsal attire—including backpacks, warm-ups, leggings, and sneakers—to the company's 92 dancers of all ranks to further the sportswear brand's efforts to expand its women's training category."We were excited about the possibility of working with the dancers of NYCB as a way to further our brand commitment to women's training, as a new opportunity to test and refine our performance products with top athletes, and as a chance to broaden our brand's presence in the world of arts and culture." said Adam Petrick, Puma's global director of brand and marketing.In addition, NYCB dancers will be featured in Puma's print and digital campaigns. The Kering-owned brand will also explore ways to support a variety of NYCB initiatives, including the ballet company's education, audience development, and dancer health and wellness efforts.The partnership, NYCB's first activewear deal, coincides with the sportswear industry's emerging demand for dance-centric marketing campaigns. American Ballet Theatre's principal dancer Misty Copeland partnered with Under Armour in a viral campaign two years ago."Many of the members of the NYCB rehearse and perform as much as 12 hours a day, and that extreme physical work out is clearly of interest to athletic companies," said Petrick. "Anywhere we see people pushing their bodies to extremes in such a demanding environment with the added dimension of creativity and new ideas is highly interesting territory for [us]."While Petrick said the brand is considering NYCB-Puma merchandises, the possibility of developing technical pointe shoes is not in the works at the moment.The announcement photos feature NYCB soloist Savannah Lowery, and corps de ballet members Olivia Boisson, Meagan Mann, Unity Phelan, and Mimi Staker. The photos show the dancers at the company's rehearsal space in Lincoln Center, dressed in Puma-emblazoned shirts and leggings along with practice tutus and leg warmers."The leggings, which are my favorite, fit so well," said Boisson, a dancer with the company since 2012. "They really hug my legs just enough so that my muscles feel supported. The fabric isn't so thin or transparent that they rip or sag, but also not so thick that it covers the outlines of my muscles."Boisson, along with the cast members featured in the first round of photos from Puma, is an up-and-coming dancer at the company. Similar to NYCB's own casting system in which dancers of lower ranks are given opportunities to debut in principal roles, Puma's choice to present younger dancers offers a chance to support the stars of tomorrow."As one of the younger dancers, I think it can be hard to try stand out and show people that you have what it takes," said Boisson. Hear us out: While Wimbledon has long enforced a dress code of (mostly) white ensembles that wouldn’t look out of place at a British prep school, the U.S. Open offers up a platform for creativity and bold self-expression, as demonstrated by the Williams sisters’ brightly colored and bedazzled outfits and Caroline Wozniacki’s vividly hued Adidas by Stella McCartney outfits. It’s the place where players get to break free of the sport’s unofficial uniform. Even so, this year, it seems that flashy pieces may be passed up in favor of a willing return to the crisp, classic, all-white ensembles that once helped to define the sport.In this spirit of the back-to-school metaphor, here’s a brief history lesson. Toward the end of the nineteenth century, alabaster outfits were associated with sunny-day luxury and leisure. “White was chosen, especially for women, as the color of on-court outfits because it never showed perspiration,” says Ben Rothenberg, the author of The Stylish Life: Tennis. “For a woman to be outside sweating was seen as unladylike, so it was actually a fairly functional choice.”Members of the South African tennis team at Wimbledon in 1929Throughout the subsequent decades, court-ready uniforms continued to mirror the overarching trends of the era (long skirts in the 1900s, headbands and hats in the 1920s, tailored shorts in the 1940s, and cinched waists in the 1950s). But it was not until the '60s and the introduction of Penn’s now-iconic “optic yellow” tennis ball that the game began to gradually welcome an infusion of color, which led to the animal prints and neon spandex that may spring to mind at the mention of the sport.Despite the fun that comes with runway-influenced looks, a resurgence of whites serves as a welcome palette cleanser. Even Venus Williams seems to agree—the powerhouse offers up a selection of blanched pieces in her own line of activewear, EleVen. “I think that white does really well,” says Rothenberg. “Designers enjoy the challenge of trying to do something original and creative with no color at their disposable.” Case in point: The aforementioned Williams’s 2003 Wimbledon dress, which featured a corset-inspired lace-up back, immediately proving that white can indeed turn heads.Many activewear designers are championing the shift back to subtlety. “Tennis whites are the very embodiment of both class and tradition,” says Yesim Philip, L’Etoile Sport’s creative director, whose most recent collection centers on blanched pieces embellished with pleats, mesh, and lace. “Wearing silhouettes in crisp white but with textured fabrics is what really is giving the classics a revival that won’t quit.”From left: Tory Sport dress, $225 (torysport.com); L'Etoile Sport dress, $245 (letoilesport.com); Monreal London skirt, $225 (net-a-porter.com). Above: Adidas Stan Smith shoes, $90 (adidas.com).Tory Sport, Tory Burch’s line of activewear for women, has embraced a similar approach as of late, with preppy polos, skirts, and sweaters in cream with retro stripes of color, while Monreal London’s pleats and ruching ensure the spirit of the classically inspired offerings remains squarely in the present tense.In addition to tournaments like the U.S. Open, Philip is hoping to spot L’Etoile Sport's all-white, active-minded pieces off the court while the sun is still high in the sky. “Pairing pleated skorts with tailored athletic tops or wearing a drop-waist tennis dress with a cashmere cardigan allows for a look that combines the old with the new, creating the resurgence of a bygone era.”If you need us, we’ll be frolicking around in our immaculate, quietly ornamented sportswear for the remainder of the summer.Serena Williams Pelts a Heckler With Tennis Balls:Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. After all, bridesmaids and groomsmen are up there with the folks getting married and are often featured prominently in many of the wedding photos. Because of this, many of us assume that the reason why bridesmaids dresses traditionally match is purely for aesthetic reasons — the bridal party looking uniform creates a pleasing backdrop for the main event. However, as Refinery 29 is reporting, that's not where the tradition of matching bridesmaids dresses started. The origin of a uniform bridal party is actually steeped in the paranormal.According to a video Refinery 29 found on Buzz60, the custom of matching bridesmaids dresses goes as far back as ancient Rome and has supernatural origins. Rather than starting the tradition out of a desire to simply look similar, the entire bridal party (including the bride herself) dressed alike to confuse anyone who may attempt to steal the bride — be it a mortal suitor or a demonic spirit.The tradition has evolved in modern times and though bridesmaids still often dress alike, the bride is now meant to stand out, rendering the origin of the story moot. Perhaps this is why many brides are opting for nontraditional weddings and allowing their bridesmaids to wear different dresses within a certain color range, or forgoing the whole bridesmaid dress trend altogether.More on weddings:The Most Iconic Celebrity Wedding Gowns of All Time:Follow Rosemary on Instagram and Twitter.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. But these aren't the in-your-face graphic T-shirts from the '90s. Fashion's new favorite tees are sophisticated and luxurious.Take Vetements. When the brand released its popular yellow-and-red DHL tees from the spring 2016 collection, the fashion set was so enamored that the tops sold out—even with a $330 price tag. Scores of knockoffs are being sold on eBay starting at less than $10. The French label also recently added American T-shirt manufacturer Hanes to its roster of collaborators for its couture debut earlier this month. Even Gucci jumped on the bandwagon by showing logo tees in its recent resort collection.From Gucci's Resort 2017 collectionThe trend is not limited to the runway. One of the most popular looks of the summer, worn by "It" girls such as Gigi Hadid and Kendall Jenner, is a slip dress styled over—what else?—a basic tee. Justin Bieber is selling $195 T-shirts as part of his tour merchandise at Barneys New York.The T-shirt wasn't always a covetable piece in a woman's wardrobe. The modern-day tee has a rather unfashionable predecessor: a men's underwear staple from the early 1900s. By the '50s, shirts emblazoned with university and rock-band logos emerged, affecting the T-shirt's popularity.Its resurgence may be tied to the fashion industry's cyclical nature; labels are now aiming to become more consumer-friendly by offering practical, mass-produced pieces. "We're seeing a return to the sensibility of the '90s, which was the last time logo mania was everywhere," says Stephanie Solomon, the fashion director at Lord & Taylor. "It was also a time when there was an upheaval in fashion, [similar to] now with the changing of the guard with Demna Gvasalia at Vetements and Balenciaga and Alessandro Michele at Gucci. Part of the fashion uniform then was the logo tee and showing belief in the brand's values by wearing it. Today, everyone's reasserting their brand fidelities."From Vetements's spring 2016 collectionThe T-shirt acts as a gateway item for many of these luxury labels, opening up the demographics of each brand. "These T-shirts are usually the most inexpensive thing in designer collections," Solomon says. "[Women are] buying into the brand at their opening price point. The customer is making a statement that she's aligned with the brand."The best part about the trend: You probably have some form of it in your closet already. "The trend has no age boundaries—it resonates at all age groups—and price isn't necessarily going to be a restriction," Solomon says. It's a piece of fashion now claimed by high-end designers, yet completely accessible. And though her words were indeed memorable, it was her communicative brooch that stole the show.The former secretary of state has a long history of letting her pins speak for themselves, a trend that began after the Iraqi media called her an “unparalleled serpent” during her time as the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. In response, Albright secured a gilded snake pin for her next meeting with Iraqi officials and from then on allowed her brooches to perform nonverbal acrobatics for her. (In 1999, the politician donned an arrow-shaped pin while negotiating the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty with the Soviet Union.) Her diplomatic take on jewelry has led to a book and a traveling museum exhibition. And last night’s brooch—a glitzy take on the Great Seal of the United States—silently screamed patriotism and offered sparkly style in spades.Here, six more women who have embraced the power of the pin.Queen Elizabeth wearing her Cullinan V brooch during her 1982 tour of the South PacificQUEEN ELIZABETHWhen it comes to twinkling additions, few can match Queen Elizabeth's collection. The Cullinan V brooch may be the most iconic, but Her Majesty has been known to embrace Art Deco styles, crests, feathers, ferns, and flowers; many of her brooches were gifts from family or admirers. When it comes to amassing an impressive and enduring jewelry collection, it’s good to be queen.The Duchess of Cambridge wearing the queen's maple-leaf brooch during her 2011 tour in CanadaDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”KATE MIDDLETONKate Middleton is tasked with bringing new life to the queen’s assemblage of brooches, and the duchess imbues even the most vintage of pins with a modern sensibility. As brooches were a mainstay on the 2015 runways—fastened to tweeds at Balenciaga, clustered on sweaters and in updos at Dolce & Gabbana, quirky renditions pinned to Proenza Schouler’s collection of boxy bags—Middleton is taking full advantage of the opportunity to reinvigorate the storied accessory.Elizabeth Taylor wearing a brooch by Jean Schlumberger in 1968ELIZABETH TAYLORThough first and foremost an actress, Elizabeth Taylor is perhaps better known for her iconic assemblage of jewelry—and her penchant for Bulgari. Taylor was known to fasten the brand’s emerald offerings on her neckline and in her hair. She also favored more whimsical pieces by French jewelry designer Jean Schlumberger, known for his designs for Tiffany & Co.Jackie Kennedy wearing her sunburst brooch in 1963JACQUELINE KENNEDY ONASSISJackie O.’s most famous brooch was no doubt the eye-catching diamond-encrusted sunburst that she pinned on dresses—and in her brunette bouffant—for an instant dose of 1960s luxury. The incomparable trendsetter continued wearing brooches throughout her life in the spotlight, accessorizing with glimmering pins in the shape of berries and blooms, and elevating political style to an aspirational and feminine level still mirrored by celebrities and First Ladies alike.Sarah Jessica Parker wearing a flower pin in Sex and the CitySARAH JESSICA PARKERFrom oversize fabric flowers to exaggerated cameos, Sex and the City’s Carrie Bradshaw was known to rock a brooch. Bradshaw's real-life counterpart, Sarah Jessica Parker, partnered with Hong Kong–based jewelry designer Cindy Chao in 2014 to create the Ballerina Butterfly, an eye-catching, ethereal pin inspired by the butterfly engravings inside a rehearsal room at the Palais Garnier in Paris. For her part, Parker has long adorned ensembles with a varied assortment of shimmering and uniquely shaped pins worn at the neckline, the waistline, and just above the hairline.KATNISS EVERDEENKatniss Everdeen—the fictional heroine of The Hunger Games—initially fastened on her gold mockingjay brooch as a good luck charm. But what began as a simple token soon took on a wealth of meaning, eventually becoming the symbol of an all-out rebellion, inspiring duplicates and even tattoos. I know her. Everyone knows her, and it’s all because of one dress. Or rather the dress—the one Kate Middleton wore to announce her engagement to Prince William in 2010. Timeless yet current, the royal-blue silk jersey wrap dress (that perfectly complemented her 12-carat sapphire stunner) has come to represent and exemplify the Duchess of Cambridge's poise and elegant style. And just like that, this one moment in time catapulted Issa—Helayel’s brand—to meteoric fame, and consequently, its downfall.And while Helayel is back with a shiny new brand this season—DHELA, a mashup of her first initial and last name, but it also means “belonging to her” in Portugese—it’s important to understand what happened to Issa that led her to this point.She first launched the London-based brand in 2001 after being unable to find anything exciting or inspiring on the market. “All my beautiful friends in London were wearing a lot of black and gray and dressing in a very unfeminine way, and I was keen to change that! So I wanted my designs to be full of bright colors and prints, joyful dresses in flattering, seductive shapes,” she tells Allure, going on to explain that Issa grew slowly and steadily for the first few years until it began to garner recognition among the A-list set. “There was nothing as well cut, easy to wear, or effortlessly elegant on the market.”Then the Great Kate Effect happened.“It was a fairy-tale moment, pure magic, and I’m incredibly flattered that she chose one of my designs for such a special moment,” Helayel says. “I think the reason it resonated around the world is because that dress would suit every woman, of every race, every nationality, and every body shape.”Kate Middleton wearing the Issa dress on the day of her engagement announcementThe good news: The dress sold out in minutes. The bad news: Helayel couldn’t keep up with the demand, financially. What she needed was an investor. She sold a majority of her company to Camilla Al Fayed, the daughter of Egyptian billionaire Mohamed Al Fayed, in 2011. Two years later, Helayel left the company due to creative differences. And in 2015, Issa shuttered.“At the time of leaving, global retail sales were about 27 million pounds and the label was achieving year-on-year double-digit growth,” Helayel recalls. “However, at a time of rapid expansion, a new design team took over, and from my perspective, they didn’t understand the DNA of the brand. Shortly after my departure, sales started to significantly drop and the label was closed two years later.”Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”The story has become something of a cautionary tale, but Helayel has resolved to look forward rather than dwell on the past. Enter her new brainchild, DHELA. It’s hard not to draw comparisons between the two brands, which Helayel says she won’t fault you for. They’re both born from the same place, after all: a design ethos that empowers women through flattering silhouettes, rich colors, and playful prints.Helayel’s famous silk jersey dresses are there, though updated in a poppy-fuchsia hue and cut with a plunging neckline or as an impossibly chic one-shoulder evening gown. Her signature chiffon caftans make an appearance as well but made over in of-the-moment shapes, like off the shoulder or with a sexy open back.“I’m keen to keep and update these signature styles at DHELA but am also very excited to be developing new fabric groups as well—knitwear in particular has interested me lately and is becoming a bigger part of my collections,” she says. “There is also a clear evolution as I have grown up, seen and experienced new things, had new ideas and been inspired to develop and build on my past.”Inspired by the Amazon, the spring 2017 collection is rooted in nature, particularly orchids and plants found in the forest, under a '70s lens (her favorites: an off-the-shoulder chiffon metallic dress and a long chiffon set in teal, green, and blue, which was inspired by giant fronds in the Amazon).Another big difference for Helayel this time around is her approach to business. “I am definitely in a stronger position to deal with all the challenges that will come with DHELA—nothing beats experience, and I’ve seen every part of the process from the very first mood boards of a collection to the shop floor,” she says. “But it’s important to remember that the world is changing hugely. For example, social media, online shopping, and shopping straight from the runway are things that just didn’t exist when I started Issa. The only way we can face new problems or questions is with an open mind and fresh perspective.”And does she think Kate Middleton will be a fan? Her lips are sealed, but she hopes “women around the world will find something at DHELA.”Scroll through to see the Helayel’s first DHELA collection.More fashion brands we love:Check out Kate Middleton's best looks from 2016:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. According to the brand, these women all represent the spirit of Jimmy Choo. With so many fashion campaigns lacking diversity both in race and age—it's great to see Jimmy Choo leading by example and being inclusive of both.Founded by Jimmy Choo Yeang Keat in 1986, the label's signature styles are pointed-toe pumps and strappy sandals. The shoes rose to fame in the late '80s after being featured in the pages of Vogue, and Princess Diana frequently wore them during the '90s.The campaign images feature models against a minimalist background wearing classic pumps, jewel-tone velvet booties, knee-high leather boots, and sandals. Sarah Richardson styled all the looks, and Craig McDean served as the photographer. Richardson and McDean also collaborated on the label's men's fall 2016 campaign. Richardson has styled campaigns for labels including Lanvin and Roberto Cavalli, while McDean is known for his photography in top fashion magazines, such as W and Vogue.The ads will be officially released in September and will be accompanied by a video on the Jimmy Choo website."The fall 2016 campaign is a reflection of the characters who embody the Jimmy Choo brand values both during the past 20 years and into the future," said Sandra Choi, the label's creative director, in a statement. They should be versatile enough to pair with your favorite trousers or midi skirts, last for more than a couple of wears, and be relatively affordable. Alix (a.k.a. fashion stylists’ secret weapon) meets all those criteria with its range of sleek, flattering, and minimal bodysuits. Known for its beautifully constructed one-pieces that come in various colors and luxe fabrics, Alix is the brainchild of Alexandra Alvarez, the New YorkCity–based designer who launched the label two years ago. The Parsons grad decided to take on the bodysuit when she couldn’t find the perfect top to pair with the bottoms she designed during her senior year. The result is a line of cool, foolproof garments that work seamlessly with everything in your closet, from voluminous skirts to wide-legged pants. “I wanted to make bodysuits a staple for every woman’s wardrobe, not a ‘wear once’ statement piece,” says Alvarez. Beloved by Kendall Jenner, Kim Kardashian, and Gigi Hadid, the brand expanded to slip dresses and recently released swimwear this summer. We sat down with the designer to chat about the direction of her brand, how to wear a bodysuit, and why confidence is key when it comes to style.Why did you decide to start Alix? "Everything started when I was searching for a cool bodysuit to style with some bottoms I made during my senior year at Parsons. I realized that they literally had gone extinct, and there was no contemporary brand that offered them. After I graduated, while I was in the process of interviews and applying for jobs, I started drawing different variations that felt modern but still timeless. It was then that I knew I was onto something and began to pursue starting my own brand. I saw the serious need for sleek, modern, and versatile bodysuits in the market, and I steered Alix in that direction."Do you have advice on how to wear a bodysuit? "The possibilities are endless! That’s what’s so great about bodysuits. You can wear one of my classics with denim and a blazer for fall or switch it up with a maxiskirt and flat sandals in the summer. The beautiful thing is seeing how everyone has the opportunity to add their personal style to each suit and always make it work."Alexandra AlvarezGabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsLuxury basics have been making a comeback. Why do you think this is so?"Everyone loves statement pieces. But when it comes to what women feel they need or rather spend money on, it's investment pieces—a.k.a. luxury basics. There’s something special about getting a piece of clothing that feels luxurious and timeless but also you know you can wear it in so many different ways. Quality, fit, and versatility are everything. I feel that people are shopping differently and are more conscious of making smarter purchases. It’s important for women to have staples in their closets, or 'go-to pieces' as I call them. For me, I realized that bodysuits can be a go-to piece with incredible versatility."  So you’ve conquered the bodysuit and the slip dress. What is next on your list?"I’ve been focused on finding the right fit and figuring out bodysuits for four years now. I think the next step for me that feels organic is swimsuits. They are very similar products, and what I love most about designing bodysuits is how much I can connect with women and the way they feel about themselves. My mother always ingrained in me that confidence is beauty despite what you wear. I love the idea of empowering women by creating a product that makes them feel beautiful inside and out. Hopefully with the swimsuits I can continue to do this!"Lily Aldridge Talks Beauty and Wellness:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. And that's exactly what happened to French figure skater Gabriella Papadakis during her routine with partner Guillaume Cizeron.According to Yahoo Sports, Papadakis suffered a wardrobe malfunction during the pair's ice dancing Olympics routine that caused the top of her costume to come undone, exposing her left breast for a few moments. The costume had a halter top (though it did include additional shoulder straps), and in the beginning moments of the routine, Cizeron's hand must've accidentally caused it to come loose. However, because of the additional straps, the costume mostly held up except for a few seconds. You wouldn't have known anything had gone wrong by looking at Papadakis' face; she went about the rest of the routine flawlessly, like a true professional.She did address the mishap afterwards saying, "It was my worst nightmare happening at the Olympics. It happened in the first few seconds [of the routine]. I told myself I didn’t have a choice; I have to keep going.” She told reporters that she got through the rest of the routine by praying. Even with the malfunction, she kept a positive attitude, saying, "I think we should be proud we were able to deliver a strong performance with that happening." Alice’s powder-blue dress tumbles down a rabbit hole, Dorothy’s gingham version survives cyclones and new lands, and Wendy’s sky-colored nightgown flutters into the night. In To Catch a Thief, Grace Kelly’s Frances is seen wearing an ethereal blue gown when she meets the retired cat burglar who will free her from the monotony of life; and in Westworld, Dolores’s seeking nature is reflected by a bodiced blue. With the forthcoming release of Disney's Beauty and the Beast, we will once again meet Belle, who yearns for “so much more than this provincial life” as she strolls around the town clad in blue linen.And as Goethe observed, we are indeed compelled to follow.Judy Garland as Dorothy in The Wizard of Oz.According to Leatrice Eiseman, executive director of the Pantone Color Institute, our near-universal inclination toward the cool color can be partially attributed to the sky. “It's something to look forward to, to see that blue sky,” says Eiseman. “It’s dependable. It's reliable. It might cloud up, but we know it’s there.” These positive connotations—dependability, constancy, loyalty—may explain why the hue was traditionally attributed to boys, as the qualities, should they stick, could commingle to create a strong, decent man.But what happens when the color is given over to girls? Onscreen, their diminutive worlds tend to expand. “You’re adding a bit of power to the character by giving her the blue,” says Eiseman. “It's a very subtle way of saying, ‘Yeah, but young women, young girls, can be empowered, too.’”Emma Watson as Belle in Disney's Beauty and the Beast.Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Such is the case for Belle, who, after expressing a desire for “adventure in the great wide somewhere,” encounters new experience in wholly unexpected guise. And it’s the blue dress, worn while she devours books and aids in her father’s inventions, that serves as a physical symbol of her impending transition from a limited reality to an eye-opening one.Costume designer Jacqueline Durran, who helped bring Beauty and the Beast to life with her tangible takes on the original animated attire, says the shade fits Belle's role as an active heroine. “There is a sort of refinement and crispness to light blue, but there's also blue in workwear,” she explains. “It is a practical color, and a color that you can work in. In that sense, it is full of active strength.”For Durran, the use of the iconic blue was a given, but she knew the costume had plenty of room for improvement. “It was important to play with the textures and subtly introduce pattern and detail into the blue,” says Durran, who drew inspiration from eighteenth-century France. Underneath Belle’s embroidered skirt, there's a printed white petticoat layered over a pair of bloomers (long trouser-style underwear), which allowed for more movement than a floor-grazing frock. “The bloomers were really popular with Emma [Watson],” she says. “She was always wanting to pull up the skirt and show the bloomers underneath.”A peek at the bloomers worn by Emma Watson in Beauty and the Beast.The ensemble was made even more utilitarian with the addition of external pockets. “During that era, women had pockets that were on strings, which they tied around their waist under the dress, with a slit in the dress for access,” says Durran. “But because Belle is concerned less with her appearance and more with being practical, she wants her pockets to be on the outside, so the useful things are right there when she needs them. It's a bit like having an eighteenth-century tool belt.”While the blue of Belle’s dress was preordained, it was still a factor in filming, and steps were taken to ensure viewers took note of the hue. “Though we didn't completely take blue out of the village, Belle is distinct within the town as the only one who wears a column of blue,” says Durran. “She stands out as different than her environment.”And therein lies the essence of the blue dress. Whether worn by a Disney princess or an A.I. country girl stuck painting the same horse-freckled landscape, the skyward tone hints at a woman to whom viewers should pay attention—a woman bound for more.Love the color blue? A single mother named Vi Erker, wearing a skirt suit, hugs a child on a suburban lawn. At first glimpse, the women in photographer Charlotte Brooks’s photographs appear to live very different lives. The women’s clothing and settings indicate their distinct roles in American society at a particular point in time. During her tenure at Look magazine from 1951 to 1971 when the publication closed, Brooks photographed several stylish celebrities of her era as well: Audrey Hepburn, Lucille Ball, and Jean Seberg (who starred in Jean-Luc Godard’s Breathless).According to Ileana Selejan, the curator of the first-ever retrospective of Brooks’s work—which opens on September 28 at the Davis Museum at Wellesley College—the similarities of the subjects in the images rather than the differences point to Brooks’s real interest: the struggles of working women across class, ethnicity, and occupation. While the clothing in the photos provides clues into the women’s lives, Selejan says that it reveals more of a “sociological perspective on fashion.” Brooks herself was one of only a small group of women in her era that worked as full-time photographers, and she lobbied for women’s rights and equal pay. Selejan also noted that the male photographers at Look fought over the fashion assignments, so Brooks didn’t receive many herself.La Lupe performing in 1970.“Brooks basically stalked La Lupe for a couple days,” Selejan told Allure. At that point, the singer was already famous, “very extravagant, very diva-like.” When she went shopping, she’d exit a store and find her fans outside, begging for autographs. Though Brooks captured the glamour, which is evident in the printed image included in the exhibition, she also photographed a more relatable side of the woman and her private, domestic life.Brooks took a similar approach when she shot photos of comedian Lucille Ball. “It was about her going home and spending time with her daughter and kind of everyday interactions,” said Selejan. With Seberg, too, the image is “about the all-American girl coming back home after her glamorous life in Paris and Hollywood.”While presenting the subjects in a less gilded manner might have made them more relatable to the magazine readers, Selejan also believes that this kind of portrayal was particularly important to Brooks. She describes the photographer as an empathetic documenter of women attempting to succeed in all types of circumstances. “A majority of the stories are not about famous people,” she said. “It’s really about everyday challenges and how they impacted huge numbers of people…most women will have encountered similar struggles that these women encountered themselves.”RELATED: Yayoi Kusama's "Infinity Mirrors" to Go on a TourFor a story about Joan Murray, one of the first African-American woman to report the news for a major network show, Brooks captured the extensive lengths to which her subject went to present herself. “The photographs and also the text place a lot of emphasis on her appearance,” said Selejan. In the images, she puts on her makeup and picks out her clothing. “With Brooks, I think she’s interested in how elaborate the process is.” Regardless of how talented these women were, they had to worry about superficial details that men could neglect.In gowns, suits, and meticulously applied makeup, the subjects in the exhibition’s images provide a glimpse into the conditions for women (including Brooks herself) at a particular point in time. They ask us to reconsider how equity can still be improved. "Charlotte Brooks at Look, 1951—1971" reveals how photographers can shape a national narrative about the way we live and draws the public’s eye to certain societal concerns not unfamiliar today.Josina Anderson, the first-and-only female NFL Insider, on what it takes to get "camera ready":Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Designers seem to be stuck in a perpetual #TBT, churning out fresh takes on past trends and bringing back some of our old favorites. The latest designer to join the old-is-new-again club is Isabel Marant. Through a partnership with fashion retailer Net-a-Porter, the designer is relaunching the Otway and the Soono boots next week.When the suede styles debuted as part of Marant’s 2009 collections, both styles sold out almost instantaneously, despite having hefty four-figure price tags (starting at $1,180). Even before the boots became available for purchase, the brand was hounded with inquiries about pre-orders and advance pairs. Definition cult favorite.“The reaction we received the first time we launched the Soono and Otway was incredible. Since then, we’ve noticed that both styles have become cult pieces with women scouring the internet to find them,” Lisa Aiken, fashion director at Net-a-Porter, tells Allure.Isabel Marant spring 2009 collectionRELATED: The Ultimate Fall Fashion Shopping GuideYour days of searching on eBay are long gone: The Isabel Marant boots are back for real. The exclusive Net-a-Porter partnership means shoe aficionados can now get their hands on a fresh recut of the Otway style, which features chain detail and comes in black and taupe, and the studded Soono cone heel boots in black.“The Soono and Otway are both timeless and chic wardrobe pieces that are not only fashionable but also functional with a mid-heel,” says Aiken. Thanks to the chain and stud detailing, the Isabel Marant boots totally nail the rock-and-roll twist on a classic. Plus, the cut makes yours leg look ultra-slimming.Isabel Marant Sonoo bootsRELATED: The Easiest Way to Transition Your Wardrobe Into Fall? Taking a cue from street-style vintage label finds, designers are reissuing capsule collections packed with iconic faves, like Tommy Hilfiger’s 90s throwback collection at Urban Outfitters, Levi’s classic 505 relaunch and Adidas’s Kate Moss-inspired resurrection of the Gazelle sneakers that will all have you wishing you’d hung on to your original versions. “More than ever, the idea of trends is in flux and fashion is defined by personal style,” says Aiken. “For me it’s about zeroing in on those cult pieces that have longevity in your wardrobe.”Allure Fashion Director Rachael Wang Shares Her Fashion Tips:Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The listing in question, which is seeking a “Senior Brand Manager” for plus-size fashion in the Seattle area, reads: "Amazon is looking for a passionate industry veteran, with the proven ability to create credible fashion assortments and establish a strong point of view to lead the product and merchandising strategy for one or more brands within Softlines Private Label.”The rest of the details on the job listing are in line with what any buyer for a major fashion brand would do, and it doesn’t give any specifics about what the brand will look like. However, Amazon has enjoyed success with its current in-house brands, specifically womenswear labels Society New York, James & Erin, and Lark & Ro—all of which currently carry select items in plus sizes. There are also chic clothes from brands, including Melissa McCarthy Seven7 and Vince Camuto. Amazon is also reportedly launching an in-house lingerie line with bras for $10. Yes, the company seems to be taking over the world.Though there has recently been a shift towards inclusivity in the fashion industry—with brands such as Nike and online styling service Stitch Fix launching plus-size collections—the plus-size womenswear market remains largely untapped. As Racked reports, 65 percent of American women wear a size 14 or larger, and the plus-size market is a $20 billion industry, it’s kind of crazy that it’s taken the industry this long to recognize the need for stylish and affordable plus-size womenswear. Just this year, beloved retailers Charlotte Russe, Victoria's Secret, Gap, Abercrombie & Fitch, and plenty more have closed numerous stores nationwide. According to surfacing reports, Forever 21 may be joining their ranks.Earlier this month, Bloomberg reported that the retailer was struggling to secure financing from outside lenders, and on August 28 it published an article speculating that the company could be preparing for a "potential bankruptcy filing," based on information from "people with knowledge of the plans." Forever 21 did not respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.According to Bloomberg, the fast-fashion retailer is  working with a team of financial advisers and has been in talks with outside lenders for additional financing. However, sources told the publication that conversations about that funding have been stalled. What a potential bankruptcy would mean for shoppers is the closure of as many unprofitable Forever 21 store locations as the company, its vendors, and its lenders see fit — the specific amount has yet to be confirmed by the company or reported by any media outlets. Allure has reached out to Forever 21 for a statement on the matter.This potential bankruptcy is just one example of many financial crises other retailers in the industry have faced within the past year. Charlotte Russe filed for chapter 11 in February and closed nearly 100 before reopening under the guidance of new ownership. In April, Victoria's Secret announced the closure of 53 stores in North America and cancelled its annual televised runway show. Gap Inc. also announced in February its plans to close 230 Gap stores after a plunge in sales.Forever 21's financial struggle is also reflected in its public reputation, which it has recently struggled to uphold. Most recently, customers on Twitter chastised the retailer for mailing diet bars with plus-size online clothing orders, after which it issued an apology. In 2018 it was accused of selling a T-shirt design that resembled that of an independent creator. Months after that, Forever 21 came under fire for featuring a Black Panther sweater on a white model; it promptly issued an apology and removed the photo from its site.Controversy aside, Forever 21 is one of the retail industry's biggest remaining real estate tenants in the shopping mall industry, according to Bloomberg. Should it shutter its doors, it would only be the nail in the coffin of an already dying industry. Earlier this month, Business Insider reported that more than 8,000 brick-and-mortar stores have closed in 2019, endangering malls and shopping centers everywhere. If a giant like Forever 21 is having reported trouble staying afloat in the digital age, what's going to be left?Now, read more on fashion:Now, see what it's secretly like to be a fashion supermodelDon't forget to follow Allure on Instagram and Twitter.asGabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade’s 12-Year-Old Son Wore Fake Nails, and Some Idiots Got Upset About ItDr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. What’s missing? A bra of the push-up, underwire variety. “I just don’t see the point in wearing one,” the 31-year-old says. Richards would rather go au naturel or slip on a bralette—the less structured, more laidback style that’s become the underpinning of the moment.Fashion trendsetters such as Kendall Jenner and Gigi Hadid have been frequently seen sporting the relaxed, unrestrained style, while designers, including Alessandro Michele (of Gucci) and Marc Jacobs, sent out a host of sheer and airy bra tops on the runway for spring/summer 2016. Even Victoria's Secret, the brand best known for its cleavage-enhancing push-up bras, released a collection of bralettes this year.Gucci spring 2016While Richards concedes that she doesn’t have “much to hold up,” the barely-there bralette has qualities of ease and comfort that appeal to modern, millennial-minded women. “I think there’s been a movement toward wearing less and less in the way of bras,” says Marissa Vosper, 31, who together with Lauren Schwab, co-founded lingerie company Negative Underwear in 2014. Their Sieve Non-Wire bralette has become so popular that it’s sold out twice (there’s currently a waitlist). Vosper credits its success to the rise of athleisure and an emphasis on casual undergarments that don’t constrain your body. “It’s more about how you feel than just look,” she says. Minus the sharp underwire, bulky padding and frilly embellishments that often come with traditional bras, the undone bralette is a—radically—fresh alternative.For many brands, the nonconformist, come-as-you-are attitude of the bralette is their major selling point. New York-based lingerie designer Araks Yeramyan, 41, whose namesake line is a favorite among millennials and fashion influencers such as Leandra Medine and Michelle Williams, notes that the minimalist design show off your natural shape, quirks and all. “In a soft cup, everyone’s chest looks different, it gives you a sense of those imperfections,” she says. It’s the antidote to the normcore bra, with its stiffly molded, contoured cups, “where every chest looks the same,” she says.  Or as Vosper puts it: “It’s about owning what you’ve got, versus the whole shapewear get-up that makes you look like someone else.”Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Still, there’s a fine line between loosening up and letting it all hang out. Some element of support is essential for those who aren’t members of the A-cup tribe. Los Angeles-based intimates designer TyLynn Nguyen, 29, who recently had her second baby and has subsequently gone up a few cup sizes, says that the construction of her bralettes prevents any side-boob or nipple mishaps. “Having an elastic that’s primarily made of nylon or lycra is very important,” she says. “That way, you have stretch and proper hold, but the feel is still soft and it doesn’t dig into the skin.” She also utilizes a curved seam down the center of her triangle cups. “It helps shape your breasts a little,” she says.The History of the Bra:Vosper, meanwhile, opts for performance-level fabrics in her Negative Underwear pieces. “We use a technical form of power-mesh that supports a larger cup size,” she explains, adding that there’s a middle seam that “connects both cups and helps with separation, so [you] get a more curved neckline.” The more straight-across cuts can land you in sports-bra territory or, worse, the dreaded mono-boob situation. Yeramyan combines flattering styling with functionality: She will often double up her Araks bralettes, wearing the brand’s Lara and Uma styles in contrasting colors—they not only look chic under a sheer top, but also lend support.From top: Negative Underwear non-wire bra, $55 (negativeunderwear.com); Araks Uma bralette, $125 (araks.com); TyLynn Nguyen Petit Noir bra, $320 (tylynnnguyen.com)Dr. Pimple Popper Made the Switch to Paid Video, and Fans Are Not PleasedTaylor Swift Looks Totally Different With Side-Swept BangsKourtney Kardashian Says People Are Jealous of Her Son’s “Tarzan Hair”Much of the bralette movement, of course, is about intentionally showing it off—an idea that sound pretty great in the heat of summer. New York-based designer Haley Boyd of the super-coveted shoe line Marais USA, often opts to wear Caron Callahan bralettes as a form of a crop top, pairing it with a full skirt. “I love that it’s made from cotton canvas and has this retro ‘50s vibe,” the 31-year old says. Nguyen also wears her namesake brand’s Petit Noir bra as a top, pairing it with high-waist jeans and a blazer thrown over her shoulders, “so you can just see my midriff.”RELATED: Calvin Klein Launches Its Prettiest Lingerie YetFor a slightly less exposed but equally subversive look, Nguyen is fond of wearing a “pristine button-up that’s unbuttoned to the point where it’s almost a little too risky, so you can see that little peek of lace edge.” Still, there are certain situations that do call for a bit of modesty. Richards says she would pair a Only Hearts bralette with a sheer Rick Owens T-shirt, so you can see a subtle hint of it. Vosper, on the other hand, is all about loose tank tops—with scooped necklines, low backs, and wide armholes—that reveal more or less of her underpinnings, and exude breathability.When the heat is really on (like: now!), the easiest option might be to ditch the bra entirely, which offers its own form of freedom. Richards will often go that route with a summer dresses or anything with a cut-out, a style that’s been all over the runways lately—from Jason Wu’s backless dresses to Victoria Beckham’s shoulder-baring corseted tops, which makes wearing a bra more complicated than its worth. Besides, now is the time to just do your own thing sans lingerie, says Boyd, who is channeling the vibe of Kate Moss braless in her Calvin Klein shirts, circa 1993. “Everything about that look is so paired back—to the point where you’re not even wearing a bra,” she says, wistfully. “It’s so simple and sexy.”See what's inside Diane Lane's makeup bag:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast.
