Typically, the content of the site or app is used to make inferences about your interests, which inform future selection of advertising and/or content.Select All3 PurposesConsent PurposesLocation Based AdsConsent AllowedLegitimate Interest PurposesPersonalizeFeaturesLocation Based AdsClear FlitersYou may not realize it, but Sam McKnight has probably influenced the way your hair looked at some point in your life. Over the past 40 years, the Scottish-born hairstylist has cut and coiffed the hair of some of the most famous women in the world, style and beauty icons like Kate Moss, Princess Diana, Madonna, and Lady Gaga. He’s worked for the most prestigious fashion houses in Europe (Chanel, Fendi, Burberry, to name a few), and he’s been featured in every major fashion and beauty magazine you can imagine (including multiple appearances in Allure dating back to as early as 1992). He may not own a salon or have his own line of products (although—fingers crossed—he’s considering the latter), but McKnight is arguably one of the most important, most influential people in the hair and fashion industry of the past four decades. And never has that been more clear than today, when his book, Hair by Sam McKnight, officially goes on sale on Amazon; the publication will be followed by an exhibition at Somerset House in London starting November 2. “It’s not really a hair book,” McKnight told me during fashion week in Milan. “It’s a reference book of hair and fashion over the past 40 years through my eyes and my hands. It’s my story.” Which is why I wanted to let McKnight tell his own tale of how this book came to be.On why he wanted to do a book:“I was so fed up carrying around 40 years worth of magazines and tear sheets. They've been with me in every house, in every apartment, and when I moved into my current home five years ago, the amount of space they were taking up was ridiculous. I said, 'I'm not doing this again; it’s going on digital,' and the woman who was doing the digital archive for me happened to work for Somerset House. She showed my archive to them and that was the catalyst for them wanting to do the exhibition with me. I had been talking with people about doing a book for a while—the same people at Rizzoli who did Kate Moss’s book—but we hadn’t decided what it should be. After meeting with Somerset House, I realized, OK, the book should be an archive of the past 40 years. Having said all that, I kept the papers and the magazines. They’re just in storage now.”On what you’ll find inside:“It’s a chronology of my work, starting at the beginning, when I was working in New York City in the 1980s. To tell that story, the chapters are broken up by looks and styles that have become my trademarks over the years, as well as the major influences throughout my career, like Kate Moss, Karl Lagerfeld, Princess Diana, and the collaborations backstage at fashion shows. The pictures are a mix of my own personal photos, professionally shot photos from backstage, and my editorial work. For the editorial images, I tried to include some that haven’t been overexposed. It’s hard with Google now, but I did try to throw in a few things you wouldn’t find searching the Internet.”The biggest challenge of making a book:“The hardest part was the beginning, when I was like, How on earth do we put this together? Once I got over that, the hardest part was letting go of the images we couldn’t include because there was just not room. It was so hard narrowing down the nearly 40,000 editorial images because there are so many good ones and it feels like you’re losing a child when you edit them out. As for the personal photos, that was easy. I’d just look at them and say, 'No, too fat in this one, too old in that one.'”On how he got into the industry:“When I was 18 or 19, I was in college, training to be a teacher. But I was bored. My friends in Scotland owned a hair salon, as well as a restaurant and a disco, which were all in the same complex. I tried to DJ. I tried to work in the restaurant, but I was no good. I found myself helping out at the salon, sweeping up and driving the van, and then one day I tried blow-drying hair and thought, Well, I could do this. It really was by accident. Some people are very serious about their career path. Me, still to this day, I have no big plan. I take it as it comes.”On his big break:“My first cover shoot for British Vogue in 1977 with photographer Eric Bowman. I was terrified. But it was also the moment when I realized that this is what I want to do—I don’t want to work in a salon. I guess you'd consider it my big break because they kept calling me again and again afterward. I lasted two more years at the salon I was working at in London, and then I moved to New York City, where I got straight into shooting with American Vogue and Irving Penn and Bruce Weber. There was work every day, every evening, trips to the Caribbean. Not that I knew it back then, but it was the golden age of fashion photography.”On the biggest lesson he's learned over the years:"Too keep my mouth shut. Not at all times, but learning that it's not all about you. Because in the beginning, I thought it was all about me, which I think everyone does when they're young. So learning when it's the right time to speak up and when it's just best to stay quiet. The other big lesson I've learned is that you can be really talented, incredibly gorgeous, but if it's not your time, it's not going to happen. Like everything in life, it's all about timing."Watch top models and designers in the industry talk about what makes Sam McKnight so special:On how the hair and fashion industries have changed:"There is so much demand for change these days and expectation to change, which is different from the past, when change happened as a spontaneous reaction to something, when change happened as a natural progression, an evolution. I think there is a lot of pressure for change now, just with all the [fashion] collections that have to be done and the Internet in general. I know a lot of people, myself included, are bored with that and are wanting to take more time to concentrate on their work. But I'm rambling. The other way the hair industry has changed is the modern products and modern tools. The technologies have come leaps and bounds since I started doing hair and that has been what has helped us do all these crazy things we do, ten times a day, backstage at the shows or on set. Twenty years ago, for example, if you put grease in a model's hair for the first fashion show of the day, she has greasy hair for two weeks. Now, you can have grease products that are water-soluble so that they just wash out quickly, and because we have so many dry [styling] products, we now don't even have to wet a girl's hair to get a change. We have products that allow us to make fast changes, but fast changes that don't compromise the health of the hair."On the Somerset House exhibition:“It's not an exhibition of the book. It’s similar, and some of my work will be on display, but the exhibition is more about showing the cultural context of hair and fashion over the past 40 years. Shonagh Marshall, the curator at Somerset House, also felt that people want to see what they can’t see on Google, so we’re exposing the process of creating a hairstyle for a photo shoot or fashion show and the collaboration that goes into it. One of the first exhibits is one of our kit bags—we’ve built what looks like a backstage area, and we’ve re-created some of the looks from past shows on wigs, so it’s a whole process. For me, it’s a way to highlight the hairdressing trade. The hairdressing trade is always thought of by the public as salons. But that’s not what we do, so this helps explain that. I also hope it will help give inspiration to young people who want to get into the business.”On including Princess Diana in his book:“I still don’t talk too much about my time with Diana. And the chapter in the book isn't a tell-all or me divulging any secrets. I just put my favorite pictures of her along with a couple of funny little stories that I’ve told before. You know what, it was a hugely important part of my career. For me, I got to see places and things and meet people through that relationship that I would never, in a million years, have done if I hadn’t been a hairdresser. It was because of my trade that all of that stuff happened and that’s kind of what I’m saying with the book and the exhibition—that when you have a trade like this, there is no limit to the possibilities.”Executive Producer/Director/Journalist: Karen Morrison, DP Cameraman/Giovanni SicignanoVideo by MODTVRELATED LINKS:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Gucci featured pearls and studs on the heels of its Peyton loafers. Chanel and Nicholas Kirkwood have been experimenting with the lustrous orbs on footwear, too, while Dries Van Noten put forth a collection that included an array of pearl-encrusted sweaters, dresses, sheer gloves, and block heels. Last year, Pat McGrath glued pearl studs on models’ faces for Riccardo Tisci’s macabre, Victorian-inspired collection for Givenchy.A look from Dries Van Noten's fall 2016 collection.All this and yet not a sight of the traditional strands of pearls we know best—as seen draped around the necks of Hollywood icons and royals around the world.New York City-based stylist Micaela Erlanger, who has dressed clients such as Lupita Nyong’o and Jared Leto, says the latest pearl extravaganza is focused on not reinventing, but reinterpreting the wheel. Pearls have been a wardrobe staple for years, but fashion’s latest unconventional take on these classic gems shows that they are ready to be taken out of their ladylike element and become a statement piece of their own.Lupita Nyong'o at the Academy Awards in 2015.Take it from Lupita Nyong’o, who, dressed by Erlanger, wore a Calvin Klein gown covered in 6,000 pearls and the aforementioned pearl-studded Nicholas Kirkwood platform heels at the Academy Awards in 2015. The eye-catching gown showcased the use of pearls as a textural decoration rather than just a chaste accessory.RELATED: How You Should Carry Fall's New "It" BagsKnown as the world’s oldest gem, the earliest form of pearl as jewelry was found in Elam, now better known as modern-day Iran, and it dates all the way back to the 4th century B.C. In contemporary fashion, icons such as Princess Diana and Grace Kelly have all donned the simple strands. Coco Chanel was possibly the gem’s biggest fashion fan—she sported heaping piles of pearl necklaces over everything from the little black dress to striped tees.“I love pearls as an unexpected accessory,” says Erlanger. “I think they’re so whimsical. There’s something so ladylike about them, but when you balance [the jewels] with the ‘70s quirk that we’re seeing a lot of, they feel cooler.”According to Erlanger, the key to pulling off the trend in real life is to wear them as a subtle statement accessory. You don’t have to don an entire ball gown covered in the real thing, but the look works best when you use the gems as an accent to your outfit. “Pick a uniform, a base, then you jazz it up with your pearl accessories,” says Erlanger. “I would stay away from the traditional A-line tea-party dress shapes. It’s too Jackie O. Wear it with jeans and a T-shirt—think about the juxtaposition.”For the world’s oldest accessory, the future is looking bright.Dries Van Noten Fall 2016 Ready-to-Wear:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Zara's inventory is always on point, leaving many coworkers asking, “Who are you wearing?” when the answer is, naturally, Zara. Ad ChoicesThis nail art is the merry manicure inspo you've been looking for.Everyone has a different way of celebrating the holidays. Some go full-throttle, wearing a different "ugly" Christmas sweater for every day of December, decking their halls (and the entire exterior of their homes) with more lights than Paris, and practicing for a perfect cork-pop on New Year's Eve. Others prefer a more subtle approach, hardly dabbling in the traditional red-and-green shades of the season, preferring hints of sparkle over in-your-face festiveness.The same goes for holiday manicures. If you're picturing your nails covered in three-dimensional merry motifs — perhaps a cotton-bearded Santa and all of his reindeer, complete with pointy antlers and working light-up nose for Rudolph — there's a nail artist who can make that happen for you. Prefer a simple coat of silver that will take you through to 2020? Your polish options are endless.There's really no wrong way to get your nails ready for the holidays, but if you're having a hard time deciding on what manicure to get in these jovial last couple weeks of the year, we've rounded up some of our favorites. From Instagram's greatest nail artists to Fashion Week inspiration to our very own editor in chief Michelle Lee's lovely hands, you'll find the perfect holiday-party mani that's right for your particular level of spirit.All products featured on Allure are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.Paintbox put it best in describing this option available at its salons: "Sophisticated negative space tempers ultra-luxe, luminous glitter." And while this would look amazing with a glitter polish in any color, the green makes it a perfect, festive pick for the holidays.Stick-on star nail art was trending all summer, but it carries over beautifully into the winter, especially with the extra touch of glitter alternating between the tips and cuticles on otherwise bare nails, like in this Olive & June masterpiece.Prefer your stars painted on? Try this manicure by Betina Goldstein. She used Lauren B. Beauty's gorgeously glittery 33 Carats polish to paint stars on her bare nails, defining them with the brand's black Paparazzi polish.Tortoiseshell nails have been having a capital-M Moment, and they're made holiday-perfect by simply switching up the usual color scheme of browns and yellows to one focused on greens, like this manicure by nail artist Savannah Walker.Seen on the runway during Christian Siriano's Spring 2020 New York Fashion Week show, these nails are perhaps the most holiday-ready take on the French manicure resurgence. The light green tips (Essie's Turquoise & Caicos) pick up on the minty vibes of the season, while the sparkly silver flecks (Essie's Set in Stones) feel like snowfall.No polish is required for this elegant nail art idea by Betina Goldstein. Glued-on faux pearls in two rows down the center of each nail are reminiscent of snowballs ready to be thrown at family members visiting for the holidays.There's plenty of champagne to be enjoyed around the holidays, so let that extend to your fingertips with this simple yet stunning frosty manicure created with OPI's Many Celebrations to Go to from the brand's Hello Kitty collection.Another shade that looks super-festive when it's especially shimmery: green, of course. This KB Shimmer nail polish shade, Vested Interest, is a multichrome color pack with holographic flakes that will remind you of snow glistening on evergreen trees.An ombré French manicure (sometimes called a "baby boomer" manicure) seems like just another pretty mani any other time of year, but it has a magically snowy feel around the holidays. Dress it up a little for holiday parties by adding a metallic dot near the cuticle, like Savannah Walker did.Red nails are always appropriate for the holidays, but you can update the classic look with a chic negative-space twist like Miss Pop did for the Prabal Gurung Fall 2019 show with the berry-hued Zoya nail polish shade Vanessa.The curved, deep green polish partially covering each nail is dressed up in this Paintbox manicure with a wavy swipe of glimmering gold, making the manicure look like beautifully wrapped little gifts.Allure editor chief Michelle Lee's red and black buffalo plaid manicure will make you want to throw on some flannel and chop down your own Christmas tree.New York City-based manicurist Marilyn Garcia gave her client a sophisticated spin on wintry dark green with striped tips and a pretty, pale base.Artsy swipes of red, green, gold and black really stand out on the white base painted by New Orleans' M.A.D. Nails.Worried you can't paint 10 perfect stars? Miss Pop proves that painting partial stars on a few nails gives this manicure a stylish twist, especially with all the rhinestones added on top.There's no snow in South Florida, but Boca Raton's Nails by Marcy proves there's still plenty of holiday spirit with this holly-inspired manicure. The red berries are even three-dimensional.There was no need to expertly dot polish onto the red and gold base of this manicure — manicurist Marisa Carmichael used tiny, reflective stickers for an extra-perfect finish.Who says a manicure requires nail polish? Naomi Yasuda attached crystals of different shapes and sizes to Tina Leung's long, uncolored nails, adding glamour to literally everything she'll do with her hands.Manicurist  Mar y Sol Inzerillo is responsible for our latest holiday nail obsession: this red-and-white-striped candy cane imitation she posted to Instagram with the caption, "🤤❣️❌⭕️❣️🤶🏻🎅🏻🎄🎁 Candy cane peppermint patty #nails are always a good idea! Don't you agree?" Of course we do.This mesmerizing manicure by Hamptons-based nail artist Regina Rodriguez is all you need to accessorize any basic black and white party look. The shimmering rainbow hues will catch the light wherever you walk, so people are bound to be asking you about your digits all night.The nail artist known as @fresh.claws on Instagram made this gorgeous holiday look come to life with different colored jewels and metallic accent, which gave the finished look a whimsical "Christmas lights" effect.Nail artist Katie Masters took Christmas cuteness to new levels with this nail look, which consisted of tiny bird-inspired Santas and dainty holiday trinkets, like cranberries and hanging ornaments.Inspired by the night sky, Natalie Minerva of @nail_swag on Instagram created this magical star and moon-studded masterpiece, which stood out beautifully against the pale, shimmering ivory base shade.Allure's senior social media manager Danielle Odiamar is the brains behind this gorgeous, millennial-pink and glitter nail look. "Some pre-holiday sparkle ✨ I painted the glitter polish onto a foundation sponge and dabbed it on the tips of each nail — a super easy and fast #nailart hack I snagged from @heymichellelee!" she wrote on Instagram. Running late to a holiday soiree? This five-minute look will save the day.Allure's commerce editor Lauren Swanson got in the holiday spirit this year with nail art; namely this adorable candy cane creation she says was inspired by Paintbox. To get the look, she used Jin Soon's red and gold glitter polishes (and scotch tape for the precise diagonal lines.)Ugly Christmas sweater was the name of the game when it came to this Santa and candy cane-centric design, which was crafted by Elle, aka @enamelle on Instagram.We adore the contrast of the deep, moody merlot base color paired with silver and gold crystals — the perfect design for completing any holiday party ensemble this season.Holiday nail inspo courtesy of Blake Lively's digits. The same Elle of @enamelle on Instagram gave the A Simple Favor star a basecoat of glittery black polish before crafting an adorable mini martini glass for Lively's ring finger.To re-create these majestic, winter snowstorm-themed nails, you'll need crystals from your local craft store, a tiny detail tool to make your snowflake, and various shades of white, creamy ivory, pale pink, and blue.We can't get over this ornate creation by nailee_yj, which used tiny pearl, crystal, and sequined appliques to form Christmas trees.An organized cluster of sequins, diamond studs, and stars made for the most epic festive mani on Glossier founder, Emily Weiss, which was created by nail extraordinaire Naomi Yasuda.These geometric, sequin-emblazoned nails are the work of nail technician Damisa Ramdin, who used shimmering bronze and ivory accents against the baby-pink base shade for a festive finish.International nail artist Tracylee is the mastermind behind this holiday-perfect creation, which is complete with emerald appliques and glittery half moons to match. One, solid shimmering gold nail ties everything together.Mia of @superflynails on Instagram is responsible for this work of art consisting of little gold stars and silver circles set over a clear base.Brooklyn-based nail artist Savannah Walker incorporated the most prominent colors of the season into glittery vertical stripes. She switched up the order of the colors on each finger to make the look even more interesting.Portland nail artist Sarah Kane put a retro spin on this manicure, featuring shapes that look straight out of the intro to a 1960s Christmas TV special. The matte finish on a nude base gives the fun design a more subtle look.It's simple yet super festive: Los Angeles nail artist Glennis McCarthy coated her client's nails in what she calls a "green glitter bomb" as a glamorous way to celebrate with a single color.Seen backstage at New York Fashion Week, these low-key jolly nails take the traditional white tips of a French manicure and add a cool swipe of mint green. It's a perfect holiday manicure for minimalists.Miss Pop used real diamonds from nail-art jeweler Vero Krew to create this especially luxurious holiday manicure for Nail Pro. There's no better season for nails covered in ice.Classic red is perfect for Christmas on its own, but the stripes expertly placed by London-based nail artist Jay Deau make her client's ring-finger nails look like they're wrapped in pretty, plaid paper.New York nail artist Naomi Yasuda created a manicure that works all the way through New Year's Eve with multicolored metallic glitter in various sizes and shape. The crystal-confetti effect looks especially gorgeous on stiletto nails.There's so much to celebrate about these nails. Florida-based nail artist Devin Strebler incorporated multiple themes into this manicure, from a cable-knit texture in royal blue to a red gift bow to an incredibly detailed nutcracker. Shimmering gold details and Swarovski crystals make it especially festive.Kane combines the subtlety of glossy, nude nails with eye-catching colors by dotting shimmering circles on her clients nails to create the look of ornaments. They're "strung together" with delicately painted, curving black lines.Spotted backstage at New York Fashion Week, this silver manicure gets a wintry upgrade with snow-like dots scattered not only on the nails, but on one of the fingers as well.Prefer gold over silver? Try a look like this one sported by Allure editor in chief Michelle Lee. Whether she's wearing a cute crop top under a furry jacket or pairing a metallic puffer with a chunky sweater, it’s clear the model has mastered the art of winter fashion.She was recently seen wearing a printed Tory Burch coat, proving that standout outerwear is all you really need to survive the frigid temperature in style. The long jacquard coat from the brand's fall 2015 collection popped against her sleek, all-black outfit, making it the perfect statement piece to wear on the weekends and to a casual holiday party. Hadid kept the rest of her look simple, opting for her tried-and-true Mansur Gavriel Lady bag and a slender choker. The discreet, understated look of the bag balances the loud pattern on the coat, and the pairing also provides the perfect solution for minimalists who might find the vibrant coat a challenge to pull off in an everyday setting.More style inspirations from Gigi:While most of us above the Mason-Dixon line have zipped our coats up to the neck, Hadid opted to leave her coat open for that hurriedly put together look. Take note: If it’s really, really cold where you live, take inspiration from one of the model’s other recent looks and pair a seriously chunky cable-knit turtleneck underneath—you can proudly wear your statement coat open without the fear of getting frostbite. It also provides a great opportunity to show off those heavy sweaters that've been sitting in the back of your closet all year long.Celebs such as Kendall Jenner, Kate Moss, and Rihanna have also experimented with the statement coat this season in variations ranging from printed fur to leopard jackets. Plus, the statement coat was seen all over the runway in the form of extreme puffer jackets from designers like Balenciaga and Vetements. Even labels like J.Crew presented larger-than-life statement coats for fall 2016.Now you know, when planning your #OOTD for your next holiday party, take a tip from Hadid. You don’t have to wear an elaborate dress or even a skirt. Plus, you’re guaranteed to stay warm, no matter how low the temperature may drop.Gigi Hadid's most surprising style moments:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. Ad ChoicesHere’s what Khloé has to say about it.Another day, another controversial Kardashian story. This time, Khloé is front and center, as is her brand Good American. Designer Destiney Bleu claims that designs from Kardashian's new video are reminiscent of styles her own brand sells. Not only that, but she also says Khloé apparently bought one of everything from Bleu's site in December and was never seen wearing any of it before the release of the new video. Hmm...https://twitter.com/destineybleu/status/870733561682210820https://twitter.com/dbleudazzled/status/870760590389633024The garments in question are crystalized bodysuits (something a certain famous friend of the Kardashian-Jenners loves to wear) and the side-by-side photos are enough to raise some eyebrows. However, Good American has made a statement to Cosmopolitan denying the accusations, saying, "Under no circumstances did Good American or Khloe Kardashian infringe on another brand’s intellectual property." They also told Cosmopolitan they're going through legal channels to handle the situation, and Bleu says she's "lawyered up" as well.Though Bleu and her brand Dazzle aren't yet a household name, she's certainly dressed a few, including Ashley Graham, Serena Williams, Beyoncé, and Lady Gaga. Just scrolling through her Instagram is amazing, and everyone she dresses looks fabulous in her designs. Though Good American has said their new bodysuits aren't copies of Bleu's work, we'll have to see how this case shakes out. Heading into the fall '17 shows, many designers used their runways as platforms for social commentary. Some sent out feminist messages via graphic tees and Planned Parenthood buttons, while others spoke to our rich and varied culture by casting a diverse range of models who best represent our multicultural world in age, race, gender, and size.NYFW wrapped with two high-profile shows that made powerful statements about diversity. Marc Jacobs’s cast was nearly half black, and also included a handful of transgender models. Kanye West’s Yeezy Season 5 show starred Halima Aden, the first-ever hijab-wearing model to sign with a major modeling agency.We also witnessed plus-size models truly break through this season, with super Ashley Graham making her NYFW runway debut at Michael Kors, and multiple appearances from curve phenoms Candice Huffine, Marquita Pring, and body-positivity champion Iskra Lawrence.According to The Fashion Spot's post-fashion week Runway Diversity Report, every single runway (116 shows in total) included at least one model of color—a NYFW first. But there's still room for improvement: 31.5 percent of shows and events included models of color, which is a slight improvement over the 30.3 percent we saw last season.Read on for a recap of this season’s most diverse shows, and check back for updates throughout the fall '17 season.Models at the Marc Jacobs showLeave it to Marc Jacobs to end the week with a bang. In a stunning tribute to our country’s melting-pot culture, the designer shook things up with a colorful cast of models including a handful of trans heroes like Casil McArthur and Stav Strashko. Harlem-born Slick Woods opened the show, and it felt like a deliberate statement that approximately half the cast was black (including vitiligo spokesmodel Winnie Harlow). Jacobs has clearly set the diversity bar high for the remainder of this season.Halima Aden at the Yeezy Season 5 showOn Wednesday morning, top agency IMG Models announced it had signed model Halima Aden, who made her runway debut hours later at Kanye West’s hyped Yeezy Season 5 show. The stunning Somali-American, who was born in a Kenyan refugee camp, donned a long, luxe fur coat over her hijab. She made a splash last year as the first Miss Minnesota contestant to wear a hijab and burkini during the pageant. Now, she’s encouraging Muslim women to break down stereotypes on the global fashion stage. Aden was the high point of Yeezy’s all-around diverse cast.Ashley Graham on the runway at the Michael Kors show.Hard to believe that Ashley Graham had never done a major NYFW runway before this season’s Michael Kors show, where she became the first plus-size model to walk for the designer. Graham’s appearance capped off a week that was widely considered a victory for curvier models. At Kors, she joined an impressive roster of seasoned supermodels, including Carolyn Murphy, Amber Valletta, Natasha Poly, Isabeli Fontana, Arizona Muse, and more.A model poses at the Tracy Reese presentation.As one of the most prominent black designers working today, Tracy Reese has always celebrated women of color. This season, her presentation featured a diverse mix of inspiring women, including four poets (Aja Monet, Leslie Reese, Jenny Zhang, and Dorothea Lasky) who stood amongst the models to present their poetry on female empowerment.Liya Kebede on the runway at the Calvin Klein Collection show.Raf Simons’s highly-anticipated debut at Calvin Klein laid out his fresh new vision for the all-American label, which emphasizes a more inclusive approach to model casting. Established runway stars such as Liya Kebede, Elise Crombez, and Kinga Rajzak mixed with a unique crop of youngsters.A cast of models at the J.Crew presentation.J.Crew gained much praise when it enlisted a group of friends and family of the brand to model last season. The American label repeated its successful formula again this week by casting nonmodels from ages 9 to 67, including comedian Sandra Bernhard, street style star Taylor Tomasi Hill, photographer Alice Gao, and a range of personalities.A model on the runway at the Christian Siriano show.Christian Siriano is a longtime champion of body positivity and of making clothes for all types of women. The designer’s fall show included models of diverse ages, races, and sizes. The lineup was bookended by supermodels Alek Wek and Karolina Kurkova, and included a bevy of curvy beauties, including Iskra Lawrence, Candice Huffine, and Marquita Pring.Jesi Taylor walks the runway at the Gypsy Sport show.There’s never been anything typical about Gypsy Sport or the atypical cast of characters representing the brand. This season, designer Rio Uribe stirred up an activist spirit with a fall collection inspired by people who live on the streets. Through a series of open calls and street casting, he assembled a motley crew of game-changing activists, Instagram personalities, and a diverse group of models (like albino activist Diandra Forrest), and even Jesi Taylor, star of Allure’s “Dispelling Beauty Myths” video series.Iskra Lawrence walks the runway at the Chromat show.Diversity is nothing new for Chromat, which has become a hot ticket during NYFW thanks in part to its #woke approach to casting. The swimwear label designed by Becca McCharen has been a pioneer in breaking down barriers for trans, curve, and handicapped models. Highlights from this season’s roster included Iskra Lawrence, Carmen Carrera, and Sabina Karllson.Joan Smalls walks the runway at the Prabal Gurung show.Prabal Gurung set himself apart as a capital-F Feminist this season with his finale series of graphic tees stamped with political slogans. He also demonstrated appreciation for women of all sizes by sending out plus-sized stars Candice Huffine and Marquita Pring alongside household names like Bella Hadid. It was the first domino to fall in a series of victories for curvy models.Imaan Hammam walks the runway at the Brandon Maxwell show.Brandon Maxwell has quickly become one of the most talented young acts during NYFW. All eyes were on Lady Gaga’s fashion director, who closed his fall show with British super Jourdan Dunn, and filled his cast with black beauties (both new and established) from Joan Smalls to Imaan Hammam to Dilone and Adwoa Aboah.Alek Wek on the runway at The Row show.The Row’s Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen make elegant, understated clothes, and often showcase them on more mature models reflective of their refined customer base. This season, the duo cast icons, including Angela Lindvall (38), Erin O’Connor (39), Alek Wek (39), and Kirsten Owen (46). Last season, the brand featured zero models of color, so we're glad there's been an improvement with the casting—here's to a bigger success in fall.Jacky O’Shaughnessy walks the runway at the Tome fashion show.Tome is another label that’s been ahead of the diversity curve for years, and it didn’t disappoint this season. Plus-sized models Candice Huffine and Marquita Pring (who both clearly had a great week) mingled with gray-haired doyenne Jacky O’Shaughnessy and young models of every color.A model on the runway at the Eckhaus Latta show.This cult NYC label has always had an art-school cool vibe, and attracted downtown darlings like artist-models Camille Deterre and India Menuez, who mixed in with a unique street cast and other friends of the brand.Check out the most diverse shows at New York fashion week:How one plus-size model learned to love her body:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesWhen Demna Gvasalia landed at Balenciaga last winter, insiders couldn’t wait to see what the Vetements designer had cooked up for the storied French house. And while there was much to absorb, the hero piece of the collection was a red puffer jacket styled off-the-shoulder and paired with a crystal-embellished turtleneck, minimal envelope clutch, and floral-bedecked satin pumps.In one fell swoop, Gvasalia made the lowly utilitarian jacket—reserved for the most frigid of temperatures—cool and chic. “It may just be my new favorite snow coat this season,” says Hollywood stylist Jamie Mizrahi, whose clients include Katy Perry, Riley Keough, Sasha Lane, and Suki Waterhouse. “I am a fan of the color as well as the warmth.”Gigi Hadid wearing a puffer jacket by Tommy Hilfiger.Now that winter is upon us, how does one brave the elements in style? Taking cues from Gvasalia, there's no need to fear putting on that baggy, voluptuous coat you previously abhorred. Just look at Rihanna, who wore a cotton candy-colored, quilted variation by Ella Boucht during Paris fashion week this year. Even Gigi Hadid sported a metallic puffer coat by Tommy Hilfiger during her recent outing, proving that the style might be replacing the covetable fur as the statement topper of the season—just in time for holidays! “It's definitely the more eco-friendly version instead of a fur,” adds Mizrahi.Rihanna wearing a puffer jacket by Ella Boucht.“Puffers for holiday are the perfect yin and yang of a skinny-to-full look,” says designer Norma Kamali, who created one of the first high-fashion down numbers back in 1973 after using her sleeping bag as a coat when on a camping trip with Bob Currie in the woods. “Think about wearing it with slinky gowns that are close to the body, or sequin leggings with a white graphic T-shirt, leopard turban, and long gloves—just roll the sleeves of the jacket up.”More winter styles we love:Rita Ora wearing a orange coat by Acne Studios.Mizrahi, for her part, suggests looking for more “evening versions” like Stella McCartney's velvet navy coat or Alexander Wang’s chevron-striped cropped jacket. For those on a budget, Zara has a red puffer very similar to the one that was showcased on the runway by Balenciaga.And if you're afraid you'll stick out like a sore thumb at your next holiday soirée, Kamali suggests using the term “festive” as a litmus test because that’s what the season is about—you are celebrating. “Dress happy, cozy, and glamorous all over, and you’ll be set.”Check out Gigi's most surprising style moments:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesOn Wednesday, Peter Copping announced he is leaving Oscar de la Renta after less than two years at the company.Since the founder's death in 2014, Copping has been designing feminine and romantic collections for the company. Though his time was short—after all, he only worked on three ready-to-wear collections, excluding bridal and prefall—a slew of celebrities have donned the creative director's pieces for red carpets, Hollywood parties, and more.Let's take a look back at some of the best of those looks.Sienna Miller at the Oscars in 2015Miller wore one of Copping's gowns from his first Oscar de la Renta collection. The black dress, accented with black velvet bows and lace, stood out on a red carpet full of colorful looks. Copping's fall 2015 collection featured eye-popping geometric prints, ruffled Edwardian blouses, and floor-sweeping gowns rendered in jet black or with touches of black lace.Amanda Seyfried at the Tony Awards in 2015Proving once again that Copping has an elegant approach to combining black and lace in evening attire, Seyfried wore a black off-the-shoulder brocade dress that hit right above the knee. The dress was from the designer's debut collection for Oscar de la Renta, which put a focus on using modern trends, such as off-the-shoulder necklines and subtly sexy lace panels, to make gowns feel fresh again.Diane Kruger at the Venice Film Festival in 2015Kruger wore a floor-length black-and-white gown made of organza, lace, and beads. The flowers on the gown are motifs that Copping has used time and time again, especially in the fall 2015 collection.Carey Mulligan at the Suffragette premiere in Los Angeles in 2015Straight from Copping's spring 2016 show, Carey Mulligan wore a slightly ruffled, lacy lavender dress, which tied in the back like a halter top. For this collection, the designer continued to integrate his trademark lace, feminine bows, florals, and modern silhouettes. The main difference from the designer's debut collection was his approach to color. This collection was full of powder-puff blue, white, and grays.Gwendoline Christie at the Star Wars: The Force Awakens premiere in Los Angeles in 2015The actress wore a custom-made dress that featured the brand's billowing, voluminous silhouette. The gown is comprised of separates: an organza top embellished with velvet bows and a fishtail skirt made out of ten yards of tulle. Ad ChoicesThe British brand joins the "see now, buy now" movement.Fashion week is almost here—really, tomorrow is September. And with its arrival comes a flurry of changes.Today, Topshop Unique announced that consumers will be able to directly buy certain items from its runway show in London on September 18. The goods will be up for grabs at select Topshop stores around the world and on topshop.com.“We see this season’s shift to the runway-to-retail format as the logical conclusion in our drive to democratize fashion and, given Topshop’s real-time fashion model, something that feels like a very natural evolution for the brand,” said Sheena Sauvaire, the brand’s global communications and marketing director.RELATED: Burberry Reveals Details About Its First "See Now, Buy Now" CollectionThe direct-to-consumer concept has been floating around the fashion biz for a while now, with many brands following the new business model (see: Burberry, Tommy Hilfiger, Tom Ford). Misha Nonoo recently announced that she is forgoing the runway entirely and offering up her collection via Snapchat. From her site, you’ll be able to shop the pieces. Normally, retail buyers select what will be in stores, and then you have to wait months to buy the items. But it seems that being a buyer is no longer a secure position to have. Fashion, it is a-changin’.RELATED: Misha Nonoo Opts for a Snapchat-Only ShowSo where will Topshop showcase its new spring 2017 collection? Old Spitalfields Market.“The starting point for the Unique collection is always the celebration of British style and its rich heritage, so we feel Spitalfields provides the perfect backdrop to showcase our new collection,” said Kate Phelan, the brand’s creative director.In keeping with the theme of the venue, Topshop will also open a pop-up stall at the market immediately after the show to sell its new collection.Spitalfields has been a popular shopping destination for centuries, and it’s as British as one can get as far as inspiration goes. Ever since the news of the Brexit, many in the fashion industry have been questioning what the recent political events could mean for their businesses. For Topshop, perhaps focusing on a major destination known for its diversity of people and offerings is the answer.Kendall and Kylie Jenner’s Topshop Collection Revealed:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesIf you’re reading this, you probably like to shop. Money can't buy happiness, but it can buy shoes. And that’s close enough.But, shopping at fast-fashion stores (read: Forever 21) can be a massive headache. Of course, you can shop online, but even that has drawbacks. Without trying on an item first — whether it be shoes, or a fancy dress— you can’t tell if you’ll love it, or if it will fit.That’s where Forever 21’s new online feature comes in. As Cosmopolitan reports, the fast-fashion retailer recently launched a major upgrade to its website, replacing still product shots with short videos of a model wearing the item and modeling it in motion. This provides the shopper with a much clearer idea of the product’s fit, drape and movement, effectively eliminating what is, perhaps, the only drawback to online shopping. Though the new feature hasn’t been rolled out site-wide yet (you’ll only find the videos for a handful of items on Forever 21’s site, we have a feeling it’ll only be a matter of time before the entire website — and the rest of the e-commerce industry  — catches up. Truthfully, we’re a bit mystified nobody thought of using videos as a marketing tool sooner.More reasons to love Forever 21:Unsurprisingly, Twitter is all over the site upgrade, with many pointing out the similarities between Forever 21’s moving ads and the moving pictures imagined in the Harry Potter series. And while we know Forever 21’s new online feature includes GIFs, and not actually enchanted photos, we can’t deny that the effect is, well, magical.Check out the site’s cool new feature below.https://twitter.com/youngshels/status/813123093765980160?ref_src=twsrc%5EtfwNow learn how this model stays superhot at all times:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The heavy-duty fur itself is pretty over-the-top with a silhouette we have a feeling only Rihanna could pull off. Even if the weather called for a statement coat, the look is pretty ridiculous (though we'll admit, those of us on the freezing East Coast can't help but look with envy).More winter style tips from Gigi:Bieber is certainly no stranger to the world of statement-making style. Since outgrowing his signature swoop and purple hoodie, the singer has elevated our expectations for tour merch with both Barneys and more affordable Forever 21 collabs, and he's even spoken candidly about his pre–red carpet beauty routine. And we have to give him credit for his DGAF attitude towards his personal style. Given the crisp collared white button-down, paint-splattered jeans, and vaguely creepy pair of wire-frame aviator glasses Bieber paired with his arctic outerwear, it’s clear the singer isn’t afraid of taking on several trends at once. Ad ChoicesStreet style photos are popular for a good reason. They often show wearable and fun ways to sport new trends in real life—and they’re definitely guilty of encouraging fashion purchases. Lyst, the online shopping tool with a focus on data, is well aware of this, too. While the rest of us were keeping up with the coolest new trends on the runway, the analysts at Lyst collected information on which stylish street style pieces experienced a surge in searches and purchases during the four-week time period. The answers might surprise you.Searches for “plaid,” a classic fall and winter staple, jumped to 61 percent, while sales were increased by 23 percent. The checkered print was also seen on the runways for fall 2017, from brands including J.Crew, Public School, and Junya Watanabe.It was raining in Paris for almost the entire duration of fashion week, so it’s no surprise that shoppers were searching for “vinyl.” The search term increased by 79 percent, and sales rose by 27 percent. Yves Saint Laurent and Raf Simons for Calvin Klein also included a plethora of vinyl dresses for fall 2017.No surprise here. Alessandro Michele's logo-laden Gucci bags were popular in all four cities and coveted by many. So much so that searches increased by a whopping 102 percent, while sales rose by 32 percent.Searches for “white boots,” perhaps one of the most challenging items to pull off, rose by 82 percent, while sales increased by 30 percent. There were plenty of these on Dior’s spring 2017 runway.Whether worn off-the-shoulder or layered underneath a structured coat, this wardrobe staple was a favorite among the fashion set this season. The searches for “striped shirts” rose by 42 percent, while sales increased by 31 percent.You might be wondering what the new “It” sunglasses of the season may be—according to Lyst, look out for an “octagonal” shape, a style favored by brands like Miu Miu and Chloé. Searches for these increased 98 percent, while sales increased by 46 percent.Embroidered jackets, which Jonathan Simkhai and Altuzarra both experimented with for their fall 2017 collections, are a fun way to get in on the customization trend. Searches increased by 78 percent, while purchases increased by 42 percent.Searches for “dark florals,” perhaps inspired by Valentino and Simone Rocha’s flower-covered, black dresses and coats, rose by 62 percent.Thanks to the current socio-political climate, pantsuits made a strong comeback on the runway, specifically in New York where designers experimented with bold hues like pink. Searches jumped 78 percent, and sales increased by 40 percent.The most popular search and increase in sales may be the most surprising due to its simplicity. Searches for red clothing jumped 120 percent, while sales grew by an astonishing 108 percent. Politics may have played a big part behind the surge—last week, many women wore the color as a sign of solidarity for International Women’s Day.More on street style:London's top fashionista shares her style advice:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. In a paper just published in British Medical Journal Open, a University of Michigan Health System team has compiled a supercomprehensive collection of info on the topic, gathered from 30 studies involving 11,533 adult patients in 14 countries. The team also plans to launch their own international study: "Targeting Attire to Improve Likelihood of Rapport," or TAILOR. (I see what your did there, you sassy scientists!) What they've found so far is fascinating.While it seems logical that a slovenly appearance would make a patient uneasy, the perception that a well-dressed doc is more capable and professional does not appear to be universal. There are cultural and generational differerences of opinion. Science Daily reports, "In general, Europeans and Asians of any age, and Americans over age 50, trusted a formally dressed doctor more, while Americans in Generation X and Y tended to accept less-dressy physicians more willingly."Personally, I've only especially taken note of my doctor's clothes when I visited a specialist who wore a right-off-the-runway dress to give me an exam. True story! The dress she had on easily cost over $1,000, and she was wearing it with latex gloves. Weeks later, when I had to have surgery, she came to my hospital bed wearing a dress with fur-trimmed sleeves. At that point, I was already on sleepy drugs, so I laughed uncontrollably at the ultrafancy sight of her. I'm told she did change into scrubs for the surgery itself, but I never saw her in them, so I like to imagine her still wearing that dress and maybe also a jewel-studded capelet and a little crown while she did the deed. (Excellent surgeon, BTW.)My sharp-dressed surgeon aside, this study also reminded me of another anecdote. I'd read years ago that it was important for patients to dress well for a doctor's appointment to get the MD to really listen to their concerns. I hadn't really thought about it since, until a few months ago when, as a new freelancer, I went to a late-afternoon appointment makeup-free and in gym gear (I was planning to run home). Suddenly, a doctor whom I'd previously had a great rapport with while wearing just-came-from-the-office work skirts treated me very differently. Once I'd had my vitals taken, there was a long gap before I was seen by him. (Because I clearly had nowhere to get to?) His greeting to me was unusually cold. During the exam, when I—clad in a Celtics T-shirt, leggings, and a messy ponytail—told him my insurance would change soon because I was phasing out my corporate-chosen plan, he even railed into me about how I would have no job security and being a freelancer would prove to be a huge mistake. He followed that up by saying I'd regret not having kids later in life. Um, cool. Can I get my zit cream refilled now? Visual cues play a huge role in our interactions with others for better and worse. (And clearly that dude is also just kind of a jerk.)Have you ever been impressed or unimpressed by a doctor's clothes? Or felt judged by them because of the way you were dressed?Like Allure on Facebook and get more beauty news and daily tips in your feed.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. Stores in the U.K. are banning mirrors in changing rooms to promote self-confidence."We want to ensure that everyone feels comfortable and confident when trying on clothes, so that's why we're trialing banning the mirrors," Alex Thomas, regional marketing manager of Hammerson, said. "We hope that women in particular will try something on and feel gorgeous and glamorous. Hopefully, this will be a success and we can roll it out across our shopping centers for the summer."The drastic action came about after a study claimed that over 70 percent of British women didn't like what they saw in the changing rooms.But what about if we want to see how something looks on us? We can't be the only ones wondering if this is a bad idea. Not everything we try on is going to be the perfect outfit. Sometimes it takes 10, 15 or even 20 other not-so-ideal looks to hit your jackpot. And if you can't see how something fits—especially in the back—would you buy it?Fitting-room mirrors are pretty much like fun house ones. Depending on the angle and lighting, you can look different from your reflection at home. Some mirrors aim to make you look thinner than you are, in the hopes of selling to you. Last year, Buzzfeed sent a reporter to snap her reflection in 20 different changing rooms. The result? She looked different, tanner, and, yes, way more svelte in almost every one.A better way to tackle this issue? Know that you're facing down a weird mirror and bizarre lighting, and that you're awesome even if that swimsuit doesn't fit you. Also, may we suggest taking a page out of Cher from Clueless's book and snapping a selfie of your outfit to get a better sense of how you look? You'll have to do just that if the ban spreads. Typically, the content of the site or app is used to make inferences about your interests, which inform future selection of advertising and/or content.Select All3 PurposesConsent PurposesLocation Based AdsConsent AllowedLegitimate Interest PurposesPersonalizeFeaturesLocation Based AdsClear FlitersEsther Gauntlett and Jenny Cheng are redefining how we dress with their unconventional design aesthetics.New York-based designers Jenny Cheng and Esther Gauntlett are open about how they financially support their city lives and their fashion label, Gauntlett Cheng. Cheng works with a knit consultant, assisting in swatch and garment development for big brands such as Calvin Klein and Coach. Gauntlett works at skin-care company Aesop. After days in the corporate world, they head to their decidedly un-corporate Williamsburg studio—the same workroom that once quartered Eckhaus Latta, where the duo met as interns. The space—a spare white room with old wood floors coated with chipping paint, a couch strewn with purses and fabrics, and a table coated with papers and other materials—houses the pair’s eccentric, offbeat designs that have become the brand’s signature since their spring 2015 debut collection.For their upcoming show at New York Fashion Week, they’ll be riffing on their work experiences. The collection will feature office-inspired wardrobe with a nighttime edge (think a tattered Diane von Furstenberg-style wrap dress covered in “GC” monogram). Formerly known as Moses Gauntlett Cheng—cofounder David Moses left to design for up-and-coming brand Vaquera last season—the label has been making waves in recent months. Rihanna just wore one of their custom do-rags at the 2016 VMAs. Clearly, this is a pair to watch. We spoke to Gauntlett and Cheng about their upcoming show, their recent photo shoot in an RV, and how they juggle their day jobs with their fashion career.I heard you’re showing on a boat this season.Esther Gauntlett: We showed at VFiles, and then we showed at Milk. We’re really excited to be going back to something that isn’t a traditional runway kind of space. Having a venue that has a lot of personality and something to do with the clothes themselves is really important. Previously, we showed in Jenny’s boyfriend’s RV in a garage in Chinatown.Jenny Cheng: And the models were walking out in the dead of winter in, like, a bra.Gauntlett Cheng fall 2016 campaignWhere’s the RV now?JC: We recently did a campaign shoot on the RV. It was parked in the Rockaways. It was these two models just being really intimate—kind of living the RV life—in bed, [then] driving and coming out with luggage or a suitcase. It was kind of inspired by Michael Kors ads, the ones where they’re coming off a helicopter.EG: This season, the RV got an upgrade. It’s got a mural on the outside, a granite floor, and flashing LED lights.Tell us about your spring 2017 collection.EG: This season, the clothes definitely have a kind of “corporate life gone wrong” vibe to them. We always come at it from things that we’re experiencing in our lives—concerns, anxieties, reactions we have. It’s about faking our day jobs a little bit and coupling that with this persona of someone who’s a nightlife personality, who doesn’t have to get up for work in the morning, or someone who doesn’t have to work at all. It’s trying to project both of those things to the world. Everything starts to get really messy—like you’re going to work from the club kind of vibe.How does this vibe present itself in the clothes?EG: There’s definitely a mix of some really trashy evening stuff. We’re also doing a lot of suiting and little skirt suits. We’re doing a kind of monogram gone wrong.JC: Like a monogram that says GC and SOS, and it’s all chopped up.RELATED: Up-and-Coming Brands to Know at New York Fashion WeekHave your relationships with the corporate world changed now that you’re becoming well known? How are you mixing the original spirit with success?EG: Both of us still work. While we would definitely love to be able to [design] full time, I think it’s still a ways off. I guess we try and express those frustrations a little bit with making clothes. It’s a ridiculous life. We go to work, come here after. We’re in the studios until very late at night. We get up after a few hours of sleep. We don’t get a day off, more so at this time of year.Anyone helping out?EG: Last season we had two girls from Australia and my mom—so three girls from Australia. Now we have four interns.Since you’ve been interns yourself, do you see it as a role reversal?EG: It feels weird, definitely. I was so grateful when I interned somewhere like Eckhaus Latta, where it was small and we were making everything in-house, and I could see and learn the aspects of everything. I got such an understanding of the business side of things from working somewhere really small, and I enjoyed making things. I think watching Mike [Eckhaus] and Zoe [Latta] do it made [starting a brand] feel possible. We went into it very naïve. But if me and Jenny had sat down and been like, 'Let’s start a business,' there’s no way it would have happened.RELATED: Would You Wear Hood by Air's Crazy New Boots?Your clothes are so cool, but they’re not flattering in a traditional sense. How do you want people to feel when they wear them?EG: I think it changes every season. Last season definitely had a kind of comfort, wrapping yourself, worn in, lived in, falling apart kind of vibe. The season before that got so overtly sexy. I think we play with things like that by making clothes that are unexpectedly sexy, and then making expected sexy clothes more interesting and strange.I saw the [September 2016] Playboy shoot with Kelly Gale wearing a Gauntlett Cheng bikini bottom.EG: I noticed that because we got tagged. It’s really funny to see a chunky, knitted bikini bottom in Playboy, you know? Like on the sexiest girl ever. She’s so beautiful and she’s wearing this kind of cozy bikini.How have things changed since David left?JC: Work-wise, we’re still doing the same thing. Our process hasn’t changed.EG: The name is in the process of changing. It’s just going to be Gauntlett Cheng going forward. It’s funny, we get asked this a lot and I still don’t quite know how to answer. It feels like someone’s voice is missing. I think the way we tried to approach that was by involving as many people as we could—getting peoples’ input and opinions on everything. I think the more voices you have, the better.This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.Talking fashion with Olivia Palermo:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesLots of lace and feminine details—and not a logo in sight.Calvin Klein has been one of the fashion industry’s go-to brands for basics since it emerged on the scene in the late ‘60s. Ready-to-wear, denim, sportswear, underwear—you name it, the label sells it. Fast-forward more than four decades later, the brand is still reinventing and perfecting what it does best. And with Raf Simons heralding a new era for the iconic American brand, we are seriously in for a treat next year. Until then, we are excited for the launch of its new lingerie collection for its Seductive Comfort line, which goes on sale this week.Calvin Klein Underwear may be best known for its traditional logo-emblazoned undies—most recently seen on the seductive ads starring the likes of Kendall Jenner, Justin Bieber, and Bella Hadid—but the brand decided to go a more feminine route this time with possibly its most visually appealing undergarments yet. The collection features the brand’s beloved lift-demi and strapless bras in floral scalloped-lace trims in a variety of colors, including black, tan, and red. Ad ChoicesYou're standing in front of your closet, scanning the neat lines of your color-coded, Kondo-approved, joy-inducing wardrobe. It is Schrödinger's bureau: There are dozens of outfits; there are no outfits at all. No matter how many closet clean-outs you go through, the problem never seems to go away. We know. We go through exactly the same thing every morning. We'll have to take our comfort in solidarity, though, because the numbers, well, the numbers are just depressing.Those numbers are 17, 4, and 6. Specifically, each day the average woman spends 17 minutes picking out what to wear. That comes out to four full days every year, or six solid months between high-school graduation and retirement of doing absolutely nothing but choosing a damn shirt. The stats come from a poll by Marks & Spencer, a major U.K. retailer, so we're not exactly talking about highly scientific study parameters here. Big grain of salt aside, the idea that you might spend half of your yearly vacation days trying to match the exact shade of black in your favorite dress pants with an equally black top is a sobering thought.If it makes you feel better, the boys aren't much better off (no surprise to anyone who's ever lived with a guy.) While the men in the poll reported spending slightly less time on their morning wardrobe debate, it's not nearly as dramatic a difference as mediocre stand-up comedians would lead you to believe. In fact, guys spent 13 minutes a day on their outfit selection, just four minutes shy of the ladies' totals. And while a whopping 62 percent of women succumbed to what the poll calls "wardrobe rage," more than a third of men have also fallen prey to the "I have nothing to wear and everything's terrible" blues. Consider that the bright spot of this whole sad affair: Next time a guy in your life teases you about staring into the abyss of your closet, you can at least rest assured that he's as screwed as you are. The material on this site may not be reproduced, distributed, transmitted, cached or otherwise used, except with the prior written permission of Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesI don’t like handbags. Never have. In my nearly 30 years, I’ve acquired five and discarded three, well below the average number of bags most women possess. And while I admired the expensive-looking hardware and black leather quilting of my first Marc Jacobs tote—proudly purchased to take to my very first fashion magazine internship a decade ago—and the clean lines of the Mansur Gavriel bucket bag I’ve carried around for past three years straight, I have always loathed carrying them.Filled on a given day with a wallet, hand sanitizer, lip balm, comb, SPF powder, a paperback, a jacket or scarf, and half a dozen other things that inevitably wind up inside over the course of time, bags are consistently heavy and cumbersome, weighing down my right shoulder and bumping into passersby. The friction of their straps has pilled many a sweater and coat. Year after year, I’ve looked on enviously as boyfriends have strolled about to museums and shops and dinners, straight-shouldered and hands-free.I’m not the first fashion writer to loathe handbags. Carine Roitfeld famously eschewed them during her early years as a stylist and as the editor of French Vogue (though recently she’s been seen toting a Loewe bucket bag, and even professes to find it useful). Diana Vreeland, who took great advantage of the interior pockets of her Chanel shirts, found them frivolous. “What do I want with a bloody old handbag that one leaves in taxis and so on?” she recalled asking a Harper’s Bazaar colleague in her memoir, D.V. She even suggested creating an issue entirely free of the things, to show everything one could do with pockets.A look from Rachel Comey spring 2017 collection.For centuries, both men and women carried handbags. It wasn’t until the late 17th century that pockets became permanent fixtures on men’s jackets and trousers. Women, meanwhile, continued to carry handbags. And once they entered the workforce? The bags got bigger. Some designers, like Rosetta Getty and Rachel Comey, have done a terrific job at incorporating pockets into their womenswear, but others omit them in favor of leaner lines and trimmer silhouettes.So I proposed to my editor a little experiment: What if I gave up using a handbag altogether for a week? As it happened, those seven days fell halfway between a trip to sunny Newport Beach, Calif., to visit my parents, and a cold, rainy visit to New York. (I didn’t count the day flying between the two, because hand luggage was simply inevitable.)Strangely the lack of my pockets in my wardrobe was something I’d hardly noticed before.By day one, I was already regretting my experiment. My mom asked me to run a quick shopping errand with her to the mall—could I be ready to go in five? Usually, I’d just grab my handbag and head out the door, but now I had to attach its contents on me. It was 70 degrees out, too warm to throw a jacket over my long-sleeved tee—and I suddenly realized that the skirt I was wearing, nor any of the ones I’d packed, had pockets. (Strangely the lack of my pockets in my wardrobe was something I’d hardly noticed before.) Scrambling, I found an old pair of paint-stained jeans and slid a credit card, ID, a couple of gift cards, a phone, and keys in their generously sized back pockets.Getting dressed on subsequent days did not get easier, nor faster. See, the nice thing about carrying the same handbag every day is that it’s pretty much already packed and ready to go whenever you need it. So I resorted to wearing the same jeans every day—and then had to fish my credit card and ID out of the washing machine. This had always struck me as a ridiculous mistake that boys make; now I’m sympathetic. Things did get easier when I got to New York, where it was cold enough to wear a Uniqlo down vest (hooray for four pockets!) and a Burberry coat every day.I missed having lip balm at the ready. I missed having a scarf or jacket at my disposal when it got cold. But what really drove me nuts was how often I had to use disposable bags. Whether shopping for groceries or a pair of jeans, I generally refuse to take a bag—even if that means hand-carrying a carton of grapes on the mile walk home. Now, I didn’t always have a choice.More fashion survival tips:But the real challenge was my laptop. I carry my Macbook Air with me everywhere I go, slipping into coffee shops to pound out emails and copy between meetings and whatever else I’ve got going on in a given day. In California, the idea of walking 20 minutes to the nearest coffee shop carrying my laptop clutched to my chest, even in a secure neighborhood, seemed ridiculous. So I worked at home. If there was a silver lining, I saved money on coffee, but I paid for it in productivity. In New York, where coffee shops are in much closer proximity, I cradled it in my arms like a textbook, which worked alright until I got stuck in a rainstorm. I took off my trench, wrapped it around my laptop, and arrived home soaking wet. My laptop, thankfully, remained dry.But, for all the above-stated inconveniences, going without a handbag for a week was pretty damn great. I felt light and free, nimble and quick. How nice it was to simply tuck my hands in my front pockets and go for a walk without anything tugging against my shoulder, bouncing against my hip. How liberating, at a cocktail party, to have one hand grasping a drink and the other at its leisure, while other women shifted their clutches from one elbow to the other.I’m not going to stop carrying handbags anytime soon. But I am going to aim to go handbag-free as much as possible, particularly in the evenings. Perhaps the biggest impact will be on my shopping habits—no coat, skirt nor dress will enter my closet without a thorough examination of its pocket situation.4 denim trends we love:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The designer’s namesake line is well-known for its mystical, boho-luxe accessories that feature unconventional materials in delicate settings. Her dagger charm necklace, for example, is made out of turquoise beads and a real shark tooth that has been adorned with pavé diamonds.“I source materials from all over the world, including butterfly-shaped tourmalines carved in Brazil, bone carved in Hawaii, and shark teeth from the oceans,” says Aiche. “However, all of my jewelry is designed and handcrafted in Los Angeles.”Her delicate diamond bra chains and teardrop ear jackets have quickly gained a loyal fan base. Margot Robbie, Bella Hadid, Miranda Kerr, Rihanna, and Brie Larson are just a few of the women who’ve worn a piece of Aiche’s work this summer.The designer, who works in Beverly Hills but grew up in a multicultural home, takes inspiration from her own blended Native American and Egyptian heritage—think moonstone necklaces covered in glittering pavé diamonds and a magic eye ring with two cerulean blue diamonds. She has also recently branched out to offer more than just accessories. Both Gigi Hadid and Karlie Kloss have stepped out in Aiche’s customizable denim shirts—complete with their names and an eye motif on the back—which were made in collaboration with Los Angeles–based clothing brand Mother.One of our favorite pieces (and Rihanna’s, too) is the hand-carved agate cameo ring. A type of art that’s been around for over hundred years, the bas-relief technique was used in mourning cameo brooches during the nineteenth century. The demure Old World jewelry style has gotten a cool new look since then. Aiche’s versions feature elegant roses, unicorns, and even tattoo-esque “Best Mom” lettering. “I always enjoy working with pieces that have meaning and connection, and I felt that cameos were sentimental keepsakes that needed to be reintroduced in a modern way,” Aiche says of her signature rings.When it comes to her design process, Aiche is adamant about making a woman feel beautiful on the inside. “The right piece of jewelry has the power to make a woman feel more sensuous or playful or beautiful,” she says. “And when she feels that way inside, it can have a profound effect on who she is and how she is perceived on the outside.”How to Wear Statement Jewelry:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. For one, it's always around the Fourth of July, a time when most of us are busy barbecuing and sitting by the pool rather than scanning the Internet. Second, not as many people go to couture—the shows are smaller, more intimate—and the clothes you see on the runway are either ridiculously expensive or never get produced. But regardless, I love couture. It's a spectacle, where the clothes are exquisite and the hair and makeup are either fantastical or totally far-out. Most of the looks you see on couture runways you'd never wear, but for the beauty obsessed, you'll appreciate what I consider to be true hair and makeup works of art. Case in point: the amazing beauty moments we saw the past few days in Paris.The glittery red lips at Atelier Versace dazzled as the models came down the runway (above). And judging from makeup artist Pat McGrath's Instagram posts, this is one look you may just be able to re-create in the coming months.At Chanel, graphic false lashes (on top and bottom!) and a pile of fluffy curls made the models look positively doll-like.At Maison Margiela, McGrath and hairstylist Eugene Souleiman are encouraged to stretch their creative wings and go wild. This season, nearly every model had her own unique beauty look—the looks included hot-pink brows, sculptural hair rolls, metallic lipstick, mosquito nets, and splatters of multicolored paint across each and every feature. But my favorite one? This quirky lip look that incorporated two colors and a thin line of silver glitter. Totally not wearable, but definitely cool as hell.Here's an example where the hair and makeup wasn't extravagant or crazy but just exceptionally beautiful—like a modern Veronica Lake style. The combination of sleek waves with winged liner and red lips is perfect for a cocktail party of evening fete.The cat eyes at Christian Dior weren't just simple flicks—they were graphic, dramatic, and personalized for each model.Also worth a mention—the few models at Dior who wore gold winged shadow to tie in with the gilded accents in the collection.Last but not least, model Soo Joo's makeup for the finale at Jean Paul Gaultier. With white lashes and liner and dots of different shades of red lipstick, the effect was part ice queen, part Impressionist painting.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. The New York-based fashion retailer is known for its frequent collaborations with multiple (and sometimes unexpected) brands that conjure up highly covetable products that bring out the '90s fangirl in all of us. The label recently launched a throwback line featuring Power Rangers, which consists of an assortment of hoodies, tees, crewnecks, and caps that seriously brought on some waves of nostalgia. For foodies, Kith built pop-up shops in New York City and Miami earlier this month in partnership with beloved cereal brand Cap'n Crunch.On Friday, the streetwear purveyor will unveil its latest collection with French fashion brand Iro. Kith owner Ronnie Fieg met with the Iro team in Paris during fashion week and immediately fell in love with the brand's chic-meets-edgy aesthetic and the quality of its products, including the fabrics. "From there it was about translating Iro's unique design language through the Kith lens in a way that could resonate with both the Iro and the Kith customer," Fieg tells Allure.4 denim styles you should try now:Within the nine-piece collection, you'll find elements of effortless Parisian style mixed with New York's downtown edge. There are cream-colored shearling coats with asymmetrical zips and a bomber jacket embroidered with the names of both brands. The New York sensibility comes through in the laid-back lace-up crewneck, sweatpants, and men's oversize hoodie. Best of all? You can pull off the looks in an urban setting as well as the countryside. For proof, just take a look at the gorgeous look book, which was photographed in upstate New York. There’s no reason why you can’t stage your own fall foliage inspired #OOTD."The partnership with Iro was very organic," says Fieg. "I believe the end result is a strong statement on what is considered 'high fashion' today, as the lines continue to be blurred. Kith and Iro share this vision, which has culminated into this beautiful assortment of products."Kith made its New York fashion week debut in September with a collection that emphasized the many collaborations Fieg experimented with in the past, including capsules with brands such as Columbia, BAPE, Aimé Leon Dore, Timberland, and Off-White, to name a few. Priced between $175 to $2,495, the Iro x Kith collection will arrive in stores, online, and Bergdorf Goodman this Friday, and will likely be worn by the likes of Hailey Baldwin and Gigi Hadid, who are both fans of the brand. Here's how a practical uniform became so much more.16th: The approximate century indigo-dyed, stiff cotton pants first became popular in Nîmes, France, and Genoa, Italy; for centuries, they would be favored by sailors. "De Nîmes" (French for "from Nîmes") is the origin of the word "denim."139,121: The patent number obtained by Nevada tailor Jacob Davis and businessman Levi Strauss in 1873 for the first riveting process for denim jeans, which increased their strength and made them a durable uniform for miners, farmers, and mechanics.3: The approximate number of inches too long that 1870s Levi's buyers would order their jeans. The fabric would shrink when washed, but until then, men would cuff the legs and use the folds to store tobacco.1951: The year singer Bing Crosby was refused entry to a Canadian hotel (until an employee recognized him) because he was wearing jeans. In response, Levi's created a more formal look for him made entirely of denim—a "Canadian tuxedo."27: Marlon Brando's age when he wore jeans in the 1953 film The Wild One, about a motorcycle gang, establishing the look of young hoodlums.1955: The year Levi's overdyed jeans to a vibrant blue for James Dean to wear in Rebel Without a Cause.12th: The grade in which Elvis Presley began wearing sports coats, popped- collar shirts, and pants to school; his peers favored jeans, but they reminded Presley of the work clothes his family wore at their poorest.1957: The year Presley had a line of jeans named after him, when Levi's created black "Elvis Presley Jeans" like the ones he wore to perform "Jailhouse Rock" in the movie of the same name.$394.9 million: The worldwide box-office sales of the 1978 film Grease. To promote the musical, which was set in the 1950s, Sedgefield Sportswear created Grease jeans with the movie's logo on the back pocket. With every purchase, buyers received a movie poster or foam dice to hang from a rearview mirror.63: The number of episodes of the Sonny & Cher Comedy Hour, which began airing in 1971. The entertainers helped popularize bell-bottomed jeans.15: Brooke Shields's age when she appeared in ads by Richard Avedon for Calvin Klein Jeans. In one she said, "Do you want to know what comes between me and my Calvins? Nothing." It was pulled from the air because it implied that the model wasn't wearing underwear.34: The years later Shields recalled in her memoir There Was a Little Girl that she and her mother hadn't thought the line was a double entendre, writing, "It would hurt me to think that the creative team was trying to exploit my innocence."1990s: The decade oversize carpenter jeans with a loop on the leg to hold a hammer were adopted as a fashion statement by both the hip-hop community and ravers.100,000: The number of pairs of used American jeans that Thailand imported annually in the mid-'90s. Still, U.S. denim dealers said Japan was their biggest market abroad.10,000 to 100,000: The number of yen (approximately $100 to $1,000) used Levi's 501s would sell for in Tokyo in the '90s, depending on their age and condition.108: The approximate age in years of the Levi's 501 jeans found in an old mine in California's Mojave Desert in 1998.$60,000: The amount the jeans sold for in an eBay auction in 2005 to an anonymous buyer and collector in Japan.6: The number of days after his inauguration that President George W. Bush banned jeans at the White House.85: The percentage of women in a 2007 study who said they kept clothes that did not fit for sentimental reasons or weight-loss motivation—particularly their smallest sizes.6: The season of Sex and the City when Miranda fit back into her skinny jeans after having a baby and finding "no time to eat."1984: The year fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent said, "I wish I had invented blue jeans.... They have expression, modesty, sex appeal, simplicity—all I hope for in my clothes."28: The season of Saturday Night Live in which Tina Fey,Amy Poehler, Maya Rudolph, and Rachel Dratch appeared in an ad parody for "Mom Jeans," high-waisted denim "cut generously to fit a mom's body."9: The length in inches of the zipper on Mom Jeans. The tagline: "Give her something that says, I'm not a woman anymore—I'm a mom.'"2009: The year President Barack Obama defended his oft-mocked "dad jeans," saying, "Those jeans are comfortable, and for those of you who want your president to look great in his tight jeans, I'm sorry—I'm not the guy."6: The number of "mean Tweets" about himself that President Obama read on Jimmy Kimmel Live! in 2015, including one about his jeans.
