Gobbetti, who's currently the chairman and chief executive of French luxury brand Céline, will join the company next year.The change in leadership comes after months of rumors that a senior manager would be brought in to support Bailey on the corporate side, as first reported by The Financial Times in May."I am very excited that Marco Gobbetti is joining us as chief executive officer and as a partner to me," said Bailey in a statement. "On a personal level, I know that we are going to enjoy a wonderfully collaborative partnership that makes me very excited for our future at Burberry."Gobbetti has worked in luxury for more than 20 years on brands including Givenchy and Bottega Veneta. His appointment comes at a challenging time for Burberry. The company announced last month that Bailey had received a 75 percent pay cut last year after it missed its profit targets.Bailey made history as the first designer in a publicly traded fashion company to become CEO. The digitally skilled designer replaced the company's former chief executive Angela Ahrendts two years ago.Last year, Burberry announced it would combine its three lines—Prorsum, London, and Brit—into one. This fall, the company will unite the men's and women's ready-to-wear shows, and the collections will be available to buy immediately after they are presented on the runway.Update (July 14, 2016): Bailey has addressed the senior management shake-up at the brand, following the news on Monday that Gobbetti has been appointed as its new CEO."I clearly have a very full time role based on my responsibilities. But as with all of these things, you work to lead a team," Bailey told the Business Of Fashion. "I think the role of any leader is to take themselves out of the situation and to say what is right for the company going forward."Bailey mentioned his strong chemistry with Gobbetti and took the opportunity to compliment his expertise in the luxury sector."He has a profound understanding of retail and retail execution," the former CEO said. "He has also got an incredibly global experience; he is somebody that has done a lot of work in the US, of course in Europe but also in Asia, so he thinks very globally and that is relatively unusual."Bailey also shared his thoughts on Brexit, admitting that "it certainly was not the result that we were looking for at all. The capsule collection – originally conceived by LPA alongside Lena Dunham, Emily Ratajkowski, Cara Delevingne, Suki Waterhouse and Paloma Elsesser – was set to debut tomorrow as a direct commentary on the modern day normality of cyber-bullying and the shared desire to create a community for those most affected by the epidemic. Proceeds were set to benefit Girls Write Now, a charity focused on mentoring underserved young women and helping them find their voices and tell their stories through writing."The prematurely released images featured on Revolve.com was not only included without context of the overall campaign but regrettably featured one of the pieces on a model who's [sic] size was not reflective of the piece’s commentary on body positivity. We at Revolve sincerely apologize to all those involved – particularly Lena, Emily, Cara, Suki and Paloma – our loyal customers, and the community as a whole for this error."The collection has been pulled. We are proud to donate $20,000 to Girls Write Now in the hopes that those who need it can still benefit from what was to be a meaningful, insightful and impactful collaboration by LPA."This story was originally published on September 13, 2018, at 3:00 PM:Shopping website Revolve is coming under fire for a questionable marketing move. The retailer was selling sweatshirts by clothing brand LPA with the quote “Being fat isn’t beautiful it’s an excuse” on the front, and they have since taken the item down. It’s apparently a comment that plus-size model Paloma Elsesser has heard before — the words “as said to @palomija” are printed below in a much smaller font. While it appears to be an attempt at reclaiming fatphobic messages, many people believe Revolve missed the mark by choosing to put the design on a skinny model and making the quote attribution barely readable.In a statement to Teen Vogue, Revolve spokesperson Simone Kuhfal said that the images of a forthcoming LPA collection were "prematurely released" on its website. She explained that the capsule collection, which was originally conceived by LPA alongside Paloma, Lena Dunham, Emily Ratajkowski, Cara Delevingne, and Suki Waterhouse, was intended to be "direct commentary on the modern day normality of cyber-bullying and the shared desire to create a community for those most affected by the epidemic." Proceeds were set to benefit Girls Write Now, a charity focused on mentoring underserved young women."The prematurely released images featured on Revolve.com was not only included without context of the overall campaign but regrettably featured one of the pieces on a model whose size was not reflective of the piece’s commentary on body positivity," Kuhfal said. "We at Revolve sincerely apologize to all those involved – particularly Lena, Emily, Cara, Suki, and Paloma – our loyal customers, and the community as a whole for this error. The collection has been pulled." Kufhal continued, saying, "We are proud to donate $20,000 to Girls Write Now in the hopes that those who need it can still benefit from what was to be a meaningful, insightful, and impactful collaboration by LPA."Despite Revolve's intentions, the internet had a lot to say about the actual impact of the piece. The sweatshirt currently has a rating of 1.2 stars (out of five) on its product page, with many consumers expressing their outrage about Revolve’s decision to sell an item that seemingly perpetuates body negativity. One person called the move “heinous” and wrote, “If this is supposed to be a range of jumpers that points out hate of body types...it's doing the exact opposite...the message is not clear...it's insulting!” Another added, “Zero stars weren’t an option so I had to go with one. I can’t decide if you’re fat shaming or skinny shaming or both. Whatever it is, it’s disgusting, why are you sending negative messages to women about their bodies?”On Instagram, reactions were just as vocal. London-based artist and social advocate Florence Given posted a screenshot of the sweatshirt in question, and people quickly chimed in with their perspectives. One commenter called the whole fiasco “horrendous,” and another person put it bluntly, “This is disgusting! Really unbelievable. Chanel has a wide range of skin-care products, but its eye cream is the best when it comes to achieving younger-looking eyes. Last year’s Allure Best of Beauty winner, the cream features 3.5-DA, or dicaffeoylquinic acid, which has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. Easy to dab on and scent-free, this one will stay on my vanity for many years to come. $105 (chanel.com).When it comes to perfume, I like to experiment. I haven’t found my signature scent yet, but I’m currently loving this new fragrance from Hermès. My favorite flower is lily of the valley, which translates to “muguet” in French. Side story: In France, friends and family celebrate the first day of May by offering bouquets of the flower for good luck. The scent lingers for hours and creates the illusion of spring (even on a scorching day in New York City). $255 for 3.3 fluid ounces (hermes.com).I switched to this shampoo last year after years of using random drugstore products. Three people told me my hair looked good the day I switched over. I’m not exaggerating. Designed for thinning hair, the shampoo uses turmeric as one of its main ingredients, which has anti-inflammatory qualities. Just pour a quarter-size amount on your hands and lather as you would typically wash your hair. I like to use the thickening conditioner as well. $30 for 6.7 fluid ounces (aveda.com).I’m not a big makeup wearer, especially during summer. But one cosmetic product I always remember to apply is this mascara from Dior. I have short and thin eyelashes, but a couple of strokes makes them look thick and long. Plus, the curled brush catches and lifts almost all my lashes. $29.50 (dior.com).I have two requirements when it comes to sunscreen: 1) It has to be noncomedogenic because I’m acne-prone. 2) It should feel smooth and easy to slather on (translation: not chalky). This sunscreen meets both of these standards and more. It leaves my skin feeling so soft that I forget I’m even wearing sunscreen. Plus, it contains antioxidants and anti-inflammatory ingredients that prevent fine lines and wrinkles. The price is pretty hefty (I don’t waste a drop), but then again it has the same qualities as a $200 anti-aging moisturizer, so you could say you get more bang for your buck. $185 (laprairie.com).This New York–based brand has just about all the essentials you need to complete your wardrobe. In keeping with its name—“ligne”means "line" in French—everything sold on the site features stripes. My favorite is this light cotton shirt in bright blue. You can wear it with a skirt or jeans or pair it with heels or sneakers. I’ll probably get one in black, too. $115 (lalignenyc.com).I'm a light packer—prepare a shirt or two, cosmetic kit, and undergarments, and I'm all set. For a quick weekend trip outside New York City, this carry-on suitcase from Steamline Luggage perfectly holds all my essentials. Modern yet vintage-inspired, the bag is completely made out of vegan leather, but feels smooth and looks luxurious like the real deal. If it's too precious to travel with, you can also use it as a chic decoration—I like to store old keepsakes like ticket stubs and photos inside. $230, (steamlineluggage.com)What can I say? I love stripes. And I love reading about the designer who practically invented stripes for women. Coco Chanel was so inspired by the nautical style worn by sailors that she incorporated the stripes in her 1917 collection. This trilogy is filled with beautiful iconic photos of the brand’s history, from Coco’s designs to Karl Lagerfeld’s current innovations. $75 (assouline.com).Who doesn’t love a good A-line skirt? With its slim waist and flared hip, the silhouette works on almost every body type. And it’s pretty versatile, too: I can see myself wearing this almost all year long with loafers, heels, boots, or sneakers. $590 (net-a-porter.com).More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. As style influencers and denim-heads prove, there are no rules. A jean jacket really comes to life when you put your own spin on it, and pull it off in a way that says something about your personality. You can make it pretty or punk, or hey, maybe a little of both. In the end, no two ways to wear this essential are exactly alike, and that’s the beauty of it.That personal, individualistic attitude inspired AMO’s Lola jacket, which launched last spring (and promptly sold out). It’s back in production this fall with the same ripped-off collar and raw, unfinished hem, but in a darker wash and accented with fun, emoji-like pins that you can take on and off. “It feels like a more feminine version of a jean jacket,” says AMO co-founder Kelly Urban. She recommends throwing the jacket over a blouse or even a one-piece bathing suit with low-slung shorts and sandals for casual Cali vibe.RELATED: The West Coast Lines “It” Girls Are Loving Right NowTo further ride that transition from summer into fall, consider an ultralightweight option, like Rebecca Taylor’s indigo chambray jacket, which is part of her new La Vie collection. With its cropped, boxy silhouette, patchwork details and front tie closures, the breezy topper has “a tom-girl feel,” says Taylor. Layer it over sheer shirts and dresses with Vans, or channel the ‘70s by pairing it with flared jeans. “I’m loving denim on denim at the moment,” says the designer.Balenciaga fall 2016There were, of course, louder interpretations of the jean jacket on the fall runways, which packed a lot of punch. Gucci’s Alessandro Michele sent out an oversized, acid-washed number with fur cuffs while Demna Gvasalia did his usual, amazing thing with denim—deconstructing it and sewing it back together to create an askew, supercool jean jacket at Balenciaga. Marc Jacobs blew up the proportions and went crazy with gothic-glam embellishments (chains, spider webs, and pompoms!). For a dose of Parisian chic, Karl Lagerfeld toughed up ladylike tweed with denim at Chanel; while Sonia Rykiel’s bomber-style jean jacket exuded Left Bank sophistication with its raccoon sleeves and suede trim.RELATED: The Experts’ Guide to Transitioning Your Wardrobe Into Fall“I love denim jackets because they’re just as versatile as jeans,” says Salt Lake City-based style blogger Christine Andrew of Hello Fashion. “You can tie it around your waist or layer it over a hoodie or cozy sweater, and it also adds dimension under a trench.” Or get creative and remove the sleeves, says Elizabeth Parks Kibbey, founder of Los Angeles-based Collection boutique, which specializes in vintage denim. “I’m a huge advocate of the cut-off jean-jacket vest, layered over oxford shirts and blouses.” Don’t bother making it perfect or going to a tailor. This vest is better when the edges are undone, and some strings are left exposed. Pull it on with a slip dress and this season’s combat boots for a sexy, rebellious romp.From left: AMO denim jacket, $334 (shopbop.com); Sonia Rykiel jacket, $2,300 (soniarykiel.com); Rebecca Taylor chambray jacket, $325 (rebeccataylor.com).But to really stand out, take a style cue from Rihanna (when isn’t she blazing a trail with denim?) and play with proportions. “I have a picture of Rihanna in an oversized Matthew Dolan jean jacket that I adore,” says Kibbey. Sizing up, she says, “is a big leap, but it looks so great.” Pick a jacket that’s roomy enough to fit a bulky sweater underneath—but not so large that you’re drowning in it. Then, roll up the sleeves to expose a bit of skin, and just have fun with it. As Kibbey says of the look, “It’s the perfect amount of street plus chic.”Supermodels Reveal Their Denim Obsession:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. Ad ChoicesScroll through Instagram, and you’ve likely come across the “Ark” bag, the crescent-shaped bamboo carryall from Los Angeles–based fashion brand Cult Gaia. Timeless yet modern—with a budget-friendly price tag to boot (it currently retails for $118)—the bag has been spotted in the hands of sartorial darlings such as Jessica Alba and blogger Chriselle Lim since last summer.Yet despite its seemingly runaway success, the accessory struggled to find customers when it first debuted back in 2013. “No one actually bought it for two years,” says Jasmin Larian, the brainchild behind Cult Gaia. “So much of fashion is based on trend. It took time, but we had to train the customers to think that they could pull it off.” The 28-year-old's perseverance paid off last February when she sold a few of the bags to Clare Distenfeld of Fivestory, the buzzy lifestyle boutique in New York City. The label soon garnered the attention of the city’s stylish social circle, cementing Larian’s status as an emerging accessories designer.Known for her Cali–meets–Grace Kelly aesthetic, Larian, whose assortment of offbeat yet elegant offerings includes everything from oversized rattan bangles to '50s-inspired turbans, says her goal is to make statement pieces that stand the test of time. This now includes a debut ready-to-wear collection, which launched online today. Priced between $118 to $198, the lineup includes an array of punchy pieces that recall tranquil, beachy vibes.We recently spoke with Larian about the inspiration behind her brand, sustainable fashion, and her connection to the Bratz dolls.Why did you decide to launch your own brand?My mom was a fashion designer when I was growing up, and my dad had a toy company that started the Bratz dolls (Yasmin, one of the four original Bratz dolls, was named after Jasmin). I grew up around fashion designers who made miniature clothes for dolls. Fashion has been a part of my life forever. I started Cult Gaia in 2012, straight out of FIT [the Fashion Institute of Technology]. I was making headpieces and flower crowns for friends as a hobby, and people started to take notice. I think the cornerstone of our brand is making things that are conversation starters. Even with the crown, it was something that brought a lot of attention—a recognizable and wearable art piece.Who is the “girl” you design for?Someone who is really easygoing, effortless, pays attention to subtle details. Her statement pieces are her accessories. She puts her bag in bed at night. She loves luxury, but doesn’t think she needs $7,000 to obtain that. My muse is Haley Boyd, the designer behind footwear brand Marais USA. She’s been wearing our bag for a long time.The Gaia Ark is everywhere on social media. To what do you attribute its popularity?It’s so recognizable. It’s an amazing conversation starter. If you carry this bag, I bet you everyone will ask, “Where did you get that? What is that? Is that a bag?” It garners so much attention. It’s also something that looks amazing with every outfit. I’ve worn it with a black-tie gown. It’s designed to stay on your coffee table and look just as beautiful as home decor as it is [as an accessory].A look from the spring 2017 collectionTell us about your new spring collection.Everything I make is superfeminine. Before my trip to Italy, I made some clothes to wear on my trip. My friends said they really wanted to wear them as well, so I decided to put a capsule collection together. Everything is really effortless; nothing’s too frilly, nothing’s overdesigned. I feel like everything’s something you might find in your mother’s closet. My aesthetic is super-vintage-inspired, like Grace Kelly on the beach. There’s a triangle wraparound dress that looks good on everybody. My friends have been begging me for the linen tent dress. It’s so easy to throw on.As a new designer, how important is it to maintain an affordable price range for your customers?It’s a constant struggle to maintain that price point, but it’s so important. Our bags come in boxes and dust bags. I don’t know if you can find that everywhere with the price point we are giving. I believe in making handmade, high-quality items that will last forever and be passed down like an heirloom piece. But I don’t think everything should cost over $1,000. From a customer standpoint, it’s shocking when you see this bag compared to other “It” bags that cost more. They’re not buying one. They’re buying two, getting one for a friend or family member.A look from the spring 2017 collectionWhere do you source your fabrics and produce your line?I was just so apprehensive about producing a whole collection. Loving and making one piece of clothing is so different than manufacturing a line. Plus, I was superapprehensive of the waste that it would create. Everything is made in L.A. Everything in our collection is made from deadstock fabric. We’re taking fabrics that would be in a landfill if we didn’t use it. I’m not interested in making clothes if I’m going to create more waste. It kills the passion of what you to do.What’s next for Cult Gaia?A lot more innovation. The biggest compliment for me is seeing how people react whey they come to our space to see our products. I just want to blow everyone’s mind all the time and give you beautiful things.A look from the spring 2017 collectionA look from the spring 2017 collectionMore bags we love:Jessica Alba shares what's in her beauty bag:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. This is the first time the jewelry company has featured celebrities in a campaign.Each actress and model was photographed portrait style against a classic Tiffany Blue background. A black-and-white close-up of each woman's jewelry, including diamond studs and the Tiffany T Square bracelet, accompanies each portrait.The decision to cast Nyong'o and Fanning in the campaign came shortly after Grace Coddington was hired by the brand as a creative partner in April."I'm also known not to like celebrity very much," Coddington told Business of Fashion. Instead, she wanted to "find people who are beyond the average celebrity." The former Vogue creative director sought to keep some elements of the campaign classic. Case in point: the iconic Tiffany Blue, "which was kind of a lovely blue anyway," she said.Since joining the company earlier this spring, Coddington has been working to reshape the brand's advertising, starting with these ads, which were shot by David Sims and will run in September magazine issues. A short film documenting the process by R. J. Cutler, the director of The September Issue, will also debut.Tiffany & Co. is making a big effort to become more fashionable. Before Coddington's hire, the company tapped modernist jewelry designer Francesca Amfitheatrof as its first female design director. Also, last week it was announced that Reed Krakoff would join the company to design home and accessories collections. The brand also recently started selling an archive collection, called Out of Retirement, at Dover Street Market in New York City. For a 179-year-old jewelry brand, things are looking new again.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. Ad ChoicesWhen you reach a certain level of celebrity, a fashion line seems almost inevitable. The latest star to add "designer" to her resume is actress Eva Longoria, who just dropped her own line of modern feminine staples.Unlike a lot of celebs-turned-designers, Longoria, who learned how to sew at the age of 7, has actually spent more time in the sartorial world than in the celebrity spotlight. Known for her killer red carpet looks, the star says that launching her own fashion brand is a childhood dream come true.The spring 2017 collection, available at evalongoria.com and HSN.com, is largely based on the actress’s personal style, ranging from a crop of leave-little-to-the-imagination body-con dresses to a strong array of menswear-inspired staples.The true standout look from the line is Longoria’s all-white, wide-leg power suit—especially timely considering the persistence of Pantsuit Nation and the critical mass of suffragette white seen on the streets and the red carpet during awards season. Basically, Longoria’s suit is the stuff of badass suffragette dreams.Other standouts in Longoria’s collection include a cropped faux leather jacket, a quilted denim bomber, and a flounce-hem pencil skirt perfect for the office and a night on the town. The lineup also features an array of office-appropriate blouses fit to shake up a standard button-down look. The collection skews more towards trendy than timeless, with a price range to match—you can score everything in the collection for $159 or less. As for the size, it currently offers XS–XXL and 0–18.For eager shoppers, the Eva Longoria fall 2017 collection is already in the works. Ad ChoicesScarlet velvet, pale pink, and matching metallics — these bold separates prove dresses aren't the only way to get creative for awards season (and beyond).Gone are the days when every woman is expected to wear a gown and every man a tuxedo on the red carpet. Regardless of gender, the looks at the 2019 Academy Awards and other shows this year prove more celebrities than ever are choosing suits as their go-to black-tie wear. Whether it's a pastel pink number (with a matching scrunchie) a la Game of Thrones and Aquaman star Jason Mamoa, or the chic metallic suit worn by Awkwafina, these looks go way beyond the typical black tuxedo or “menswear for women” we've been accustomed to for too long.As someone with a deep fondness for matching separates and an aversion to wearing dresses and skirts — I like them on other people, just not on me! — I am impressed by all the beautiful, vivid colors, luxurious fabrics, and unique cuts, and feel like this awards season actually featured some style inspo for people like me. Don't get me wrong, I always find huge excitement in the gorgeous hair and makeup, particularly given all the prep work by hair pros, makeup artists, facialists, and nail artists that goes into creating these looks, but it's amazing to see Oscars 2019 red carpet fashion extend to folks who love creative, chic suits and separates, too.On the Oscars 2019 red carpet, comedian, writer, producer, director, and all-around amazing human being Amy Poehler wore a chic black suit with a ruffled shirt, pairing it with an easygoing hairstyle and simple makeup.On the Oscars 2019 red carpet, If Beale Street Could Talk actor Stephan James rocked a beautiful velvet suit from Etro, white Giuseppe Zanotti boots, and a Swarovski earring as a pendant on the lapel — a creative accessorizing idea for those of us who love a bit of sparkle, but don't actually feel like wearing earrings. Stephan James, if you're reading this: Can we trade wardrobes?Of all the suits on the Oscars red carpet, it is the shimmering pink ensemble worn by Awkwafina that was the most unforgettable. To prep her skin for this gorgeous, glowing look, makeup artist Mai Quynh used two face masks from Kiehl's — the Buttermask for her lips and the Calendula & Aloe Soothing Hydration Mask on the rest of her face — plus the brand's Ultra Facial Cream (which was reformulated sans parabens late last year). For her makeup, Quynh used Giorgio Armani's famous Luminous Silk Foundation in the shade 5.75, which gave her complexion its Oscar-worthy radiance.It's only February, sure, but don't you just wish you could wear this look for New Year's Eve in 10 months?At just 15 years old, Elsie Fisher is already acing the red carpet in a unique way. And to complement her chic black suit for the Oscars — which, like Stephan James's, was made from a luxurious velvet — the Eighth Grade actress wore her first set of false lashes, according to makeup artist Kristin Hilton. “Elsie is wearing a Thom Browne suit and stick-straight hair, so we wanted a graphic eye look with similarly clean lines,” explains Hilton, who used Lashify products (a brand Allure editors are already quite fond of thanks to its your-lashes-but-better results) to achieve the look.It's easy to overdo a young star's hair and makeup on the red carpet, but the playful cat eyeliner, natural-looking falsies, pinky-nude lips, and ultra-simple hair kept things fun — making me wish I had started wearing suits like this a long, long time ago... perhaps in eighth grade? (I'm sorry, I'm sorry.)Not only did Aquaman and Game of Thrones star Jason Momoa wear a beautiful pale pink look on the Oscars 2019 red carpet, he matched it to a perfectly coordinated scrunchie.For his 2019 Academy Awards look, Chadwick Boseman proved a straight, tailored look isn't the only way to wear a suit on the red carpet. Many women and femme people wear wide, flowy silhouettes for awards shows, but it's relatively rare to see a man experiment with a unique cut like this. Here's hoping that more celebrities (and non-famous folks, of course) aren't afraid to play around and try something new.As I mentioned above, I'm not big on dresses; nevertheless, I am just plain obsessed with the stunning feathery gown worn by makeup artist Annamarie Tendler on the Oscars 2019 red carpet. And the dark floral suit jacket worn by her husband, comedian John Mulaney, is perfect to wear for any meeting, date, night out, or casual bunch. (What, you don't do casual brunches in tuxedo jackets?)OK, so the jaw-dropping, show-stopping Christian Siriano gown that Billy Porter wore to the 2019 Oscars isn't a suit, technically. However — however — it is concrete proof that we need more ensembles with a tuxedo top half and ball-gown bottom, and a perfect example of everything good that is now happening in the world of red carpet fashion. For such a painfully long time, Worst Dressed lists and snarky commentators prevented artists from taking risks with hair and makeup, and especially their wardrobes. But the reason no one has stopped talking about Porter's gorgeous dress is that it's new and fresh, and it bypasses all the shitty gender norms many of us feel subject to in our regular lives, and he wore it on the grand scale of a world stage.Melissa McCarthy always kills it on the red carpet, but this black-and-white look featuring a floor-length cape is exceptionally glamorous.Legendary director Spike Lee's highly lauded BlacKkKlansman did not win the 2019 Academy Award for best picture — a bad call, in my opinion, and an overall controversial one — but he shined nonetheless on the red carpet in this all-purple suit, which was a gorgeous tribute to Prince. As for Tonya Lewis Lee, the Hollywood producer and author opted to wear a head-turning strapless dress featuring a velvet, deep-cut bodice and flowy, asymmetrical train. Bonus: Her gown featured pockets, aka the best red carpet accessory of all.For Oscars 2019, Captain America himself had one of the most subtle jackets of the evening — and that's really saying something about the growing range of suits, considering a deep aqua like this would've been viewed as a risk just five years ago.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. For her spring 2017 debut as the fashion house's creative director, Maria Grazia Chiuri presented a "We Should All Be Feminists" T-shirt inspired by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's 2014 essay of the same name. Not only did the buzzy shirt take over our Instagram feed, it's also become the uniform of choice for many fashion-forward celebs, including Natalie Portman, Jennifer Lawrence, and Rihanna. To make the tee even more impactful, the brand announced today that it will donate a portion of the proceeds from sales of the shirt to the Clara Lionel Foundation (CLF), Rihanna's nonprofit organization.The multitalented singer-philanthropist started the group in honor of her grandparents back in 2012. Since then, CLF—which supports and funds global education, health, and emergency-response programs around the world—has offered need-based scholarships for college students in the U.S. and held an annual fund-raising gala called the Diamond Ball. Last week, the Harvard Foundation named Rihanna its 2017 Humanitarian of the Year (previous recipients of the award include former United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon and Pakistani activist Malala Yousafzai).Regardless of its empowering message, the shirt—which retails for $710—initially drew criticism from skeptics who questioned whether or not the brand was capitalizing on the current feminist wave. Earlier this month, actress and teen activist Rowan Blanchard tweeted her concerns regarding the plethora of feminist merch on the runway: "The Dior one 'we should all be feminists' that's popping up everywhere supposedly retails for 700$ hope that $ goes to @PPact or @audrelorde."https://twitter.com/RowanBlanchard/status/833416669644984322Despite the delay (which could be attributed to the brand's traditional six-month production schedule), Dior delivered—and it's not only brand to do so. At New York fashion week this month, both Christian Siriano and Jonathan Simkhai sent down graphic shirts with powerful messages on the runway. Even better: The designers announced they'll donate 100 percent of the proceeds to the ACLU and Planned Parenthood, respectively.Fashion with a mission is something we can all get behind. Sure, the shirt carries a (very) hefty price tag, but maybe now you can treat yourself knowing that a portion of the splurge will be going to a great cause.The tops will be available in Dior boutiques worldwide until May 15 this year. Lovesick, the trendy new sister brand of plus-size retailer Torrid, is expanding its size offerings to correspond with a fierce new campaign celebrating body positivity—giving smaller ladies an opportunity to shop the brand's affordable threads.In a statement, the brand, which launched in April last year, announced all of its clothes will now be available in sizes 8-26—previously, the smallest size it offered was a 10. And while the words "body positivity" and "inclusivity" have been thrown around a lot in fashion lately, Lovesick is committed to backing up its promises. In fact,the brand's size expansion represents one of the first times a plus-size retailer has broken out of its mold and offered threads for straight-size shoppers.In addition to practicing what it preaches, Lovesick is partnering with child rights organization Plan International's "Because I Am A Girl" campaign, which works to empower girls and young women around the world through education. One percent of all sales are donated to the development, which provides uniforms, tuition, and school supplies to girls in need.Lovesick's new sizes launch today, January 5. Ad ChoicesIt's safe to say there's been an eclectic range of collaborations in recent years. Last year alone we saw Christopher Kane put a fresh new spin on Crocs, Vetements bring back Juicy Couture sweats, and Kith take on the '90s with its Power Rangers-inspired streetwear. The latest mash-up to join the list? Coach's new line with indie luxe brand Rodarte.As first reported by WWD, the 15-piece collection includes one handbag and an array of apparel items, and is expected to launch in April at select Coach stores, coach.com, and specialty retailers. According to a Rodarte representative, the capsule is the result of a mutual friendship between Coach's creative director, Stuart Vevers, and Rodarte designers, Kate and Laura Mulleavy, and it'll explore “the idea of mixing the vocabularies of New York and Los Angeles.”At first blush, the partnership between the American brand and the Los Angeles-based label might seem odd given their contrasting aesthetics. The former is best known for its leather goods and a quirky range of millennial-centric offerings, including a Mickey Mouse capsule with Disney and a set of accessories inspired by its mischievous T-rex mascot, Rexy. Rodarte, on the other hand, is the darling of fashion editors and Hollywood A-listers. Its avant-garde and ethereal gowns are a favorite among celebs like Natalie Portman, Ruth Negga, and Kirsten Dunst.And yet despite all the differences, the Coach and Rodarte collab checks all the boxes when it comes to the two brands' end goals. Under Vevers's direction, Coach has been going through a massive brand overhaul in the past couple of years, eschewing its signature logo-heavy bags in favor of Americana-inspired heritage pieces like biker jackets and shearling coats. It enlisted fashion photographer Steven Meisel to shoot ad campaigns, and even announced a new partnership with Louis Vuitton muse Selena Gomez. Last November, the brand unveiled its new flagship store on Fifth Avenue, paving its way into the realm of high fashion.In contrast, the Mulleavy sisters have taken the opposite direction with a series of commercial-focused projects. The label has worked with a diverse range of lower-priced brands and mass-market retailers, including Target, Superga, and even Starbucks. Last March, it launched a lust-worthy ready-to-wear collection—with an equally attractive price tag—in collaboration with H&M's sister brand, & Other Stories. Earlier today, the brand announced it will move its show from New York to Paris, and plans to add a third collection, which will focus on more "lifestyle" items like leather goods and trousers, according to Business of Fashion.If anything, the limited-edition Coach and Rodarte collection finally gives us a chance to snag a Mulleavy sisters original without breaking the bank. Though the price range hasn't been revealed yet, the line will likely fall below Rodarte's four-figure price tag if the brand's past collaborations are any indication.More on our favorite fashion collabs:Check out Rodarte's spring 2017 collection:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesLast night, M.A.C. hosted a party to celebrate their fall makeup collection with Guo Pei. As in the designer who dressed Rihanna for the Met Gala. As in the designer whose epic yellow train has been compared to omelets, egg yolks, and—my personal favorite—pizza crust. So, through a very nervous translator, we went ahead and asked her about these comparisons. And her response was genius."I saw that last night when I was very hungry. I don't care if people make fun of it as long as they love it. People should be happy, and all the works I've done are to express happiness," she said. So basically, she wins.Pei's designs inspired the products in her M.A.C. makeup collection, which features hand-drawn illustrations and actual fabrics on the packaging. This is one of the coolest M.A.C. collections launching this year, which isn't surprising considering it's coming from one of the coolest women we've met in fashion.Fore more M.A.C. news, check out:• See the Entire M.A.C. Ad ChoicesAlso, an explanation of what a VSCO Girl actually is.VSCO Girls. If you're one of the few grown adults who secretly downloaded the TikTok app this year, you've heard the phrase countless times there and eventually saw the teenage archetype become a rapid-fire meme across Twitter and Instagram, too. And, of course, all memes are subject to becoming Halloween costume trends. Chances are, every party you attend this year will be littered in adults dressed like teen girls who just really, really like sandals and Hydro Flasks. If you're looking for a hyper-timely get-up for 2019 (or just want to appear cooler and younger than you actually are), the VSCO Girl is probably one of the easiest to put together.Luckily, Allure's chief TikTok meme poster (hi, yeah, that's me) can walk you through the concept, including what a VSCO Girl actually is, what you'll need to wear, and what to say to really get into character. All it takes is a few staple wardrobe pieces you'll probably use again, a couple of memorable phrases, and a laid-back beauty approach.The "VSCO" in VSCO Girl refers to the photo-editing app of the same name, pronounced "vis-co." The term began as a catchall phrase for teen girls who post pictures on the app's social feed or use its colorful photo filters exclusively on other social media. The VSCO Girl aesthetic, coined in 2017, basically snowballed from there thanks to TikTok and its instant virality.Watch an Actual Youth go shopping and you'll get this aesthetic down pretty quickly. It's part athlete, part hiker, part beach bum.There are three items you absolutely, 100 percent need if you're going to pull off a recognizable VSCO Girl: An oversized T-shirt, athletic shorts, and sandals. Like other teen stereotypes of years past, VSCO Girls have a documented affinity for certain colors and brand names. The key to finding a VSCO Girl-friendly shirt, like this one, is to stick to pastels or intentionally faded colors and to pick a size that's large enough to hit mid-thigh. Contrary to most high-school dress codes, shorts must be so short, they disappear entirely underneath the shirt — can't go wrong with a pair of black Nike Tempo Shorts, a common VSCO Girl staple.As far as shoes go, sandals, clogs, and slides are the primary shoe choices of VSCO Girls everywhere. Have a pair of Crocs lying around? Go to town with some cutesy, customizable Jibbitz (that's the hilarious name of those charms you can attach to the holes in the top) and revel in their squishy comfort. How about some Birkenstock slides? Congratulations, you're already most of the way there.Anyone who wants to take their VSCO Girl costume to the next level certainly can't do so without a Hydro Flask, an arm full of colorful scrunchies, and a puca shell necklace, all main factors of any TikTok meme.The best part of the VSCO Girl Halloween costume is that you can be pretty easygoing when it comes to makeup and hair. These teens are rather laid-back in that regard, so feel free to stick to sheer complexion products and a tinted pink lip balm, like one from E.L.F. Cosmetics'. High messy buns and long, beachy waves are easy to do, too, with the help of a little Not Your Mother's sea salt spray.Study up, y'all, because this is where the fun really comes in. The overall joke about VSCO Girls is that they're overwhelmingly white, inherently wealthy, and more than a little self-absorbed. Ergo, parodied takes on VSCO Girls have spawned a ton of hilarious catchphrases, inspired by a general lack of self-awareness, pseudo-passion for the environment, and obsession with social media.The most important of them all has to be "and I oop," which originates from a viral video of RuPaul's Drag Race star Jasmine Masters. Use it any time something shocking or unexpected happens, even if that something is as plain as one of your scrunchies falling off your wrist. The second most important is "sksksksksksk," which is pronounced exactly how you'd think and is basically the VSCO Girl equivalent of "lol" and the like. It works as a response to everything. Lastly, just tell everyone you see to "save the turtles" — that's why you carry that Hydro Flask, after all, to save plastic.More on Halloween:Trying something more elaborate? The dress is now sold out online.Trump has a history of taking fashion risks. She wed Donald Trump wearing a Christian Dior gown designed by John Galliano. Her mother, Amalija Knavs, was a fashion designer, and Trump herself worked as a model at the young age of 16 with top photographers such as Arthur Elgort and Helmut Newton. She also had her own QVC jewelry and watch collection.Known for her simple and modest silhouettes with graphic pops of color, Ilincic has dressed multiple high-profile women. First Lady Michelle Obama has worn the brand several times, including a violet frock on a state visit to England in 2011. Samantha Cameron donned a navy and coral dress by the label when she left Downing Street with her family last week. During her 2014 visit to Australia, Catherine, Duchess of Cambridge, wore a yellow Roksanda Illincic dress that her husband, Prince William, said made her look "like a banana."Since making her London fashion week debut in 2005, Central Saint Martins grad Ilincic has become a fashion powerhouse with collections sold in over 40 countries.Here are five things to know about the designer.1. She doesn't have a favorite color, which may be why her pieces contain all the colors of the rainbow. "Color brings happiness," Ilincic told the Net-a-Porter magazine The Edit last year. "It's a point of difference, a way of making a statement with something that is not shape or fabric, but something that just makes you feel comfortable and positive. I think that positive energy is very important."2. She's a serious collector of vintage Yves Saint Laurent clothes. "My love for his work comes from my mum because she was crazy about his designs when I was a little girl," she told The Telegraph in 2011. "I probably have about 500 pieces of vintage YSL. I used to find them in car boot sales and charity shops, but now I'm so busy that I go to specialist boutiques—I pay the price for not having enough time to browse the shops."3. Her dream is to see a man wearing her designs. "I have been so lucky, lots of wonderful people have worn it," Ilincic told British Vogue in 2014, when asked whom she'd love to see wearing her pieces. "But I've never seen a man wearing it—I'd love to see a really exciting man wearing it!"__4.__Her love of fashion stems from customizing her mother's clothes in Serbia. "It is hard to get vintage back home. I always used to customize my mum's clothing—she has quite a big wardrobe so there was plenty to choose from," she told The Guardian in 2008. "I already had a love of vintage, but it was just dependent on the wardrobes of my mum, my aunts and my grandma."5. She takes inspiration from the femininity of Serbian women. "My roots are very closely tied to the DNA of the brand," she told Interview magazine in 2014. "Growing up in Serbia where women are unapologetically very feminine, I came to London and realized that I wanted to keep this feminine element but give it a twist and challenge ideas of classical beauty."More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Between that and Christian Siriano's gorgeous dress for Leslie Jones, mainstream fashion is getting its plus size on. It's about damn time.I've worked in fashion for 17 years, and I'm a size 12. I have F-cup boobs. Do you know how hard it is to find designer clothes that fit my figure? When you work at fashion magazines and sites, you have to dress the part. Having a chic look is mandatory.I admit I know little about the plus-size market in terms of brands. I've always covered mainstream lines—designers whose largest offering was a 10. Years ago, the plus-size world wasn't taken as seriously, though the financial impact was always known. (It's a $17.5 billion market, according to the Business of Fashion).I've tried my best to fit into the world I was covering, swathing myself in layers of black in the hopes of hiding my curves. Do you know how many times a fashion pal has said to me, "Oh, my God, your boobs are so big!" I've lost count. Your body is dissected for conversational fodder. The message is: Always be on a diet; always talk about your diet. Show that you're trying to attain an impossible size 2. That's how I lived my life. Screw that.Things have changed, and for the better. Bloggers like Nicolette Mason and models such as Tess Holliday and Ashley Graham are getting the spotlight they deserve. There are more retail brands offering up a variety of sizes (Asos Curve, ModCloth, and Eloquii, to name a few). I've always craved that feeling of a high-end designer's dress zipping up my back with ease. And these Lane Bryant collaborations will satisfy that for me (Siriano debuted his line with the retailer earlier this year, and it sold out within a week)."With our ready-to-wear collection, we reach a more limited consumer, so it is exciting for us to be able to bring fashion to a different demographic," Gurung said in an email. "They've [Lane Bryant] also done a great job at marketing the brand with innovative and powerful campaigns that really resonated with me."Siriano, whose next Lane Bryant collection drops in the fall, told me he doesn't even think about size."I don't know if it's ever been an issue for us," he said. "I've never even thought about it. I grew up with a mom who was a size 14 my whole life. And some of my best customers are over a size 10. I'm a huge fan of tons of women that are every size. I'm not going to say no to dressing Oprah!"Gurung is on the same page: "We've always been able to cut up to a size 22 as we do not want to put a size limit on what we offer, but now's the time to talk more about it and be heard," he said.I want to tell my younger self that she doesn't have to hide in all black, opting for a caftan because it's just easier (but for real, caftans do rock). If you've been feeling self-conscious about your body, take my advice and stop it. You're gorgeous, so own it.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. Ad ChoicesRihanna, Cara Delevingne, and Beyoncé are fans.When NYX Cosmetics founder Toni Ko sold her makeup line for over $500 million to L’Oréal two years ago, she decided to start a line of sunglasses called Perverse, which she launched earlier this spring.With NYX, the entrepreneur broke through the barriers of luxury beauty by offering name-brand-worthy products at an incredibly affordable price point (think $6 matte lipsticks in an assortment of colors). Now she’s doing the same with Perverse by offering quality, fun sunnies that almost anyone can afford. Most Perverse sunglasses retail for less than $50.Celebs have taken notice of Ko’s cool aesthetic. Rihanna, Cara Delevingne, Beyoncé, Kylie Jenner, and Bella Thorne have all worn the sunglasses. Suki Waterhouse and Chanel Iman wore the sunnies at Coachella, while others have been spotted donning them on casual days out.RELATED: Looking Shady: Essential Sunglasses for the Summer“I like things that are simplified with a hint of punk,” Ko told Allure. “I don’t care for too many patterns or colors; I probably wear head-to-toe black about 80 percent of the time. I like to mix femme with hints of masculinity, but simplified.”Many of the frames are retro-inspired, such as tinted aviator frames or round, 1960s-inspired glasses.Toni Ko at Perverse headquarters.“I sold NYX because I thought I wanted to retire. But once I retired, I realized how boring, unproductive, and meaningless life was without working,” says Ko. “I really wanted to start another company because I truly feel happy when I’m working, creating products, and building a brand.”And though she loves beauty, Ko signed a noncompete contract with L’Oréal that lasts five years, so sunglasses, which she collects, were a natural choice. The decision to go into sunglasses also came from Ko’s business research of want versus need. “Food is an absolutely must-purchase, but lippies and sunnies are not,” she says. “So for both businesses, it’s imperative to build an emotional connection with your consumers. I believe the way to connect emotionally is to empower and by sending positive messages to our audience.”With two brick-and-mortar stores already in Los Angeles and six more in the works for other locations in California, it’s safe to say we’ll be seeing more celebs wearing styles like the geek-chic-inspired Bookish frames or the subtle cat eye dubbed the Cool Cat.View From the Fashion Closet: SunglassesMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Described as "a good balance between edgy, sexy, and feminine," the cool girl brand sells an array of #OOTD-worthy pieces like silk maxi dresses with high slits and cute button-downs with funny slogans (“There’s daggers in men’s smiles," one shirt reads), rather than the typical hippie style tees or hemp bracelet we've come to associate with most eco-friendly labels.Just this week, Reformation opened a brand new San Francisco store decked out with seriously high-tech gadgets for all your seamless shopping needs. Touchscreen monitors throughout the shop and in the dressing rooms help keep track of items, styles, colors, and even the wait time for the next available room. Last week, the brand also launched a new eco-conscious denim line called #refjeans for the first time. Here, we caught up with Aflalo to talk about the new store, the brand's vintage-inspired style, and the surprising girl she designs for.What’s your favorite thing about your new store?Basically, we’re using technology to make a high-volume store feel really high-end. I used to work retail, and I remember all I did was clean up, fold, and put stuff away. We’re not going to have that, because the front of the store is a big showroom space and the back of the store is where all the inventory is, which goes right into the dressing room. It’s a very clean, magical space. Yeah, there’s going to be lines for the dressing room, but you’ll know exactly how long your wait time is. You don’t have to stand there, you can do whatever you want in the meantime.Inside the new San Francisco storeWhy is it important now to open a brick-and-mortar store when everyone is so into online shopping?We have three stores right now, and this is going to be our fourth store. Our stores do really well. Stores are actually more profitable for us than online, because between the free shipping and the returns, it just ends up that our stores do better. I like going into stores and going shopping. I like trying things on and I like the whole experience.Yael AflaloSustainable brands tend to have a high price point. How do you keep Reformation affordable, while still making cool clothes girls want to wear?We make stuff in America in our factory, and pay everyone living wage—I would say we’re probably one of the higher paying factories in our area. I don’t know why they can’t make it for cheaper. It's probably because they buy it from another factory who buys it from another factory. There’s a lot of in-between, I’m guessing. Going direct has a lot of value.Who is the girl you are designing for?I design for this waitress girl. She made $200 in tips the night before and she is obsessed with the dress. We’re kind of trading the dress for those tips she made the night before. We try really hard to make sure that we earn that money, and that she’s going to feel really happy and pretty in her new dress.A campaign shot from the brandA lot of your pieces look vintage inspired. How do the silhouettes of the past influence your designs?I love vintage because there’s so much potential. I’ve never found a vintage piece where I was like, ‘Oh, this is perfect.’ I love buying vintage or getting it from a warehouse, and just adding to it. I prefer starting there than starting from scratch. We do it a lot with denim, tops, and dresses.I love to take what’s going on with street style from Pinterest, or just being out and about. I love Alexa Chung and Jeanne Damas. Something else we’ve been doing lately is just looking at old pattern books and DIY sew-it-yourself stuff from the ‘40s and ‘50s. They have a lot of really great silhouettes. I’ve been combining those two lately.If you had to pinpoint the best-seller of all time, what would you say it is?There’s a dress called the Winslow. I think it looks good on a lot of different body types. It’s one of those dresses that a cool girl would buy, but also a girl who's more conservative would buy, as well. It’s just an overall crowd pleaser. It has a lot of versatility in terms of where you can wear it. You could wear it to an event, but you could also just wear it to brunch.A campaign shot from the #refjeans lineWhat other exciting projects do you have coming up for Reformation?We’re really excited about the denim collection we just launched—it sold out, so we have a new re-order coming. We’re going to be focusing more on denim and building out the line.More fashion brands we love:Now, watch how one plus-sized model learned to love her body:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesThe event's theme is "Heavenly Bodies."It's probably safe to assume that Rihanna throws incredible parties. And in just a few short months, we'll get to see her in action, when she hosts the 2018 Met Gala alongside Amal Clooney and Donatella Versace, according to Vogue.The magazine — whose editor-in-chief, Anna Wintour, has chaired the Met Ball since 1995 — noted that the three guests of next year's event have attended a combined 24 Met Galas. Rihanna has attended the event seven times, performed twice, and, earlier this year, she was praised for being one of only a handful of attendees who truly embraced the 2017 gala's theme, "Rei Kawakubo/Comme des Garçons: Art of the In-Between." For the event, she wore a sculptural Comme des Garçons gown covered in fabric "petals." Amal has only attended one Met Ball, 2015's "China: Through the Looking Glass" exhibition, but it was one to remember: She wore a scarlet Maison Margiela Artisanal gown with a fitted bodice and narrow A-line skirt made of layers and layers of ruffled fabric. Donatella has attended a whopping 16 Met Galas since 1995, always in one of her ultra-luxe, form-fitting designs.Last year's hosts were Katy Perry, Pharrell Williams, Gisele Bündchen, and Tom Brady. In the years before that, celebs from all across the entertainment and fashion spectrum, including Taylor Swift, Marc Jacobs, and Jennifer Lawrence, have joined Wintour in cohosting the glamorous event.Vogue also revealed that the theme for next year's event will be "Heavenly Bodies: Fashion and the Catholic Imagination." The exhibit, which aims to "create a dialogue between fashion and the masterworks of religious art" in the Costume Institute's archives, is co-sponsored by Donatella and will juxtapose actual religious pieces — like the papal robes on loan from the Sistine Chapel, many of which have never left the Vatican — with modern-day items by Coco Chanel, John Galliano, and more, that were inspired by Catholic ornamentation and symbolism.The 2018 Met Gala will take place at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City on April 30. The "Heavenly Bodies" exhibit will be open to the public at the Met, the Anna Wintour Costume Center, and the Met's uptown branch, The Cloisters, from May 10 through October 8.Related:For nostalgia's sake, check out last year's absolute best hairstyles:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad Choices"Back-to-school" chic for adults.With fall fashion on the rise but the impermeable summer heat still in the air, backless loafers, or mules, may be your best bet.They've been worn recently by celebrities such as Emma Roberts and Olivia Palermo as well as fashion insiders, including Style Bubble’s Susanna Lau and British Vogue’s Sarah Harris.The shoe style can literally be worn with almost anything (jeans! dresses! sweaters!) and can easily be slipped on or off. While the style comes with or without heels, the flat version is comfortable enough to wear on less formal occasions, but the look is decidedly chicer than a pair of dated ballet flats. The open back provides a cooling sensation, while the preppy style is on point with what’s coming up in fall fashion.Olivia PalermoA hybrid of a shaggy slipper and a classic loafer, Gucci’s fur-lined shoes, as envisioned by Alessandro Michele for his debut fall 2015 collection, became the season’s most coveted footwear. Editors, bloggers, and models alike went head over heels for the style, which quickly sold out at many retailers. Earlier this year, Acne Studios, Céline, and Brother Vellies came out with their own versions of the babouche, a sister style to the backless loafer. As luck would have it, tons of fast-fashion chains from Zara to H&M have released their own iterations in patent leather, floral patterns, and even with cutouts.Want to try the trend yourself? The secret to pulling it off might just be in how you style them. When worn with bare feet, backless loafers come off as bohemian chic. Paired with a pair of preppy socks and trousers, the look is decidedly old-school (and perfect for back to school). Fall-ready fashion that suits the current summer temps? Ad ChoicesIn an age where everyone and their mother seems to have a personal stylist or shopper, or a really opinionated fashionable friend, a celebrity with great style is expected. What's unexpected, though, is a celebrity whose awesome style is 100 percent her own doing, like Ashley Madekwe.Check out how Ashley Madekwe styled this fall's biggest trend:Not only is Madekwe a talented actress (she's had starring roles on Revenge and WGN America's Salem), she also runs a screenshot-worthy fashion blog on the side, called Ring My Bell. Before I chatted with Madekwe for Allure (she's featured in our September issue), I quickly browsed her blog for background research. Two hours later, I had a dozen browser tabs open on my computer, a page-long wish list, and a crazy admiration for the actress's style. Unlike tons of fashion blogs that only feature pieces from Gucci, Prada, and every other gorgeous-but-unattainable designer, Madekwe always features a mix of both high and low items, like an outfit comprised of Steve Madden, Topshop, Forever 21, and a touch of Balmain. Plus, she links to more affordable options of whatever she's wearing, so you really can re-create her style, regardless of your budget. All of which are reasons why we chose Madekwe for the "User's Guide to Style" story in our September issue, in which we asked her to dress up—and down—a pair of Tommy Hilfiger denim culottes with items from her own closet. Exploring Chanel’s relationship to literature, the show takes inspiration from the designer’s impact on an unlikely personality—the French literary critic Roland Barthes. Remember reading about the death of the author in college? That’s him. He once wrote, “If you were to open a text about the history of literature today, you should find in it the name of a new classic author: Coco Chanel. Chanel does not write using paper and ink (except as a pastime), but with fabric, forms, colors.”RELATED: 5 Ways Coco Chanel Changed the Way We DressThe legendary designer knew and admired such writers as Pierre Reverdy, Max Jacob, and Jean Cocteau. In fact, the multitalented and influential Cocteau met her through actress Cecile Sorel in 1917 and introduced her to some of the major artists of their time. In1924, she created costumes for the Blue Train, a ballet which featured a libretto by Cocteau and stage curtain by Pablo Picasso. Other favorite literary minds included Homer, Plato, Virgil, Sophocles, Lucretius, Dante, Montaigne, Cervantes, Madame de Sévigné, and Stéphane Mallarmé.If all this sounds a bit academic, never fear—a wardrobe of fashion creations will be on view alongside dedications, archives, photographs, paintings, and drawings. Curator Jean-Louis Froment is also displaying jewelry, perfumes, and art objects from her Paris apartment, some never before seen. Each element, the exhibition asserts, contributed to Chanel’s unique aesthetic and vocabulary.The exhibition opens with a handwritten note by Chanel that reads, in French, “The life we lead always amounts to so little, the life we dream of, that’s the great existence because it continues on after our death.” Books gave her an escape she craved and fueled the creativity that led her to run one of the world’s most important fashion houses and make “a novel out of her own life,” according to Culture Chanel, the organization behind the exhibition.Coco's Chanel and Karl's Chanel: The Evolution of a Fashion House:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Dreading the Monday blues? The millennial pink-and-sky-blue jumper is bound to help you get through the bleakest 9-to-5 grind. Ready for a cozy Sunday curled up on the couch? The gray pullover is a chic alternative to your tried-and-true Champions hoodie. From high-waist skinnies to fitted straight-legs, the supermodel can make just about any pair a runway-worthy piece, thanks to her enviable frame and impeccable sense of style. Now, Kerr is translating her true blue obsession into a new collaboration with Los Angeles-based denim brand Mother.Available in stores and online now, the 12-piece, limited-edition capsule includes foolproof pieces with hints of '60s and '70s vibes. Think: a flared mini skirt, a figure-hugging jumpsuit, cropped white tees, and a pair of everyday skinny jeans fittingly called “Easy Does It.” The best part? A portion of the proceeds will be donated to The Royal Hospital for Women Foundation, an Australia-based organization that provides support for premature babies and their families. “The whole process was a lot of fun, but I think the best part was creating something meaningful that gives back to others in need,” Kerr tells Allure. “I was a premature baby myself, so the cause is very close to my heart.”Kerr, a long time Mother fan, seized the opportunity to design her first-ever denim collection when the brand’s co-founders, Lela Becker and Tim Kaeding, approached her last May. And though she is no stranger to collaborations—having racked up serious design cred with her line of everyday jewelry for Swarovski and even a porcelain teaware set for Royal Albert—the model admits this design process was different from her past creative endeavors. “You need to take into account the comfort, and how the design and the cut can best flatter the different body shapes of women,” says Kerr, who looked to her own closet for sparks of inspiration. “I worked on every detail—the washes, the pink suede patch, logo, and hardware.”When it comes to putting together the perfect look, Kerr knows comfort is key. Instead of low-rise jeans, she always reaches for a high-waist style because “it nips you in at the smallest part of your waist and elongates the legs." She finishes off her look with wardrobe staples like an oversize tee or a tailored blazer. As for the shoes, Kerr can't resist a pair of cool kicks or dainty ballet flats à la Jane Birkin and Audrey Hepburn—two icons with effortless style, just like the supermodel.More style advice:Four denim trends we love:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The designer, who launched her label Made Gold in 2014, created a capsule collection earlier this year with London artist Yuki Haze that consisted of graffiti slogans and hand-painted faces on denim shorts, jackets, and jeans.Her latest project? A partnership with Los Angeles–based artist Step Son. The two met a few years ago when the artist started showing up at parties Goldschmied was hosting for her brand. “Every single party—one was at an art gallery, one was at a warehouse—he would sneak up and doodle on the men’s bathroom walls,” Goldschmied told Allure. “We’d get in trouble every time. We just thought it would be superfunny to put him to work on an actual denim piece.” The collection, which marks the brand’s first foray into unisex pieces, includes three jackets and two pairs of jeans covered in the artist’s textural drawings and paint splatters.Denim pieces from the new collection.As the daughter of Adriano Goldschmied, the founder of AG Adriano Goldschmied, Diesel, and Replay, Marta puts a focus on high-quality denim with an edge—whether it’s through artist collaborations or rule-breaking, unexpected design quirks. “I think fashion and art are very similar. Our brand is very conceptual, so we resonate with artists,” she said.RELATED: Stella McCartney x Ed Ruscha and Other Memorable Fashion and Art CollaborationsCollaborations aside, Bella and Gigi Hadid are just a few of the celebs who have been seen wearing Made Gold’s sold-out Betty jeans, which have the added detail of lace-up ties on each side of the leg. “That specific design was a way of me rebelling against the system and the way everyone was telling me to do things,” she said. “I wanted to do this really risqué style. It’s very hard to put on, because of the whole side being open. But there is something very feminine [about the jeans] when you’re putting [them] on. It brings you back to the old times when women were helping each other with corsets.” According to Goldschmied, her company advised her to not include the jeans in the collection when it came out last year.A denim jacket from the collection.“Our girl is badass at the end of the day,” said Goldschmied, who is inspired by grunge and continues to rebel by pushing the idea of what denim can be. Cobalt-blue ribbons and bag handles will complement the bright color.The new packaging started arriving in stores over the weekend, along with a new rolling suitcase designed by Marc Newson. According to Michael Burke, the chairman and chief executive officer of Louis Vuitton, the packaging will eventually roll out to the brand's 450 stores worldwide.RELATED: Selena Gomez Is the New Face of Louis Vuitton"We don't want the packaging to be fashionable. It's supposed to have quite a long life cycle," Burke told WWD. "In most cases, brand colors play off of black and white. We wanted to be different."The label has a close relationship with the color scheme. The yellow hue was featured on a vintage Vuitton trunk, the Citroën, which was commissioned by the French carmaker for an expedition in 1924. The color is also similar to the shade of the brand's handles, trim, and labels since 1860. Since Vuitton's inception in 1854, blue details have been used for personalization in the form of initials and ribbons.Most recently, Nicolas Ghesquière, the brand's artistic director, featured the shade on many of its popular handbags, including the Petite Malle and the Twist MM. Saffron also showed up on the fall and spring 2016 catwalks at various labels, including Gucci, Prabal Gurung, and Prada.The new packaging is made to last longer than the old packaging—it's thicker and more resilient—and is more collapsible than ever before.h/t: WWDMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesTo make way for its expansion into Asia.Get ready to see a whole lot less of Michael Kors in your local mall — unless you live in Asia. On Wednesday, the luxury retailer announced it would be closing 100 to 125 stores in the next two years, the Los Angeles Times reports.The reasons for the closures are twofold: It's partly to make way for the brand's expansion into Asia and partly to adjust to the increase in online shopping over in-person purchasing. It's unclear which of the 827 global stores (a number that's actually up by 159 locations from last year) the company is looking to shut down, but the decision is expected to save around $60 million per year, according to the Los Angeles Times."In order to optimize our store base, we performed an in-depth analysis on our entire fleet. Based on the results of this evaluation, we plan to close between 100 and 125 lifestyle stores globally over the next two years," the brand told Allure in a statement. "This will enable us to focus on the most productive locations, as well as those that we believe are important and supporting our brand image."This is not necessarily bad news for the London-based retailer. In an earnings call on Wednesday morning, Michael Kors Chief Executive John Idol said that closing these few stores will help the company focus its resources on its most lucrative locations in "key cities" around the world. He also spoke about the company's plans to expand its influence in Asia, where 50 stores are expected to open this year.“We believe in our retail fleet. We think it's critical to our business,” Idol said. “We think that the key to success there again revolves around product, and revolves around the store environment and creating excitement.”In addition to the closures, Michael Kors also has plans to renovate around 100 of its standing stores, mostly in North America, in the same two-year time frame. According to a statement from the brand, the new store layout is built around a center runway opening into luxurious rooms that distinctly showcase accessories, footwear, women's wear and menswear categories. This will allow sales associates to provide consumers with a unique and elevated styling experience based on the flagship Regent Street store in London.More style stories:Rapper Lizzo Talks Bodysuits and Body Image:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. There’s nothing better than when a revered classic brand like J.Crew and a cutting-edge retailer like Net-a-Porter team up to bring us the fall-fashion love child of our dreams. Pinch yourself because that’s exactly what the two brands are doing with an effortlessly chic capsule collection this season.Set to launch on September 13, the exclusive partnership pays homage to the classic and somehow always edgy Breton stripe—an existing signature in J.Crew’s collections season after season. The signature stripe has storied roots. Originally a part of the official navy uniform for French sailors in 1858, Coco Chanel spotted its ultrachic potential and introduced it to the fashion set with her 1917 collection.RELATED: Isabel Marant Is Bringing Back the Ultimate Cool-Chick ShoesThe 25-piece J.Crew x Net-a-Porter collection lives up to the stripes’ honorable past with a solid balance of wardrobe staples, like the classic navy double-breasted blazer, funky seasonal statement pieces, like the faux-fur (vaguely skunk-like) wrap scarf, and spot-on seasonal trends, like the wide-leg navy trousers.For J.Crew president and creative director Jenna Lyons, the magic is all in the mix. “The edit, which is Net-a-Porter’s strong point, is the result of an extremely fun collaboration,” she said in an interview with WWD. “My favorite pieces are the craziest—the bias-striped fur coat, and the most simple—a striped boatneck T-shirt with a tulle hem.”The collection is also a monochrome addict’s dream—the entire capsule comes in navies and neutrals—and with the balance of safe and daring styles, it’s the perfect injection for a fall wardrobe update.Talking Fashion With Olivia Palermo:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesAnd get this: The new collection will be sold directly to you online.With New York Fashion Week soon approaching (September 8), we’re ready for the onslaught of designer shifts that accompany it. Misha Nonoo is already ahead of the crowd. After staging an “Insta-show” on Instagram last year, she’s skipping the runway format once more in favor of a Snapchat presentation, according to Business of Fashion (BoF). But wait, there’s more: The designer is ditching her wholesale business and selling directly to consumers via her website, mishanonoo.com.“This new model allows me to continue to leverage technology and innovation to interact with my customer directly,” Nonoo said in a statement. “We can now better meet our customer’s wardrobe needs wherever she is, and continue to dress her for every intention.”The switch from wholesale is a major move, one that other designers may soon follow. There’s been grumbling in recent years (and it’s growing louder) that the current fashion calendar makes no sense. The timeline to show the clothes and get them in store is months long, and consumers want instant gratification (sometimes via knockoffs if they’re available sooner).Famed style critic Suzy Menkes likened the fashion schedule—usually two ready-to-wear collections a year, plus haute couture, menswear, resort, and pre-fall—to a “fashion treadmill,” back in 2013. She argued that the schedule was the reason so many designers were burning out. "If we accept that the pace of fashion today was part of the problem behind the decline of John Galliano, the demise of Alexander McQueen and the cause of other well-known rehab cleanups, nonstop shows seem a high price to pay for the endless 'newness' demanded of fashion now,” she wrote in T Magazine.RELATED: Donna Karan and DKNY's Best Fashion MomentsShe’s not the only one who’s questioning the calendar. Public School designers, Dao-Yi Chow and Maxwell Osborne, decided to ditch traditional shows. Instead of adhering to the standard schedule, the duo decided to do two shows a year—one in December and one in June—that combine men’s and women’s collections.RELATED: Burberry Reveals Details About Its First "See Now, Buy Now" CollectionBurberry has already shifted to a direct-to-consumer model. Even Diane von Furstenberg, head of the CFDA, noted to British Vogue, "We have designers, retailers and everybody complaining about the shows. Everything needs to be rebooted."All of this means Misha Nonoo is moving in the right direction, and we expect even more designers to follow her lead. Like Public School, she’s combining the seasonal collections, offering up to three a year: Fashion Essentials, Fashion Specialty, and Evergreen Essentials (the latter will be offered year-round). And unlike her last show, which allowed consumers to preorder an item, they can now buy it instantly. Snapchat, she said to BoF, “is more raw and real life. The thing to expect is new uses of native Snapchat functions. It’s experimental, ephemeral, and speaks to this girl where she is.”The fashion world is changing, and in the end, we’ll all likely benefit from it.Kylie Jenner Teaches You How to Use Snapchat:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesYour days to shop cheap and cheerful strappy sandals in bulk — for less than a Benjamin — are dwindling, as Payless ShoeSource has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Tuesday. Adding to the news, the mass retailer announced its plans to immediately close 400 storefronts in both the U.S. and in Puerto Rico. To be fair, the news isn't entirely shocking. Back in February, we reported on rumors circulating about that very possibility.Devastating, right? I know I'm not alone when I say Payless was my ultimate go-to for budget basic black flats and glittery prom shoes when I was a teen. However, the bankruptcy news isn't all that bad. With the closings, the shoe retailer plans to make lemonade out of lemons by boosting its online e-commerce presence — and reducing its debt by almost half. "This is a difficult, but necessary, decision driven by the continued challenges of the retail environment, which will only intensify," Payless CEO W. Paul Jones said in a statement. "We will build a stronger Payless for our customers, vendors and suppliers, associates, business partners and other stakeholders through this process."Payless ShoeSource was originally founded in 1965, in Topeka, Kanas, where its global headquarters remains today. Since its inception, the discount shoe retailer has opened 4,400 stores in 30 countries and employs nearly 22,000 people. It's also garnered a slew of celebrity fans, including Star Jones and "smize"master Tyra Banks. "My shoes were $20 from Payless and actually only $13 because it was the end-of-summer sale," Banks previously told InStyle. "I went in and bought myself four pairs of shoes. I don't play. And my friends were like, 'Oh my gosh, are those the new Pradas?' And I'm like, 'If you want them to be, sure!'" she said. "Don't they look kind of Prada-ish?"More fashion news:With or without the backing by Banks, it's a time of systemic change for Payless ShoeSource and the state of brick and mortar retail. The shoe store joins American Apparel, Bebe, and The Limited, all of which have made the decision to shutter storefronts this year after sliding profits. Ad ChoicesIn wintertime, my work uniform usually involves leather pencil skirts, snug turtleneck sweaters, boots, and pants, pants, pants. So when it's hot and my choices seem to be all-floral, all-peasant everything, I'm screwed. I can get away with wearing a Mets tank to the office only so many times. Allure's fashion director, Rachael Wang, came to the rescue and shared her top pieces for looking and staying cool in the heat.1. Menswear button-down tops. Cotton means breathable. Plus, with this style, "you can unbutton and push up the sleeves, you can have it tucked in or tucked out, and you can go really oversize and do a half-tuck into a skirt," says Wang.2. Wide-leg pants. "I really love breezy palazzo pants; they're work-appropriate and can also be sexy," says Wang. She recommends pairing them with a blouse and lacy bra to keep the look flowy without veering into hippie. "Culottes are also really nice in a lightweight fabric, like silk or linen, so air can pass through."3. Sandals. It's a little obvious, but when your feet are covered, the trapped heat can warm up your whole body. Flat gladiators or sandals with a little heel allow your toes to breathe. You may still want to consider alternate footwear if you commute to avoid dirty feet, though. "I'm totally the commuter lady who wears sneakers on the subway," says Wang.4. Kimono tops. Versions that have wrap waists and full sleeves bring a little structure and tailoring to summer dressing. The cut may seem like a lot of material, but in light fabrics, it's actually pretty cool.5. Dresses. If you want to avoid the frilly, ruffled look, wrap dresses and shirtdresses tend to have cleaner silhouettes that are feminine, not girlie. The skirts can be as straight or full as you like. "And I generally think midcalf is appropriate, but you can go above the knee if you want," says Wang.6. Midi skirt. They're the Vans of bottoms—comfortable, classic, and easy to wear with anything. To sneak sexy into your midi skirt, look for one with a slit up the leg. The most important detail is fabric. "Choose cotton, silk, linen, any of the natural fabrics," says Wang. "You obviously want to stay away from wool and also polyester. You could probably pull off rayon if it's really breezy and doesn't touch your body, but anything synthetic is going to trap heat and make you sweat."Check out more of Wang's fashion favorites here:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast.
