Since 2014, Aerie has stopped using Photoshop on its visuals for intimates and swimwear as part of its #AerieReal body-positive movement.The video features 40 Aerie girls, including British model Iskra Lawrence, the brand’s role model and a National Eating Disorder Association ambassador. Artists, bloggers, social-media fans, and Aerie designers star alongside Lawrence, plus models Barbie Ferreira, Fo Porter, Amber Tolliver, Annie McGinty, Diana Veras, and Eli Almeida."Aerie continues to transform the industry by eliminating retouched photos and encouraging women to discuss important issues like body image, self care and education," said Iskra Lawrence in a statement. Together, we can learn to love our real selves and change the world."The “Share Your Spark” campaign is an inspiration to women of all ages, and follows the body-positive trend that’s been sweeping the fashion industry. Last month, Nike released a sports bra campaign featuring plus-sized model Paloma Elsesser. Plus-sized retailer Lane Bryant started its #ImNoAngel campaign last year in response to Victoria’s Secrets “The Perfect ‘Body’” ads. The brand also created a campaign called #PlusIsEqual, which highlights underrepresentation of plus-sized women in the media and the fashion industry.RELATED: Nike's Body-Positive Bra Campaign Is All About the CurvesAccording to the apparel brand, 67 percent of women in the US are sizes 14 to 34. In addition, the NPD Group, a market research company, recently reported that teens purchasing plus-size clothes has almost doubled to 34 percent since 2012. Tapping into a more extensive variety of sizes—and creating campaign imagery that represents a wider array of body types, much like Aerie’s new campaign—is incredibly beneficial for fashion brands.Here’s to more celebrations of body empowerment.My Look: Paloma ElsesserMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesIf you’re a street-style fan, you’re probably familiar with the highly Instagrammable minimalist bags from Mansur Gavriel. After hitting the scene four years ago with the now signature bucket bag, the simple, chic line of pastel and poppy-hued carry-alls have become instant style stars. Now, Mansur Gavriel is about to take that "It" girl whisperer know-how into the realm of apparel with its first ready-to-wear collection. Brace yourself.After conquering the world of accessories (cofounders Rachel Mansur and Floriana Gavriel were dubbed the accessories designer of the year by the Council of Fashion Designers of America, NBD) with its clean, sculptural bags and equally simplified shoes, the completely self-funded brand announced today that they were ready to take on the world of ready-to-wear.“Creatively, we were always ready,” Mansur said in an interview with Business of Fashion. “We had such fast growth with the bags that we felt that we needed to be operationally prepared. Now the time is right.”The brand will debut its freshman collection of autumn/winter apparel at New York Fashion Week in September, a move that also signals a shift to the see-now-buy-now trend that took over NYFW last year and hasn’t left the runways since. “With social media today, the whole system just doesn’t make much sense to us,” said Mansur. “It also feels much more exciting creatively to share the collection at the same time that it will be offered to the public.”To the delight of stylists everywhere, the good news continues. Along with the expansion into our closets, Mansur Gavriel also announced that it'll be sticking around its brick and mortar pop-up shop in NYC’s SoHo neighborhood. To celebrate its new seasonal schedule, the space will be turned into a "fully immersive Candy shop environment" to showcase its spring 2017 collection on February 14. The pop-up will be open to the public the next day for four weeks. Customers will be able to shop the existing collection while enjoying candy and cake imported from Italy. They’re flattering and work well for day, evenings, and work meetings.Uniqlo V-neck sweater, $19.90 (uniqlo.com); Uniqlo Crewneck Sweater, $19.90 (uniqlo.com).Two cashmere sweaters, one in charcoal from Uniqlo and the other in burgundy from Everlane, have been all I’ve needed this winter, thanks to savvy use of under-layers (see next slide).Uniqlo cashmere V-neck sweater, $59.90 (uniqlo.com); Everlane cashmere sweater, $100 (everlane.com).I am a huge, huge fan of Uniqlo’s heat-trapping body-wear line, HeatTech, which I wear under all of my clothes in the winter. In my suitcase I keep two pairs of opaque black tights, one black turtleneck, and a nude scoop-neck long-sleeved tee to layer under my skirts and sweaters. Typically, the content of the site or app is used to make inferences about your interests, which inform future selection of advertising and/or content.Select All3 PurposesConsent PurposesLocation Based AdsConsent AllowedLegitimate Interest PurposesPersonalizeFeaturesLocation Based AdsClear Fliters“She is on a boat, clutching her two-year-old son, so tight, wishing she could protect him from all he’s seen. She thinks of her war-torn country — or what remains of it. Her two-year-old cries, hungry and shivering. She is aware that she is of the lucky few who were able to secure a spot on this raft, but is terrified of what lies ahead. She wonders what will become of her husband who was unable to join her on this journey but told her he would catch up to them. She never thought they would be separated like this. Choking back tears, she stares down at her son's eyes that ache from crying. His ribs have become clearly visible. She stares to the point where an endless blue sea meets an endless blue sky and wonders if that is where hope lies.”This excerpt is from a prose poem entrepreneur Shahd Alasaly wrote when she was trying to decide what to name her Syrian-influenced ethical clothing brand. Alasaly, who is of Syrian descent, founded Blue Meets Blue, an initiative that marries social consciousness and ethical fashion in a clothing line that boasts flowing silhouettes, dark hues, and sophisticated beadwork.Blue Meets Blue is more than a just a brand, though. It's a community of artisans who support, employ, and encourage Syrian refugee women to create gorgeous clothes, made in the U.S. Made by seamstresses and designers from several countries (including Turkey and Jordan), the pieces are products of an inclusive and promising Middle Eastern–heritage local collective. I sat down with Alasaly to delve in on her ambitions, hopes, and projects toward a brighter, ethical future.ALLURE: Please tell us more about your background and the challenges starting this clothing line.SHAHD ALASALY: When I learned we were facing the biggest refugee crisis since World War II, I wanted to find a way to help. So, I combined my background in psychology with my background in design [to create a] form of art therapy, with a little spin of fashion psychology. We wanted to create a luxury clothing line that empowers refugees. We wanted them to find employment as soon as they arrived in the United States and we wanted them to work in their skill set.We noticed as they sew, having many deep conversations about the difficult experiences they had endured, it helps to reduce a lot of their anxieties, a lot of their depression, and they express themselves through the intricate work that they do. This is their skill set, so they definitely feel empowered while they are doing it. This definitely has been our focus. Then to move on, the list of challenges they face is very long, but they’re resilient, they’re strong, and they want the best for their families.We have a few goals at Blue Meets Blue. First of all, we want to empower the refugees, especially Syrian, by providing them with fair employment and an opportunity to take care of their families. We want to create a sense of community for them. A lot of their depression and PTSD comes from coming to a new country, having language barriers, not having any friends, not having any support. So this is a support system for them.Steering away from fast fashion, we want clothing with a meaning — meaning for people who are making it and people who are buying it. Lastly, we wanted to eliminate a lot of the misunderstanding about refugees by spreading love through our fashion. Art is a very common language. Whether it’s music or fashion, people can all relate. When people see beautiful clothing, there’s something they are connected to and can talk about.ALLURE: What do you think of fast fashion today, and how do think you are helping to fix some of the problems that come with it?SA: Fast fashion right now, starting with consumers, is definitely losing track. Fast fashion is very detrimental to the environment — to the people involved. The sweatshops are not cutting it anymore. People are aware of how their products are being created, made, and manufactured. It’s very important to us to have a high-quality model, to create and produce in the United States, to provide and bring jobs to the United States.Those are all things that we are focusing on. We want to focus on creating quality clothing, things that people will keep in their closet for a long time. When they buy it, they have a connection to it; they have a connection to the story behind it, and they want to keep it for a long time. It’s not something that’s as easily disposable, and that’s what we want our clothing to be.ALLURE: I am always impressed with Syrian craftsmanship, like the skilled beading, sewing, and mix of fabrics. What is your recruitment process like, and how do you scout women with the skill set to help you create the luxury clothing?SA: We partner with a lot of resettlement agencies in Chicago right now, like the Syrian Community Network, RefugeeOne, and a bunch of [other ones]. They [see] who [is] skilled in certain things and [give] me the information. Aside from that, we’ve also had a lot of refugees personally reaching out to us via email, which has been so exciting to me but also very heartbreaking, because I can’t reply to everybody, and that makes me very sad. The fact that they are excited about it — the amount of people that have reached out to us and wanted to be part of our team has been just very, very, incredible. So it really comes from everywhere.ALLURE: How would you say you are contributing to the shift in attitudes toward Syrian refugees in America? How does being based in Chicago allow you to do so?SA:  Just focusing on something that is a common language for everyone has helped a lot. When people come [to see the clothes], whether we have a pop-up shop or a trunk show [or] a booth, first they’re coming and seeing a product and then they hear the story behind it. Then they hear a little bit about each of the artisans that are working, like: “Oh, this person came to the United States and she wants a better life for her child,” and they see points they can relate to. We also have these facts we hear, for example, [that] there are 65 million people displaced from their homes around the world.About seven out of 10 Syrians are now displaced from their home. Homeland Security found out that not one refugee has committed an act of terror. All these things bring it back to perspective. Having open conversations and dialogues have really helped these shifts. We had an interview on WBEZ, the public radio [station] in Chicago, and after that interview, we had a few people reach out to us and say, “You really changed my misconceptions about refugees from the things that you’ve said,” or “I am so interested to learn more,” and that alone to me is success.ALLURE: Given that we’re facing the biggest crisis of global displacement from countries including Iraq, Somalia, and Sudan — just to name a few — what are your hopes and concerns for 2018?SA: Obviously, like everybody, you want peace to return to their [countries]. Nobody wants to be displaced from their home. For the people who have left their home and starting over, to be able to start over in peace. My hope is for all the wars to end [and] for more understanding and dialogue in the world.ALLURE: With a climate of uncertainty, what can fashion do to address the crisis in Syria?SA: What we’re doing, for example, I think that’s a great model. Whether it’s in fashion or any other industry, to be able to think of a problem and say: “I can help.” You have doctors who are doing missions out in places like Haiti, Turkey, and Greece; anybody can find a way to help out in their skill set. Specifically, in fashion, my hope for Blue Meets Blue is to open a warehouse or a factory so that when refugees enter the United States, they automatically have a job upon arriving. Specifically, the ones [who are skilled at] embroidery, beading, and pattern-making, or [who] were seamstresses. It’d be really wonderful for them to have workshops and teach others who are interested. My hope is to have a warehouse soon, [and to be be] able to employ as many as possible in as many states as we can, because there are many refugees in every state. There’s a lot that every industry can do, and people who can do should take that stance and think [about] how they can serve their community.ALLURE: Finally, what does Blue Meets Blue stand for?SA: When I was thinking of a name, the same image kept popping into my head. Them leaving their country and take a very challenging route. Sometimes involving being on a boat, the only thing they see is blue of the ocean meeting the blue of the sky. In my head that was symbolizing their journey to freedom. Their journey to hope.More stories to check out:Now, watch this video about popular eye makeup styles from the past century:Follow Jihane on Twitter.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesSince the debut of the smartwatch a few years ago, the market has been flooded with wearable technology. Across brands, the basic features are nearly identical, but details like OS compatibility (and design, of course) need to be taken into account. We broke down the key differences between the six major smartwatch brands to help you determine which is the best fit for you—whether you're #TeamiPhone or #TeamAndroid.Apple WatchThough not the first wearable to debut on the market (Pebble is responsible for that), this smartwatch is definitely the most widely known. Apple watches can only run on iOS (sorry, Androids) but with a Remote app (for controlling Apple TV) and Apple Pay capabilities, it's a must-have for die-hard Apple fans. And with 11 customizable watch faces, availability in two sizes (38 millimeters and 42 millimeters), and 22 interchangeable bands, it looks damn chic, too. Prices start at $299.Android WearGoogle's entry is both iOS and Android compatible, spans 12 different brands (including Tag Heuer, Fossil, and soon, Michael Kors), and has the most body options of any of the smartwatches. With thousands of interchangeable watch faces and new Mode snap-and-swap bands, this device can track your heart rate through Zumba and also elevate your dinner-to-drinks outfit. It's the chicest of all smartwatches, if you ask us. Prices vary by brand.Samsung smartwatchesMost of Samsung's Gear S2 watches run on Samsung's own Tizen OS (currently only the Gear Live runs on Android Wear), so if you don't have a Samsung smartphone, this might not be the best option for you. But with a standalone music player, WatchON (a built-in IR blaster a.k.a. remote control), and over 1,000 apps in its app store, this smartwatch brings greater accessibility to the palm of your hand. Er, wrist. Prices start at $299.99.PebblePebble entered the smartwatch game in 2012 with the release of the first modern wearable financed through Kickstarter. Since then, the "people's smartwatch" has evolved to run on both Android and iOS, is compatible with plenty of apps, and is the most affordable smartwatch on the market. Offered in five styles (Time, Time Steel, Time Round, Steel and Classic), this waterproof but non-touchscreen superwatch strikes just the perfect balance between underdog and hipster cool. Prices start at $99.99.Vector WatchesThis watch's long-lasting battery life (30 days!) is probably the biggest draw; throw in the fact that it's compatible with Android, iOS, and Windows phones, and you've got a serious (though largely unknown) contender in the smartwatch competition. Like Pebble, these watches aren't touchscreen, but the water-resistant, always-on interface makes it a great watch—with the added benefit of being smart. Prices start at $299.BlocksLike Pebble, Blocks was born through Kickstarter and is touted as the first modular smartwatch, meaning you can customize the technology around your needs, adding and upgrading features to infinitely expand and customize functionality. The individual modules form the links in the band and can do anything from extend battery life to convert motion into energy to monitor air-quality control. If only everything in our lives were so customizable. Available for preorder, with prices starting at $330.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. Ad Choiceswww.allure.comhttp’s server IP address could not be found.Try:nullWhat do you think of when you hear the word "neutral"? For many of us, it's black, white, gray, and the occasional brown. Cue the silver, your new favorite neutral for everyday wear. When it comes down to it, metallics are actually quite wearable. Gone are the days when these shiny shoes came out to play for their late-night Studio 54 debut. Pair them with a plain white tee and jeans, and you have the perfect outfit for day. To narrow down the overwhelming range of shopping options in the French fashion capital, we asked designers and stylists for their go-to magasins and favorite hidden gems. So whether you’re heading to the City of Light for the grand finale of fashion month or just planning a fromage-filled voyage there this fall, here are seven chic shops you won’t want to miss.Isaac ReinaBarcelona-born Isaac Reina crafts simple yet incredibly soft and luxurious bags and small leather goods for his eponymous line, and the full collection can only be found in his Right Bank store. [LD Tuttle] (http://ldtuttle.com/) designer Tiffany Tuttle loves to visit the boutique for this very reason: “It’s a very hard-to-find brand. In their store, you can see the whole collection in all different colors, and the person in there is so happy and willing to show you all of the details that make their bags special.” The boutique is tiny, but its sleek, minimalist design reflects the overall aesthetic of the brand and is a welcome respite from the white noise of the city's visuals. “In Paris, everyone really seems to put so much into their stores so that they really tell a complete story about the brand; I especially appreciate this,” says Tuttle. 12 Rue de Thorigny, isaacreina.com.RELATED: 6 Places So Gorgeous, You'll Forget About SnapchatHosesHosesNestled in a discreetly chic area in the heart of Le Marais, Hoses carries a tightly edited selection of shoes, bags, and jewelry from under-the-radar brands (Unutzer, Mimi Berry) and highly coveted labels (Saint Laurent, Church’s) alike—many of which are exclusive to the store. Julia Leach, creative director of [Chance] (http://www.chanceco.com/), has been buying the “tailored and tomboy” styles for almost a decade. 41 Rue de Poitou, hoses-limited.com.SpreeSpreeThis Montmartre-based gallery and boutique sells an artful mix of designer fashion and mid-century modern décor, thoughtfully curated by the husband-wife duo Bruno Hadjadj, a visual artist, and Roberta Oprandi, a fashion designer and Isabel Marant collaborator. “They always have a wonderful selection that is of-the-moment but not too trendy, along with vintage furniture, books, and artwork for sale,” says Leach. So you can actually buy the whole flatlay look and the Friso Kramer table it’s presented on. 16 Rue la Vieuville, spree.fr.L'Atelier RenardL’Atelier RenardIf you’re looking for a completely one-of-a-kind artisan-crafted leather bag that only gets even better with age, don’t miss a trip to the storied L’Atelier Renard, which has been creating designs for famous fashion houses as well as in-the-know individuals. Perfumer [Francis Kurkdjian] (http://www.franciskurkdjian.com/?lang=en) frequents the workshop for bespoke travel accessories and recently collaborated with the company on his own line of card holders laced with notes from his signature scents. 3 Place du Palais Bourbon, atelierrenard.com/.RELATED: What a Headache It Is to Find the Perfect ScentBulyL'Officine Universelle BulyEntering this apothecary-style beauty emporium is like stepping back in time a few hundred years—probably because it’s inspired by the nineteenth-century French perfumery after which it’s named. Although the fragrances, skin-care, and bath products have been updated with modernized formulas, they are still packaged in gorgeously illustrated, Old World-feeling jars and vials that [Preciously Paris] (http://www.preciously.fr/en/index.php?) designer Carole Tessier stocks up on to display on her bathroom shelves. 6 Rue Bonaparte, buly1803.com.Lydia CourteilleLydia CourteilleLydia Courteille’s Saint Honoré boutique is a sparkling cabinet of curiosities filled with fantastical, sculptural jewelry. Tessier says about the pieces, “I like the rare and one-of-a-kind stones used, which can be worn with everything from jeans to couture dresses.” The prices are as one would expect for such meticulously crafted precious gems, but whether you’re in the market or not, at the very least it makes for some theatrical window shopping and a close-up look at the kind of baubles Rihanna wears while performing. 213 Rue Saint Honoré, lydiacourteille.com.MerciMerciHoused in a historic tri-level converted factory, this one-stop supershop carries everything from understated but chic lingerie and cult-favorite beauty products, to handmade ceramics and marble-patterned stationery, and much more—making for some seriously cool souvenir shopping. Costume designer and celebrity stylist Negar Ali Kline says, “It’s a very inspired curation. I find things there that I haven’t seen anywhere else.” Take a break from the inevitable hours of combing the wares at one of their three in-house cafés (our favorite is the one lined with thousands of used books that you can flip through while waiting for your eggs en cocotte). Plus, a portion of profits go to a children’s charity in Madagascar—as if you needed another reason to visit. 111 Boulevard Beaumarchais, merci-merci.com.RELATED: Beyond the Birkin: 3 Investment Handbags From HermèsA day in Paris:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad Choiceswww.allure.comhttp’s server IP address could not be found.Try:nullFew things get me as excited for the arrival of summer as a new pair of sandals. There are those who have embraced the Birkenstock and the shower shoe, but I tip my hat to a designer determined to make beautiful, feminine ones—behold Stuart Weitzman's leg-wrap sandals, which take the season's ever-popular gladiator to new heights with a four-and-a-half-inch stiletto heel. (Bonus: Proceeds from the four-color, limited-edition collection will benefit cancer research at the Boston Children's Hospital's Folkman Institute.) I recently spoke to Weitzman about his charitable collaboration, the three iconic muses always on his mind, and how he really feels about designer copycats.How did your collaboration with Dr. Martha Moses to benefit cancer research at the Folkman Institute come about? "This is not the first time that we've put together a fashion collaboration. I recognize the wonderful work that she does in her foundation, and we have kind of adopted women's cancer as the charity that we try to raise the most money for. And this is the third time that we are doing something to raise funds for her organization. We started to have tremendous demand for this particular lace-up-the-leg sandal, and we knew it would be a shoe with high visibility, which would then allow what we're doing to be highly publicized and hopefully encourage other people to support this noble work as well."How does fund-raising for ovarian and breast cancer research connect specifically with your customer? "Almost everyone we know has had some sort of family with both of these. My sister had ovarian cancer—she's a survivor. My mother-in-law is not a survivor. She died from breast cancer 40 years ago, before we were all aware of what needs to be done. Our customer is a woman, and these are two ailments that afflict her."When starting a new collection, where do you look for inspiration? "I really design for women, and I have my muses that I think about as the collection progresses. We are very, very good at making and engineering the shoe in a comfortable, fitting way. There's a lot of faces of ladies that enter my mind when I'm designing the shoes, and I give most of my inspiration to the fact that I'm doing it for women and not for some abstract dream."Do you have any specific muses? "There are two icons who are always there, and I'm always thinking, What would she wear today? Audrey Hepburn and Jackie Onassis. They were always ladies who had so much confidence in how they dressed and how they looked and how they felt that they never needed the use of a high heel to give them another personality or enhance anything about themselves. And yet they looked very cool and chic in these wonderful flats. And then their contemporary, Marilyn Monroe. She had to have show-off footwear. And I've always felt that if I can design for both of those types of women, then I've covered the range."Your 50/50 boots have become some of the most sought-after styles around—and the most copied. What makes them so popular, and how do you feel about other designers replicating them? "I always try to think back to what my father said: 'If they don't copy you, you're not doing something right.' Well, that's sort of a truism. In one sense, it's a compliment. And in the other sense, I'm also a businessman, and it's disturbing when the laws of the land allow them to have something almost identical for a quarter of the price, made in an inferior way in a far-off land, but that's the way it is."Do you keep an eye on the work of other designers? "I never design in a vacuum. I don't lock myself in a studio and close the other world away from me. Ready-to-wear design will affect trends and attitudes, so I'm always on top of both ready-to-wear fashion and what other footwear fashion there is out there."What are you doing for your next collection? What new colors and silhouettes are on the horizon? "Throughout our collection are all kinds of materials: the softness of suede and the exotic nature of crocodile, as well as patent leather. We're building upon the boot business that women have told us they love. We think we can push the envelope by making the boot even longer. In contrast to that, there's the boldness of platforms and the big heels of the '70s this coming fall and next spring. I think next season it will be the sexy pump with the big heel. In a woman's mind, she thinks, That's a heel I could wear all day, as opposed to a thin heel, which she's buying for an evening out."For more on fashion, check out:• 10 So-Pretty Flats to Get You Through Spring• Manolo Blahnik: 10 Beautiful Things• How to Look Great When You TravelMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Say bonjour to these stylish kicks.Veja, the chic French sneaker brand made in Brazil, already has a reputation for being a favorite of fashion’s elite.The label, known for its use of sustainable and organic materials, is sold worldwide at some of the coolest boutiques, including Dover Street Market, Kith, and Colette. Marion Cotillard, the French actress and epitome of Parisian style, is also a fan.Now, 12 years after its inception, Veja will make its biggest U.S. debut to date. Until October 11, the brand will open a pop-up shop inside New York's SoHo boutique Anthom. The store will carry the most extensive range of Veja sneakers ever to hit the States—from the bestselling Esplar 3 Locks, which feature three Velcro straps, to the V-10, a classic lace-up that comes in neutral shades. These shoes look even better when worn over time like your favorite leather jacket or that pair of distressed vintage jeans. Oh, and did we mention that all of Veja’s styles are unisex?We sat down with co-founder François-Ghislain Morillion, one half of the creative duo alongside his partner, Sébastien Kopp, to talk French inspiration, sustainable materials, and the celeb he would love to see wearing the brand's shoes.Veja is a French brand, but everything is made in Brazil. How do the two different cultures affect the aesthetic?I think our sneakers are a bit more French than Brazilian. Brazil is about tons of colors and a lot of information, and we try to reduce it. It’s about going to the core of the product. When we designed our retro runner shoes, we tried to do it in the simplest way. In the end, we like it when it’s sharp and clean. Though, Brazilian architecture is magnificent. It’s simple and brutal.What French style icons do you find inspiring?One of our style icons is Marion Cotillard. She’s wearing our shoes with a Dior dress, and we find that pretty cool. It’s kind of a bohemian thing. She’s chic, but she’s not dressed up—that’s very Parisian. In London, the girls are very dressed up. In Paris, they’re a bit more relaxed, and they can wear sneakers with a dress. There’s no problem with that.What artists inspire the different textures of each sneaker?Lots of artists. My favorite artists are Rothko and Richard Serra. I love the thickness of Serra’s materials. For shoes, it’s not only visual, you have to touch it. In a way, it transmits an energy. You always have some shoes that you prefer to others, and it’s not always because they’re more beautiful. It’ also because when you touch them, they’re nicer.RELATED: 9 Eye-Catching Shoes From NYFWWhy is it important for your brand to be sustainable?We created this company with this ideal: To be able to make really beautiful pieces that respect men and the environment. Then, it really started to be a game—to be able to innovate and always go forward. Two years ago, we launched shoes using fish leather. We always want to be the leaders in the market and be really ahead of the others. It’s fun, to be able to get rid of plastics. It’s really something that the big brands are also working on. But they’ll be doing it more in five or ten years.All of the shoes are made in Brazil in a factory that respects the rights of workers. We do social audits every year to be sure that the social rules are respected. That’s different. All our raw materials come from Brazil. The rubber comes from the Amazon forest.What’s the most groundbreaking thing you’ve done in terms of sustainability with your sneakers?We are working on a way to get rid of leather. I’m not able to talk about it much yet, because it’s a big research project, but we’re working on it with scientists. Leather is still not so sustainable. It’s a product of the meat industry. It’s not our dream material. For now, we have not found a material that is as beautiful as leather. The main thing is the texture and the way it wears with time. If you use synthetic leather, it’s actually plastic and it doesn’t age.In twelve years designing for Veja, what’s the most surprising thing you’ve come across?Korean craze. Koreans are crazy about our shoes. All these K-pop stars are wearing them. It was totally unexpected. If you go to Seoul, you’ll see them everywhere. We started really booming this year. They love the V-10. It’s very French and also very American. They also love to dress like couples. They even match the underwear.Who would you love to see wearing your sneakers?I’d say Obama. That’d be really cool.Marion Cotillard on the celebrity who makes her swoon:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. Go ahead and ask Sunny Co. Clothing — but it might take the house a little while to get back to you.The California-based clothing company is currently dealing with potentially having to give away tens of thousands of free bathing suits after an Instagram promotion massively backfired. The swimsuit saga began on Thursday, when Sunny Co. posted a photo promising a free "Pamela" bathing suit (which retails for $64.99) to everyone who reposted the image and tagged the company over the next 24 hours, Buzzfeed reports. The only stipulations mentioned in the original post were that the offer was valid only in the U.S. and that individuals were responsible for covering the shipping and handling. NBD, right?That's when all hell broke loose. The post has since gained more than 338,000 likes, and thousands of people began reposting the image in an attempt to cash in on the free Baywatch-style swimsuit. The massive response led Sunny Co. to adjust the rules of the giveaway several hours after the initial promotion was originally announced. A second Instagram post added a rule stipulating that Sunny Co. "reserves the right to cap the promotion...due to the viral volume of participants." Additionally, the brand warned that processing and shipping would most likely be delayed due to the "overwhelming volume of orders."But Sunny Co. has more problems to deal with than fulfilling thousands of free swimsuit orders. Multiple people are claiming on Facebook that they were charged for the full price of the swimsuit, rather than just the $12.98 for shipping and handling. Buzzfeed reports that customers have reached out to Sunny Co. on various platforms; the queries have thus far gone unanswered. We've has reached out to the brand for comment.Sunny Co. may not be responding yet, but Twitter is. In the 1920s, American tennis player Bill Tilden impressed fans with his forehand and his preppy style, according to The Stylish Life: Tennis by Ben Rothenberg. Tilden's understated white V-neck sweaters and matching trousers remain a classic ensemble in men’s fashion today.Advances in technology have also changed the way tennis uniforms look and function. Spandex, nylon, and other synthetic fabrics created to wick away perspiration are essential—and a far cry from what athletes were wearing 100 years ago. Keren Ben-Horin, a fashion historian and coauthor of She’s Got Legs: A History of Hemlines and Fashion, told Allure, “When Victorian women played tennis in the 1880s and 1890s, they were wearing their street clothes, which included heavy undergarments like corsets, bustles, and petticoats, and voluminous skirts that grazed the ground."Let’s take a look back at how tennis uniforms have changed through the ages.Tennis grew popular in Victorian England, and the clothing matched the fashion of the day: dresses with high collars and long sleeves. White clothing, which dirties easily, became a symbol of the rich, much like the sport itself. "Tennis whites" gradually became a rule, with Wimbledon mandating all-white uniforms for its players in 1890. In the early 1900s, women played tennis in floor-length skirts, stockings, and long-sleeved tops (all of which prevented range of mobility). British tennis player Dorothea Douglass (shown here) won the Wimbledon Women’s Singles title seven times.French tennis player Suzanne Lenglen caused a stir when she played Wimbledon with bare arms and a knee-length hemline. Her outfit was made by French designer Jean Patou. Lenglen also wore flapper-style headbands on the court. During that decade, French tennis player René Lacoste created lightweight, breathable cotton shirts (now known as polo shirts) and started mass-producing them in 1933. Today, the Lacoste brand continues to manufacture the tops emblazoned with the iconic crocodile (“The Crocodile” was Lacoste's nickname).Helen Wills Moody’s courtside uniforms fit in with the loose and boxy silhouettes of the 1930s. Instead of impractical long skirts, Moody preferred to wear pleated knee-length skirts and her signature white visor.The ultrafeminine outfit worn by American tennis player Gertrude Moran at Wimbledon in 1949 was a hint of 1950s trends to come. Her top had ruffles, and she (intentionally) wore shorts designed by British couturier Ted Tinling with lace that peeked out as she played. Photographers lay flat on the ground to try to get pictures of the lace shorts.Women’s tennis uniforms in the 1950s were all about cinched waists, decorative cardigans, and feminine pleated skirts, seen here on the American player Maureen Connolly. And following his retirement, British tennis player Fred Perry launched his namesake sportswear brand in 1952.Mod fashion took the 1960s by storm and showed up in tennis uniforms. Streamlined tunics with pops of gingham were popular, as were the graphic shorts worn by English players Virginia Wade and Lorna Greville-Collins, and Marlys Burel of France.Americans John McEnroe and Vitas Gerulaitis opted for terrycloth headbands, colorful striped polo shirts, and short shorts. Originally a knitwear company, Fila started making sportswear with the endorsement of Swedish tennis star Björn Borg, shown here.At the height of the 1980s, uniforms became tighter and leaner all over. American tennis player Anne White, shown here, wore a white unitard to Wimbledon in 1985. Officials reportedly requested that she dress more traditionally the next day. At the 1987 U.S. Open, American Chris Evert lost her diamond bracelet on the court during a match, and the game was paused until it was found. That incident led to the diamond "tennis bracelet."American tennis player Andre Agassi paired denim shorts with fluorescent cycling shorts and flamboyant shirts. Agassi refused to play Wimbledon from 1988 to 1990 because he didn’t approve of the all-white dress code.Russian tennis player Maria Sharapova’s early 2000s outfits included menswear elements and plenty of Swarovski crystals. At Wimbledon 2008, Sharapova debuted a Nike-designed, tuxedo-inspired ensemble.At the 2010 French Open, Venus Williams, who has been known to wear edgy uniforms (as has her sister Serena), wore a black transparent lacy piece that looked like it was inspired by lingerie. The tennis star wore a pair of nude shorts underneath.At this year’s Wimbledon tournament, Nike-sponsored women wore pleated shift dresses that kept flying up and exposing the stomach (shown: Eugenie Bouchard of Canada). According to the New York Times, players who were uncomfortable with the loose dresses were given traditional skirts and tops. Brand endorsements are one of the biggest influencers of modern tennis style today.At the 2016 Wimbledon Championships, Serena Williams won her 22nd Grand Slam title wearing a white high-collared dress with a pleated skirt by Nike. Some Twitter users critiqued the outfit for being too revealing: "I wouldn't usually comment on another woman's body, but could someone give Serena Williams something to cover her nipples...very distracting," one user tweeted. Many of her fans clapped back in defense of her body and the dress, which was applauded for its simple yet classic design.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. All rights reserved. Since Sunday, a t-shirt has been at the center of one such fast-spreading cause.Los Angeles indie designer Creepy Gals took to Instagram to ask its followers whether a t-shirt by fast-fashion company Forever 21 looks quite similar to one of Creepy Gals’ popular products. The post shows a side-by-side image of the shirt Creepy Gals sells and the new item from Forever 21. They're both t-shirts with similar fonts spelling out singular words that are surrounded by hearts. Though the words are different (the Creepy Gals tee says "Sickening" and the Forever 21 tee says "Fabulous"), Creepy Gals pointed out the similarity in style and font, asking followers if they thought it was a coincidence or not.The post reads, "Forever 21 released this shirt that is eerily similar to my Sickening design. Not sure if their team designed it or they got it through some third party, but this is too close for comfort. The word they used may be different but the placement of the hearts is copied verbatim; the font, the color scheme, the feel is way too similar to my original design. What do you think? Do you agree that it's pretty much the same design as mine or am I being irrational?"Creepy Gals acknowledges that Forever 21 may have obtained the design through a third party and that the text is different, so it may not have been intentional. However, the post continues, "This is my livelihood. This is super disheartening and I'm not sure how to navigate this. This is the same ole story once again. I have seen many of my fellow artist's designs blatantly stolen by big corporations like Forever 21. What is to be done about this??"This isn't the first time Forever 21 has been accused of copying designs, as the brand has released slides in the past that were similar to Rihanna's Fenty x Puma collection and has also sold a phone case eerily similar to one sold by indie brand Valfré. The brand has mostly avoided commenting on past controversies, at least in those two cases.Forever 21 isn't the only brand that's come under fire as of late — in fact, many fast fashion brands have been under the microscope lately for a number of issues. There are many concerns over cultural appropriation, of course, as well as accusations of appropriating LGBTQ+ terms for profit.Allure has reached out to both Forever 21 and Creepy Gals for comment on this story, and will update if we hear back.Read more stories about fashion:Now, watch Paris Jackson try nine things she's never tried before:Follow Rosemary on Instagram and Twitter.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesIt's been six months since it was first announced that former Dior creative director Raf Simons was taking over the reins at Calvin Klein as its chief creative officer. On Friday morning, the designer made his highly anticipated debut with a men's and women's collection for the American brand during New York fashion week.Guests were invited to the brand’s corporate offices in Midtown, where they sat inside a space festooned with an installation by Simons’s longtime collaborator and friend, artist Sterling Ruby. Inspired by the "unique beauty and emotion of America," the collection (titled "Parade") featured an array of Western-themed streetwear full of bold color combinations, masculine silhouettes, and of course, a dose of sex appeal. Similar to the designer's fall 2017 menswear collection for his eponymous line, the lineup included various forms of crisp tailored jackets with wide shoulders. Corporate attire in glen plaid checks and vibrant shades of turquoise and violet were showcased on the catwalk, while nudity in the form of transparent tops with knit sleeves were worn by both genders. Other standout pieces included denim-on-denim iterations, patchwork quilt outerwear, and cutout dresses with a peek of underboob.To accompany the Americana theme, the show featured a mix soundtrack by fashion's favorite sound designer Michel Gaubert, which included snippets from The Virgin Suicides, "In Dreams" by Roy Orbison, and David Bowie’s “This Is Not America.” The choice of the last song was not lost on the audience, considering the present sociopolitical climate. “It reflects the environment,” Simons wrote in the show notes. “All of these different people with different styles and dress codes...It is the coming together of different characters and different individuals, just like America itself." This message was especially clear in the casting choices: a group of fresh-faced newcomers and old favorites of the designer from diverse backgrounds. It is worth noting that Simons, whose career established its roots in Europe, is a Belgian who now calls New York his home.The audience, too, featured a parade of stars from the world of art, film, music, and fashion. The Academy Awards is a little over two weeks away, but the show included the many buzzy names we'll probably see on the red carpet, including Julianne Moore, Naomie Harris, Sarah Jessica Parker, and Gwyneth Paltrow. Ad ChoicesHere are the rules for when to drop the cash.I recently found myself at a James Perse store trying on a $300 shirt dress. Black, ribbed, with a slight V-neck, the dress fit well and would pair seamlessly with many pieces in my wardrobe. My only hang-up? I had about a dozen cheaper versions of the same thing already hanging in my closet. Plus, the thought of dropping that much cash on a piece of clothing that didn’t feel totally special gave me a headache.I have a love-hate relationship with high-end basics. After finally getting rid of the last cheap ill-fitting vestiges of my early twenties, my wardrobe is a happy mix of simple yet well-tailored black, white, and neutral basics and great consignment store finds. And as much as I love my olive-green Zac Posen dress, I would choose classic and foolproof basic essentials like denim jeans and a killer black shift dress over flashier trendy pieces any day.RELATED: The Ultimate Fall Fashion Shopping GuideWhile I completely believe in investing in the items you'll get the most use out of, I always seem to have the same urge to tighten my purse strings whenever an expensive piece is just too basic. Each time I reach for my credit card, I am reminded that I could simply pick up the cheaper version of that T-shirt dress at the Gap and use the extra cash on a plane ticket to catch some West Coast sun or a ridiculously impractical yet amazing pair of shoes (thanks to Carrie Bradshaw, I have a serious weakness for Manolos).Further igniting my constant dilemma, it seems like tempting high-end basics are everywhere. Retailers like James Perse and the Line have built their entire brand on what are basically high-end versions of a Hanes tee, while fashion collectives like Vetements are catapulting the trend into the highest echelons of the high-end fashion world. Since coming on the scene in 2014, Vetements and its avant-garde take on basics have been dominating the pages of fashion glossies and street-style blogs alike. (Both have audiences who are enthusiastic about dropping $800 for a faded black hoodie.)Major fashion houses are even starting to launch their own (très pricey) basics lines. In part inspired by the success of Phoebe Philo’s artistically minimalist Céline, these capsule collections feel slightly more personal when it comes to the details. Take Valentino for example. Earlier this year, the label best-known for its over-the-top elegance and opulent designs released the Rockstud Untitled collection, a capsule that features classic staples with Valentino’s signature edgy studs including a $2,290 crewneck sweater and a $1,195 white poplin button down (both of which I will own only in my high-end basics dreams.) Even Céline’s simplest silk shifts have Philo’s fingerprints all over them.So how do we know when it’s worth it to drop a couple grand on a basic button-down rather than just pick up the $20 version from H&M? In some cases, the quality difference or presence of subtle-yet-covetable design details are obvious.RELATED: The West Coast Lines “It” Girls Are Loving Right NowFor Vanessa Traina, executive creative director at the Line—which recently launched it’s own brand of upscale tees called Tenfold Los Angeles—the life expectancy of the item justifies the cost. “I tend to invest in quality, especially when they are items that make consistent appearances in my wardrobe cycle,” she says. “A higher quality item generally has a longer life cycle so you really are making an investment.” For example, Tenfold, according to Traina, developed a heavier-weight washed-cotton shirt with a more sculpted fit than what you would expect from a standard tee. “The end result makes it feel more like a fitted top than a T-shirt,” she says.Of course the upkeep on that life cycle is more intensive. Tossing the $9 H&M tee is no biggie if it shrinks in the dryer, but you might not be so callous about your $90 investment tee. Traina swears by hang-drying her shirts and tossing her jeans in the freezer to disinfect.“If you're looking for quality, it's important to check fabric content and details like the neatness and even hems, seams, and other details,” says Rachael Wang, Allure's fashion director. But the number-one reason to justify the price hike is simple: impeccable fit. In other words, that button-down is worth the extra money when it makes you look like the extra money.When I tried on that James Perse dress, I felt like a million bucks. And in my book, that’s worth the investment. So I ditched a couple of the cheaper versions in my closet and went back to the store to claim the new dress—while I mentally prepared myself for all the air-drying and hand-washing in my future.Allure Fashion Director Rachael Wang Shares Her Style Tips:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Her bare butt, slightly out of focus, faces the camera, and in the mirror we see she's holding a deliberately positioned crab-shaped handbag, also by Thom Browne. Ad Choiceswww.allure.comhttp’s server IP address could not be found.Try:nullwww.allure.comhttp’s server IP address could not be found.Try:nullThink about power dressing. Start by considering shoulder pads. In the 1980s, women tried to extend their professional clout by forging a masculine silhouette. Double-breasted suits obscured actual breasts, while pinstripes were like natural camouflage, allowing the wearer to blend seamlessly into the red-blooded environs of the boardroom. Well, not quite seamlessly.That’s because a woman trying to dress the way a man would dress if he were a woman was a confusing (and condescending) proposition on its own. And when hair and makeup came into play, it actually backfired. In the name of power dressing, women began piling their hair into scaffold-like updos, practically giving it a head start up the corporate ladder. They may not have gone to a barber, but a stripe of blush revealed cheekbones as sharp as a razor’s edge, and aggressive shades on eyes and lips were the makeup equivalent of an executive decision: unflinching and unapologetic. Clothes may have made the man, but makeup armored the woman inside men’s clothing.Times have changed. As women reach the top of every profession, their desire to be one of the guys is as dead as the three-martini lunch. If a woman wears a tie, it’s only because she doesn’t have to.Allure Fashion Director Rachael Wang shares her own personal style:But the real leap forward in the evolution of power dressing is in the hair and makeup. Think about that. We’ve gotten to a place where it’s possible to display both femininity and authority, where prettiness doesn’t equal weakness, where you can lean into your work as successfully as you can lean into wearing long, wavy hair while you’re doing it. There may be no more famous a poster child—make that a poster woman—of this pivot in our national psyche than the formidable president of J.Crew, Jenna Lyons. Her famously tomato-red lips represent the type of creative insight—and, going out on a limb here, business acumen—that generates billions in revenue. More evidence that the women who indulge their preferences, and even dare to have fun with beauty, mean business.RELATED:Hillary Clinton's Power Suit Gets a Reebok MakeoverDecoding Hillary Clinton's White Suit at the DNC8 Items to Help You Rock a Power SuitMore from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ball-Hopkins, a reporter and model who also uses a wheelchair, took to Twitter on July 4 to discuss the collaboration. "So over the last several months I have been working with @ASOS to create a fashionable, yet practical waterproof all in one!" she wrote. "Not just for people like me in a chair but for anyone. It's about making fashion accessible! So what should be next?!"https://twitter.com/chloe_ballhopzy/status/1014444230830419969In another tweet, Ball-Hopkins explained what was special about the jumpsuit. At best, it’s functional and gets the job done—it’s something you probably don’t even think about. But in the hands of Monse, Alexander Wang, Adam Selman, and more, it’s being reinvented.At Alexander Wang, the classic shirt came cropped with strips of jersey fabric layered underneath—a styling trick we’d easily try with a more subdued tank top for work. The designer also sent models down the runway wearing pinstriped shirt dresses with thigh-high slits—an outfit we can imagine at afterwork events rather than the office. The top can also easily be paired with tailored pants for a more formal occasion.MonseMonse, which has a history of deconstructing the classic button-down and making it covetable, styled the look in every way imaginable. Models wore crisp white off-the-shoulder shirts and striped blouses with different fabrics patched together for the ultimate contrast. The major takeaway from Monse’s collection? Try wearing a white shirt you already have, slightly off-the-shoulders and pair it with a tailored dress or a dark skirt for a cool, prep school twist.RELATED: 5 Monse Signatures We Expect to See at Oscar de la RentaAdam Selman took a similar approach and presented the classic work shirt in the form of pinstriped dresses and as baggy tops that opened below the bust. To get this look, open a few buttons from the bottom of your shirt and wear a pretty camisole underneath to keep the look suitable for work.BurberryAt London fashion week, designers including Eudon Choi and Burberry loosened up the classic silhouette and added details, such as fabric ties, floppy bows, and ruffles, which can easily be recreated by dressing up an old shirt with a coordinating scarf or belt.The great thing about designers reinventing the work shirt is that it can easily become the focus of your look, rather than something that just blends in with your outfit. The key to transforming the piece is balance. Ad ChoicesIn sad fashion-related news today, designer Azzedine Alaïa has passed away at the age of 82 in Paris. According to an obituary in The New York Times, the cause of his death was a heart attack. This news has been confirmed by his company. Alaïa's passing is a huge loss for the fashion industry, as his work spans many decades and has many famous fans.According to the obituary in The New York Times, Alaïa has been designing clothing since at least 1957, when he paid rent partially by designing clothing for Comtesse Nicole de Blégiers while working with Christian Dior in Paris. News of his talent spread and many other famous insiders at the time became his clients. In recent years, he's dressed the likes of Michelle Obama and Lady Gaga. Apparently, he did things on his own time, and preferred to design on his own creative clock rather than allow the constraints of the fashion world and the press to dictate his work schedule.He recently returned to the world of couture just this July after a six year hiatus with a gorgeous show. According to The New York Times, he is survived by "his nieces and nephews; his partner, the painter Christoph von Weyhe; his closest collaborator, Carla Sozzani, and all those who worked with him." They also happen to be good friends, so it makes sense that they’d trade style secrets both on the street and on the runway.The latest example comes courtesy of Hadid, who stepped out in a pair of black transparent mesh boots by one of her favorite shoes brand, Public Desire. A similar style was previously recently worn by Jenner, who opted for a clear pair with a lucite heel. While Jenner styled hers with a pair of white fishnet tights, jeans, and an extravagant gold shearling jacket, Hadid kept hers minimal and used them to upgrade an all-black outfit of cozy sweats, crop top, and perfectly-fitted bomber jacket. This is peak athleisure made chic.If you’re interested in trying the naked boot trend yourself, you can definitely take a cue from either of the “It” girls. Hadid’s streamlined pants hit right before the boots to elongate her silhouette, whereas Jenner’s rolled-up jeans add a bit of casual fun to an otherwise extreme statement-making shoes. Both girls have really capitalized on the cool-meets-casual factor here, meaning this is a look you can easily replicate with some of the items you probably already own in your closet.Hadid also emphasized her look with some covetable accessories. An oversized pair of sunglasses shields her from the aggressive paparazzi while a structured box tote adds a pretty ladylike detail to her all-black #OOTD.If you want to get in on the look, check out the brand, which carries more than a few similar options in various shades. Ad ChoicesThe ballet is about to get a NYFW-worthy makeover.The world of fashion and the world of ballet have always been soul sisters of sorts (just look at the ballerina takeover at New York Fashion Week this fall as proof). It’s a pas de deux between two art forms that makes perfect sense—both revolve around the supreme beauty of the body. That cerebral connection is coming to life more and more. Last year, Opening Ceremony brought ballerinas to the runway for its NYFW show, and this year, the spring 2017 Sachin & Babi show was entirely inspired and modeled by ballet dancers.RELATED: A New Pas de Deux: Puma Partners With New York City BalletThe symbiosis is getting stronger thanks to ultrachic patrons of the arts like Sarah Jessica Parker, who has leveraged connections and some serious coin to facilitate major designer collaborations. This year is no exception for the New York City Ballet, which—largely thanks to SJP—will be unveiling custom costumes by some of the top fashion designers for the company’s fall gala this month. Historically, the gala has featured handpicked choreographer-designer collaborations, including Thom Browne, Valentino Garavani, and Peter Copping for Oscar de la Renta. This year’s roster looks a lot like the runways we’ve seen this month, and there will be ethereal costumes fit for our childhood (OK, grown-up) ballerina dreams from Narciso Rodriguez for a piece by principal dancer Lauren Lovette, Jason Wu for Peter Walker, Rosie Assoulin for Annabelle Lopez Ochoa, and Dries Van Noten, who will be working with soloist and resident NYCB choreographer Justin Peck.Sketches by Narciso Rodriguez and Rosie Assoulin. Above: sketches by Dries Van Noten and Jason Wu.Though designed specifically for dancers, we have a feeling the performance looks will play heavily in our spring wardrobe inspiration. Rodriguez, for one, has created a mini collection of sweet-meets-spicy looks—think ballet-pink flowing dresses slashed with inlays of jet-black mesh. Jason Wu went in the opposite direction: An early sketch indicates a seductive and bold dress in lace. Rosie Assoulin brought workwear to the stage, and Van Noten's pieces will keep with the ethereal ballet theme—he’s created a simple shift for principal dancer Sara Mearns that might look just as at home in our wardrobe as it does on stage.With any luck, some of that famous dancer’s grace might rub off on us as we snag the ballet-inspired trend for ourselves.How Ballet Skills Translate to Lifelong Success:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. The decision does not apply directly to other towns that have imposed similar bans.While some European designers have embraced clothing in line with Islamic guidelines (Dolce & Gabbana’s abaya collection and Uniqlo’s hijab collaboration with U.K.-based Hana Tajima, to name a few), modest wear has once again caught flak in France. The country, home to an estimated 4.7 million Muslims, according to the Pew Research Center, has recently seen cities such as Nice and Cannes impose bans on swimwear that covers the body and the head: a.k.a. the burkini.Last Wednesday, French prime minister Manuel Valls said the burkini is a “translation of a political project for a counter-society based on woman’s enslavement.”Designers of the swimwear have been quick at voicing their disagreement. “I personally feel that [this ban] is more of an attack on women,” says Kausar Sacranie, the U.K.-based designer of Modestly Active, a conservative activewear brand that sells burkinis. “Taking the right away from a woman to choose what she wears or doesn’t wear is much more important to question.”Australia-based designer Aheda Zanetti, who designs burkinis for her label Ahiida, says it’s unfortunate that a woman’s choice of clothing has been a pawn in politics. “I don’t believe that a French politician, Taliban, or anyone in general should enforce women on what we should wear or not,” she says.The enforcement is the latest example of the tension between France and its Muslim community following a series of terrorist attacks that has traumatized the nation, including last month's Bastille Day mayhem in Nice that claimed 86 lives. In Cannes, offenders risk a fine of €38 (about $42) for wearing the burkini, according to the mayor's ordinance.Several opponents of the ban are speaking out for the fundamental rights of women, including Rachid Nekkaz, a wealthy real estate entrepreneur who has offered to pick up the tab for women fined under the ban. "I decided to pay for all the fines of women who wear the burkini in order to guarantee their freedom of wearing these clothes, and most of all, to neutralize the application on the ground of this oppressive and unfair law," Nekkaz told CNN.Paris-based designer Vanessa Lourenco started making burkinis for her boutique Madamme BK with the idea that every woman should have the freedom to enjoy life, regardless of her clothing guidelines. "I’m not Muslim, and people do ask me why I design for Muslim women," says the designer. "My answer to that is simple: At the end of the day, women are women. We all want to look beautiful and feel feminine."When asked whether the new ban would affect sales, Lourenco says she intends to continue selling worldwide regardless, while Zanetti has seen a rise in inquiries regarding sales, particularly in Europe, since the ban.Lourenco adds that fashion should be democratic, with options for everyone. A ban like this limits that privilege. “Creating awareness is already a large step forward in changing people’s attitudes to this innocent but liberating fashion,” she says.Or as Zanetti concisely sums it up: “It’s just a swimsuit!”Here, 12 more instances of clothing and beauty bans for women around the world:1. Ancient Greece During the seventh century B.C., women in Greece were forbidden from wearing embroidered robes or jewelry outside—unless they were prostitutes. The color purple was also reserved for nobility, since the dye was considered rare and precious.Models wearing pants designed by Yves Saint Laurent in 19682. France Overturns a 200-Year-Old Ban on Women Wearing Pants According to a law imposed on November 17, 1800, French women needed permission from the local police to wear pants or “dress like a man.” Though the law was ignored for the decades following, it wasn’t officially overturned until 2013, more than 200 years later.3. New York City in 1936Women in New York City were banned from wearing any tops that left their navel exposed in public according to a law in 1936. The ban was lifted almost 50 years later in the '80s. Revealing the midriff has gained popularity since then.The new 'bikini' swimwear by Louis Réard4. The Invention of the Bikini in 1946 Five years after the creation of the modern bikini in 1946, the Vatican denounced the two-piece bathing suit as sinful. Prior to the introduction of the two-piece, Hollywood's Hays Code prevented the showing of the navel onscreen.  5. The Island of Paama Shorts and Pants Ban in 2001 In March 2001, chiefs from the island of Paama in Vanuatu banned women from wearing shorts or pants in public. They claimed both articles of clothing were too revealing and could potentially incite rape and adultery.Traditional Greek footwear on sale in Greece6. Greece Bans Heels In 2009, Greek authorities moved to ban women from wearing stiletto heels at archaeological sites out of fear they would damage the monuments.7. Karamay, China, in 2014 In 2014, the law in Karamay, a city in the Xinjiang region of China—home to a population that is around 45 percent Muslim—banned any clothing that seemed too Islamic on public buses. This included the hijab, niqab (face covering), burqa (a loose-fitting long garment), and even clothing with the Islamic star-and-crescent symbol. The law warned that perpetrators would be “handled by the police.”  8. Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan Ban Lace Undergarments in 2014 Lacy underwear was banned in Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan after regulations were made that undergarments could not contain less than 6 percent of cotton for proper moisture absorption (a criterion most lace lingerie did not meet). That same year, several women were detained in Kazakhstan after protesting the ban on lace underwear.   9. Iranian Cleric Says Western Clothes Are Causing Rivers to Run Dry A cleric in Iran recently called for a crackdown on women wearing clothes deemed too “Western,” saying that the provocative dress is causing the country's rivers to run dry. In 2010, a different cleric warned that women who dress immodestly would spread adultery in society and, by doing so, increase the frequency of earthquakes in the area.Members of the Qatar women's basketball team walking off the court after withdrawing ahead of their preliminary-round match against Mongolia at the Asian Games10. International Basketball Federation Headdress Ban The Qatar women's basketball team withdrew from the 2014 Asian Games when players refused to remove their head scarves before competing against Mongolia. Ironically, the motto of the games was “diversity shines here.”11. Uganda Miniskirt BanFollowing an anti-pornography bill, which banned “indecent” dressing, women took to the streets in 2014 to protest in miniskirts. Known as the “miniskirt law,” the bill did not explicitly name miniskirts but rather considered any clothing that exposed the breasts, thighs, or butt as unlawful.  12. BBC Producer Bans Red Lipstick At a BAFTA panel event in 2014, Melissa Hardinge, the executive producer of BBC's children's programming, said she stresses the importance of presenting suitable content for younger viewers. She then disclosed she has asked presenters of children's programs to remove their red lipstick before going on air because "they shouldn’t look too sexy."#AskAMuslimGirl: Muslim Girls Get Real About the Hijab:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Since her diagnosis, the actress has been open about her condition and its effect on the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves. “I am disabled. I fall sometimes. I drop things. My memory is foggy. And my left side is asking for directions from a broken GPS. But we are doing it,” she wrote on Instagram.Though I don't have MS, I can relate to some of what Blair is saying. My twin sister and I were born with Crouzon syndrome — a craniofacial condition that caused the bones in our skulls to fuse before being fully developed. As a result, our eyes were large, wide-set, and crooked. We grew up with faces that set us apart from both our family and society. I appreciate the awareness and visibility she's bringing to important conversations.In addition to her openness about the challenges of MS, the actress has also embraced the ways in which her life and identity have shifted — most notably through fashion. For her first public appearance post-diagnosis, the actress attended the Vanity Fair Oscar party in a Ralph and Russo dress. She also used a cane that was designed just for her.Though people with disabilities, scars, and facial differences are rarely seen at A-list award shows, mainstream events, or even on television at all, Blair remained stunning, confident, and unapologetic throughout the event. And to see her in attendance, cane and all, sends a positive message to those of us who are different, those of us who have spent our lives feeling as though we have to hide parts of ourselves in order to be accepted.Selma Blair’s openness as she navigates her MS, as well as the increase in body-positive representation, is inspiring because for me, accepting my Crouzon syndrome — and my resultant physical differences from others — has taken a lifetime.In the United States, an estimated 1 in 750 babies is born with a craniofacial disorder. While the effects of these conditions vary depending on the type and severity, craniofacial disorders are believed to cause a third of all facial differences in the U.S.Living with an unconventional face made me hyperaware of my differences. Even as a child, other kids (and sometimes their parents) made a show of pointing out the ways my face did not match theirs. They would stare too long and loudly whisper unkind comments. All I wanted was for it to be OK to be myself. Instead, from the time I was old enough to be aware of my existence, I was also aware of just how much my face defined me.Selma Blair’s openness as she navigates her MS is inspiring because accepting my own medical condition and physical differences has taken a lifetime.When I entered elementary school, I became adamant about being allowed to dress myself. Because I was constantly surrounded by ignorance and the judgments of others, I wanted some agency over my appearance. So every morning, I would fight my mother and older sisters when they picked out my clothes and got me ready for school.My mother wanted our outfits to distract others from our appearance. She bought my sister and me dresses with velvet ruffles and matching shoes; plaid shorts paired with matching vests and sunglasses; and heavily patterned shirts with matching hats that partially hid our eyes. If strangers in public were focused on our cute clothes, maybe they wouldn't stare at our faces. If we were fashionable enough, she hoped, we could blend in.Some mornings, after my clothes had been picked out for me, I would wait until my mother left for work and my sisters were busy getting themselves ready for school to find my own outfit. I would stand in my closet and grab the pieces that excited me the most. Sometimes it was a polka-dot shirt with floral leggings under striped shorts. Other times, it was a pajama shirt paired with a skirt I was only to wear on special occasions.I realize now that their intention wasn’t to stop me from expressing myself through my style; they just wanted to shield me from the unkind comments I was often subjected to. Having me wear clothes that allowed me to blend in more easily was their way of protecting me. However, I didn’t want to always wear clothes and outfits that distracted from what I looked like. I didn’t want to hide who I was. By the end of elementary school, I was already tired of carrying around a shame I was too young to understand.The older I got, though, the more I realized their point. Fashion started to become a sort of camouflage — an attempt to blend in in a world that was not meant for me. Though I didn’t want to care about what I looked like on the outside, I did.In high school, there were days when I woke up early, curled my hair, and found an outfit that made me feel beautiful. But when I got to school, I was still ridiculed for my appearance. I’d usually pretend not to notice, but the moment I was alone, I would break down. While clothing could cover my body and make my differences less noticeable, it did not prevent me from feeling the pain I felt inside. Fashion couldn’t hide the fact that I was different, so I stopped trying.One afternoon after school, I plopped down on the couch in my family’s living room and turned on the television to find an episode of The Tyra Banks Show. It was the “Rock Your Ugly” episode, where Tyra talked about the importance of accepting our appearance — even the parts of ourselves we want to hide. After the episode, something clicked. Fashion became empowering. I couldn’t change the way my bones were structured or the ways my eyes were shaped, nor could I control what others thought about me, but I could control the version of myself that I put out into the world. My style became my voice. If people were going to stare at me, I’d at least give them something I was proud to have them look at. On days when I felt insecure and unattractive, I looked at myself in the mirror and told myself to rock it.These days, choosing an outfit is about more than just personal taste. It’s about having the confidence to wear clothes I like. It’s about knowing who I am, what my style is, and holding my head high, regardless of other people’s opinions. Embracing myself and my style gave me a sense of agency I’d been missing.Now, as a 28-year-old woman, I am empowered by individuals like Selma Blair who believe fashion to be a form of self-expression, who can embrace their changing identities with grace and inspire self-acceptance.Blair’s impact is also exposing able-bodied folks to disability and helping them understand the importance of normalizing physical differences. “You want to still be part of the living, not a shuffling person people get out of the way for because they’re queasy,” she told Vanity Fair last month. And in addition to becoming a voice for the disability community, the actress has also expressed interest in designing a chic and accessible clothing line.“I really feel like people with disabilities are invisible to a lot of people. Because they’re uncomfortable, or don’t have the energy to dress up, don’t want to be seen,” Blair said.This is part of a larger cultural shift. Other brands, like MIGA swimwear, a swimwear line inspired by individuals with bodily disfigurements, are also realizing the importance of having fashionable options that are not only accessible, but that celebrate the diverse experiences that make up a person. This includes disfigurement. The swimsuits, which are not only made for people with a physical difference, is similar to the line Blair wants to start because it all comes back to the importance of celebrating individual experiences and identities.Like Selma Blair's MS, my medical condition will not go away. It is forever a part of me. And every day when I get dressed, my face is still asymmetrical. But wearing clothes I love allows me to rock my differences the best I can. It allows me to proudly show the world who I am. While my love of fashion taught me that it's how I feel about myself that matters, I’m grateful for people like Selma Blair and companies like MIGA Swimwear who show the world that having a medical condition does not devalue who you are — that being different is beautiful.Read more stories about body image on Allure:Now watch Lizzo try 9 things she's never done before:Don't forget to follow Allure on Instagram and Twitter.More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Ad ChoicesGone are the days of whitewashed runways—we hope.Despite efforts made by a few designers (remember Zac Posen's multiracial casting for his fall 2016 show?), diversity on the New York Fashion Week runways is still a huge issue. But hopefully things are about to get better, thanks in part to a mandate from the Council of Fashion Designers of America, according to WWD. In the midst of the industry's intensifying cultural conversation on race and diversity, the CFDA released its biannual health initiative letter yesterday that included (for the second year in a row) guidelines encouraging designers to “be inclusive of racial diversity when preparing casting of models for their company needs,” as they prep for the September shows. The letter was penned by designer Diane von Furstenberg and CFDA CEO Steven Kolb.RELATED: When Diversity in Beauty Should Mean More Than RepresentationAccording to the CFDA letter, seeing models of color on the runway should be the norm, not the exception. That means designers have an explicit responsibility to request that agencies include models from all backgrounds in every casting session. Modeling agencies also have a responsibility to scout a diverse talent pool. “Our objective is to make a shift on how the model of color is viewed so it becomes natural to see them participating each season in a greater number than seasons past,” the mandate reads.RELATED: Model Ebonee Davis Speaks Candidly About Racism in FashionThe CFDA’s discussion on diversity began back in 2007 when the Diversity Council started championing a public conversation about the issue among designers. The organization also recently partnered with Equinox to up the ante on the gym's health and wellness initiatives. It's all part of a bigger revolution happening in the fashion industry, one that advocates for a changed culture around the way we view beauty. In addition to the CFDA’s statements about diversity, the council also included advice on how to screen for signs of eating disorders on the catwalk.If the CFDA’s statements this week are any indication, we look forward to the day we can officially (finally!) say goodbye to the days of whitewashed runways and models struggling with dangerous eating habits, which will make a much better fashion week for all.Now, watch model Paloma Elsesser talk about what it means to be body positive and how important diversity is in fashion:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast. Since the election, enthusiastic residents of Chappaqua, New York, have spotted the former Secretary of State around town, picking out a turkey at the local market or hiking in the woods. The go-to staple that’s typically reserved for “casual Fridays” and the weekends have gotten an upgrade, coming in a variety of cool washes, shapes, and designs that pretty much anyone can pull off. And with so many iterations out there, it’s practically a disservice to stick to one silhouette. Some days I feel like a '70s bohemian flower child wearing my flares, while other days I gravitate toward skinnies because they look awesome paired with a sleek pair of ankle booties.If you’re stuck in a fashion rut and craving trendy ways to update your denim style, Rachel Wang, Allure's fashion director, has got you covered. For starters, there is the fiesta flare, a funky interpretation of the classic flare but with a flamenco twist. Then there's the high-waist, boot-cut style and the beloved mom jeans (who knew they could be totally chic?). Retro style has come back full throttle in the most badass way, and I’m here for every moment of it. Finally, for the days when you’re seeking a relaxed fit, there is the wide-leg jean—think loose-fit pants from '90s streetwear brand JNCO, but better. Just like your favorite pair of lived-in boyfriend jeans, these styles can easily be incorporated into any wardrobe. Ad ChoicesOne of the most influential figures in fashion history has passed away.The fashion and beauty worlds are in mourning today. Karl Lagerfeld, larger-than-life designer, creative director behind Chanel and Fenti, and fashion industry icon, passed away in Paris on Tuesday. He was 85.It was rumored that Lagerfeld was ill when he didn't attend the Chanel Haute Couture show in January, though WWD reports that he worked right up until the end. His Fendi fall ready-to-wear collection is scheduled to show in Milan on Thursday.The House of Karl Lagerfeld confirmed news of the designer's death on his official Instagram page. "He was one of the most influential and celebrated designers of the 21st century and an iconic, universal symbol of style. Driven by a phenomenal sense of creativity, Karl was passionate, powerful and intensely curious," read the caption accompanying a tribute posted to his feed. "He leaves behind an extraordinary legacy as one of the greatest designers of our time, and there are no words to express how much he will be missed."The German designer, who moved to Paris a teenager, began his career in fashion as Pierre Balmain's assistant in 1955. With stints at  Jean Patou, Chloé, and Fendi, Lagerfeld rose through the fashion ranks to become creative director at Chanel in 1983. His revitalization of the brand is legendary in the industry. It was Lagerfeld who introduced the world-famous "CC" monograph. During more than 35 years at the fashion house, Lagerfeld and Chanel became inseparable in fashion lexicon.Lagerfeld in his Paris studio, 1979.In addition to designing for luxury fashion houses, Lagerfeld collaborated with H&M, Coty, and Diesel. Even his beloved cat, Choupette, had her own fashion and beauty collaborations, earning a reported $4.4 million in 2014. Lagerfeld had the power to make even his cat an international fashion icon, but he also used his influence to encourage up-and-coming designers like Jeremy Scott and Victoria Beckham.Lagerfeld with his models at Chanel's fall/winter ready-to-wear show, 2005.Designers, models, and fashion editors have come out to pay tribute to Lagerfeld and his legacy. Victoria Beckham wrote on Instagram, "So incredibly sad to hear this. Karl was a genius and always so kind and generous to me both personally and professionally. RIP." Olivier Rousteing also took to Instagram to describe what Lagerfeld meant to him: "You have been a school for all of us, you will always be present, reminding and defining what fashion is." It's hard to underestimate Lagerfeld's legacy as tributes pour in from all corners of the fashion world.Lagerfeld kisses his godson Hudson Kroenig at Chanel's fall/winter ready-to-wear show in Paris, 2016.Lagerfeld will be remembered as one of the most prolific and influential figures in fashion, and his trademark white collared shirt, black jacket, sunglasses, and ponytail will remain an iconic image in the fashion-history books.More on Karl Lagerfeld's enduring impact:More from AllureContact© 2019 Condé Nast.
